# Migrating to melonJS 20.x

> What changed in melonJS 20.x, and which older APIs are gone, deprecated, or
> renamed. Read this before writing melonJS code from memory — much of what is
> published about melonJS predates 20.0.

**Why this skill exists:** most melonJS material in circulation describes 19.x or
earlier. Code written from that knowledge looks correct and fails at runtime.
The items below are ordered by how likely they are to be reproduced from memory.

## 1. `Application.init()` is mandatory and asynchronous

Since 20.0, constructing an `Application` no longer initialises it.

```js
// ✗ pre-20.x — the constructor called init(width, height, options) for you
const app = new Application(800, 600, { parent: "screen" });
app.world.addChild(sprite);          // added, but nothing ever renders

// ✓ 20.x
const app = new Application(800, 600, { parent: "screen" });
await app.init();                    // REQUIRED
app.world.addChild(sprite);
```

`init()` is async because acquiring a WebGPU device is async. There is no
synchronous alternative, and no automatic fallback that papers over the missing
call. Nothing that then breaks names it: the constructor still builds
`app.world`, so children can be added and simply never draw — no canvas is
appended, the app never subscribes to the frame tick, and `app.renderer` /
`app.viewport` stay `undefined` — while constructing a `Sprite` or `Text` first
throws a `TypeError` on the unset global `game` instead.

The signature changed too: 19.x took `init(width, height, options)`, 20.x takes
none, and anything passed is ignored (settings come from the constructor).

**`video.init(...)` no longer exists.** The `video` module now exports only the
four renderer constants (`AUTO`, `CANVAS`, `WEBGL`, `WEBGPU`) — there is no
`init` on it to call. Any code shaped like `me.video.init(800, 600, {...})` is
from a removed API. Build an `Application` and await `init()`. Its siblings
went with it: `video.renderer`, `video.createCanvas()` and `video.getParent()`
are now `app.renderer`, `app.renderer.createCanvas()` and
`app.getParentElement()`.

`init()` runs once: a second call is ignored with a console warning, and after
`app.destroy()` it throws. A destroyed `Application` is final; build a new one.

Note that `import * as me from "melonjs"` still works, so `me.Sprite` style is
fine. It is the *globals bootstrap* that is gone, not the namespace import.

## 2. Post effects replaced the `shader` property

`renderable.shader = …` is **deprecated since 19.2.0**. Use the post-effect API:

```js
// ✗ deprecated
mySprite.shader = new ShaderEffect(app.renderer, glslBody);

// ✓
mySprite.addPostEffect(new ShaderEffect(app.renderer, glslBody));
```

Related trap: **`removePostEffect()` destroys the effect** — and so does
assigning `renderable.shader`, which destroys whatever it replaces. Only an
effect carrying `shared = true` is spared. To turn one off temporarily, toggle
`effect.enabled` instead: remove-and-re-add hands you back an object whose GPU
resources have already been freed.

## 3. WebGL 2 is the baseline; WebGPU is the default attempt

`video.AUTO` now tries **WebGPU → WebGL 2 → Canvas**. WebGL 1 is gone.

Consequences:

- Which backend runs is a runtime fact. Do not write code that assumes WebGL.
- Custom shaders can carry both GLSL and WGSL in one asset, so one effect runs
  on either GPU backend.
- Features needing a programmable pipeline are inert on Canvas and warn once
  rather than throwing.
- Test capabilities, not the backend: `renderer.shaderLanguage` and
  `renderer.supportsDepthBuffer` replace checks on `renderer.gl` or
  `instanceof WebGLRenderer`, which answer "no" on WebGPU.
  `renderer.WebGLVersion` is always `2` (deprecated), and the `preferWebGL1`
  setting and the `#webgl1` URL flag are gone.
- A custom WebGL batcher extends `WebGLBatcher` (`Batcher` is now the
  backend-neutral base), and a custom shader on a `Mesh` receives model-space
  geometry: position with
  `uProjectionMatrix * uViewMatrix * uModelMatrix * vec4(aVertex, 1.0)` and
  tint with `uTint`. Sprite and post-effect shaders are unchanged.

## 4. Deprecated exports still present

These resolve but should not be used in new code:

| deprecated | since | use instead |
|---|---|---|
| `CanvasTexture` | 17.1.0 | `CanvasRenderTarget` |
| `Compositor` | 18.1.0 | `WebGLBatcher` |
| `PrimitiveCompositor` | 18.1.0 | `PrimitiveBatcher` |
| `QuadCompositor` | 18.1.0 | `QuadBatcher` |
| `Math` (capitalised) | 18.0.0 | `math` (lowercase) |
| `device.requestFullscreen` / `exitFullscreen` | 19.7.0 | `app.requestFullscreen()` / `app.exitFullscreen()` |
| `renderable.shader = …` | 19.2.0 | `addPostEffect()` |
| `Entity` | 18.1.0 | `Sprite` / `Renderable` + a `Body` |
| `loader.onload` / `onProgress` / `onError` | 18.2.0, **removed 20.3** | the `LOADER_*` events, or `preload(assets, onloadcb)` |
| `response.overlap` / `overlapN` / `overlapV` | 19.5.0 | `response.depth` / `response.normal` |
| `setLineWidth()` | 17.3.0 | the `lineWidth` property |
| `pool.register` / `pool.pull` / `pool.push` | 18.0.0 (a console notice since 20.9) | `createPool()` / `getPool()`; `registerObjectClass()` for a class a level names |
| `registerTiledObjectClass` / `registerTiledObjectFactory` | 20.18.0 (no console notice) | `registerObjectClass` / `registerObjectFactory`: the same functions, named for every kind of level |
| `TMXRenderer`, `TMXOrthogonalRenderer`, `TMXIsometricRenderer`, `TMXHexagonalRenderer`, `TMXStaggeredRenderer` | 20.18.0 (no console notice) | `TileMapRenderer`, `OrthogonalRenderer`, `IsometricRenderer`, `HexagonalRenderer`, `StaggeredRenderer`: the same classes |
| `TMXTileMap`, `TMXTilesetGroup` | 20.18.0 (no console notice) | `TileMap`, `TilesetGroup`: the same classes |
| `loader.getTMX` | 20.18.0 (no console notice) | `loader.getTileMap`: the same function |
| `body.fromJSON()`, a shape list given to `addShape()` | 20.7.0 (the `Body` constructor form throws) | `bodyDef = { type, shapes: "<json asset>", id }` |
| `body.ignoreGravity` | 19.5.0 | `gravityScale = 0`, or `body.setGravityScale(0)` |
| `app.updateAverageDelta` | 20.0.0 | `app.lastUpdateDelta` |
| `loader.crossOrigin = …` / `loader.withCredentials = …` | 20.4.0 (assigning throws) | `loader.setOptions({ crossOrigin, withCredentials })` |
| `UITextButton#bitmapText` | 20.13.0 | `label` |

Two of these deserve emphasis:

- **`Entity`** is still exported, so code using it compiles and runs while being
  the wrong shape for 20.x. Compose a `Sprite`/`Renderable` with a `Body`
  instead.
- **The capitalised `Math`** shadows the global `Math` if imported carelessly.
  `me.Math.random()` from older docs resolves to the deprecated re-export.

## 5. The global `game` is not the modern shape

`game` is still exported, but since 20.0 it names the most recently
**initialized** `Application` and is `undefined` until the first `init()`
resolves — so anything reading it at module scope gets `undefined`. Take the
`Application` instance as a parameter instead: `Stage#onResetEvent` and
`onDestroyEvent` are handed it, and any renderable can reach it through
`parentApp`.

## 6. Node and SSR

melonJS imports cleanly under Node — useful for isomorphic apps and for tooling.
It has **no runtime dependencies** as of 20.3. Do not add polyfills for
`globalThis`, `String.trimStart` or `String.trimEnd`: the published bundle
targets ES2022, so every environment that can parse it already has them.

## 7. Browser support

The published bundle targets **ES2022** and uses private class members. A browser
that predates that cannot parse the file at all — it fails at load, not when a
feature is used. Transpile if you need older browsers, and note that transpiling
handles *syntax* only: built-in methods need separate polyfills, which a
bundler's `target` setting will never add.

## 8. Changed again during 20.x

Code written against an early 20.x release can still trip on these:

- **`world.adapter` is read-only** (20.14): assigning it throws a
  `TypeError`. `app.world.setAdapter(adapter)` switches adapters, rebuilding
  every body from its `bodyDef`.
- **`renderer.uvOffset` and the `textureSeamFix` setting are removed** (20.11).
  Code that added `uvOffset` to a size should drop it.
- **The engine's classes are no longer in the legacy pool** (20.9):
  `pool.pull("Sprite")`, `pool.pull("Text")` and the other built-in names
  throw `Cannot instantiate object of type`. Call the constructor, or
  `getPool("text")`, `getPool("tween")`, `getPool("particle")`,
  `getPool("colorLayer")` to recycle. `pool.register(name, Class, true)` no
  longer returns an instance to the pool on removal either; `createPool` does.
- **A container sorted on `"x"` or `"y"` re-sorts its children as they move**
  (20.11, `autoSort` on by default). Turn `autoSort` off to keep an order set
  by hand. A `"z"` sort is unchanged.

## What the shipped examples still show of the old API

The examples in this repository are the best reference for how melonJS is
assembled. Two things in them are easy to misread:

- `platformer/entities/player.ts` and `enemies.ts` read and change
  `response.overlapV` in a legacy `onCollision`. On the built-in world that is
  not the deprecated field: the legacy handler gets the solver's own response,
  which has no `normal` or `depth`, and changing `overlapV` there is how a
  one-way platform or a slope changes the push-out. In a new handler
  (`onCollisionStart` / `onCollisionActive`), and on every adapter, read
  `response.depth` / `response.normal`.
- Particle speeds tuned before 20.2 look wrong now: the particle transform fix
  changed how far a burst travels, and the examples' emitters were retuned
  upward to match. An emitter copied from an older version of an example needs
  the same.

Older copies of the examples (before 20.17) also assigned `viewport.shader = …`
/ `sprite.shader = …`, set `this.z = Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` on a HUD,
extended `Entity` and called `device.requestFullscreen()`. None is current: use
`addPostEffect()`, `addChild(hud, z)`, a `Sprite` (with a `bodyDef` when it
needs a body) and `app.requestFullscreen()`.

## Checklist when code "should work" but doesn't

1. Is `await app.init()` there?
2. Is the code assuming WebGL when it might be running on Canvas or WebGPU?
3. Is it using `renderable.shader =` instead of `addPostEffect()`?
4. Is it importing a deprecated symbol from the table above?
5. Is it referencing a global `game`?
6. Is it relying on something section 8 lists as changed during 20.x?

## Related skills

- `melonjs-getting-started` — the correct 20.x bootstrap in full
- `melonjs-renderables` — post effects, pointer events and custom draw code

# Loading 3D assets

> glTF/GLB is the primary path for 3D content, and it goes through the **level
> director** rather than the world directly: `level.load("scene")`, the same call
> a Tiled map uses. OBJ/MTL is the simpler path for a single static model.

## Loading a glTF/GLB scene

```js
await loader.preload([
    { name: "diorama", type: "glb", src: "data/scenes/diorama.glb" },
]);

level.load("diorama", { scale: 50 });
```

`type: "gltf"` (JSON plus external buffers) and `type: "glb"` (single binary)
are both loader types. A self-contained GLB is the better shipping format — one
request, nothing to resolve relatively.

The scene loads under whatever camera the stage has; view it under a `Camera3d`
or it renders flat. See `melonjs-3d` for the camera.

### `level.load` options for glTF/GLB

| option | default | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `scale` | `1` | pixels per glTF unit, applied to the whole scene. Blender's metre-scale export usually needs 20–100. |
| `container` | `game.world` | where the nodes are added |
| `onLoaded` | `game.onLevelLoaded` | called with the **level id**, not the scene |
| `async` | `false` | return a promise that settles once the scene is in the world, instead of a boolean |
| `rightHanded` | `true` | see below |
| `lights` | `true` | instantiate authored `KHR_lights_punctual` lights as `Light3d` children of `container`; `false` also builds the meshes unlit |
| `lightIntensityScale` | — | keep authored intensity ratios instead of normalising every light to 1 |
| `castGroundShadow` | inherits the app setting (**on**) | blob shadows for this scene's meshes |
| `shadowGroundY` | each object's own base | world Y of the floor the blobs land on |
| `shadowOpacity` | `0.45` | how dark the blobs are |
| `shadowScale` | `1` | blob footprint multiplier; `0` or less hides them |
| `shadowOffset` | `0` | slide them along the light, in blob radii; needs `shadowGroundY`, which is the only way a scene load can name its floor |
| `shadowStretch` | `1` | lengthen them along it, clamped to 3 |
| `shadowDirectionX` / `shadowDirectionZ` | `0` | the ground direction they are cast along |
| `shadowGroundNormal` | world up | up normal of the floor, for a scene that is not level |
| `shadowLight` | — | a `Light3d` to take the direction from, re-read every draw |
| `toonBands` | `0` | cel-shade every lit mesh into this many bands (see `melonjs-3d`) |
| `outlineWidth` / `outlineColor` | `0` / black | an ink outline round every mesh, in world units (see `melonjs-3d`) |
| `outlineMode` | `"world"` | `"screen"` measures `outlineWidth` in pixels, the same thickness near or far |
| `rimLight` / `rimColor` | `0` / white | a rim light on every lit mesh (see `melonjs-3d`) |
| `pickable` | `true` | `false` has `camera.pick` pass over the scene's meshes (see `melonjs-3d`) |
| `crossfade` | `0` | an animated or skinned asset's default blend between clips, in ms (see Crossfading below) |

Those `game.` defaults are the engine's, not a recommendation. `game` is
whichever `Application` finished `init()` last, so **pass `container`
explicitly** from a `Stage`, where the right one is in your hand:

```js
onResetEvent(app) {
    level.load("sceneId", { container: app.world, scale: 40 });
}
```

`shadowGroundPoint` is **not** on that list, and a scene load drops it without
a warning. One floor POINT shared by every part of a scene would stack the
whole thing's blobs on a single spot, which is nonsense where one floor
HEIGHT is perfectly sensible. Ground that is not flat is a per-object answer:
set it on the parts you want once the load has finished.

`onLoaded` receives the level id — it is a "done" signal, not a handle on the
scene. You need it, or `async`: with the game loop running, `level.load` stops
the loop and defers the actual load to a timer, so by default it returns
*before* anything is in the world.

```js
await level.load("diorama", { scale: 50, async: true });
// the scene is in the world here
```

Note `await level.load("diorama")` without the flag does not await the load — the
call returns a boolean, and `await true` resolves immediately. To get at what was
loaded, load into a container you own, or look the nodes up by their authored
names:

```js
level.load("diorama", { scale: 50, onLoaded: () => {
    const sun = app.world.getChildByName("Sun")[0];   // note: returns an array
    sun.intensity = 2;
}});
```

### The same options from a Tiled `Trigger`

A `Trigger` authored in Tiled forwards these to `level.load()`, so a trigger that
walks the player into a glTF level carries the scene's settings as Tiled
properties:

```js
world.addChild(new Trigger(x, y, {
    shapes: [new Rect(0, 0, 100, 100)],
    to: "diorama",              // the level id — `to`, not `level`
    scale: 50,
    rightHanded: false,
    castGroundShadow: false,
}));
```

Every `level.load` option above travels, including the whole ground-shadow set,
and so do `container`, `onLoaded`, `flatten` and `setViewportBounds`. The list is
**derived** from the options each level format declares beside the code that
reads them, rather than restated, so an option added to a level format arrives
here for free. It used to be hand-written and had fallen three releases behind
the glTF path (#1649).

**`async` is deliberately excluded.** A trigger with a `color` + `duration`
sets it itself, because it needs the promise to sequence its fade and reveal; a
trigger without one loads fire-and-forget and never sets it. Either way an
authored `async` property is ignored rather than honoured.

## `rightHanded` — and the default that differs between the two APIs

glTF is authored **Y-up, right-handed**; melonJS is **Y-down, +Z forward**.
There are two ways to bridge that, and they are not equivalent:

- a **rotation** — preserves chirality, matches the authoring tool
- a **mirror** (negate Y only) — flips the scene left/right

`level.load` defaults `rightHanded: true`, so a scene loaded through the level
director comes in correctly. **The `Mesh` constructor defaults it to `false`**,
so glTF or OBJ geometry you feed to a `Mesh` yourself comes in mirrored unless
you pass `rightHanded: true`. A model that is subtly wrong — text backwards, a
character's gear on the wrong side — is this and nothing else.

Do not add a flip of your own on top; two corrections cancel back to wrong.

## Materials — what actually arrives

The importer covers a deliberate subset:

- `pbrMetallicRoughness` **base colour texture and factor**
- `COLOR_0` **vertex colours**, multiplied with the factor and the texture
- metallic/roughness **factors** converted to the engine's specular model
- `emissiveFactor`, including `KHR_materials_emissive_strength`
- `KHR_materials_unlit` — honoured, for baked/stylised workflows
- `alphaMode: "MASK"` — the cutout threshold is applied
- `doubleSided`
- the base colour texture's sampler: `wrapS` / `wrapT` (repeat by default, as
  the spec says) and `magFilter`

`alphaMode: "BLEND"` is read as opaque: the loader does not set `transparent`,
because one loaded mesh can merge materials and the flag routes the whole mesh.
Set `transparent: true` on the part yourself (see `melonjs-3d`).

Not imported: **normal maps**, metallic/roughness *textures*, occlusion maps,
`KHR_texture_transform`. Nothing errors — the material simply
arrives without them, which reads as "flatter than the preview in my authoring
tool". Bake what you need into the base colour. (OBJ/MTL does carry a normal
map, see below.)

**Mesh compression is the exception that does error.** Draco
(`KHR_draco_mesh_compression`) and meshopt (`EXT_meshopt_compression`,
`KHR_meshopt_compression`) cannot be decoded. A file that requires one warns in
the console, naming it, and fails to load; a file that only uses one (it also
carries its meshes uncompressed) warns and loads the uncompressed copy. Export
without mesh compression.

`textureFilter` on the Application settings (`"auto"` / `"nearest"` /
`"linear"` / `"linear-mipmap"`) drives sampling; glTF materials that declare
their own sampler carry it through. Pixel-art models want `"nearest"`. A mesh
already samples mipmaps under `"linear"`, so `"linear-mipmap"` changes nothing
for one.

### `baseColorFactor` is LINEAR; a `tint` is sRGB
**Pass the factor as a setting and the encoding is done for you.** `Mesh`
takes `baseColorFactor` — `[r, g, b]` in 0..1, linear, which is the form the
loader hands back — so a mesh built from a node passes the node's own field
straight through:

```js
const node = loader.getGLTF("palm").nodes[0];
const mesh = new Mesh(x, y, {
    vertices: node.vertices, normals: node.normals,
    uvs: node.uvs, indices: node.indices, normalize: false,
    baseColorFactor: node.baseColorFactor,   // encoded, not scaled
});
```

The setting's type admits `undefined`, because the loader declares the field
optional and that line has to compile under `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`.
`Sprite3d` forwards it too, and `mesh.setBaseColorFactor(f)` applies one after
construction. For an ordinary sRGB colour use `setTint` instead — the rest of
this section is why the two are different.


The loader handles this for you. It only bites when you build meshes yourself
from `loader.getGLTF(name).nodes` — which is what you do for per-node control,
since there is no public per-node `Mesh` factory — and reach for the obvious
`* 255`:

```js
// WRONG — every untextured material renders far too dark
mesh.tint.setColor(f[0] * 255, f[1] * 255, f[2] * 255, 1);
```

glTF defines `pbrMetallicRoughness.baseColorFactor` in **linear** space (spec
3.9.2), while a melonJS `tint` is 8-bit **sRGB** — the same space as a CSS
colour or a texel out of a PNG. They are not the same number, and the gap is
widest exactly where art tends to live:

| linear | `* 255` | correct | 
|---|---|---|
| 0.05 | 13 | 63 |
| 0.20 | 51 | 124 |
| 0.42 | 107 | 173 |
| 0.72 | 184 | 221 |
| 1.00 | 255 | 255 |

`Color.setLinear` does the encoding for you — it is the linear-space sibling of
`setFloat`, which takes the same `0..1` range but treats it as already-sRGB:

```js
mesh.tint.setLinear(...node.baseColorFactor);   // encodes; what you want
mesh.tint.setFloat(...node.baseColorFactor);    // does NOT encode; too dark
```

It clamps, so the slightly out-of-range factors some exporters emit cannot turn
into `NaN`, and it keeps the encoded value as a float rather than rounding
through 8 bits.

Measured on a scene whose every material went through `* 255`: mean frame luma
85.5 against 147.8 once encoded, with each channel sitting 60 to 73 counts low.

**Fix it early.** It is nearly invisible as a bug, because the scene still
looks coherent — just moody — so lighting and bloom thresholds get tuned
against the wrong values. Correcting the encoding afterwards blows the frame
out and forces a lighting retune, which is a much bigger job than the encode.

This applies only to factors coming out of glTF. Colours **you** author for the
screen, a HUD tint or a glow, are already sRGB: `* 255` is right for those.

## Lights

Authored `KHR_lights_punctual` lights — sun, point, spot — become `Light3d`
children of the container the scene loads into, plus a soft white ambient fill
at intensity 0.3, and each keeps its authored name. A scene carrying any of them
renders through the **lit** path automatically (except `KHR_materials_unlit`
materials); one carrying none renders unlit.

glTF stores physical units — lux for suns, candela for lamps — and a Blender
daylight sun is 1000+, which blows out the engine's stylised shading. So every
light is normalised to intensity 1 by default. To keep the *ratios* the artist
set, scale instead of normalising:

```js
// a 1000-lux sun lands at 1, a 500-lux fill lands at 0.5
level.load("diorama", { scale: 50, lightIntensityScale: 0.001 });
```

Pass `lights: false` to leave the authored lights out. The meshes are then built
**unlit**, so a `Light3d` of your own does not shade them either. To light a
scene your own way, keep the authored lights and retune them by name, or remove
them once the load has finished and add yours: the meshes stay lit.

## Animation

Node-TRS animation **is** supported: translation, rotation and scale channels,
the rigid hierarchical animation used by blocky/low-poly character packs. An
animated asset instantiates as a single `GLTFModel` keeping the node hierarchy
intact, with an API deliberately mirroring `Sprite`. The model carries the asset
name, which is how you get hold of it after loading:

```js
const model = app.world.getChildByName("hero")[0];   // the GLTFModel

model.getAnimationNames();                           // ["idle", "walk", ...]
model.setCurrentAnimation("walk", { loop: true, speed: 1, onComplete });
model.setCurrentAnimation("jump", { next: "idle" }); // chain
model.isCurrentAnimation("walk");
model.play();
model.pause();
model.setAnimationTime(500);                         // like Sprite#setAnimationFrame, in ms
model.getCurrentAnimationTime();                     // like getCurrentAnimationFrame
model.reverseAnimation("open");                      // like Sprite#reverseAnimation
```

`speed` is a playback multiplier (1 = authored speed), not a frame delay. Only
an explicit `loop: false` stops looping. `setCurrentAnimation` **throws** on a
clip name the asset does not define — check `getAnimationNames()` first. Called
with the clip that is already playing it returns at once and ignores its
options, so retime a running clip through `model.animationspeed`, not a second
`setCurrentAnimation(name, { speed })`.

Moving and turning a clip around (20.16):

- **`setAnimationTime(ms)`** moves the current clip to that time and poses it
  at once. A looping clip wraps the time (`setAnimationTime(length)` is its
  first frame); a play-once clip is held between its start and its end and
  plays on from there, even if it had finished. It throws on a time that is
  not a finite number, and does nothing with no clip playing. Use it to start
  a crowd's identical walk cycles out of step.
- **`reverseAnimation(name?)`** plays the clip backwards, as
  `Sprite#reverseAnimation` does: each call turns it around, and it stays
  reversed the next time it is played, starting from its end. A play-once
  clip played backwards ends on its first frame, where `onComplete` and
  `onended` fire. A door's "open" clip reversed is its "close".
- **A negative `speed`** plays the clip backwards as well (both together play
  it forwards). Before 20.16 it froze the clip on its first frame and never
  ended it.

### Placing and moving a model

A `GLTFModel` is placed like any other renderable — `pos`, `depth`, `rotate`
and `scale` move the **whole rig**, and compose with whatever the active clip
is doing, so a walk cycle plays wherever the character stands. They apply just
the same while the clip is paused, finished or was never played, and `scale()`
multiplies the `scale` option the model was built with:

```js
const boat = new me.GLTFModel(me.loader.getGLTF("boat"), { scale: 40, lit: false });
boat.setCurrentAnimation("paddle", { loop: true });
app.world.addChild(boat);

boat.pos.set(steerX, waterLevel);
boat.depth = travelled;
boat.rotate(lean - lastLean, AXIS_Z);   // `rotate` is RELATIVE — feed it the delta
boat.animationspeed = 0.85 + 0.9 * pace; // one authored tempo, many run speeds
```

Constructing one directly from `loader.getGLTF(name)` is fine and is the way to
go when the model is a game object rather than a scene — `level.load` is for
loading a whole scene into the world.

### Skinned characters

A **skinned** mesh — one bound to a skeleton through `JOINTS_0` / `WEIGHTS_0`
and a glTF `skin`, which is what Mixamo, Quaternius, KayKit and most rigged
character packs export — deforms with its joints (20.16). Nothing to opt in:
an asset with a skin loads as a `GLTFModel` (even with no clips), and its clips
drive the joints like any other node.

```js
await loader.preload([{ name: "fox", type: "glb", src: "models/fox.glb" }]);

const data = loader.getGLTF("fox");
// size it from the asset's own bounds rather than guessing the export unit
const scale = 200 / (data.bounds.max[1] - data.bounds.min[1]);
const fox = new GLTFModel(data, { scale, lit: true });
app.world.addChild(fox, 0);
fox.setCurrentAnimation("Walk");
```

How it behaves, so nothing about it is a surprise:

- **The skin is deformed on the CPU**, from the bind pose, on every frame the
  joints move: identical on WebGPU, WebGL and Canvas, at one pass over the
  vertices per frame. A character of a few thousand vertices costs a fraction
  of a millisecond; a crowd of hundreds of skinned characters is the wrong use
  — the GPU has nothing to share between them. Moving or turning the model
  alone does **not** re-skin it.
- **Up to four joints per vertex** (`JOINTS_0` / `WEIGHTS_0`). `JOINTS_1` /
  `WEIGHTS_1` are ignored, so an export with more influences loses the extra
  ones; limit influences to 4 in the exporter. Weights are renormalised to sum
  to 1, and a weight naming a joint the skin does not have is dropped with a
  warning.
- **The skinned mesh's own node transform is ignored**, as the glTF spec
  requires: the joints alone say where it is. Its part `Mesh` sits at the
  model's origin with a cull sphere covering the rig, so it culls where it is
  drawn.
- `data.bounds` is measured on the **skinned rest pose**, so framing a camera
  on it works for a rigged character.
- Each model deforms its **own copy** of the geometry; the descriptor's arrays
  stay the bind pose, so many models can share one loaded asset.
- **Morph targets are not read** (facial blend shapes): the mesh keeps its base
  shape.

### Crossfading between clips

`setCurrentAnimation(name, { crossfade: ms })` blends into the clip instead of
snapping to it — the difference between a walk turning into a run and a walk
*popping* into one. The clip being faded out keeps playing underneath while its
weight falls to 0 (a looping one round its loop, a play-once one, or one
chained with `next`, on to its last frame, which it then holds); with nothing
playing, the blend starts from the rest pose.

```js
fox.setCurrentAnimation("Run", { crossfade: 250 });
fox.setCurrentAnimation("Jump", { loop: false, next: "Idle", crossfade: 150 });
// `next` is entered with the same crossfade
```

Set it once rather than on every call with **`model.crossfade`** (or the
`crossfade` option of `new GLTFModel`, `GLTFScene#addTo` and `level.load`),
like `animationspeed`: every change that does not give its own blends over it,
`play(name)` and the string and function forms included. A call's own
`crossfade` wins, `0` included, which is how one change snaps on a model that
blends by default.

```js
hero.crossfade = 200;
hero.setCurrentAnimation("Run");                    // blends over 200 ms
hero.setCurrentAnimation("Hit", { crossfade: 0 });  // snaps
```

- Switching again **mid-fade** blends from the pose on screen, so mashing
  buttons never pops.
- `pause()` freezes the fade with the clip; `stop()` cancels it.
- Rotations are slerped, translations and scales lerped, per node. It works on
  rigid (node-TRS) rigs as well as skinned ones.
- `crossfade` is ignored by `Sprite` and other frame animations.

Ground speed has to follow the clip too, or the feet skate: tween the speed
over the same duration (`new Tween(pace).to({ value: runSpeed }, { duration: 250 })`).

### Holding things: nodes and attachments

Every glTF node of a model, a part or a skeleton's joint, is reachable by its
name (20.16). `getNodeNames()` lists them, as `getAnimationNames()` lists the
clips.

```js
hero.getNodeNames();       // ["Armature", "mixamorig:Hips", ..., "mixamorig:RightHand", ...]

// keep a sword in the right hand: it follows the clip, the crossfade and the hero
sword.pos.set(0, -12, 0);  // its offset from the hand, along the hand's own axes
hero.addChildToNode(sword, "mixamorig:RightHand");
hero.removeChild(sword);   // drops it

// or just ask where the hand is this frame
const hand = hero.getNodeTransform("mixamorig:RightHand");
spark.pos.set(hand.val[12], hand.val[13], hand.val[14]);
```

- **`addChildToNode(child, name)`** adds the child to the model like
  `addChild`, and moves it to the node every time the model is posed. Its
  `pos` when added is its **offset** from the node; after that `pos` is where
  it is in the world, overwritten each pose, so set the offset first. Adding a
  child already on a node moves it to the new one with the same offset.
- **What turns with the node**: a `Mesh` (either handedness) or a nested
  `GLTFModel`, from the way it was turned when added. A billboard `Sprite3d`,
  a particle emitter or any other renderable only follows the position.
- **The node's scale is never applied.** Mixamo armatures carry a 0.01 scale;
  the sword keeps its own size instead of shrinking with the bone.
- `getChildByName` finds it and `removeChild` takes it off the node; moved to
  another container or destroyed, it stops following.
- **`getNodeTransform(name, out?)`** returns a `Matrix3d`: the node's origin in
  the translation (x, y and depth, the units of `pos`) and its turn, without
  scale, in the rest. A model moved since its last pose is posed again first.
- Both throw on a name the asset does not have: check `getNodeNames()`.

## Instancing

A node using `EXT_mesh_gpu_instancing` loads as an `InstancedMesh` — one draw
call for every copy, which is the difference between a hundred trees and a
hundred thousand. Export with instancing enabled where your tool supports it.
Sparse accessors on the instancing attributes are rejected with a clear error
rather than silently misplacing every instance.

Face culling is decided once per mesh, so instances with a **negative scale**
(mirrored linked duplicates) render inside-out. Building the scene or model
warns when it meets them; mark the material `doubleSided`, which turns culling
off for the set.

## Ground shadows

```js
level.load("diorama", { scale: 50, castGroundShadow: true, shadowGroundY: 0 });
```

`castGroundShadow` is tri-state: set it and it overrides the application setting
for this scene in both directions; omit it and the scene inherits — and that
setting is `true` by default, so shadows are already on. As a scene-wide opt-in
it skips nodes with no vertical extent — a ground plane is exactly that, and
shadowing it with itself smears a blob across the whole floor. Blob shadows need
a GPU backend and a `Camera3d`; nothing is drawn on the 2D-camera or Canvas
paths.

Omit `shadowGroundY` and each blob sits at its own object's base at full
strength, which is right for props already resting on the ground. Set it when
things jump or fly, so the shadow stays on the floor and shrinks with height.

A blob sits on its caster's x/z by default, so a wide flat-bottomed prop hides
its own shadow under itself. The knob for that is `shadowScale`, which widens
the blob until its edge shows past the prop, or `shadowOffset` plus a direction,

sets it itself, because it needs the promise to sequence its fade and reveal; a
trigger without one loads fire-and-forget and never sets it. Either way an
authored `async` property is ignored rather than honoured.

## `rightHanded` — and the default that differs between the two APIs

glTF is authored **Y-up, right-handed**; melonJS is **Y-down, +Z forward**.
There are two ways to bridge that, and they are not equivalent:

- a **rotation** — preserves chirality, matches the authoring tool
- a **mirror** (negate Y only) — flips the scene left/right

`level.load` defaults `rightHanded: true`, so a scene loaded through the level
director comes in correctly. **The `Mesh` constructor defaults it to `false`**,
so glTF or OBJ geometry you feed to a `Mesh` yourself comes in mirrored unless
you pass `rightHanded: true`. A model that is subtly wrong — text backwards, a
character's gear on the wrong side — is this and nothing else.

Do not add a flip of your own on top; two corrections cancel back to wrong.

## Materials — what actually arrives

The importer covers a deliberate subset:

- `pbrMetallicRoughness` **base colour texture and factor**
- `COLOR_0` **vertex colours**, multiplied with the factor and the texture
- metallic/roughness **factors** converted to the engine's specular model
- `emissiveFactor`, including `KHR_materials_emissive_strength`
- `KHR_materials_unlit` — honoured, for baked/stylised workflows
- `alphaMode: "MASK"` — the cutout threshold is applied
- `doubleSided`
- the base colour texture's sampler: `wrapS` / `wrapT` (repeat by default, as
  the spec says) and `magFilter`

`alphaMode: "BLEND"` is read as opaque: the loader does not set `transparent`,
because one loaded mesh can merge materials and the flag routes the whole mesh.
Set `transparent: true` on the part yourself (see `melonjs-3d`).

Not imported: **normal maps**, metallic/roughness *textures*, occlusion maps,
`KHR_texture_transform`. Nothing errors — the material simply
arrives without them, which reads as "flatter than the preview in my authoring
tool". Bake what you need into the base colour. (OBJ/MTL does carry a normal
map, see below.)

**Mesh compression is the exception that does error.** Draco
(`KHR_draco_mesh_compression`) and meshopt (`EXT_meshopt_compression`,
`KHR_meshopt_compression`) cannot be decoded. A file that requires one warns in
the console, naming it, and fails to load; a file that only uses one (it also
carries its meshes uncompressed) warns and loads the uncompressed copy. Export
without mesh compression.

`textureFilter` on the Application settings (`"auto"` / `"nearest"` /
`"linear"` / `"linear-mipmap"`) drives sampling; glTF materials that declare
their own sampler carry it through. Pixel-art models want `"nearest"`. A mesh
already samples mipmaps under `"linear"`, so `"linear-mipmap"` changes nothing
for one.

### `baseColorFactor` is LINEAR; a `tint` is sRGB
**Pass the factor as a setting and the encoding is done for you.** `Mesh`
takes `baseColorFactor` — `[r, g, b]` in 0..1, linear, which is the form the
loader hands back — so a mesh built from a node passes the node's own field
straight through:

```js
const node = loader.getGLTF("palm").nodes[0];
const mesh = new Mesh(x, y, {
    vertices: node.vertices, normals: node.normals,
    uvs: node.uvs, indices: node.indices, normalize: false,
    baseColorFactor: node.baseColorFactor,   // encoded, not scaled
});
```

The setting's type admits `undefined`, because the loader declares the field
optional and that line has to compile under `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`.
`Sprite3d` forwards it too, and `mesh.setBaseColorFactor(f)` applies one after
construction. For an ordinary sRGB colour use `setTint` instead — the rest of
this section is why the two are different.


The loader handles this for you. It only bites when you build meshes yourself
from `loader.getGLTF(name).nodes` — which is what you do for per-node control,
since there is no public per-node `Mesh` factory — and reach for the obvious
`* 255`:

```js
// WRONG — every untextured material renders far too dark
mesh.tint.setColor(f[0] * 255, f[1] * 255, f[2] * 255, 1);
```

glTF defines `pbrMetallicRoughness.baseColorFactor` in **linear** space (spec
3.9.2), while a melonJS `tint` is 8-bit **sRGB** — the same space as a CSS
colour or a texel out of a PNG. They are not the same number, and the gap is
widest exactly where art tends to live:

| linear | `* 255` | correct | 
|---|---|---|
| 0.05 | 13 | 63 |
| 0.20 | 51 | 124 |
| 0.42 | 107 | 173 |
| 0.72 | 184 | 221 |
| 1.00 | 255 | 255 |

`Color.setLinear` does the encoding for you — it is the linear-space sibling of
`setFloat`, which takes the same `0..1` range but treats it as already-sRGB:

```js
mesh.tint.setLinear(...node.baseColorFactor);   // encodes; what you want
mesh.tint.setFloat(...node.baseColorFactor);    // does NOT encode; too dark
```

It clamps, so the slightly out-of-range factors some exporters emit cannot turn
into `NaN`, and it keeps the encoded value as a float rather than rounding
through 8 bits.

Measured on a scene whose every material went through `* 255`: mean frame luma
85.5 against 147.8 once encoded, with each channel sitting 60 to 73 counts low.

**Fix it early.** It is nearly invisible as a bug, because the scene still
looks coherent — just moody — so lighting and bloom thresholds get tuned
against the wrong values. Correcting the encoding afterwards blows the frame
out and forces a lighting retune, which is a much bigger job than the encode.

This applies only to factors coming out of glTF. Colours **you** author for the
screen, a HUD tint or a glow, are already sRGB: `* 255` is right for those.

## Lights

Authored `KHR_lights_punctual` lights — sun, point, spot — become `Light3d`
children of the container the scene loads into, plus a soft white ambient fill
at intensity 0.3, and each keeps its authored name. A scene carrying any of them
renders through the **lit** path automatically (except `KHR_materials_unlit`
materials); one carrying none renders unlit.

glTF stores physical units — lux for suns, candela for lamps — and a Blender
daylight sun is 1000+, which blows out the engine's stylised shading. So every
light is normalised to intensity 1 by default. To keep the *ratios* the artist
set, scale instead of normalising:

```js
// a 1000-lux sun lands at 1, a 500-lux fill lands at 0.5
level.load("diorama", { scale: 50, lightIntensityScale: 0.001 });
```

Pass `lights: false` to leave the authored lights out. The meshes are then built
**unlit**, so a `Light3d` of your own does not shade them either. To light a
scene your own way, keep the authored lights and retune them by name, or remove
them once the load has finished and add yours: the meshes stay lit.

## Animation

Node-TRS animation **is** supported: translation, rotation and scale channels,
the rigid hierarchical animation used by blocky/low-poly character packs. An
animated asset instantiates as a single `GLTFModel` keeping the node hierarchy
intact, with an API deliberately mirroring `Sprite`. The model carries the asset
name, which is how you get hold of it after loading:

```js
const model = app.world.getChildByName("hero")[0];   // the GLTFModel

model.getAnimationNames();                           // ["idle", "walk", ...]
model.setCurrentAnimation("walk", { loop: true, speed: 1, onComplete });
model.setCurrentAnimation("jump", { next: "idle" }); // chain
model.isCurrentAnimation("walk");
model.play();
model.pause();
model.setAnimationTime(500);                         // like Sprite#setAnimationFrame, in ms
model.getCurrentAnimationTime();                     // like getCurrentAnimationFrame
model.reverseAnimation("open");                      // like Sprite#reverseAnimation
```

`speed` is a playback multiplier (1 = authored speed), not a frame delay. Only
an explicit `loop: false` stops looping. `setCurrentAnimation` **throws** on a
clip name the asset does not define — check `getAnimationNames()` first. Called
with the clip that is already playing it returns at once and ignores its
options, so retime a running clip through `model.animationspeed`, not a second
`setCurrentAnimation(name, { speed })`.

Moving and turning a clip around (20.16):

- **`setAnimationTime(ms)`** moves the current clip to that time and poses it
  at once. A looping clip wraps the time (`setAnimationTime(length)` is its
  first frame); a play-once clip is held between its start and its end and
  plays on from there, even if it had finished. It throws on a time that is
  not a finite number, and does nothing with no clip playing. Use it to start
  a crowd's identical walk cycles out of step.
- **`reverseAnimation(name?)`** plays the clip backwards, as
  `Sprite#reverseAnimation` does: each call turns it around, and it stays
  reversed the next time it is played, starting from its end. A play-once
  clip played backwards ends on its first frame, where `onComplete` and
  `onended` fire. A door's "open" clip reversed is its "close".
- **A negative `speed`** plays the clip backwards as well (both together play
  it forwards). Before 20.16 it froze the clip on its first frame and never
  ended it.

### Placing and moving a model

A `GLTFModel` is placed like any other renderable — `pos`, `depth`, `rotate`
and `scale` move the **whole rig**, and compose with whatever the active clip
is doing, so a walk cycle plays wherever the character stands. They apply just
the same while the clip is paused, finished or was never played, and `scale()`
multiplies the `scale` option the model was built with:

```js
const boat = new me.GLTFModel(me.loader.getGLTF("boat"), { scale: 40, lit: false });
boat.setCurrentAnimation("paddle", { loop: true });
app.world.addChild(boat);

boat.pos.set(steerX, waterLevel);
boat.depth = travelled;
boat.rotate(lean - lastLean, AXIS_Z);   // `rotate` is RELATIVE — feed it the delta
boat.animationspeed = 0.85 + 0.9 * pace; // one authored tempo, many run speeds
```

Constructing one directly from `loader.getGLTF(name)` is fine and is the way to
go when the model is a game object rather than a scene — `level.load` is for
loading a whole scene into the world.

### Skinned characters

A **skinned** mesh — one bound to a skeleton through `JOINTS_0` / `WEIGHTS_0`
and a glTF `skin`, which is what Mixamo, Quaternius, KayKit and most rigged
character packs export — deforms with its joints (20.16). Nothing to opt in:
an asset with a skin loads as a `GLTFModel` (even with no clips), and its clips
drive the joints like any other node.

```js
await loader.preload([{ name: "fox", type: "glb", src: "models/fox.glb" }]);

const data = loader.getGLTF("fox");
// size it from the asset's own bounds rather than guessing the export unit
const scale = 200 / (data.bounds.max[1] - data.bounds.min[1]);
const fox = new GLTFModel(data, { scale, lit: true });
app.world.addChild(fox, 0);
fox.setCurrentAnimation("Walk");
```

How it behaves, so nothing about it is a surprise:

- **The skin is deformed on the CPU**, from the bind pose, on every frame the
  joints move: identical on WebGPU, WebGL and Canvas, at one pass over the
  vertices per frame. A character of a few thousand vertices costs a fraction
  of a millisecond; a crowd of hundreds of skinned characters is the wrong use
  — the GPU has nothing to share between them. Moving or turning the model
  alone does **not** re-skin it.
- **Up to four joints per vertex** (`JOINTS_0` / `WEIGHTS_0`). `JOINTS_1` /
  `WEIGHTS_1` are ignored, so an export with more influences loses the extra
  ones; limit influences to 4 in the exporter. Weights are renormalised to sum
  to 1, and a weight naming a joint the skin does not have is dropped with a
  warning.
- **The skinned mesh's own node transform is ignored**, as the glTF spec
  requires: the joints alone say where it is. Its part `Mesh` sits at the
  model's origin with a cull sphere covering the rig, so it culls where it is
  drawn.
- `data.bounds` is measured on the **skinned rest pose**, so framing a camera
  on it works for a rigged character.
- Each model deforms its **own copy** of the geometry; the descriptor's arrays
  stay the bind pose, so many models can share one loaded asset.
- **Morph targets are not read** (facial blend shapes): the mesh keeps its base
  shape.

### Crossfading between clips

`setCurrentAnimation(name, { crossfade: ms })` blends into the clip instead of
snapping to it — the difference between a walk turning into a run and a walk
*popping* into one. The clip being faded out keeps playing underneath while its
weight falls to 0 (a looping one round its loop, a play-once one, or one
chained with `next`, on to its last frame, which it then holds); with nothing
playing, the blend starts from the rest pose.

```js
fox.setCurrentAnimation("Run", { crossfade: 250 });
fox.setCurrentAnimation("Jump", { loop: false, next: "Idle", crossfade: 150 });
// `next` is entered with the same crossfade
```

Set it once rather than on every call with **`model.crossfade`** (or the
`crossfade` option of `new GLTFModel`, `GLTFScene#addTo` and `level.load`),
like `animationspeed`: every change that does not give its own blends over it,
`play(name)` and the string and function forms included. A call's own
`crossfade` wins, `0` included, which is how one change snaps on a model that
blends by default.

```js
hero.crossfade = 200;
hero.setCurrentAnimation("Run");                    // blends over 200 ms
hero.setCurrentAnimation("Hit", { crossfade: 0 });  // snaps
```

- Switching again **mid-fade** blends from the pose on screen, so mashing
  buttons never pops.
- `pause()` freezes the fade with the clip; `stop()` cancels it.
- Rotations are slerped, translations and scales lerped, per node. It works on
  rigid (node-TRS) rigs as well as skinned ones.
- `crossfade` is ignored by `Sprite` and other frame animations.

Ground speed has to follow the clip too, or the feet skate: tween the speed
over the same duration (`new Tween(pace).to({ value: runSpeed }, { duration: 250 })`).

### Holding things: nodes and attachments

Every glTF node of a model, a part or a skeleton's joint, is reachable by its
name (20.16). `getNodeNames()` lists them, as `getAnimationNames()` lists the
clips.

```js
hero.getNodeNames();       // ["Armature", "mixamorig:Hips", ..., "mixamorig:RightHand", ...]

// keep a sword in the right hand: it follows the clip, the crossfade and the hero
sword.pos.set(0, -12, 0);  // its offset from the hand, along the hand's own axes
hero.addChildToNode(sword, "mixamorig:RightHand");
hero.removeChild(sword);   // drops it

// or just ask where the hand is this frame
const hand = hero.getNodeTransform("mixamorig:RightHand");
spark.pos.set(hand.val[12], hand.val[13], hand.val[14]);
```

- **`addChildToNode(child, name)`** adds the child to the model like
  `addChild`, and moves it to the node every time the model is posed. Its
  `pos` when added is its **offset** from the node; after that `pos` is where
  it is in the world, overwritten each pose, so set the offset first. Adding a
  child already on a node moves it to the new one with the same offset.
- **What turns with the node**: a `Mesh` (either handedness) or a nested
  `GLTFModel`, from the way it was turned when added. A billboard `Sprite3d`,
  a particle emitter or any other renderable only follows the position.
- **The node's scale is never applied.** Mixamo armatures carry a 0.01 scale;
  the sword keeps its own size instead of shrinking with the bone.
- `getChildByName` finds it and `removeChild` takes it off the node; moved to
  another container or destroyed, it stops following.
- **`getNodeTransform(name, out?)`** returns a `Matrix3d`: the node's origin in
  the translation (x, y and depth, the units of `pos`) and its turn, without
  scale, in the rest. A model moved since its last pose is posed again first.
- Both throw on a name the asset does not have: check `getNodeNames()`.

## Instancing

A node using `EXT_mesh_gpu_instancing` loads as an `InstancedMesh` — one draw
call for every copy, which is the difference between a hundred trees and a
hundred thousand. Export with instancing enabled where your tool supports it.
Sparse accessors on the instancing attributes are rejected with a clear error
rather than silently misplacing every instance.

Face culling is decided once per mesh, so instances with a **negative scale**
(mirrored linked duplicates) render inside-out. Building the scene or model
warns when it meets them; mark the material `doubleSided`, which turns culling
off for the set.

## Ground shadows

```js
level.load("diorama", { scale: 50, castGroundShadow: true, shadowGroundY: 0 });
```

`castGroundShadow` is tri-state: set it and it overrides the application setting
for this scene in both directions; omit it and the scene inherits — and that
setting is `true` by default, so shadows are already on. As a scene-wide opt-in
it skips nodes with no vertical extent — a ground plane is exactly that, and
shadowing it with itself smears a blob across the whole floor. Blob shadows need
a GPU backend and a `Camera3d`; nothing is drawn on the 2D-camera or Canvas
paths.

Omit `shadowGroundY` and each blob sits at its own object's base at full
strength, which is right for props already resting on the ground. Set it when
things jump or fly, so the shadow stays on the floor and shrinks with height.

A blob sits on its caster's x/z by default, so a wide flat-bottomed prop hides
its own shadow under itself. The knob for that is `shadowScale`, which widens
the blob until its edge shows past the prop, or `shadowOffset` plus a direction,
which slides it clear. **Not** `shadowGroundY`: raising that floats the blob up
over the object as a dark ring instead of sliding it out, because it is for
things that leave the ground, not a visibility control.

For a light that is not overhead, name one: `shadowLight` takes the direction
from a `Light3d` and is re-read every draw, so a day or night cycle carries
every shadow in the scene with it. Nothing is inferred — a scene with no named
light and no `shadowDirectionX`/`Z` gets no direction, because a scene with
several lights has no non-arbitrary answer. `shadowStretch` lengthens the blob
along that direction and fades it as it pulls; `shadowGroundNormal` lays it on
a floor that is not level. All of these apply to an `InstancedMesh` too, as one
value for the whole set.

# 3D and 2.5D in melonJS

> melonJS is a 2D engine that grew a real 3D tier: perspective cameras, meshes,
> instancing, glTF scenes and 3D lights. Most of what a model "knows" about 3D
> graphics comes from the OpenGL convention, and **melonJS's is the inverse**.
> Read the conventions section before writing any 3D code.

## Coordinate conventions — the inverse of OpenGL

This is the single most important thing on this page.

| | melonJS | OpenGL convention |
|---|---|---|
| vertical | **Y-down** — higher `y` is *lower* on screen | Y-up |
| depth | **+Z forward** — higher `z` is *farther* away | −Z forward |

`Camera3d` exposes three rotation angles: `camera.pitch`
(X, look up/down), `camera.yaw` (Y, look left/right) and `camera.roll` (Z, bank
the horizon). The view is `R(yaw) ∘ R(pitch) ∘ R(roll)` inverted, and the frustum
planes come off that same matrix — so culling follows a banked view.

The basis those angles produce is **readable and writable**: `getBasis(right,
up, forward)` reads it, `setBasis(right, up, forward)` poses the camera from
one.

`camera.rotate()` is NOT the way to bank a 3D camera. It writes the inherited
`currentTransform`, which a 3D view never reads, so the call is silently inert.
Set `roll`. (On a `Camera2d` it is the other way round: roll IS that transform's
rotation, which is why `worldToLocal` / `localToWorld` compensate for it.)

The payoff is that 2D code translates directly — anywhere you used `pos.x` /
`pos.y`, add `pos.z` and the maths still holds. The cost is that every
OpenGL-shaped instinct is backwards.

**Consequence that bites immediately:** "behind everything" is the *largest*
depth when the camera looks along +Z. Put a backdrop on the wrong side and it
either paints over the whole scene (it is nearer than everything else) or
disappears without trace (it falls in front of the near plane and the GPU clips
it). Which sign means "far" depends on which side the camera sits, so check the
camera before picking a backdrop depth.

glTF assets are authored Y-up right-handed. `level.load` converts them by
rotation (`rightHanded: true` is its default), so you do not apply a flip
yourself. The **`Mesh` constructor defaults `rightHanded` to `false`**, which
bridges by mirroring instead — geometry you hand to a `Mesh` directly comes in
flipped left/right unless you pass `rightHanded: true`. See
`melonjs-3d-assets`.

## Opting in

3D starts with the camera class, and nothing else has to change. Set it once on
the `Application`:

```js
import { Application, Camera3d } from "melonjs";

const app = new Application(1024, 768, {
    parent: "screen",
    cameraClass: Camera3d,      // ← the opt-in
});
await app.init();
```

That flips the world's sort to `"depth"`, switches the broadphase to a 3D index,
and renders sprites and meshes with perspective projection. `Camera3d` extends
`Camera2d`, so follow, fade, shake and post effects all still work (follow with
a difference, see the camera traps).

### Keep the camera, do not fish it back out

`app.viewport` is the **active stage's** default camera, so it is typed
`Camera2d`: a stage overrides the application's `cameraClass`, and the
built-in loading screen does exactly that. Reading your `Camera3d` back out of
it therefore needs a cast, and a cast that is wrong while the loader is up:

```js
const camera = app.viewport as Camera3d;   // works, until it does not
```

Own it instead. Pass the camera in and keep the typed reference, and nothing
downstream ever narrows:

```js
class GameStage extends Stage {
    readonly camera: Camera3d;

    constructor(app) {
        const camera = new Camera3d(0, 0, app.renderer.width, app.renderer.height);
        super({ cameras: [camera] });
        this.camera = camera;
    }
}
```

A freshly built camera is named `"default"`, and a stage registers its
`cameras` by name, so this IS the stage's default camera: `app.viewport`
returns the same instance.

### The two patterns differ in LIFETIME, and that decides which you want

This is the part that bites. `cameraClass` builds a **fresh camera for each
stage**, which the engine does deliberately so "Camera3d state shouldn't
bleed across stages". An owned camera passed through `super({ cameras })` is
built once and lives as long as the stage object, which for a stage you
register with `state.set()` means as long as the application.

So anything you attach to the camera now outlives the visit:

```js
// in onResetEvent — runs EVERY time the stage is entered
app.viewport.addPostEffect(bloom);
```

With `cameraClass` that lands on a fresh camera each time and is harmless.
With an owned camera it stacks: a second bloom on the second visit, a third
on the third. The symptom is text and edges appearing to double or smear,
because the scene is being post-processed once per accumulated effect.

Note that `removePostEffect` DESTROYS the effect rather than detaching it, so
"just remove it on the way out" is not a free undo.

**Choose on lifetime, not on typing:**

| your effects / camera state are | use |
|---|---|
| set up per stage visit, in `onResetEvent` | `cameraClass` — fresh camera per stage |
| set up once, in the stage constructor | an owned camera in `super({ cameras })` |

If you want the typed reference but your setup is per-visit, keep
`cameraClass` and narrow once on reset:

```js
override onResetEvent(app) {
    const viewport = app.viewport;
    if (!(viewport instanceof Camera3d)) {
        throw new Error("this stage needs a Camera3d");
    }
    this.camera = viewport;   // typed, checked, and still fresh per visit
}
```

That is what the Earth Defender example does, and why: it attaches post
effects on every reset and never removes them.

Narrowing beats asserting wherever you read the shared slot: the language
verifies `instanceof`, and fails loudly if the application was never given a
`cameraClass`, where a cast fails silently at the first 3D call.

Per-stage opt-in also works, which is useful when the loading screen is 2D:

```js
class GameStage extends Stage {
    constructor() {
        super({ cameras: [new Camera3d(0, 0, 1024, 768, { fov: Math.PI / 3 })] });
    }
}
```

## Camera traps

- **There is no sky.** The frame clears to `renderer.backgroundColor` (opaque
  black unless the renderer was created transparent), and `world.backgroundColor`
  clears over it when you set one — both are flat colours. Anything more is a
  backdrop renderable, screen-fixed or placed at a far depth.
- **Set the clip planes for your scene scale.** Defaults are near 0.1 / far 1000.
  Objects beyond the far plane clip or project with bad w-divides; a `near` that
  is too small wastes depth precision and distant props z-fight. Use
  `camera.setClipPlanes(near, far)`.
- **`camera.pos.set(x, y)` is 2-argument and zeroes z.** Use
  `camera.setPosition(x, y, z)`, which leaves the depth untouched when `z` is
  omitted; `camera.depth` is the z accessor if you only want that.
- **`lookAt(target)` solves pitch and yaw only**, so on its own it cannot
  express "up is this direction" and it leaves `roll` alone. Pass an up to
  bank the horizon too: `camera.lookAt(target, up)`, where `up` is what should
  appear UP ON SCREEN. This engine renders Y-down, so a level horizon is
  `(0, -1, 0)`. There is deliberately no default, because giving one would
  silently level every camera that had banked its own horizon.
- **When the game already has all three axes, hand them over**:
  `camera.setBasis(right, up, forward)`, the writable counterpart of
  `getBasis`. The case that needs it is a view over a curved surface, where up
  is the surface normal and differs at every point, so no pitch and yaw pair
  expresses it and integrating towards one drifts and gimbals at the poles.
  `setBasis` absorbs a triple that has drifted off orthonormal rather than
  leaving the camera holding something that is not a rotation, and it does not
  care what the axes are scaled to: a direction is a direction, so anything
  from a denormal to 1e300 resolves the same way. Note its `up` is the camera's
  local +Y column, which under Y-down points DOWN the screen: the opposite
  sense to `lookAt`'s, and one negation apart.
- **`worldToLocal` does not project.** It is a 2D camera's offset subtraction.
  To pin a label or marker to a point in the scene use
  `camera.worldToScreen(point, out?)`: it takes a `Vector3d`, applies the
  projection and returns a `Vector2d` in the camera's pixels (y down), or
  `null` behind the camera. See `melonjs-camera-and-drawing`.
- **`follow()` tracks exactly.** Under a `Camera3d` the camera sits at the
  target's position plus `followOffset` (world space, set with
  `camera.setFollowOffset(x, y, z)`) every frame. The 2D follow's axis,
  deadzone and damping are not applied. For a damped chase camera, leave the
  target unset and move the camera yourself (`math.damp`, or `slerp` below for
  its facing).

## Orbiting a point: `orbit`

`camera.orbit(target, yaw, pitch, distance)` places the camera on a sphere
around a point, looking at it: the camera of a model viewer, a level overview,
a turn-table, a third-person view. The angles are the camera's own `yaw` and
`pitch`, which it keeps: `lookAt` the other way round (that one keeps the
position and finds the angles, this one keeps the angles and finds the
position). A **negative** `pitch` looks down, from above the point.

Keep the three numbers in your own state and call `orbit` again when they
change. A drag reads screen coordinates (`gameScreenX` / `gameScreenY`), not
world ones, which move with the camera; clamp the pitch short of a quarter
turn; ease toward where the player asks with `math.damp`:

```js
const view = { yaw: 0.6, pitch: -0.4, distance: 900 };
const want = { ...view };
let dragging = false;
let lastX = 0;
let lastY = 0;
input.registerPointerEvent("pointerdown", camera, (ev) => {
	dragging = true;
	lastX = ev.gameScreenX;
	lastY = ev.gameScreenY;
});
// let go anywhere, on the canvas or off it
event.on(event.POINTERUP, () => {
	dragging = false;
});
input.registerPointerEvent("pointermove", camera, (ev) => {
	if (!dragging) return;
	want.yaw += (ev.gameScreenX - lastX) * 0.005;
	want.pitch = math.clamp(want.pitch - (ev.gameScreenY - lastY) * 0.005, -1.4, 1.4);
	lastX = ev.gameScreenX;
	lastY = ev.gameScreenY;
});
input.registerPointerEvent("wheel", camera, (ev) => {
	want.distance = math.clamp(want.distance * (1 + ev.deltaY * 0.001), 200, 4000);
});
// in update(dt), dt in ms
for (const k of ["yaw", "pitch", "distance"]) {
	view[k] = math.damp(view[k], want[k], 8, dt / 1000);
}
camera.orbit(model.pos, view.yaw, view.pitch, view.distance);
```

Release the three pointer events (`input.releasePointerEvent`) and
`event.off` the release when the stage ends. `orbit` places the camera once: a camera with a `follow()` target is put
back at the target on its next update, so orbit with no target set.

## Orthographic projection: the isometric look

`camera.projection = "orthographic"` (or `projection: "orthographic"` in the
`Camera3d` options) keeps everything 3D — depth buffer, lighting, fog, ground
shadows, billboards, sprites and particles at their depth, culling, picking,
glTF scenes — and drops the
foreshortening (20.16). Parallel edges stay parallel and a prop is the same
size at the back as at the front: the look of an isometric tactics, builder or
diorama game, without isometric tile maths.

```js
const camera = app.viewport;              // cameraClass: Camera3d
camera.projection = "orthographic";
camera.orthoHeight = 900;                 // world units tall, at zoom 1
// true isometric: a quarter turn of 45°, looking down atan(1/√2) ≈ 35.26°
const yaw = Math.PI / 4;
const pitch = Math.atan(1 / Math.SQRT2);
camera.setPosition(
    -Math.sin(yaw) * Math.cos(pitch) * 1800,
    -Math.sin(pitch) * 1800,              // up is -Y
    -Math.cos(yaw) * Math.cos(pitch) * 1800,
);
camera.lookAt(0, 0, 0);
camera.setClipPlanes(50, 6000);
```

- **`orthoHeight` frames the view, `zoom` zooms it.** `orthoHeight` is the
  height of the view in world units at zoom 1 (the width follows the aspect),
  defaulting to the camera's height in pixels, one unit per pixel. `zoom`
  divides it, as on a `Camera2d`: `zoom = 2` shows half as much world, and
  `orthoHeight` still reads what was set. `fov` is ignored; a perspective
  camera ignores `zoom` (narrow its `fov` instead).
- **`orthoWidth` keeps the width instead.** Set it (or pass it as an option,
  instead of `orthoHeight`) and the view's width survives every resize while
  the height follows the aspect: a board that must always fit across a phone
  held upright. Whichever of the two was set last is the one kept; the other
  reads what it works out to. `zoom` divides both.

```js
camera.orthoWidth = 1200;   // the board's width always fits, portrait or landscape
```
- **Still stand the camera back.** It is placed and pointed as a perspective
  one is: `near` / `far` are measured from it, so something behind it is
  clipped, and specular highlights are measured from its position.
- **Switching at run time** keeps the camera where it is; only the projection
  changes. To make the two frame alike, give perspective
  `fov = 2 * atan(orthoHeight / 2 / distance)`.
- Picking works the same: `screenToRay` returns parallel rays, one per pixel,
  each starting on the camera's plane.

## Where an up vector earns its keep

Three cases. In the first two, `lookAt(target)` on its own is already right and
an up would be noise. The third is the one it exists for.

```js
// 1. ordinary third-person: world up never changes, so say nothing
camera.setPosition(x, y, z).lookAt(player);

// 2. a deliberate dutch angle: this is a ROLL, not an up vector
camera.lookAt(player);
camera.roll = Math.PI / 32;

// 3. a view over a curved surface: up is the surface normal, and it is
//    different at every point on the globe. No pitch and yaw pair expresses
//    it, and integrating towards it drifts and gimbals over the poles.
const up = player.pos.clone().sub(planetCentre).normalize();  // surface normal
camera.setPosition(eye.x, eye.y, eye.z).lookAt(player, up.negate());
```

Note the `negate()` in case 3. The surface normal points away from the planet,
which is the direction the player's head points, and `up` wants what should
appear UP ON SCREEN. This engine renders Y-down, so `(0, -1, 0)` is a level
horizon and a world-space "up" direction has to be handed over in that sense.
Get it backwards and the view is upside down, which is the single most likely
mistake with this argument.

If the game already computes all three axes, skip the solve entirely:

```js
// a surface frame the game is already maintaining
camera.setBasis(right, up, forward);
```

`setBasis` takes the camera's OWN columns, where `up` is local +Y and so points
down the screen: the opposite sense to `lookAt`'s, one negation apart. It also
absorbs a frame that has drifted off orthonormal, which one integrated over
thousands of steps will have.

**A camera posed this way and a world rotated into a fixed camera's frame are
the same picture.** If a game already transforms its world into view space by
hand, there is nothing to gain by switching; the value of `setBasis` is not
having to write that transform in the first place.

## Turning a direction: `slerp`, not `lerp`

`lerp` walks the straight line between the two tips, which passes INSIDE the
sphere. The result points the right way at both ends, lingers near them, rushes
the middle, and comes out shorter than either input as it crosses the midpoint.
On a camera swing that reads as a lurch; on a body walking over a globe it dips
into the surface.

`Vector3d#slerp` turns along the great circle instead, at a constant angular
rate, and carries the length across linearly, so two unit vectors give back a
unit vector and nothing needs renormalizing.

```js
// a turret, a camera, a ship: a facing chasing another facing
facing.slerp(toTarget, 0.25);

// frame-rate independent, the same shape as math.damp
facing.slerp(toTarget, 1 - Math.exp((-6 * dt) / 1000));
```

`ObservableVector3d` has it too and fires its callback ONCE, so
`renderable.pos.slerp(...)` is one notification rather than three.

**`Vector2d` has the same method**, and it is not a cut-down copy: in 2D the
whole turn is one signed angle, so there is no sine to divide by and no
degenerate near-parallel case at all. What it buys a 2D game is the wrap: a
heading damped as a NUMBER from 170 degrees to -170 degrees sweeps the long 340
instead of the short 20, and an arc between directions cannot do that.

Two degenerate pairs are handled inside rather than left to the caller, and
both turn up in ordinary game code:

- **the same direction**, where every path between them is the same path.
- **opposite directions**, where infinitely many great circles pass through
  both and none is the shorter way round. The textbook formula divides by a
  vanishing sine here and hands back `NaN`, which propagates into a position or
  a matrix and the object disappears. `slerp` picks a stable perpendicular and
  turns through half a circle instead.

That second case is why a hand-rolled version is a liability rather than a
shortcut: anything orbiting a planet reaches the antipode of where it started,
every run.

**`math.damp` for a scalar, `slerp` for a direction.** Same job, different
space; what `damp` cannot do is keep a vector on the sphere.

## Depth sorting

Under `Camera3d` the world sorts on `"depth"` **every frame** (recursively), so
unlike 2D you *can* assign `depth` after `addChild` and it will reorder. That is
the one place where the usual z-ordering rule is relaxed — see
`melonjs-renderables` for the 2D rules, which still apply everywhere else.

You will often *have* to. A `Container` has `autoDepth: true` by default, so
`addChild(child)` with no explicit z **overwrites `pos.z` with the child's
index** — a real world depth in a 3D scene, and never the one you wanted. Pass
it (`world.addChild(mesh, z)`), or set `mesh.depth` afterwards. The glTF
importer turns `autoDepth` off on the container it loads into for this reason.

A `Container`'s depth carries to its children when they are drawn, as it
already did for culling and the sort: a group at depth 400 draws its sprites
and meshes 400 units further away. One more reason to give containers an
explicit z.

**`floating` does not opt out of this sort.** It skips the camera *transform*,
not the depth *order*. A floating child is ordered by `|pos.z|` alone — its
`pos.x/y` are screen pixels, and the camera does not move relative to it — so
the magnitude is the distance and the sign is ignored:

```js
world.addChild(hud, -150);       // small -> nearer than anything -> on top
world.addChild(skybox, -10000);  // large -> farther -> behind everything
world.addChild(skybox, 100000);  // equally far: sign does not matter
```

Both hold at any camera position. A HUD given the huge z that would put it on
top in 2D lands at the far end of the level instead, with the scenery drawing
over it. Pointer events follow the same order (20.16): of two overlapping
floating regions, the one at the smaller depth is asked first.

## Transparency

A mesh fades by setting its opacity — there is nothing else to switch on:

```js
ghost.setOpacity(0.4);
```

Meshes render in two phases. The **opaque pass** writes depth in sort order; the
**transparent pass** replays afterwards, back-to-front, blending and writing no
depth. A draw lands in the second whenever its alpha is fractional.

That default matters because the opaque path writes premultiplied colour with
blending off, so a faded mesh that stays there (as every one did before 20.4)
comes out **darkened toward black** rather than see-through — the background
contributes nothing.

**`transparent: true`** when the transparency is in the TEXTURE rather than the
opacity — a soft-edged glow, smoke, a glTF material with `alphaMode: "BLEND"`.
The automatic check reads the draw's alpha and cannot see into a texture. Watch
`alphaCutoff` here: it discards texels *before* blending sees them, so a soft
edge needs a low cutoff (`Sprite3d` drops its own default to `1/255` when you
set `transparent: true`). The cutoff thresholds the MATERIAL's alpha, not the
drawn alpha, so a fading cutout mesh keeps its shape instead of disappearing at
its own threshold.

The glTF loader does **not** set this for you: one loaded mesh can merge several
materials and the flag routes the whole mesh, so a `"BLEND"` material sharing
geometry with an opaque one would drag the opaque half into the transparent pass.

**`transparent: false`** pins a mesh to the opaque pass however it is faded.

### `depthTest: false` for something with no surface to be occluded on

`transparent` decides the PASS, and the transparent pass turns depth *writing*
off on its own so overlapping blended draws blend instead of fighting. Whether
geometry in front of a mesh **hides** it is a separate question, and
`depthTest` is where you answer it. The default, `true`, is what you want for
anything genuinely in the scene — a muzzle flash behind a wall should still be
behind the wall, and this is not a synonym for "additive".

Set it `false` for a mesh standing in for a screen-space effect: an additive
glow carrying a world position only so it can sort and move with the thing it
belongs to. A world-space caption billboarded over a prop wants it for the
same reason, since it has no surface for the prop's own foliage to be in front
of. Left depth tested, a flat billboard is sliced along a hard straight
line the moment any geometry is nearer at some pixel. That shows up worst
around something round — a glow on a rock near a planet's limb gets cut,
and no offset escapes it, because the near surface bulges further toward the
camera than any offset you would dare apply.

```js
const halo = new Sprite3d(0, 0, {
    image: glowTexture,
    width: rock.radius * 3, height: rock.radius * 3,
    billboard: "spherical",
    blendMode: "additive",
    transparent: true,     // the blended pass
    alphaCutoff: 0,        // do not cut the soft falloff
    depthTest: false,      // and do not let the world slice it
});
```

Honoured in the **transparent pass only**, on both GPU backends: a mesh drawn
in the opaque pass ignores it, so pair it with `transparent: true` as above.
The Canvas renderer has no depth buffer and ignores it.

Blending uses the renderable's existing `blendMode`, so a glow is one property.
The advanced modes (`"overlay"`, `"difference"`, and the rest that need a
compositing pass) fall back to `"normal"` here, on both backends:

```js
const glow = new Mesh(0, 0, {
    ...quad, texture: glowTexture,
    transparent: true, blendMode: "additive", alphaCutoff: 0,
});
```
