# Display and scaling

Seven settings decide how a game looks on screen, and they are easy to get
individually right and collectively wrong. This is what each one actually
does, and which one to reach for.

## The four jobs

A pixel travels from your source art to a physical pixel through four
separate decisions. Knowing which setting owns which is most of the work.

| job | setting | what it decides |
|---|---|---|
| how big the frame is drawn | `width`/`height` on `Application` | the design resolution everything is authored against |
| how it uses the space | `scale`, `scaleMethod`, `scaleTarget` | fit, fill, stretch, and what it measures to decide |
| may the factor be fractional | `scaleRounding` | whole device pixels per source pixel, or any factor |
| how a texture is sampled | `antiAlias`, `textureFilter` | nearest or linear, and the CSS upscale filter |

`subPixel` is a fifth, orthogonal to all of them: it decides whether a
renderable may sit on a fractional position WITHIN the frame. `syncToDisplay`
is about the frames in a row rather than one frame: whether motion advances
by the same amount on each.

## Design resolution

```js
const app = new Application(480, 270, { scale: "auto" });
```

The game is drawn at 480x270 whatever the window is, and the canvas is scaled
to the container. Everything in world coordinates is in those units. This is
the usual arrangement: author once, scale to whatever you are given.

## `scale` and `scaleMethod`

`scale: "auto"` turns on automatic scaling, and so does naming any
`scaleMethod` other than `"manual"`, even with no `scale` given:
`{ scaleMethod: "flex" }` alone scales to its container. A number is a fixed
multiplier, used only while `scaleMethod` is `"manual"` (the default); with
automatic scaling on, the number is ignored.

`scaleMethod` decides how the available space is used:

- **`"fit"`** keeps the design resolution and the aspect ratio, scaling to the
  largest factor that fits. Leftover space becomes margin. This is the one to
  use when the game is authored for a fixed frame.
- **`"fill-min"` / `"fill-max"`** keep the aspect ratio but RESIZE the
  renderer, so the design resolution changes with the window and the game sees
  more or less of the world.
- **`"flex"`, `"flex-width"`, `"flex-height"`** resize the renderer on one or
  both axes.
- **`"stretch"`** scales each axis independently, so the aspect ratio is not
  preserved and circles become ovals.
- **`"manual"`**, the default, does nothing automatic with a numeric `scale`.
  With `scale: "auto"` it scales as `"fit"` does.

The distinction that matters: **`fit` scales a fixed frame; everything else
changes how much of the world is visible.** A game whose layout assumes a
known frame wants `fit`.

## `scaleTarget`: what gets measured

Automatic scaling measures **the parent of the element the canvas is mounted
in**, not the element itself. If that grandparent is not the box you meant,
the canvas is sized wrongly, and the failure is quiet.

The case that bites: a canvas container that is `position: fixed` or
`absolute` contributes no height to its parent, so the parent measures only
whatever else is in it. If that parent is `<body>`, the engine falls back to
the window size and the canvas ends up larger than the box it lives in,
cropped by whatever sits above it.

```js
new Application(1024, 576, {
	parent: "screen",
	scale: "auto",
	// measure THIS, rather than guessing from the DOM shape
	scaleTarget: document.getElementById("stage"),
});
```

Either name the element with `scaleTarget`, or give the canvas container a
parent whose box is the area you want filled. If the canvas is cropped or
overflows on resize, this is the first thing to check.

## `scaleRounding`: whole device pixels

```js
new Application(480, 270, {
	scale: "auto",
	scaleMethod: "fit",
	scaleRounding: "integer",   // default "fractional"
});
```

`"fractional"` fills the container exactly, at whatever factor that takes. A
480 wide design in a 1280 wide container is scaled by 2.667, so some source
pixels cover three screen pixels and some cover two. Pixel art shows this as
uneven glyph stems and shimmering edges, and browsers resolve the unevenness
differently, so the same scene can look crisp in one and soft in another.

`"integer"` rounds the factor DOWN so every source pixel covers the same whole
number of device pixels, and letterboxes with the space left over. That trade,
crisp pixels for black bars, is the whole decision.

### What it costs

More than "some letterboxing", and the size of it is decided by
`devicePixelRatio` as much as by the window. A higher ratio has more device
pixels to round among, so it lands closer to the factor it wanted. For a
480x270 design, which is exactly a quarter of 1920x1080:

| container | ratio | fit | integer | presented | area lost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1920x1080 | 1 or 2 | 4.000 | 4 / 8 | 1920x1080 | none |
| 1440x810 | 1 | 3.000 | 3 | 1440x810 | none |
| 960x540 | 1 | 2.000 | 2 | 960x540 | none |
| 1280x720 | 2 | 2.667 | 5 | 1200x675 | 12% |
| 2560x1440 | 2 | 5.333 | 10 | 2400x1350 | 12% |
| 1280x720 | 1 | 2.667 | 2 | 960x540 | **44%** |
| 1366x768 | 1 | 2.844 | 2 | 960x540 | **51%** |

So the decision is mostly made when the design resolution is chosen, not when
this setting is. One that divides the sizes you expect costs nothing; one that
does not can give up half the screen on a 1x display, and 1366x768 laptops are
not rare. A game that must fill the window on any machine should stay
fractional and accept the uneven pixels.

Two things to know:

- It applies to **`scaleMethod: "fit"` only.** Every other method resizes the
  renderer to the container, so the design resolution moves and there is no
  fixed factor to round.
- The rounding happens in **device** pixels. `devicePixelRatio` multiplies the
  CSS size on the way to real pixels, so rounding the CSS factor would let the
  fraction straight back in: a factor of 2 at a ratio of 1.25 is 2.5 device
  pixels per source pixel.

## `antiAlias` does three things

This is the setting most likely to surprise, because it is not one switch:

1. the texture filter, but only while `textureFilter` is `"auto"` (the
   default), which TRACKS it: linear when on, nearest when off. Setting
   `textureFilter` explicitly decouples the two
2. `imageSmoothingEnabled` on the 2D context
3. the canvas CSS `image-rendering`: `pixelated` when off, `auto` when on

So `antiAlias: false` gives hard-edged textures AND a hard-edged upscale of
the whole frame. That is usually what a pixel-art game wants, and usually NOT
what a smooth 3D scene wants, because it also disables MSAA.

`textureFilter: "nearest" | "linear"` separates the texture half, so a scene
can have smooth model edges and nearest-sampled sprites. The presentation half
is not separable: there is no way to get MSAA silhouettes and a hard-edged
upscale at the same time.

## Drawn small: `textureFilter: "linear-mipmap"`

A sprite drawn much smaller than its texture (a zoomed-out camera, a minimap,
a scaled-down sprite) shimmers as it moves, even with linear sampling: each
screen pixel covers many texels and linear sampling blends only four of them.
`"linear-mipmap"` samples the texture's mipmaps, smaller copies averaged in
advance, wherever something is drawn below its size:

```js
const app = new Application(1280, 720, { textureFilter: "linear-mipmap" });
```

At its size or larger a texture draws as it does under `"linear"`, so a game
whose main view is at its size and whose minimap is zoomed out gets a smooth
minimap and an unchanged view. It covers sprites, text and tile layers, not a
video nor a texture the engine renders into, and a `nearest` texture keeps to
its full size. GPU backends only; on WebGPU each texture it applies to takes
about a third more memory.

A small mipmap level's texels span many of the art's pixels, so a sample near
the edge of a frame would reach into the next frame of the atlas. Under
`"linear-mipmap"` every sprite and tile keeps its samples half a texel of the
level it reads inside its own frame, so the next frame no longer streaks along
its edges. Two limits:

- a level's texel is an average of a square of the art, 2, 4, 8 pixels a side
  and so on. Where a frame's edge falls inside such a square, its outermost
  texel already holds some of the neighbour: drawn very small, a frame of an
  atlas packed edge to edge can show a faint line of it. Frames on a grid of
  a power of two (a 32 or 64 px sheet) are free of it, and a padding of a few
  pixels between frames removes it elsewhere;
- a sprite drawn through a `ShaderEffect` samples the texture in the effect's
  own program, which is not kept to the frame.

A repeating pattern is left to wrap.

## `subPixel` is about position, not scale

`subPixel: false` (the default) draws everything on whole pixels. The snap
happens **once, where a draw lands**, the same on every renderer: each edge of
a sprite, a shape or a clip is rounded to the nearest pixel after every
translation and scale it is drawn under. So:

- nested containers add their positions up exactly first (10.6 then -6.5
  lands on 4, the pixel 4.1 is in);
- a flipped sprite covers the pixels it covers unflipped;
- a sprite and a `fillRect` at the same position cover the same pixels, and a
  shape has no half-grey edge on the Canvas renderer;
- a position floating point error leaves a hair short of a pixel, such as a
  body resting on the floor at `223.99999999999997` after a collision
  push-out, draws on that pixel (224), so it does not shake every other frame.

The camera's view starts on a whole pixel too, in world units (zoomed 2x, it
moves in 2 px steps), and culling and the pointer use that same position:
things standing still stay still against each other while the view scrolls,
and a click lands on what is drawn under it. A rotated draw, and anything a
`Camera3d` draws, is left where it is.

It does nothing about how the frame reaches the screen. A game that carefully
snaps positions and is then scaled by 2.667 has thrown that work away at the
last step, which is the contradiction `scaleRounding: "integer"` exists to
resolve.

`subPixel: true` alone does not make motion smooth: with nearest sampling a
sprite between two pixels is still drawn on one of them, so a scene moving
4.5 pixels a frame jumps by 4 and 5 in turn. Rendered art (not pixel art)
moves smoothly with `textureFilter: "linear"` as well, which blends it across
the two, while the upscale stays crisp (`antiAlias: true` would also smooth the
whole canvas as it is scaled up, which is what makes it look blurry). A still
scene is only sharp when the camera rests on a whole pixel, so give it a
target on whole pixels:

```js
const app = new Application(1280, 720, {
	scale: "auto",
	subPixel: true,
	textureFilter: "linear",
	syncToDisplay: true,
});
// the camera follows a point on whole pixels, kept on the hero: it glides
// between pixels while following, and comes to rest on one
const focus = new Vector2d();
app.viewport.follow(focus, app.viewport.AXIS.BOTH, 0.12);

// in the hero's update(dt)
focus.set(Math.round(this.pos.x), Math.round(this.pos.y));
```

## `syncToDisplay` is about steady motion

The game updates in fixed steps, 60 a second by default, as many as the time
since the last frame holds. Browsers report that time with up to a millisecond
of jitter, so on a 60 Hz display a frame now and then gets no update and the
next one gets two: the world holds still for a frame, then moves twice as far.
Scrolling, and anything else moving steadily, stutters while the frame rate
reads a solid 60.

```js
const app = new Application(1280, 720, { scale: "auto", syncToDisplay: true });
```

With it on, frame times are counted in whole display frames and what is
rounded off is carried to the next frame: one update every frame at 60 Hz, one
every other frame at 120 Hz, and the game keeps its speed. A display within 2%
of `timer.maxfps` (60 by default), or of 2, 3 or 4 times it, or a half, a third
or a quarter of it, is counted at exactly that rate, so a 59.94 Hz screen runs
the game 0.1% slower than the wall clock; leave it off when the updates must
keep to the wall clock exactly. The display's rate is learned as the game runs,
and again when it changes (the window moved to another screen). At a refresh
that is no multiple of the update rate (144 Hz, 165 Hz) the steps cannot fall
evenly however the time is counted.

It is off by default. It sets `timer.syncToDisplay` when the application is
initialized, which a game can also switch at any time.

## Soft text next to crisp sprites

If everything is crisp EXCEPT the text, the scale factor is not the cause: a
fractional factor softens the whole frame equally. The text is different
because of how it is made.

`Text` draws through the browser's `fillText`, which anti-aliases glyph edges
into partial-alpha pixels. Measured on one label at 16px: **171 distinct
partial alpha levels**. Nothing in the canvas API turns that off. `antiAlias`
and the `imageSmoothingEnabled` that `CanvasRenderTarget` sets govern IMAGE
drawing, not glyph rasterisation.

So the label arrives already soft, and the upscale then magnifies each grey
edge pixel into a grey block, sitting beside sprites that were hard-edged to
begin with and stay hard-edged under nearest sampling.

It also explains the same scene looking crisp in one browser and soft in
another at identical size and settings: engines use different font
rasterisers, with different hinting and anti-aliasing, so they bake DIFFERENT
textures from the same font at the same size.

**Use `BitmapText` for a game that upscales.** A pixel-font atlas is
hard-edged source art like every other texture, so it survives magnification
the way the sprites do. Raising the design resolution only shrinks the
magnification of anti-aliasing that is still there, so it softens the symptom
rather than removing it, and `scaleRounding` does nothing for this at all.

Keep `Text` where the frame is not upscaled much, or where the label is meant
to look smooth.

### Baking an atlas from a face you already use

Swapping in a bitmap face means generating one, and three things decide
whether it comes out looking like the original:

- **Threshold the coverage.** Hard edges are the whole point, so every pixel
  has to end up fully on or fully off. Hardening only the ALPHA is not enough:
  an outlined glyph keeps a soft stroke-to-fill blend INSIDE the silhouette,
  which still reads as blur once magnified. Pick the colours from a mask.
- **Bake each size at that size, and draw it at a ratio of 1.** `size` on
  `BitmapText` is a ratio of the authored size, and a bitmap face has the sizes
  it was baked at. Doubling a smaller atlas halves the detail; a ratio below 1
  drops whole stems; a fractional ratio resamples hard pixels unevenly. One
  atlas per step of the type scale.
- **Grow the outline outward, but carve it INWARD around a counter.** This is
  the one that costs the most time. A stroke drawn by the canvas is centred on
  the contour, so around an enclosed hole it eats into the letter and the hole
  keeps its size. Dilating a mask outward instead grows black INTO the hole
  from every side, which closes anything under about 3px: the letter loses its
  counter and reads as a blob. Take the rim from the fill side and the hole
  survives at every size. Neither leaving holes unrimmed nor closing the small
  ones is a substitute — both were tried and both look wrong.

Two traps in the generator itself:

- A face whose glyphs overshoot the `textBaseline` origin is clipped by a tight
  cell, and the symptom is an outline that goes missing along one edge of some
  glyphs. Pad the cell by a fraction of the size, and assert that no glyph's
  ink reaches its border.
- The threshold decides the TOPOLOGY, not just the weight. A notch or a narrow
  gap in a letterform closes over at a full threshold and becomes an isolated
  hole, which then bakes as a black blob sitting on the glyph. Thinner, the
  same feature stays joined to the background and reads as the face intends.
  So a small size may want a thinner fill than a large one, and the way to see
  it is to magnify one glyph, not a whole line.

## A pixel-art setup

```js
const app = new Application(480, 270, {
	scale: "auto",
	scaleMethod: "fit",
	scaleRounding: "integer",   // whole device pixels, letterbox the rest
	antiAlias: false,           // nearest textures, hard-edged upscale
	// subPixel: false is already the default
});
```

## A smooth 3D setup

```js
const app = new Application(1024, 576, {
	scale: "auto",
	scaleMethod: "fit",
	antiAlias: true,            // MSAA and a filtered upscale
	textureFilter: "nearest",   // but keep blocky textures if the art is blocky
});
```

## Symptoms

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| pixel art is blurry or shimmers | the frame is upscaled by a fractional factor; set `scaleRounding: "integer"` |
| crisp in one browser, soft in another | the same fractional factor, which engines distribute differently under `pixelated` |
| the canvas is cropped or overflows its box | automatic scaling measured the wrong element; name it with `scaleTarget` |
| the canvas grows on every resize | the measured ancestor is auto-sized around the canvas itself |
| things shimmer as they move | fractional positions; check `subPixel`, and that the scale factor is whole |
| scrolling stutters while the frame rate reads 60 | a frame now and then runs no update and the next two; set `syncToDisplay: true` |
| moving rendered art jumps by whole pixels with `subPixel: true` | nearest sampling still draws it on one pixel; add `textureFilter: "linear"` |
| the whole game looks blurry with `antiAlias: true` | it also smooths the canvas as it is scaled up; use `textureFilter: "linear"` instead |
| a minimap or a zoomed-out view shimmers as it moves | linear sampling blends 4 texels where a pixel covers many; use `textureFilter: "linear-mipmap"` |
| faint lines along sprites drawn small, from the next frame of the atlas | under `"linear-mipmap"` the built-in sprite shaders keep to the frame, but not a `ShaderEffect`'s own sample, and the smallest levels still mix a frame not on a power-of-two grid with its neighbour: pad the atlas |
| a still scene looks a little soft with linear sampling | the camera rests between two pixels; follow a target rounded to whole pixels |
| 3D model edges are jagged | `antiAlias: false` also disables MSAA; turn it on and use `textureFilter` for textures |
| textures are smoothed when they should be blocky | `antiAlias: true` makes the default texture filter linear; set `textureFilter: "nearest"` |
| `scaleRounding: "integer"` changes nothing | it applies to `scaleMethod: "fit"` only; the others resize the renderer |
| text is soft but sprites are crisp | the glyphs were anti-aliased when `Text` baked them; use `BitmapText` (see below) |
| the game shows more world on a bigger window | that is `fill-*` or `flex-*` doing their job; use `"fit"` to keep a fixed frame |
| a numeric `scale` (say `2`) is ignored | a `scaleMethod` other than `"manual"` turns automatic scaling on, which ignores the number |
skills.bodyMd:
# Display and scaling

Seven settings decide how a game looks on screen, and they are easy to get
individually right and collectively wrong. This is what each one actually
does, and which one to reach for.

## The four jobs

A pixel travels from your source art to a physical pixel through four
separate decisions. Knowing which setting owns which is most of the work.

| job | setting | what it decides |
|---|---|---|
| how big the frame is drawn | `width`/`height` on `Application` | the design resolution everything is authored against |
| how it uses the space | `scale`, `scaleMethod`, `scaleTarget` | fit, fill, stretch, and what it measures to decide |
| may the factor be fractional | `scaleRounding` | whole device pixels per source pixel, or any factor |
| how a texture is sampled | `antiAlias`, `textureFilter` | nearest or linear, and the CSS upscale filter |

`subPixel` is a fifth, orthogonal to all of them: it decides whether a
renderable may sit on a fractional position WITHIN the frame. `syncToDisplay`
is about the frames in a row rather than one frame: whether motion advances
by the same amount on each.

## Design resolution

```js
const app = new Application(480, 270, { scale: "auto" });
```

The game is drawn at 480x270 whatever the window is, and the canvas is scaled
to the container. Everything in world coordinates is in those units. This is
the usual arrangement: author once, scale to whatever you are given.

## `scale` and `scaleMethod`

`scale: "auto"` turns on automatic scaling, and so does naming any
`scaleMethod` other than `"manual"`, even with no `scale` given:
`{ scaleMethod: "flex" }` alone scales to its container. A number is a fixed
multiplier, used only while `scaleMethod` is `"manual"` (the default); with
automatic scaling on, the number is ignored.

`scaleMethod` decides how the available space is used:

- **`"fit"`** keeps the design resolution and the aspect ratio, scaling to the
  largest factor that fits. Leftover space becomes margin. This is the one to
  use when the game is authored for a fixed frame.
- **`"fill-min"` / `"fill-max"`** keep the aspect ratio but RESIZE the
  renderer, so the design resolution changes with the window and the game sees
  more or less of the world.
- **`"flex"`, `"flex-width"`, `"flex-height"`** resize the renderer on one or
  both axes.
- **`"stretch"`** scales each axis independently, so the aspect ratio is not
  preserved and circles become ovals.
- **`"manual"`**, the default, does nothing automatic with a numeric `scale`.
  With `scale: "auto"` it scales as `"fit"` does.

The distinction that matters: **`fit` scales a fixed frame; everything else
changes how much of the world is visible.** A game whose layout assumes a
known frame wants `fit`.

## `scaleTarget`: what gets measured

Automatic scaling measures **the parent of the element the canvas is mounted
in**, not the element itself. If that grandparent is not the box you meant,
the canvas is sized wrongly, and the failure is quiet.

The case that bites: a canvas container that is `position: fixed` or
`absolute` contributes no height to its parent, so the parent measures only
whatever else is in it. If that parent is `<body>`, the engine falls back to
the window size and the canvas ends up larger than the box it lives in,
cropped by whatever sits above it.

```js
new Application(1024, 576, {
	parent: "screen",
	scale: "auto",
	// measure THIS, rather than guessing from the DOM shape
	scaleTarget: document.getElementById("stage"),
});
```

Either name the element with `scaleTarget`, or give the canvas container a
parent whose box is the area you want filled. If the canvas is cropped or
overflows on resize, this is the first thing to check.

## `scaleRounding`: whole device pixels

```js
new Application(480, 270, {
	scale: "auto",
	scaleMethod: "fit",
	scaleRounding: "integer",   // default "fractional"
});
```

`"fractional"` fills the container exactly, at whatever factor that takes. A
480 wide design in a 1280 wide container is scaled by 2.667, so some source
pixels cover three screen pixels and some cover two. Pixel art shows this as
uneven glyph stems and shimmering edges, and browsers resolve the unevenness
differently, so the same scene can look crisp in one and soft in another.

`"integer"` rounds the factor DOWN so every source pixel covers the same whole
number of device pixels, and letterboxes with the space left over. That trade,
crisp pixels for black bars, is the whole decision.

### What it costs

More than "some letterboxing", and the size of it is decided by
`devicePixelRatio` as much as by the window. A higher ratio has more device
pixels to round among, so it lands closer to the factor it wanted. For a
480x270 design, which is exactly a quarter of 1920x1080:

| container | ratio | fit | integer | presented | area lost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1920x1080 | 1 or 2 | 4.000 | 4 / 8 | 1920x1080 | none |
| 1440x810 | 1 | 3.000 | 3 | 1440x810 | none |
| 960x540 | 1 | 2.000 | 2 | 960x540 | none |
| 1280x720 | 2 | 2.667 | 5 | 1200x675 | 12% |
| 2560x1440 | 2 | 5.333 | 10 | 2400x1350 | 12% |
| 1280x720 | 1 | 2.667 | 2 | 960x540 | **44%** |
| 1366x768 | 1 | 2.844 | 2 | 960x540 | **51%** |

So the decision is mostly made when the design resolution is chosen, not when
this setting is. One that divides the sizes you expect costs nothing; one that
does not can give up half the screen on a 1x display, and 1366x768 laptops are
not rare. A game that must fill the window on any machine should stay
fractional and accept the uneven pixels.

Two things to know:

- It applies to **`scaleMethod: "fit"` only.** Every other method resizes the
  renderer to the container, so the design resolution moves and there is no
  fixed factor to round.
- The rounding happens in **device** pixels. `devicePixelRatio` multiplies the
  CSS size on the way to real pixels, so rounding the CSS factor would let the
  fraction straight back in: a factor of 2 at a ratio of 1.25 is 2.5 device
  pixels per source pixel.

## `antiAlias` does three things

This is the setting most likely to surprise, because it is not one switch:

1. the texture filter, but only while `textureFilter` is `"auto"` (the
   default), which TRACKS it: linear when on, nearest when off. Setting
   `textureFilter` explicitly decouples the two
2. `imageSmoothingEnabled` on the 2D context
3. the canvas CSS `image-rendering`: `pixelated` when off, `auto` when on

So `antiAlias: false` gives hard-edged textures AND a hard-edged upscale of
the whole frame. That is usually what a pixel-art game wants, and usually NOT
what a smooth 3D scene wants, because it also disables MSAA.

`textureFilter: "nearest" | "linear"` separates the texture half, so a scene
can have smooth model edges and nearest-sampled sprites. The presentation half
is not separable: there is no way to get MSAA silhouettes and a hard-edged
upscale at the same time.

## Drawn small: `textureFilter: "linear-mipmap"`

A sprite drawn much smaller than its texture (a zoomed-out camera, a minimap,
a scaled-down sprite) shimmers as it moves, even with linear sampling: each
screen pixel covers many texels and linear sampling blends only four of them.
`"linear-mipmap"` samples the texture's mipmaps, smaller copies averaged in
advance, wherever something is drawn below its size:

```js
const app = new Application(1280, 720, { textureFilter: "linear-mipmap" });
```

At its size or larger a texture draws as it does under `"linear"`, so a game
whose main view is at its size and whose minimap is zoomed out gets a smooth
minimap and an unchanged view. It covers sprites, text and tile layers, not a
video nor a texture the engine renders into, and a `nearest` texture keeps to
its full size. GPU backends only; on WebGPU each texture it applies to takes
about a third more memory.

A small mipmap level's texels span many of the art's pixels, so a sample near
the edge of a frame would reach into the next frame of the atlas. Under
`"linear-mipmap"` every sprite and tile keeps its samples half a texel of the
level it reads inside its own frame, so the next frame no longer streaks along
its edges. Two limits:

- a level's texel is an average of a square of the art, 2, 4, 8 pixels a side
  and so on. Where a frame's edge falls inside such a square, its outermost
  texel already holds some of the neighbour: drawn very small, a frame of an
  atlas packed edge to edge can show a faint line of it. Frames on a grid of
  a power of two (a 32 or 64 px sheet) are free of it, and a padding of a few
  pixels between frames removes it elsewhere;
- a sprite drawn through a `ShaderEffect` samples the texture in the effect's
  own program, which is not kept to the frame.

A repeating pattern is left to wrap.

## `subPixel` is about position, not scale

`subPixel: false` (the default) draws everything on whole pixels. The snap
happens **once, where a draw lands**, the same on every renderer: each edge of
a sprite, a shape or a clip is rounded to the nearest pixel after every
translation and scale it is drawn under. So:

- nested containers add their positions up exactly first (10.6 then -6.5
  lands on 4, the pixel 4.1 is in);
- a flipped sprite covers the pixels it covers unflipped;
- a sprite and a `fillRect` at the same position cover the same pixels, and a
  shape has no half-grey edge on the Canvas renderer;
- a position floating point error leaves a hair short of a pixel, such as a
  body resting on the floor at `223.99999999999997` after a collision
  push-out, draws on that pixel (224), so it does not shake every other frame.

The camera's view starts on a whole pixel too, in world units (zoomed 2x, it
moves in 2 px steps), and culling and the pointer use that same position:
things standing still stay still against each other while the view scrolls,
and a click lands on what is drawn under it. A rotated draw, and anything a
`Camera3d` draws, is left where it is.

It does nothing about how the frame reaches the screen. A game that carefully
snaps positions and is then scaled by 2.667 has thrown that work away at the
last step, which is the contradiction `scaleRounding: "integer"` exists to
resolve.

`subPixel: true` alone does not make motion smooth: with nearest sampling a
sprite between two pixels is still drawn on one of them, so a scene moving
4.5 pixels a frame jumps by 4 and 5 in turn. Rendered art (not pixel art)
moves smoothly with `textureFilter: "linear"` as well, which blends it across
the two, while the upscale stays crisp (`antiAlias: true` would also smooth the
whole canvas as it is scaled up, which is what makes it look blurry). A still
scene is only sharp when the camera rests on a whole pixel, so give it a
target on whole pixels:

```js
const app = new Application(1280, 720, {
	scale: "auto",
	subPixel: true,
	textureFilter: "linear",
	syncToDisplay: true,
});
// the camera follows a point on whole pixels, kept on the hero: it glides
// between pixels while following, and comes to rest on one
const focus = new Vector2d();
app.viewport.follow(focus, app.viewport.AXIS.BOTH, 0.12);

// in the hero's update(dt)
focus.set(Math.round(this.pos.x), Math.round(this.pos.y));
```

## `syncToDisplay` is about steady motion

The game updates in fixed steps, 60 a second by default, as many as the time
since the last frame holds. Browsers report that time with up to a millisecond
of jitter, so on a 60 Hz display a frame now and then gets no update and the
next one gets two: the world holds still for a frame, then moves twice as far.
Scrolling, and anything else moving steadily, stutters while the frame rate
reads a solid 60.

```js
const app = new Application(1280, 720, { scale: "auto", syncToDisplay: true });
```

With it on, frame times are counted in whole display frames and what is
rounded off is carried to the next frame: one update every frame at 60 Hz, one
every other frame at 120 Hz, and the game keeps its speed. A display within 2%
of `timer.maxfps` (60 by default), or of 2, 3 or 4 times it, or a half, a third
or a quarter of it, is counted at exactly that rate, so a 59.94 Hz screen runs
the game 0.1% slower than the wall clock; leave it off when the updates must
keep to the wall clock exactly. The display's rate is learned as the game runs,
and again when it changes (the window moved to another screen). At a refresh
that is no multiple of the update rate (144 Hz, 165 Hz) the steps cannot fall
evenly however the time is counted.

It is off by default. It sets `timer.syncToDisplay` when the application is
initialized, which a game can also switch at any time.

## Soft text next to crisp sprites

If everything is crisp EXCEPT the text, the scale factor is not the cause: a
fractional factor softens the whole frame equally. The text is different
because of how it is made.

`Text` draws through the browser's `fillText`, which anti-aliases glyph edges
into partial-alpha pixels. Measured on one label at 16px: **171 distinct
partial alpha levels**. Nothing in the canvas API turns that off. `antiAlias`
and the `imageSmoothingEnabled` that `CanvasRenderTarget` sets govern IMAGE
drawing, not glyph rasterisation.

So the label arrives already soft, and the upscale then magnifies each grey
edge pixel into a grey block, sitting beside sprites that were hard-edged to
begin with and stay hard-edged under nearest sampling.

It also explains the same scene looking crisp in one browser and soft in
another at identical size and settings: engines use different font
rasterisers, with different hinting and anti-aliasing, so they bake DIFFERENT
textures from the same font at the same size.

**Use `BitmapText` for a game that upscales.** A pixel-font atlas is
hard-edged source art like every other texture, so it survives magnification
the way the sprites do. Raising the design resolution only shrinks the
magnification of anti-aliasing that is still there, so it softens the symptom
rather than removing it, and `scaleRounding` does nothing for this at all.

Keep `Text` where the frame is not upscaled much, or where the label is meant
to look smooth.

### Baking an atlas from a face you already use

Swapping in a bitmap face means generating one, and three things decide
whether it comes out looking like the original:

- **Threshold the coverage.** Hard edges are the whole point, so every pixel
  has to end up fully on or fully off. Hardening only the ALPHA is not enough:
  an outlined glyph keeps a soft stroke-to-fill blend INSIDE the silhouette,
  which still reads as blur once magnified. Pick the colours from a mask.
- **Bake each size at that size, and draw it at a ratio of 1.** `size` on
  `BitmapText` is a ratio of the authored size, and a bitmap face has the sizes
  it was baked at. Doubling a smaller atlas halves the detail; a ratio below 1
  drops whole stems; a fractional ratio resamples hard pixels unevenly. One
  atlas per step of the type scale.
- **Grow the outline outward, but carve it INWARD around a counter.** This is
  the one that costs the most time. A stroke drawn by the canvas is centred on
  the contour, so around an enclosed hole it eats into the letter and the hole
  keeps its size. Dilating a mask outward instead grows black INTO the hole
  from every side, which closes anything under about 3px: the letter loses its
  counter and reads as a blob. Take the rim from the fill side and the hole
  survives at every size. Neither leaving holes unrimmed nor closing the small
  ones is a substitute — both were tried and both look wrong.

Two traps in the generator itself:

- A face whose glyphs overshoot the `textBaseline` origin is clipped by a tight
  cell, and the symptom is an outline that goes missing along one edge of some
  glyphs. Pad the cell by a fraction of the size, and assert that no glyph's
  ink reaches its border.
- The threshold decides the TOPOLOGY, not just the weight. A notch or a narrow
  gap in a letterform closes over at a full threshold and becomes an isolated
  hole, which then bakes as a black blob sitting on the glyph. Thinner, the
  same feature stays joined to the background and reads as the face intends.
  So a small size may want a thinner fill than a large one, and the way to see
  it is to magnify one glyph, not a whole line.

## A pixel-art setup

```js
const app = new Application(480, 270, {
	scale: "auto",
	scaleMethod: "fit",
	scaleRounding: "integer",   // whole device pixels, letterbox the rest
	antiAlias: false,           // nearest textures, hard-edged upscale
	// subPixel: false is already the default
});
```

## A smooth 3D setup

```js
const app = new Application(1024, 576, {
	scale: "auto",
	scaleMethod: "fit",
	antiAlias: true,            // MSAA and a filtered upscale
	textureFilter: "nearest",   // but keep blocky textures if the art is blocky
});
```

## Symptoms

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| pixel art is blurry or shimmers | the frame is upscaled by a fractional factor; set `scaleRounding: "integer"` |
| crisp in one browser, soft in another | the same fractional factor, which engines distribute differently under `pixelated` |
| the canvas is cropped or overflows its box | automatic scaling measured the wrong element; name it with `scaleTarget` |
| the canvas grows on every resize | the measured ancestor is auto-sized around the canvas itself |
| things shimmer as they move | fractional positions; check `subPixel`, and that the scale factor is whole |
| scrolling stutters while the frame rate reads 60 | a frame now and then runs no update and the next two; set `syncToDisplay: true` |
| moving rendered art jumps by whole pixels with `subPixel: true` | nearest sampling still draws it on one pixel; add `textureFilter: "linear"` |
| the whole game looks blurry with `antiAlias: true` | it also smooths the canvas as it is scaled up; use `textureFilter: "linear"` instead |
| a minimap or a zoomed-out view shimmers as it moves | linear sampling blends 4 texels where a pixel covers many; use `textureFilter: "linear-mipmap"` |
| faint lines along sprites drawn small, from the next frame of the atlas | under `"linear-mipmap"` the built-in sprite shaders keep to the frame, but not a `ShaderEffect`'s own sample, and the smallest levels still mix a frame not on a power-of-two grid with its neighbour: pad the atlas |
| a still scene looks a little soft with linear sampling | the camera rests between two pixels; follow a target rounded to whole pixels |
| 3D model edges are jagged | `antiAlias: false` also disables MSAA; turn it on and use `textureFilter` for textures |
| textures are smoothed when they should be blocky | `antiAlias: true` makes the default texture filter linear; set `textureFilter: "nearest"` |
| `scaleRounding: "integer"` changes nothing | it applies to `scaleMethod: "fit"` only; the others resize the renderer |
| text is soft but sprites are crisp | the glyphs were anti-aliased when `Text` baked them; use `BitmapText` (see below) |
| the game shows more world on a bigger window | that is `fill-*` or `flex-*` doing their job; use `"fit"` to keep a fixed frame |
| a numeric `scale` (say `2`) is ignored | a `scaleMethod` other than `"manual"` turns automatic scaling on, which ignores the number |

# Post effects and custom shaders

> melonJS ships a catalogue of post effects and a dual-language shader system.
> The recurring trap is that every shader path needs a GPU backend and
> **degrades to nothing** on Canvas rather than erroring. Blend modes are the
> exception — those work on all three renderers.

## Applying an effect

Effects attach to a renderable **or** to a camera (for full-screen grading):

```js
import { VignetteEffect, GlowEffect } from "melonjs";

sprite.addPostEffect(new GlowEffect(app.renderer));
app.viewport.addPostEffect(new VignetteEffect(app.renderer));
```

`renderable.shader = …` is **deprecated since 19.2.0**, and its setter destroys
whatever it replaces. Use `addPostEffect` / `getPostEffect` / `removePostEffect`.

### A camera effect covers the HUD too

A camera's post-effect brackets the **entire** world draw — floating children
included. So the obvious way to write a full-screen pass also washes over every
HUD label in that world, which is rarely what you want.

To land a pass *after* the world but *before* the HUD, host the effect on a
screen-filling floating renderable ordered below the HUD's z instead:

```js
const quad = new Sprite(0, 0, { image: anyImage });
quad.anchorPoint.set(0, 0);
quad.scale(viewW / anyImage.width, viewH / anyImage.height);
quad.floating = true;                 // its own uv is now screen space
quad.blendMode = "additive";
quad.addPostEffect(myEffect);
world.addChild(quad, HUD_Z - 10);     // 2D: below the labels. See the note.
```

Two things follow from the quad filling the frame: its own `uv` is screen space
(so a pass like this needs none of the `screen_uv` / `screen_texture` builtins),
and the incoming `color` is the quad's own texture, which a body that paints
from scratch can ignore entirely.

**Depth here is easy to get backwards, and the rule FLIPS between the two sort
modes.** Under the default `sortOn = "z"` a higher z draws later, i.e. on top,
so `HUD_Z - 10` puts the pass under the labels as written above. Under
`sortOn = "depth"`, which every `Camera3d` scene sets, a floating child's sort
key is `pos.z * pos.z` and the walk paints far to near, so the SMALLER
magnitude is nearer and draws on top — `HUD_Z - 10` there puts the pass OVER
the labels, the opposite of the comment.

So in a 3D scene give the overlay a larger magnitude than the HUD, and give
the HUD a small one (`melonjs-3d` and `melonjs-ui-and-text` both say a HUD
wants a small depth, not the huge z that would put it on top in 2D).

Either way, verify it rather than reasoning about it: return a flat colour from
the body for one frame and see what it tints.

## A renderable that draws with PRIMITIVES has to ask to be captured

One effect is applied the cheap way: the renderable is drawn with the effect's
own program instead of being captured offscreen and post-processed, which costs
no render target. That is equivalent only when everything the renderable draws
is a textured quad. `fillRect`, `strokeRect` and `renderer.fill(shape)` go
through a batcher that never reads that shader, so **one** effect on such a
renderable would silently do nothing, while **two** would work, because a chain
always captures.

So a renderable of your own that draws with primitives says so:

```js
class Bar extends Renderable {
    constructor(x, y, w, h) {
        super(x, y, w, h);
        this.postEffectNeedsCapture = true;   // ← or one effect is a no-op
    }
    draw(renderer) {
        renderer.fillRect(this.pos.x, this.pos.y, this.width, this.height);
    }
}
```

`ProgressBar`, `UIPanel` and `Trail` set it for you, and a sprite needs
nothing: the flag defaults to `false` and only ever changes the single-effect
case.

## Toggle with `enabled`, do not remove

**`removePostEffect()` destroys the effect** — it calls `effect.destroy()` and
frees GPU resources, so the instance cannot be re-added. Same for
`clearPostEffects()` and for reassigning the deprecated `.shader`.

```js
// ✗ destroys it; re-adding later fails or forces a recompile
sprite.removePostEffect(effect);

// ✓
effect.enabled = false;
```

An effect with `effect.shared === true` opts out of auto-destroy because it is
reused across renderables.

## Built-in effects

Twenty-five presets, every one constructed as `new XEffect(renderer, options)`
and every one shipping both a GLSL and a WGSL body, so they all run on either
GPU backend: `VignetteEffect`, `ScanlineEffect` (optional CRT curvature),
`BloomEffect`, `GlowEffect`, `BlurEffect`, `PixelateEffect`,
`ChromaticAberrationEffect`, `DropShadowEffect`, `FlashEffect`,
`OutlineEffect`, `ColorMatrixEffect`, `DesaturateEffect`, `DissolveEffect`,
`TintPulseEffect`, `WaveEffect`, `SwayEffect`, `InvertEffect`, `SepiaEffect`,
`HologramEffect`, `ShineEffect`, `RadialGradientEffect`, `SquishEffect`,
`ToneMappingEffect`, `GradientMapEffect`, `DitherEffect`.

Five of them are a `ColorMatrixEffect` with a matrix set for you, and share
its one shader: `SepiaEffect`, `DesaturateEffect`, `InvertEffect`,
`FlashEffect` and `TintPulseEffect` (the last two since 20.17). Drive them
through their own setters (`setIntensity`, `setColor`, `setTime`).

**Colors take an alpha.** Every color option and `setColor` takes `[r, g, b]`
or `[r, g, b, a]`, each 0.0 to 1.0, and the alpha is the color's own opacity: a
half-transparent outline, a glow at half strength, a flash that only half
covers. `[r, g, b]` is opaque, as it always was. Any other length throws.
`RadialGradientEffect` takes a `Color` instead, and its alpha scales the spot.

```js
sprite.addPostEffect(new OutlineEffect(app.renderer, { color: [1, 1, 1, 0.5] }));
```

**On a sprite cut from an atlas or a tileset, the effects that read around a
pixel keep to the sprite's own frame.** `GlowEffect`, `OutlineEffect`,
`BlurEffect`, `DropShadowEffect`, `ChromaticAberrationEffect`, `WaveEffect`,
`SwayEffect`, `PixelateEffect`, `DitherEffect` and `BloomEffect` read the neighbouring frames
as transparent, as if the sprite were drawn on its own, so they never show
along its edges and the atlas needs no padding for them. Past the texture's own
edge (a standalone image, or the outside of an atlas) nothing changes.

**The effects that place a pattern place it on the renderable they draw.**
`SwayEffect`'s planted row, `WaveEffect`'s `anchor`, the centre of
`VignetteEffect`, `RadialGradientEffect` and `ScanlineEffect`'s curvature all
land on the sprite itself: cut from an atlas, flipped, rotated, or with other
effects after it, the pattern sits where it sits on a sprite with a texture of
its own and that one effect. What is measured in the texture stays measured in
it: `ShineEffect`'s sweep, bands and width, `WaveEffect`'s amplitude and
frequency, `DissolveEffect`'s grain, the lines of `HologramEffect` and
`ScanlineEffect` (on an atlas sprite, fractions of the atlas, so a single shine
crosses an atlas sprite only part of the time). With other effects after them
they all stay on the sprite. `SwayEffect` measures everything across the
sprite.

nothing to pass.** Each of those effects takes the size of what it draws: the
sprite's whole texture (the atlas image, not the frame), the screen for a
camera's effect, a mesh's texture. With other effects after it, it still
measures in the sprite's own pixels, at any scale and under a camera's zoom
(on a container, in the container's own), so adding a second effect never
changes how wide the first comes out. Do not pass `textureSize` to get this: a
`textureSize` (or `setTextureSize()`) fixes the size instead, for a width
meant in some other texture's pixels.

```js
// 2 pixels of the sprite's art, whatever the size of its atlas, its scale,
// the camera's zoom, or the effects after it
sprite.addPostEffect(new OutlineEffect(app.renderer, { width: 2 }));
sprite.addPostEffect(new GlowEffect(app.renderer, { width: 6 }));
```

reads that, at the game's texture filter, as a sprite reads its own texture:
under `"nearest"` (or `antiAlias` off) a width that lands between two screen
pixels, such as 2 pixels of a sprite drawn at 0.3, stays crisp, and under
`"linear"` it blends, on WebGL and WebGPU alike. The result lands inside the
clip the sprite is drawn under, a minimap camera's view or a clipping
container, as with one effect.

top sways most and everything from its `anchor` row down stays put, so a tree's
trunk or a reed's root stays planted. It suits anything planted at its bottom;
something hanging from its top, like a banner, needs its own shader. It is a
`WaveEffect`, which takes the same `anchor`, so it adds no shader. Drive it with
`setTime(seconds)` every frame, like any time-based effect; it wraps the phase
itself, so a raw clock never costs precision on a phone's medium-precision
floats.

```js
const sway = new SwayEffect(app.renderer, { strength: 0.02, anchor: 0.9 });

// each frame
sway.setTime(timer.getTime() / 1000);
```

Its strength (a fraction of the sprite's width), its `anchor` and how it bends
are all measured across the sprite, so a sprite cut from an atlas sways exactly
like the same art with a texture of its own. `WaveEffect`'s `anchor` is a row of
the sprite too, but its amplitude and frequency are measured across the texture,
so on an atlas sprite they are fractions of the atlas.

pixels take the first color of a list of two to eight, the brightest the last,
and the rest the colors in between. The sprite keeps its shading and loses its
own hues: one enemy drawn in a palette per team, a duotone, a night scene.
With `smooth: false` each color takes a band of brightness of its own, which is
a palette swap for art drawn in a few flat shades.

```js
// the same sprite as a second team, in four flat reds
enemy.addPostEffect(new GradientMapEffect(app.renderer, {
    colors: [[0.2, 0, 0.05], [0.55, 0.05, 0.1], [0.9, 0.25, 0.2], [1, 0.8, 0.7]],
    smooth: false,
}));
```

It reads brightness and nothing else, so two colors as bright as each other
come out the same: a red and a green of equal brightness cannot be told apart
afterwards. To swap particular colors for particular others, the art has to
separate them by brightness first. A sprite's black outline takes the first
color, like any other dark pixel; give that color an alpha of 0 to drop it.
`setIntensity()` fades between the sprite's own colors and the list.

`DitherEffect` draws in a few colors with an ordered dither between them, the
pattern that made a handful of colors read as many on early hardware. It is
made for a **whole scene, on the camera**: the colors are `levels` of each
channel, so everything keeps its own hue, in pixels `size` screen pixels wide.

```js
// a lit scene in six levels a channel, in pixels three screen pixels wide
app.viewport.addPostEffect(new DitherEffect(app.renderer, { levels: 6, size: 3 }));
```

Only a color that falls **between two levels** is patterned: the turn of a lit
surface from light to dark, the soft edge of a shadow, a gradient. A flat color
that is itself a level is left alone. So a flat sky or ground that comes out
speckled all over is a color between two levels: give it one made of levels (at
6 levels, channels that are fifths of 255: 0, 51, 102, 153, 204, 255), and
remember that a **lit** surface's color is its tint times the light, which is
rarely a level; leave a flat ground unlit to keep it clean.

A `palette` of two to sixteen colors of your own takes the place of the
levels: each pixel takes one of the two nearest, the nearer more often, and a
color that is in the palette stays flat. Everything then takes the palette's
hues, the scene's own are gone:

```js
// the whole scene in four greens
app.viewport.addPostEffect(new DitherEffect(app.renderer, {
    palette: [[0.06, 0.22, 0.06], [0.19, 0.38, 0.19], [0.55, 0.67, 0.06], [0.61, 0.74, 0.06]],
    size: 2,
}));
```

`size` is the width of a drawn pixel **in pixels of the texture it draws**, as
`PixelateEffect`'s is: the screen's for a camera's effect, the art's for a
sprite's. On a sprite drawn smaller than its art, a `size` of 1 makes a pattern
finer than the screen can show, which reads as noise: for art drawn at a
quarter of its size, start at 8. `strength: 0` drops the pattern and leaves
flat bands (a posterize). On the camera it covers the HUD too, like any
camera effect (see above).

`RadialGradientEffect` is a procedural soft spot: solid at the centre of the
renderable it draws, fading linearly to transparent at the edge, and elliptical
for free on a non-square one. It is the one to reach for instead of baking a
disc into a canvas, for a pickup highlight, a trigger marker or a damage flash,
on a standalone image, `Renderer.getWhitePixel()` or a sprite cut from an atlas
alike.

`SquishEffect` bulges a sprite's middle out (`setBulge(0.3)`) or pinches it in
(`setBulge(-0.3)`), its top and bottom rows staying put. Bulging out widens the
sprite past its own frame, and the effect draws on a wider quad to make room,
so the art needs no transparent margin. On its own it is a jelly wobble; paired
with a change of height it is **squash and stretch that keeps the volume**:
scale the sprite to `scaleY` of its height about its feet and set the bulge to
`1 - scaleY`, so a stretched sprite pinches in and a squashed one bulges out.
Ease `scaleY` back to 1 with a short `Tween.Easing.Back.Out`; an elastic ease
keeps it trembling long after the landing.

```js
const squish = new SquishEffect(app.renderer);
player.addPostEffect(squish);
// every frame, from the player's update()
const feet = player.height * (1 - player.anchorPoint.y);
player.currentTransform
    .identity()
    .translate(0, feet)
    .scale(1, scaleY)
    .translate(0, -feet);
squish.setBulge(1 - scaleY);
```

Apply that from the sprite's own `update()`, not from a tween's `onUpdate`. A
physics adapter that mirrors a body's angle (matter, planck and Rapier do, and so does
the built-in once a body has an angle or angular velocity) rewrites
`currentTransform` on every step, before the renderables update, so a scale set
anywhere else is gone by the time the sprite is drawn. Let the tween animate a
plain `{ scaleY }` object and read it in `update()`.

It is made for a sprite carrying it as its only effect: chained with another,
or on the camera, the frame it measures against is the whole capture, so it
squishes the whole frame. The bulge is outside the sprite's bounds, so culling
and pointer events ignore it.

**`BloomEffect` and `GlowEffect` are not the same thing**, and reaching for the
wrong one is the usual disappointment here. `GlowEffect` draws a halo OUTSIDE a
sprite's silhouette: its body returns the colour untouched wherever alpha is
already non-zero, so on an opaque frame it returns early on every fragment and
a camera-wide glow does nothing at all. `BloomEffect` is the screen bloom —
bright pixels bleed into their neighbours — and it is the one to put on the
camera:

```js
app.viewport.addPostEffect(new BloomEffect(app.renderer));
// only the brightest highlights, with a wider halo
app.viewport.addPostEffect(

);
```

Its `radius` is in texels of what it filters, the screen on a camera, and it
follows a resize by itself.

parts; the tone map is what stops the sum of the two clipping flat at white,
which is the difference between an effect that reads as light and one that
reads as a white sticker. `exposure` lifts the image into the curve, and the
curve (`aces`, `reinhard` or `exponential`) is baked at construction:

```js
app.viewport.addPostEffect(new BloomEffect(app.renderer));
app.viewport.addPostEffect(
    new ToneMappingEffect(app.renderer, { exposure: 1.6 }),
);
```

everywhere, so the frame reaching it is already clamped and `exposure` past 1
is what gives the curve range to compress.

become half-float, so the chain carries values above 1 instead of clamping at
every write, and the bloom threshold starts discriminating genuinely
over-bright pixels rather than merely bright ones. Off by default: it costs
GPU memory on the camera's two render targets and depends on the driver.

On its own it is **not HDR output**: the frame is still presented in SDR, so
anything above 1 clamps on the final blit. What it buys is that nothing clamped
BEFORE then. Removing that last clamp is a second, separate opt-in —
`hdrOutput`, below — and it is WebGPU-only.

```js
const app = new Application(1024, 576, { hdr: true, … });
// …and check what you actually got, since a driver can refuse it
if (app.renderer.supportsHDR) { /* the chain now carries values above 1 */ }
```

bloom threshold at 1 make sense only where values above 1 exist; applied to a
chain that clamps, the same numbers tone map an already display-referred frame
and switch the bloom off, which reads as a dark, flat picture rather than as a
missing feature. Where there is no headroom, squeeze each emitter into range in
its own shader instead and put the bloom threshold back under 1.

**Nothing is added to your chain.** `hdr` is additive: the same frame, plus
additive content that no longer saturates per write and a threshold that means
something. Anything still above 1 at the end clamps on the blit, as it always
did.

A tone map is therefore a decision, not a consequence, and it is a bigger one
than it looks. Every curve maps 1 to less than 1, so a 2D look built ON the
clamp — clipped white specular, saturated neon — goes matte the moment you add
one, at any exposure. Add one when your art is authored in linear light and you
want the highlights rolled off; skip it when the clipping IS the look.

It applies to the CAMERA chain only. A sprite's chain keeps 8-bit targets on
purpose: its final blit composites with `ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, and additive
blending accumulates alpha past 1 in a float target, so that factor would go
negative and subtract the backdrop.

`hdr: true` on its own changes nothing visible. It removes a ceiling; something
still has to reach for it. No single draw exceeds 1 on its own, so a game that
turns the setting on and changes nothing else renders very nearly the frame it
did before and looks like the feature is broken. The exception is worth knowing
because it is free: additive content that already overlapped was being clipped
at every write, and stops being.

What produces over-bright pixels:

```js
// a built-in colour matrix, scaled past 1 — no custom shader needed
sprite.addPostEffect(new ColorMatrixEffect(app.renderer).brightness(4));

// in 3D, both of these were always unbounded; the 8-bit target was the only
// thing destroying the range. `emissive` is a 3-component Float32Array, set
// from the mesh settings or replaced wholesale — it is not a Color
const mesh = new Mesh(x, y, { emissive: [2.5, 1.8, 0.4], /* … */ });
light.intensity = 3;

// and additive blending, which accumulates past 1 once the target can hold it
sprite.blendMode = "additive";
```

**One effect, not two.** A renderable carrying exactly ONE post effect takes
the renderer's `customShader` fast path: no offscreen target, and it draws
straight into the camera's half-float target with its range intact. A chain of
two or more is routed through a pooled intermediate that stays 8 bits per
channel on purpose, so the energy is clamped there, before the camera ever sees
it. Adding a second effect to an emitter is enough to silently undo its
headroom.

### Everything inside the camera is graded, including your UI

The tone curve runs on the camera's whole frame. A `floating` HUD is still
inside it, so a label authored at display white arrives at the curve as 1 and
leaves at `1 - exp(-exposure)` — at exposure 0.45 that is 0.36, and the HUD
comes out at roughly a third of its brightness for no reason the author can
see.

UI in an HDR chain has to be authored for that chain, exactly as the scene is:

```js
// drive the readout so the curve lands it back at display white. `shared`
// keeps one instance across every element: it opts the effect out of the
// per-renderable auto-destroy, so the first element torn down does not take
// the program the others are still using
const energy = new ColorMatrixEffect(app.renderer).brightness(2);
energy.shared = true;
for (const element of hudElements) element.addPostEffect(energy);
```

Put it on each ELEMENT, not on their container: `beginPostEffect` clears
`customShader` for any renderable with no effects of its own, so a container's
shader is thrown away by its first child. The alternative is to keep the UI out
of the camera pass entirely, by overriding `Stage.draw` and drawing it after
`super.draw(...)` — at the cost of the bloom that makes additive UI glow.

The quad trick under *A camera effect covers the HUD too* does not help here.
It works by hosting a pass BELOW the HUD's z, and a tone map cannot live there:
it has to be the last thing before the blit to the 8-bit canvas, which is the
camera. Anything the camera draws goes through it.

Pick the multiplier by measuring against the no-headroom build, not by
inverting the curve. Inverting it over-estimates, because additive UI is inside
the BLOOM too and driving it harder also makes it spill wider into the same
pixels.

`hdr` gives the chain headroom and then throws it away at the very last step,
because the surface the browser presents into is 8 bits per channel. Values
above 1 clamp there, exactly as they did before the setting existed.
`hdrOutput` changes that surface, so they reach the compositor instead:

```js

if (app.renderer.supportsHDROutput) { /* the display is getting values above 1 */ }

app.renderer.setHDROutput(false);   // and at runtime, for a settings screen
```

# Post effects and custom shaders

> melonJS ships a catalogue of post effects and a dual-language shader system.
> The recurring trap is that every shader path needs a GPU backend and
> **degrades to nothing** on Canvas rather than erroring. Blend modes are the
> exception — those work on all three renderers.

## Applying an effect

Effects attach to a renderable **or** to a camera (for full-screen grading):

```js
import { VignetteEffect, GlowEffect } from "melonjs";

sprite.addPostEffect(new GlowEffect(app.renderer));
app.viewport.addPostEffect(new VignetteEffect(app.renderer));
```

`renderable.shader = …` is **deprecated since 19.2.0**, and its setter destroys
whatever it replaces. Use `addPostEffect` / `getPostEffect` / `removePostEffect`.

### A camera effect covers the HUD too

A camera's post-effect brackets the **entire** world draw — floating children
included. So the obvious way to write a full-screen pass also washes over every
HUD label in that world, which is rarely what you want.

To land a pass *after* the world but *before* the HUD, host the effect on a
screen-filling floating renderable ordered below the HUD's z instead:

```js
const quad = new Sprite(0, 0, { image: anyImage });
quad.anchorPoint.set(0, 0);
quad.scale(viewW / anyImage.width, viewH / anyImage.height);
quad.floating = true;                 // its own uv is now screen space
quad.blendMode = "additive";
quad.addPostEffect(myEffect);
world.addChild(quad, HUD_Z - 10);     // 2D: below the labels. See the note.
```

Two things follow from the quad filling the frame: its own `uv` is screen space
(so a pass like this needs none of the `screen_uv` / `screen_texture` builtins),
and the incoming `color` is the quad's own texture, which a body that paints
from scratch can ignore entirely.

**Depth here is easy to get backwards, and the rule FLIPS between the two sort
modes.** Under the default `sortOn = "z"` a higher z draws later, i.e. on top,
so `HUD_Z - 10` puts the pass under the labels as written above. Under
`sortOn = "depth"`, which every `Camera3d` scene sets, a floating child's sort
key is `pos.z * pos.z` and the walk paints far to near, so the SMALLER
magnitude is nearer and draws on top — `HUD_Z - 10` there puts the pass OVER
the labels, the opposite of the comment.

So in a 3D scene give the overlay a larger magnitude than the HUD, and give
the HUD a small one (`melonjs-3d` and `melonjs-ui-and-text` both say a HUD
wants a small depth, not the huge z that would put it on top in 2D).

Either way, verify it rather than reasoning about it: return a flat colour from
the body for one frame and see what it tints.

own program instead of being captured offscreen and post-processed, which costs
no render target. That is equivalent only when everything the renderable draws
is a textured quad. `fillRect`, `strokeRect` and `renderer.fill(shape)` go
through a batcher that never reads that shader, so **one** effect on such a
renderable would silently do nothing, while **two** would work, because a chain
always captures.

class Bar extends Renderable {
    constructor(x, y, w, h) {
        super(x, y, w, h);
        this.postEffectNeedsCapture = true;   // ← or one effect is a no-op
    }

```

`ProgressBar`, `UIPanel` and `Trail` set it for you, and a sprite needs
nothing: the flag defaults to `false` and only ever changes the single-effect

**`removePostEffect()` destroys the effect** — it calls `effect.destroy()` and
frees GPU resources, so the instance cannot be re-added. Same for
`clearPostEffects()` and for reassigning the deprecated `.shader`.

```js

sprite.removePostEffect(effect);

// ✓
effect.enabled = false;

An effect with `effect.shared === true` opts out of auto-destroy because it is
reused across renderables.

enemy.addPostEffect(new GradientMapEffect(app.renderer, {
    colors: [[0.2, 0, 0.05], [0.55, 0.05, 0.1], [0.9, 0.25, 0.2], [1, 0.8, 0.7]],
    smooth: false,
}));
```

It reads brightness and nothing else, so two colors as bright as each other
come out the same: a red and a green of equal brightness cannot be told apart
afterwards. To swap particular colors for particular others, the art has to
separate them by brightness first. A sprite's black outline takes the first
color, like any other dark pixel; give that color an alpha of 0 to drop it.
`setIntensity()` fades between the sprite's own colors and the list.

`DitherEffect` draws in a few colors with an ordered dither between them, the
pattern that made a handful of colors read as many on early hardware. It is
made for a **whole scene, on the camera**: the colors are `levels` of each
channel, so everything keeps its own hue, in pixels `size` screen pixels wide.

```js
// a lit scene in six levels a channel, in pixels three screen pixels wide
app.viewport.addPostEffect(new DitherEffect(app.renderer, { levels: 6, size: 3 }));
```

Only a color that falls **between two levels** is patterned: the turn of a lit
surface from light to dark, the soft edge of a shadow, a gradient. A flat color
that is itself a level is left alone. So a flat sky or ground that comes out
speckled all over is a color between two levels: give it one made of levels (at
6 levels, channels that are fifths of 255: 0, 51, 102, 153, 204, 255), and
remember that a **lit** surface's color is its tint times the light, which is
rarely a level; leave a flat ground unlit to keep it clean.

A `palette` of two to sixteen colors of your own takes the place of the
levels: each pixel takes one of the two nearest, the nearer more often, and a
color that is in the palette stays flat. Everything then takes the palette's
hues, the scene's own are gone:

```js
// the whole scene in four greens
app.viewport.addPostEffect(new DitherEffect(app.renderer, {
    palette: [[0.06, 0.22, 0.06], [0.19, 0.38, 0.19], [0.55, 0.67, 0.06], [0.61, 0.74, 0.06]],
    size: 2,
}));
```

`size` is the width of a drawn pixel **in pixels of the texture it draws**, as
`PixelateEffect`'s is: the screen's for a camera's effect, the art's for a
sprite's. On a sprite drawn smaller than its art, a `size` of 1 makes a pattern
finer than the screen can show, which reads as noise: for art drawn at a
quarter of its size, start at 8. `strength: 0` drops the pattern and leaves
flat bands (a posterize). On the camera it covers the HUD too, like any
camera effect (see above).

`RadialGradientEffect` is a procedural soft spot: solid at the centre of the
renderable it draws, fading linearly to transparent at the edge, and elliptical
for free on a non-square one. It is the one to reach for instead of baking a
disc into a canvas, for a pickup highlight, a trigger marker or a damage flash,
on a standalone image, `Renderer.getWhitePixel()` or a sprite cut from an atlas
alike.

`SquishEffect` bulges a sprite's middle out (`setBulge(0.3)`) or pinches it in
(`setBulge(-0.3)`), its top and bottom rows staying put. Bulging out widens the
sprite past its own frame, and the effect draws on a wider quad to make room,
so the art needs no transparent margin. On its own it is a jelly wobble; paired
with a change of height it is **squash and stretch that keeps the volume**:
scale the sprite to `scaleY` of its height about its feet and set the bulge to
`1 - scaleY`, so a stretched sprite pinches in and a squashed one bulges out.
Ease `scaleY` back to 1 with a short `Tween.Easing.Back.Out`; an elastic ease
keeps it trembling long after the landing.

```js
const squish = new SquishEffect(app.renderer);
player.addPostEffect(squish);
// every frame, from the player's update()
const feet = player.height * (1 - player.anchorPoint.y);
player.currentTransform
    .identity()
    .translate(0, feet)
    .scale(1, scaleY)
    .translate(0, -feet);
squish.setBulge(1 - scaleY);
```

Apply that from the sprite's own `update()`, not from a tween's `onUpdate`. A
physics adapter that mirrors a body's angle (matter, planck and Rapier do, and so does
the built-in once a body has an angle or angular velocity) rewrites
`currentTransform` on every step, before the renderables update, so a scale set
anywhere else is gone by the time the sprite is drawn. Let the tween animate a
plain `{ scaleY }` object and read it in `update()`.

It is made for a sprite carrying it as its only effect: chained with another,
or on the camera, the frame it measures against is the whole capture, so it
squishes the whole frame. The bulge is outside the sprite's bounds, so culling
and pointer events ignore it.

**`BloomEffect` and `GlowEffect` are not the same thing**, and reaching for the
wrong one is the usual disappointment here. `GlowEffect` draws a halo OUTSIDE a
sprite's silhouette: its body returns the colour untouched wherever alpha is
already non-zero, so on an opaque frame it returns early on every fragment and
a camera-wide glow does nothing at all. `BloomEffect` is the screen bloom —
bright pixels bleed into their neighbours — and it is the one to put on the
camera:

```js
app.viewport.addPostEffect(new BloomEffect(app.renderer));
// only the brightest highlights, with a wider halo
app.viewport.addPostEffect(
    new BloomEffect(app.renderer, { threshold: 0.85, radius: 4 }),
);
```

Its `radius` is in texels of what it filters, the screen on a camera, and it
follows a resize by itself.

**`ToneMappingEffect` goes after it, and goes last.** Bloom spreads the bright
parts; the tone map is what stops the sum of the two clipping flat at white,
which is the difference between an effect that reads as light and one that
reads as a white sticker. `exposure` lifts the image into the curve, and the
curve (`aces`, `reinhard` or `exponential`) is baked at construction:

```js
app.viewport.addPostEffect(new BloomEffect(app.renderer));
app.viewport.addPostEffect(
    new ToneMappingEffect(app.renderer, { exposure: 1.6 }),
);
```

It is a grade, not a colour pipeline. By default melonJS renders into `RGBA8`
everywhere, so the frame reaching it is already clamped and `exposure` past 1
is what gives the curve range to compress.

**`hdr: true` in the application settings changes that**: render targets
become half-float, so the chain carries values above 1 instead of clamping at
every write, and the bloom threshold starts discriminating genuinely
over-bright pixels rather than merely bright ones. Off by default: it costs
GPU memory on the camera's two render targets and depends on the driver.

On its own it is **not HDR output**: the frame is still presented in SDR, so
anything above 1 clamps on the final blit. What it buys is that nothing clamped
BEFORE then. Removing that last clamp is a second, separate opt-in —
`hdrOutput`, below — and it is WebGPU-only.

```js
const app = new Application(1024, 576, { hdr: true, … });
// …and check what you actually got, since a driver can refuse it
if (app.renderer.supportsHDR) { /* the chain now carries values above 1 */ }
```

Branch the GRADE on that flag, not just the feature. An exposure under 1 and a
bloom threshold at 1 make sense only where values above 1 exist; applied to a
chain that clamps, the same numbers tone map an already display-referred frame
and switch the bloom off, which reads as a dark, flat picture rather than as a
missing feature. Where there is no headroom, squeeze each emitter into range in
its own shader instead and put the bloom threshold back under 1.

**Nothing is added to your chain.** `hdr` is additive: the same frame, plus
additive content that no longer saturates per write and a threshold that means
something. Anything still above 1 at the end clamps on the blit, as it always
did.

A tone map is therefore a decision, not a consequence, and it is a bigger one
than it looks. Every curve maps 1 to less than 1, so a 2D look built ON the
clamp — clipped white specular, saturated neon — goes matte the moment you add
one, at any exposure. Add one when your art is authored in linear light and you
want the highlights rolled off; skip it when the clipping IS the look.

It applies to the CAMERA chain only. A sprite's chain keeps 8-bit targets on
purpose: its final blit composites with `ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, and additive
blending accumulates alpha past 1 in a float target, so that factor would go
negative and subtract the backdrop.

### Once it is on: putting values above 1 into the frame

`hdr: true` on its own changes nothing visible. It removes a ceiling; something
still has to reach for it. No single draw exceeds 1 on its own, so a game that
turns the setting on and changes nothing else renders very nearly the frame it
did before and looks like the feature is broken. The exception is worth knowing
because it is free: additive content that already overlapped was being clipped
at every write, and stops being.

What produces over-bright pixels:

```js
// a built-in colour matrix, scaled past 1 — no custom shader needed
sprite.addPostEffect(new ColorMatrixEffect(app.renderer).brightness(4));

// in 3D, both of these were always unbounded; the 8-bit target was the only
// thing destroying the range. `emissive` is a 3-component Float32Array, set
// from the mesh settings or replaced wholesale — it is not a Color
const mesh = new Mesh(x, y, { emissive: [2.5, 1.8, 0.4], /* … */ });
light.intensity = 3;

// and additive blending, which accumulates past 1 once the target can hold it
sprite.blendMode = "additive";
```

**One effect, not two.** A renderable carrying exactly ONE post effect takes
the renderer's `customShader` fast path: no offscreen target, and it draws
straight into the camera's half-float target with its range intact. A chain of
two or more is routed through a pooled intermediate that stays 8 bits per
channel on purpose, so the energy is clamped there, before the camera ever sees
it. Adding a second effect to an emitter is enough to silently undo its
headroom.

### Everything inside the camera is graded, including your UI

The tone curve runs on the camera's whole frame. A `floating` HUD is still
inside it, so a label authored at display white arrives at the curve as 1 and
leaves at `1 - exp(-exposure)` — at exposure 0.45 that is 0.36, and the HUD
comes out at roughly a third of its brightness for no reason the author can
see.

UI in an HDR chain has to be authored for that chain, exactly as the scene is:

```js
// drive the readout so the curve lands it back at display white. `shared`
// keeps one instance across every element: it opts the effect out of the
// per-renderable auto-destroy, so the first element torn down does not take
// the program the others are still using
const energy = new ColorMatrixEffect(app.renderer).brightness(2);
energy.shared = true;
for (const element of hudElements) element.addPostEffect(energy);
```

Put it on each ELEMENT, not on their container: `beginPostEffect` clears
`customShader` for any renderable with no effects of its own, so a container's
shader is thrown away by its first child. The alternative is to keep the UI out
of the camera pass entirely, by overriding `Stage.draw` and drawing it after
`super.draw(...)` — at the cost of the bloom that makes additive UI glow.

The quad trick under *A camera effect covers the HUD too* does not help here.
It works by hosting a pass BELOW the HUD's z, and a tone map cannot live there:
it has to be the last thing before the blit to the 8-bit canvas, which is the
camera. Anything the camera draws goes through it.

Pick the multiplier by measuring against the no-headroom build, not by
inverting the curve. Inverting it over-estimates, because additive UI is inside
the BLOOM too and driving it harder also makes it spill wider into the same
pixels.

because the surface the browser presents into is 8 bits per channel. Values
above 1 clamp there, exactly as they did before the setting existed.
`hdrOutput` changes that surface, so they reach the compositor instead:

```js

if (app.renderer.supportsHDROutput) { /* the display is getting values above 1 */ }

app.renderer.setHDROutput(false);   // and at runtime, for a settings screen
```
