# Events and lifecycle

## The bus

```js
import { event } from "melonjs";

const onUpdate = () => { /* … */ };
const unsubscribe = event.on(event.GAME_UPDATE, onUpdate);  // on() returns its own off()
event.once(event.LEVEL_LOADED, () => { /* … */ });

// two ways to undo it — the same reference, or the returned function
event.off(event.GAME_UPDATE, onUpdate);
unsubscribe();
```

`event.on`/`once`/`off`/`has` all take an optional third `context` argument,
invoked as the handler's `this`. **`off` matches on the pair — handler identity
AND context identity.** `on(EVT, fn, this)` followed by `off(EVT, fn)` removes
nothing, silently.

**Store the handler reference, or use the context argument.** An inline arrow or
a fresh `.bind(this)` in the `on` call can never be removed — that is the
standard way to leak listeners in melonJS.

```js
// ✗ unremovable
event.on(event.GAME_UPDATE, this.tick.bind(this));

// ✓ keep the bound reference
this._tick = this.tick.bind(this);
event.on(event.GAME_UPDATE, this._tick);
// later: event.off(event.GAME_UPDATE, this._tick);

// ✓ or skip the bind entirely — the context is part of the identity
event.on(event.GAME_UPDATE, this.tick, this);
// later: event.off(event.GAME_UPDATE, this.tick, this);
```

Custom event names work at runtime (`event.emit("my.custom.event", payload)`),
but `on`/`emit` are typed against a closed map of the engine's own events, so in
TypeScript a name outside that map is a compile error. Use your own emitter for
game events in a `.ts` project.

## The events worth knowing

**Per frame**

| event | when |
|---|---|
| `GAME_BEFORE_UPDATE` / `GAME_UPDATE` / `GAME_AFTER_UPDATE` | around the world update — `GAME_UPDATE` is **not** emitted while paused |
| `GAME_BEFORE_DRAW` / `GAME_AFTER_DRAW` | around the draw pass, on frames that redraw: one where no update reported a change is not drawn |
| `WORLD_STEP` | after the physics step |
| `TICK` | the raw engine tick |

**Lifecycle**

| event | when |
|---|---|
| `BOOT`, `GAME_INIT`, `VIDEO_INIT` | engine start-up |
| `STATE_CHANGE`, `STATE_PAUSE`, `STATE_RESUME`, `STATE_STOP` | state machine |
| `STAGE_RESET` | a stage was reset |
| `LEVEL_LOADED` | a Tiled level finished loading |
| `LOADER_PROGRESS`, `LOADER_COMPLETE`, `LOADER_ERROR` | asset loading: every `loader.preload()`, and a bundle loaded with `loader.load(id)` (20.14); not one asset loaded with `loader.load(descriptor)` |
| `BLUR` / `FOCUS` | the page lost or regained focus |
| `CANVAS_ONRESIZE`, `VIEWPORT_ONRESIZE` | relayout hooks |
| `POINTERMOVE` | global pointer movement |

Use `LOADER_PROGRESS` / `LOADER_COMPLETE`. The `loader.onProgress` /
`loader.onload` / `loader.onError` properties were deprecated in 18.2.0 and
removed in 20.3: they were module-level `let` bindings on an ES module
namespace, so `loader.onProgress = fn` threw and the documented migration path
never worked. For completion, `loader.preload(assets, onloadcb)` also takes the
callback directly.

## Renderable lifecycle callbacks

Prefer these over bus subscriptions where they fit — the engine calls them at the
right times and there is nothing to unsubscribe:

| callback | when |
|---|---|
| `onActivateEvent()` | `addChild`-ed into a container that is already attached to the world root (a `Container` forwards it to its children) |
| `onDeactivateEvent()` | removed from its container — including the automatic world clear on a state change. Once per `onActivateEvent`: the children of a removed container, at any depth, are told once |
| `onDestroyEvent()` | `destroy()` ran; called with no arguments from the container-removal path |
| `onCollisionStart` / `onCollisionActive` / `onCollisionEnd` | contacts |

Note the activate gate: adding a child to a *detached* container fires nothing.
The callback arrives later, when that container itself is added to the world.
And an `isPersistent` renderable survives the world clear between stages, so it
gets no fresh `onActivateEvent` on the next state.

**Pair subscriptions with activate/deactivate, not the constructor.** This is
the rule that keeps pooled objects working:

```js
onActivateEvent() {
    this._tick = this.update.bind(this);
    event.on(event.GAME_UPDATE, this._tick);
    input.registerPointerEvent("pointerdown", this, this._onDown);
}
onDeactivateEvent() {
    event.off(event.GAME_UPDATE, this._tick);
    input.releasePointerEvent("pointerdown", this);
}
```

**Pool-recycled objects never fire `onDestroyEvent` on removal** — `removeChildNow`
first tries to return the child to the pool that built it, and only calls
`destroy()` when nothing owns it. So anything taken from a `createPool` goes
back to that pool instead. Anything you clean up there will not run. `destroy()` is also what calls
`releaseAllPointerEvents(this)`, which is why a pooled object must release its
own pointer registrations in `onDeactivateEvent`.

## Guard callbacks that can fire during teardown

Events can arrive while a stage is being dismantled, when the current state is
already something else:

```js
if (!state.isCurrent(state.PLAY)) return;
```

Without this, a "children emptied" handler can reset the wrong stage.

## Removing objects from a collision callback

Contact callbacks fire inline inside the physics step, mid-iteration over the
detector's pair list. `container.removeChild()` is safe there — it defers the
actual removal to the next tick, which is exactly why it defers. The immediate
forms are the dangerous ones: `removeChildNow()` tears the object down under
the iteration, via the internal `destroy()` it calls, which nulls `pos` and
`body`. (`destroy()` is engine teardown and is not in the published types, so
`removeChildNow` is the call a game actually makes.) The builtin
detector guards the pair it is currently resolving, but nothing guarantees that
for the rest of the step or for another adapter.

Use `removeChild()`, or flag the work and drain it from `Stage.update`.

## Symptom → cause

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| handler still fires after removing the object | `event.off` given a different function reference, or a different `context` than `on` got |
| handlers accumulate on pooled objects | subscribed in the constructor rather than `onActivateEvent` |
| cleanup never runs on a pooled object | pooled removal does not fire `onDestroyEvent` |
| crash during a stage switch | callback ran mid-teardown — guard with `state.isCurrent` |
| crash after a collision | `removeChildNow()` inside a contact callback — use `removeChild()` |
| progress callbacks never fire | assigned `loader.onProgress` (removed in 20.3) instead of subscribing to `LOADER_PROGRESS` |
| a `LOADER_COMPLETE` handler (a `state.change` to the first screen) runs again mid-game | a later `preload()`, or a level's bundle loaded with `loader.load(id)`, emits it too; subscribe with `event.once`, or use `preload()`'s promise or callback |
| `onActivateEvent` never runs | the child was added to a container not yet attached to the world |
| `onDeactivateEvent` runs twice when a group is removed (a count goes negative, a light or listener is released twice) | the group's `onDeactivateEvent` and its `destroy()` both reached the children, before 20.13.0 — now once per `onActivateEvent` |
| `onDeactivateEvent` never runs on a child of a group built off-world and destroyed | it never had `onActivateEvent` either: the pair is only sent to children that entered the world |

## Related skills

- `melonjs-scenes-and-state` — the state machine and stage lifecycle
- `melonjs-performance` — pooling, and why activate/deactivate pairing matters

Without this, a "children emptied" handler can reset the wrong stage.

## Removing objects from a collision callback

Contact callbacks fire inline inside the physics step, mid-iteration over the
detector's pair list. `container.removeChild()` is safe there — it defers the
actual removal to the next tick, which is exactly why it defers. The immediate
forms are the dangerous ones: `removeChildNow()` tears the object down under
the iteration, via the internal `destroy()` it calls, which nulls `pos` and
`body`. (`destroy()` is engine teardown and is not in the published types, so
`removeChildNow` is the call a game actually makes.) The builtin
detector guards the pair it is currently resolving, but nothing guarantees that
for the rest of the step or for another adapter.

Use `removeChild()`, or flag the work and drain it from `Stage.update`.

## Symptom → cause

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| handler still fires after removing the object | `event.off` given a different function reference, or a different `context` than `on` got |
| handlers accumulate on pooled objects | subscribed in the constructor rather than `onActivateEvent` |
| cleanup never runs on a pooled object | pooled removal does not fire `onDestroyEvent` |
| crash during a stage switch | callback ran mid-teardown — guard with `state.isCurrent` |
| crash after a collision | `removeChildNow()` inside a contact callback — use `removeChild()` |
| progress callbacks never fire | assigned `loader.onProgress` (removed in 20.3) instead of subscribing to `LOADER_PROGRESS` |
| a `LOADER_COMPLETE` handler (a `state.change` to the first screen) runs again mid-game | a later `preload()`, or a level's bundle loaded with `loader.load(id)`, emits it too; subscribe with `event.once`, or use `preload()`'s promise or callback |
| `onActivateEvent` never runs | the child was added to a container not yet attached to the world |
| `onDeactivateEvent` runs twice when a group is removed (a count goes negative, a light or listener is released twice) | the group's `onDeactivateEvent` and its `destroy()` both reached the children, before 20.13.0 — now once per `onActivateEvent` |
| `onDeactivateEvent` never runs on a child of a group built off-world and destroyed | it never had `onActivateEvent` either: the pair is only sent to children that entered the world |

## Related skills

- `melonjs-scenes-and-state` — the state machine and stage lifecycle
- `melonjs-performance` — pooling, and why activate/deactivate pairing matters

# Getting started with melonJS

> Bootstrapping a melonJS 20.x game: the `Application` lifecycle, the mandatory
> `await app.init()`, the world container, and what the renderer fallback means
> for feature availability.

**Applies to:** melonJS 20.x. Older major versions differ — see the
`melonjs-20-migration` skill.

## The bootstrap

`Application` construction is synchronous but **initialisation is not**. `init()`
returns a promise and must be awaited before building any renderable, loading
assets, or entering a scene.

```js
import { Application, Text } from "melonjs";

const app = new Application(1218, 562, {
    parent: "screen",      // id of the DOM element to mount into
    scale: "auto",
    backgroundColor: "#202020",
});
await app.init();          // ← REQUIRED. Nothing below works without it.

app.world.addChild(
    new Text(609, 281, {
        font: "Arial",
        size: 160,
        fillStyle: "#FFFFFF",
        textAlign: "center",
        textBaseline: "middle",
        text: "Hello World !",
    }),
);
```

**This is the single most common thing to get wrong.** On 19.x the constructor
called `init(width, height, options)` for you; on 20.x `init()` takes no
arguments and calling — and awaiting — it is your job. Nothing that follows
names the missing call. The constructor does build `app.world`, so adding a
plain renderable succeeds and simply never draws — no canvas is appended and the
app never subscribes to the frame tick — while constructing a `Sprite` or a
`Text` throws `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'renderer')`,
because the global `game` those two fall back on is only set once the first
`init()` resolves. Either way `app.renderer` and `app.viewport` stay `undefined`
and the page stays blank.

`init()` is asynchronous because acquiring a WebGPU device is asynchronous. There
is no synchronous alternative.

## Top-level await

The bootstrap needs `await` at module scope. In an ES module that is fine. If the
surrounding tooling does not allow it, wrap it:

```js
async function main() {
    const app = new Application(800, 600, { parent: "screen" });
    await app.init();
    // …
}
void main();
```

## Choosing a renderer

`video.AUTO` (the default) tries **WebGPU → WebGL 2 → Canvas** and uses the first
that works.

```js
import { video } from "melonjs";

const app = new Application(800, 600, {
    parent: "screen",
    renderer: video.AUTO,      // default; or video.WEBGPU / video.WEBGL / video.CANVAS
});
```

Two consequences worth knowing before writing rendering code:

- **Which backend you get is a runtime fact, not a build-time one.** The same
  code runs on a different renderer depending on the machine. Do not assume
  WebGL.
- **Not every feature exists on every backend.** Shader effects and post effects
  need a programmable pipeline and are inert on Canvas. Where a feature degrades,
  the engine warns once rather than throwing — so a missing effect is a console
  warning, not a crash.

Pin the renderer explicitly (`video.WEBGL`) only when you have a reason to. It
costs you the WebGPU path and the Canvas fallback.

## The scene graph

`app.world` is the root `Container`. Everything drawn is a descendant of it.

```js
app.world.addChild(sprite, 10);   // 10 is the z / draw order
```

**Pass the z-order as the second argument to `addChild`** — it is the only form
that works. `renderable.z` does not exist as a property, setting `depth` before
`addChild` is overwritten by `autoDepth`, and setting it afterwards does not
resort. See the `melonjs-renderables` skill for the full explanation.

## Scenes

For anything beyond a single screen, use `Stage` subclasses and the `state`
manager rather than mutating `app.world` directly:

```js
import { Stage, state } from "melonjs";

class PlayScreen extends Stage {
    onResetEvent() { /* build the scene */ }
    onDestroyEvent() { /* tear it down */ }
}

state.set(state.PLAY, new PlayScreen());
state.change(state.PLAY);
```

`onResetEvent` runs every time the state is entered, not once — build scene
content there, not in the constructor.

## Loading assets

Assets are declared and preloaded through `loader`; audio needs `audio.init()`
with the formats you ship before any audio asset is preloaded.

```js
import { audio, loader } from "melonjs";

audio.init("mp3,ogg");                             // BEFORE preloading audio
await loader.preload([
    { name: "tileset", type: "image", src: "data/img/tileset.png" },
    { name: "jump",    type: "audio", src: "data/sfx/" },   // directory, not file
]);
```

A flat list suits a single-screen game. A game with several levels exports a
record of bundles instead — `{ common: [...], level1: [...], level2: [...] }`,
passed to the same `loader.preload()` — so each level's assets can later be
freed and loaded again by id; see `melonjs-loading-assets`.

Two ordering rules that produce confusing failures when missed:

- **`audio.init()` must run before any audio asset is preloaded**, and names the
  formats you actually ship. Preloading first throws *"target audio extension(s)
  should be set through me.audio.init() before calling the preloader"*.
- The audio `src` is a **directory**, not a file. The loader appends the asset
  `name` plus each configured extension, so a full filename gives you a 404.

## `anchorPoint` defaults to the centre

`Renderable.anchorPoint` is `(0.5, 0.5)`, so `pos` is an object's **centre**, not
its top-left. `Container` forces `(0, 0)` instead.

Writing top-left math against a centred anchor puts everything half a sprite off
with no error — it is the most common source of "close but subtly wrong"
placement.

## Common mistakes

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| blank page, nothing drawn, or a `TypeError` reading `renderer` from `new Sprite` / `new Text` | missing `await app.init()` |
| objects draw in the wrong order | `.z`/`depth` set instead of `addChild(child, z)` — `.z` is not even a real property |
| shader/post effect does nothing, warning in console | running on the Canvas renderer |
| audio 404s | audio asset `src` given as a file rather than a directory |
| scene content appears once and never resets | scene built in the constructor instead of `onResetEvent` |
| everything offset by half a sprite | top-left math against the centred `anchorPoint` default |
| a `Tween` or `ParticleEmitter` does nothing | `.start()` / `streamParticles()` never called |
| an asset on another origin fails to load, the error naming it | that server sends no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header (see melonjs-loading-assets) |

## Related skills

- `melonjs-20-migration` — what changed in 20.x that older code and older
  training data get wrong
- `melonjs-renderables` — custom `Renderable` subclasses, pointer events, post
  effects and the traps in each

# Input: keyboard, pointer and gamepad

## Keyboard goes through named actions

Do not poll key codes. Bind a key to an **action string**, then poll the action —
this is what lets gamepad and virtual controls map onto the same handling.

```js
import { input } from "melonjs";

input.bindKey(input.KEY.LEFT,  "left");
input.bindKey(input.KEY.RIGHT, "right");
input.bindKey(input.KEY.X,     "jump", true);   // true = locked: one press per keydown

// in update()
if (input.isKeyPressed("left"))  { /* … */ }
if (input.isKeyPressed("jump"))  { /* fires once per press, not per frame */ }
```

The third argument to `bindKey` is `lock` (default `false`). Without it,
`isKeyPressed` stays true for as long as the key is held — correct for movement,
wrong for jump or fire. A locked action stays consumed until the key is released
or you call `input.unlockKey("jump")`. Use `input.keyStatus(action)` when you
want the raw held/not-held state regardless of locking.

### A poll can miss a press entirely

`isKeyPressed` is sampled once per frame, and `keyup` decrements the key's
counter the moment it arrives — locked or not. A press that goes down and up
between two frames therefore leaves the counter back at zero and is never
seen. At 60fps that is anything under ~16ms: rare from a human finger, routine
from a synthetic event, and more likely the slower the frame rate.

For a screen where a missed press is a dead end — a splash, a "press any key",
a notice to acknowledge — listen for the event instead, which cannot be missed:

```js
import { event } from "melonjs";

// action is the bound action name, or undefined for an unbound key
const onKey = (action) => { if (action === "menuSelect") continue(); };
event.on(event.KEYDOWN, onKey);      // in onResetEvent
event.off(event.KEYDOWN, onKey);     // in onDestroyEvent — it does not self-remove
```

`KEYDOWN` fires for *every* key, bound or not, so matching on `action` is what
narrows it; it also repeats while the key is held, so guard anything that must
happen once. Keep polling for movement and for a menu cursor, where one step
per press and a key held across a state change are the things that matter.

When the window loses the focus or the page is hidden, every key and
`bindPointer` button still held is released, since its real release goes to
another window: polling sees it up when the player comes back, and a key still
held then is pressed again by its next `keydown`. No `KEYUP` is sent for it,
so code moved by `KEYDOWN` / `KEYUP` rather than by polling should also listen
to `event.BLUR`. A gamepad's presses are left to the gamepad, which is read
every frame.

The full signature is `bindKey(keyCode, action, lock?, preventDefault?)`;
`preventDefault` defaults to `input.preventDefault` (itself `true`). Pass the
fourth argument per binding, or change the global default, for the keys bound
after it, with `input.setPreventDefault(false)` — **assigning
`input.preventDefault = false` does not work**, it is a read-only module
binding. The same flag covers the keys the UI focus takes while a widget has
it, and a button's own `bindKey` key (20.15.1, read on each press): with it
off, the browser keeps its action for them too, such as scrolling the page
around the game.

### A mouse button as a key

`bindPointer` makes a mouse button press a bound key, so a click fires the same
action and `isKeyPressed` sees it:

```js
input.bindKey(input.KEY.X, "fire");
input.bindPointer(input.KEY.X);                       // the left button
input.bindPointer(input.pointer.RIGHT, input.KEY.X);  // or another button
input.unbindPointer(input.pointer.RIGHT);             // LEFT when omitted
```

As with `bindGamepad`, the key needs its `bindKey` first, or `bindPointer`
throws `no action defined for keycode N`. Turning the wheel neither presses
nor releases a bound button's key (before 20.14 it released the left
button's).

## Pointer events need `isKinematic = false`

**This is the trap.** `Renderable.isKinematic` defaults to `true`, and both the
broadphase and the pointer dispatcher skip any candidate whose `isKinematic` is
still `true`. The handler registers successfully and simply never fires.

```js
class Button extends Renderable {
    constructor(x, y, w, h) {
        super(x, y, w, h);
        this.isKinematic = false;               // ← required
    }
    onActivateEvent() {
        input.registerPointerEvent("pointerdown", this, this.onDown.bind(this));
    }
    onDeactivateEvent() {
        input.releasePointerEvent("pointerdown", this);
    }
}
```

It gates pointer **events**, not `camera.pick()`: under a `Camera3d`, `pick()`
finds the nearest mesh under a pixel whatever its `isKinematic`, and a mesh is
left out of it with **`pickable = false`** instead (an opt-out, default
`true`), which touches neither its events nor its collisions — `melonjs-3d`
compares the two side by side. Do not clear `isKinematic` just to make a mesh
pickable: that also files it in the collision broadphase.

```js
crate.isKinematic = false;                 // receives its own pointer events
input.registerPointerEvent("pointerdown", crate, onCrate);

floor.pickable = false;                    // camera.pick() looks past it...
floor.isKinematic = false;                 // ...though it still collides

const hit = camera.pick(pointer.gameScreenX, pointer.gameScreenY, app.world);
```

`Container`, `Camera2d`, `Draggable`, `DropTarget` and the `UI*` elements set it
to `false` for you, and so does giving it a physics body (a `bodyDef` on any
adapter, or a `Body`) — so plain `Renderable` and `Sprite` subclasses with no
body are the ones that catch people. Before melonJS 20.14, matter-adapter
1.6.0 and planck-adapter 1.7.0, a `bodyDef` under matter or planck left
`isKinematic` at `true`, so set it yourself there.

Register in `onActivateEvent` and release in `onDeactivateEvent`, not in the
constructor — pooled objects are reused and would otherwise accumulate handlers.

`app.viewport` works as a whole-screen region when you want global clicks. Note
it is asked **before** everything else, not as a fallback after nothing matched:
the dispatcher appends it to the candidate list and walks that list from the
end. So a viewport handler must not return `false` unless it really means to
swallow every pointer event in the game.

A state has its own viewport: the loading screen's is not the one the game's
state brings. Register on `app.viewport` once the state is in place (in the
stage's `onResetEvent`, or after `state.change(state.PLAY, true)`), not in the
`loader.preload` callback before it: that handler stays on the loading
screen's viewport and never fires.

The accepted event names are exactly `"pointerdown"`, `"pointerup"`,
`"pointermove"`, `"pointercancel"`, `"pointerenter"`, `"pointerover"`,
`"pointerleave"` and `"wheel"`. Anything else — `"click"`, `"mousedown"`,
`"touchstart"` — makes both `registerPointerEvent` and `releasePointerEvent`
throw `invalid event type`. melonJS maps the canonical name onto whichever
mouse/touch events the device actually supports, so you always register the
pointer name.

A region can listen to `"pointerup"` alone, to act on release: it gets the
release of a press made on it. With several fingers on one region, each finger
that pressed it gets its own `pointerup` / `pointercancel`; `pointerenter` and
`pointerleave` still follow one pointer per region.

## Which object gets the event

The dispatcher collects the regions near the pointer from the broadphase,
bounds-checks each one, orders them **the way they are drawn** and asks the
topmost first, walking down until something consumes.

A handler consumes by returning `false`. This is the DOM sense and it reads
backwards: `false` means handled, and anything else, `undefined` included, lets
the walk carry on to whatever is underneath.

```js
input.registerPointerEvent("pointerdown", this, () => {
    this.fire();
    return false;        // nothing under this gets the click
});
```

Three things decide the order, and only the first is obvious:

- **`pos.z`, among siblings of one container.** Higher is on top, except
  under a `Camera3d`, where the world sorts on `"depth"` and the regions follow
  that sort: a `floating` region is ordered by `|z|` alone, the **smaller** on
  top, so a dialog at depth 1 is asked before a full-screen region at depth 4.
- **Across containers, the common ancestor decides.** `pos.z` is
  container-local, since `autoDepth` numbers each container's children from 1,
  so a button at `z = 8` inside one panel does not outrank a second panel at
  `z = 2`. The pair is resolved by walking both up to their shared parent and
  comparing the two siblings there, which is exactly how drawing resolves it.
  Raise a whole panel with `ancestor.moveToTop(panel)`, not by inflating a
  child's `z`.
- **A child is asked before the container holding it**, since it draws over it.

Equal `z` between siblings falls back to child order, lower index on top. Two
callbacks registered on the **same** region for the same event run
last-registered-first.

Consuming a **move** also takes the pointer away from the regions below: each
one still holding it gets its `pointerleave`, because it is covered now and
being inside its own bounds no longer decides. Consuming a press, a release or a
wheel does not, since none of those says where the pointer is.

### Meshes under a `Camera3d`: the ray through the pointer

Under a perspective camera a region's 2D bounds say nothing about where it
draws, so a `Mesh` (and a `Sprite3d`, an `InstancedMesh`, a `GLTFModel`) is
hit-tested differently (20.16): by the **ray through the pointer**, against its
triangles. The API does not change — `registerPointerEvent` on the mesh, and
`isKinematic = false` as for any region:

```js
crate.isKinematic = false;
input.registerPointerEvent("pointerdown", crate, (pointer) => {
    const hit = pointer.hit3d;        // where the ray met the crate
    spark.pos.set(hit.point.x, hit.point.y);
    spark.depth = hit.point.z;
    return false;                     // the floor behind it is not clicked too
});
```

- Meshes are asked **nearest hit first**, after the screen-space (`floating`)
  UI, which draws over the scene. Consuming works as above: `return false` and
  the mesh behind gets nothing.
- `pointer.hit3d` carries `point`, `normal` (facing the camera), `distance`,
  `triangle`, `instance` (for an `InstancedMesh`) and `renderable` (for a
  `GLTFModel`, the part — `hit3d.renderable.name` is the glTF node). It is
  `null` on a leave, and on any event that is not a mesh's. The record is
  reused: copy what you keep past the callback.
- `pointerenter` / `pointerleave` follow the ray on and off the mesh.
- A mesh inside a moved or turned container is hit where it draws, as of the
  last frame. One in a container taken out of the world gets nothing.
- **Each event ray-tests the meshes it can reach**, every triangle of them
  (each instance of an `InstancedMesh`). A move only tests the meshes that
  listen for moves, `pointerenter` / `pointerleave` or a release: register
  only `pointerdown` on a ten-thousand-instance forest and moving the mouse
  costs nothing; register `pointermove` on it and every move pays for all of
  them.

Without registering anything, `camera.pick(x, y, app.world)` returns the same
record for the nearest mesh under a screen point, and
`camera.screenToWorld(x, y, floorY)` the point on a level floor — see
`melonjs-3d`.

## World coordinates versus screen coordinates

The pointer carries several, and picking the wrong one produces a feedback loop:

| property | meaning | use for |
|---|---|---|
| `pointer.gameScreenX` / `gameScreenY` | canvas-relative position | anything that **moves the camera** |
| `pointer.gameWorldX` / `gameWorldY` | projected into world space | picking and spawning objects |
| `pointer.gameLocalX` / `gameLocalY` | relative to the region's ancestor container | hit-testing inside a container |
| `pointer.gameX` / `gameY` | **context-dependent** — see below | region handlers on non-floating regions |

`gameX`/`gameY` is not a fixed coordinate space. The dispatcher rewrites it per
candidate just before calling your handler: world coordinates for a normal
region, screen coordinates for a `isFloating === true` region. On the global
`event.POINTERMOVE` broadcast it is set to the **screen** coordinates. When you
need one specific space, read `gameWorldX`/`gameWorldY` or
`gameScreenX`/`gameScreenY` by name rather than relying on `gameX`.

Using world coordinates for a camera-orbit drag means the same pixel maps to a
different world point every frame as the camera moves — the drag jumps wildly.
Read `gameScreenX` / `gameScreenY`, turn your own yaw and pitch by the change,
and place the camera with `camera.orbit(target, yaw, pitch, distance)` (see
`melonjs-3d`).

## Pointer move and release outside a region

Region handlers only fire while the pointer is over the region. For a drag,
press on the region, then follow and end it with the global events, which fire
wherever the pointer is: over a region or not, over the canvas or not, and for
a release, even outside the browser window while it was held:

```js
import { event, input } from "melonjs";
input.registerPointerEvent("pointerdown", handle, startDrag);
event.on(event.POINTERMOVE, followDrag);
event.on(event.POINTERUP, endDrag);       // let go, anywhere
event.on(event.POINTERCANCEL, dropDrag);  // the browser took the pointer away
// and `event.off` the three when the drag's owner goes away
```

All three hand over a `Pointer` in **screen** coordinates (`gameScreenX` /
`gameScreenY`, and `gameX` / `gameY` set to the same), outside the canvas's
range when the pointer was. `POINTERCANCEL` is a touch that became a scroll or
a pinch, a pen out of range, a system gesture: a drag that only ends on
`POINTERUP` stays stuck after one. Usually it should drop the drag rather than
act on it (no shot, no throw). Each finger has its own `pointerId`.

Do not use a raw `globalThis.addEventListener("pointerup", …)` for this any
more: it hands over the browser's coordinates, not the game's, and is easy to
forget to remove.

For plain drag-and-drop, `Draggable` / `DropTarget` already wire all of this up
(`pointerdown` / `pointerup` / `pointercancel` regions plus a global
`POINTERMOVE` listener) and emit `event.DRAGSTART` / `event.DRAGEND`, and
follow the pointer under any camera, scrolled or zoomed. `DRAGEND` still
originates from a region handler, so it only fires when the release lands on
the draggable itself.

## Gamepad

Gamepad input maps onto the same action strings, so game code does not branch:

```js
input.bindGamepad(0,
    { type: "buttons", code: input.GAMEPAD.BUTTONS.FACE_1 },
    input.KEY.X);        // → the "jump" action bound above
```

**Order matters:** `bindGamepad` throws `no action defined for keycode N` if the
keycode has not already been passed to `bindKey`.

Axes use the same call with a threshold, and bind **one half of the axis each**
— the sign selects which half:

```js
input.bindGamepad(0, { type: "axes", code: input.GAMEPAD.AXES.LX, threshold: -0.15 }, input.KEY.LEFT);
input.bindGamepad(0, { type: "axes", code: input.GAMEPAD.AXES.LX, threshold:  0.15 }, input.KEY.RIGHT);
```

**`threshold` is added to the deadzone, it does not replace it.** The test is
`abs(value) >= deadzone + abs(threshold)`, so with the default deadzone of 0.1
a threshold of `0.5` does not fire until 0.6 of full travel, and `0.15` fires at
0.25. Pick the number you want the stick to break at and subtract the deadzone.
Raising `setGamepadDeadzone` moves every axis binding with it.

`unbindGamepad(index, button, type?)`, `setGamepadDeadzone(value)` and
`setGamepadMapping(id, mapping)` complete the surface.

### Which index to bind

Bindings are per pad **index**, and the index is plug order, not identity —
nothing reports which pad is "the" controller. Slot 0 is a guess: a wheel, a
spare pad or a keyboard-shaped device left plugged in can hold it for a whole
session while the player presses buttons on slot 1.

So a one-player game binds **every slot it will accept** to the same actions,
and lets `activeGamepad()` say which one is in use when something has to go
back the other way:

```js
for (let pad = 0; pad < 4; pad++) {
    input.bindGamepad(pad, { type: "buttons", code: input.GAMEPAD.BUTTONS.FACE_1 }, input.KEY.X);
}
input.activeGamepad();   // the last pad to produce a bound input, else the
                         // first connected one, else -1
```

Binding spare slots costs nothing: the poll skips a bound index with no pad in
it. `activeGamepad()` follows **bound inputs only**, which is what makes it an
answer about the player rather than about electrical noise — a worn stick at
rest reports movement for ever and would otherwise claim to be the active pad.

### Rumble

```js
input.vibrateGamepad(input.activeGamepad(), {
    duration: 120, strongMagnitude: 0.6, weakMagnitude: 0.9,
});
input.stopGamepadVibration(index);   // cut a long effect short
input.hasGamepadVibration(index);    // for an options-screen toggle
```

Safe to call blind: no pad, no motors, or no Gamepad API at all resolves
`false` and does nothing, so game code never branches on support. Magnitudes
default to **full** and `duration` to 200 ms — the underlying web API defaults
every parameter to zero, which makes a bare `playEffect` a silent no-op. A
second call preempts the first on the same pad, so a rapid series of hits
reads as a rapid series of hits rather than as a queue. For a SUSTAINED rumble issue one effect with a
long `duration` instead of calling every frame.

Hot-plugging needs no polling of your own — the engine listens for the browser's
own events and republishes them:

```js
import { event } from "melonjs";

event.on(event.GAMEPAD_CONNECTED,    (gamepad) => { /* gamepad.id, .index */ });
event.on(event.GAMEPAD_DISCONNECTED, (gamepad) => { /* pause, show a prompt */ });
```

Bindings survive a disconnect: they are attached to the index, not to the
device, so a pad unplugged and plugged back into the same slot keeps working.
A pad unplugged with a button or the stick held lets go of the keys bound to
them, as releasing them would.

## Virtual controls

For on-screen touch controls, use `@melonjs/gamepad-plugin` (it needs melonJS
20.12 or later) rather than writing them: sticks and buttons drawn over the
game and reported as a pad in a gamepad slot, so the `bindGamepad` bindings
above answer to them unchanged.

```js
import { GamepadPlugin } from "@melonjs/gamepad-plugin";

// once the application is created: a stick and two buttons, on touch screens
plugin.register(GamepadPlugin, "gamepad", {
    buttons: [{ label: "A" }, { label: "B" }],
});
```

The left stick presses the D-pad buttons (`GAMEPAD.BUTTONS.UP` ...) in 8
directions and reports `AXES.LX`/`LY`; the buttons press `FACE_1`, `FACE_2`...
in turn, or a key with `{ key: input.KEY.SPACE }`. Each finger is followed on
its own, a touch starting on the controls does not reach the game, and they
hide while a real pad is in use. `plugin.cache.gamepad.visible` says whether
they show, to word a prompt ("tap" or a key name).

Sticks and buttons are fixed in a corner by default. **`floating: true`**
puts one under the finger wherever it lands inside its `area` (`"half"`, its
own half of the screen, by default; `"screen"`; or `{ x, y, width, height }`),
and **`hideAtRest: true`** draws it only while held. The usual mobile
two-thumb layout, nothing on screen until touched (1.1):

```js
plugin.register(GamepadPlugin, "gamepad", {
    sticks: [{ floating: true, hideAtRest: true }],                 // left half
    buttons: [{ floating: true, hideAtRest: true, label: "A" }],    // right half
});
```

Or one thumb for both: a stick over the whole screen whose quick tap (lifted
within `tap.time`, 250 ms, without leaning to `dpadThreshold`) presses a key
or button for one frame, and no button at all:

```js
plugin.register(GamepadPlugin, "gamepad", {
    sticks: [{ floating: true, area: "screen", hideAtRest: true,
               tap: { key: input.KEY.SPACE } }],
    buttons: 0,
});
```

Where areas overlap, a finger takes the first free control there: fixed
buttons, fixed sticks, floating buttons, floating sticks. So a floating button
on its `"half"` carves the right half out of a `"screen"` stick, and several
floating buttons sharing an area split it by distance to where each rests.
Every press lasts at least one frame, so a 15 ms thumb tap still reaches
`isKeyPressed`, and Safari's pinch gesture is cancelled while the controls
show, so a second thumb works on iOS.

To match the game's artwork (1.2), pass an already-loaded `TextureAtlas` as
`skin` to `GamepadPlugin`, with `base` / `thumb` region names on sticks
and `region` / optional `pressed` names on buttons. Omitted parts keep
their shapes. Regions scale to the controls' sizes without changing hit areas;
labels, floating controls, opacity, hiding and dimming keep working.

A single key can also be pressed directly, reaching the same actions:

```js
input.triggerKeyEvent(input.KEY.LEFT, true);    // press
input.triggerKeyEvent(input.KEY.LEFT, false);   // release
```

## Keyboard goes through named actions

Do not poll key codes. Bind a key to an **action string**, then poll the action —
this is what lets gamepad and virtual controls map onto the same handling.

```js
import { input } from "melonjs";

input.bindKey(input.KEY.LEFT,  "left");
input.bindKey(input.KEY.RIGHT, "right");
input.bindKey(input.KEY.X,     "jump", true);   // true = locked: one press per keydown

// in update()
if (input.isKeyPressed("left"))  { /* … */ }
if (input.isKeyPressed("jump"))  { /* fires once per press, not per frame */ }
```

The third argument to `bindKey` is `lock` (default `false`). Without it,
`isKeyPressed` stays true for as long as the key is held — correct for movement,
wrong for jump or fire. A locked action stays consumed until the key is released
or you call `input.unlockKey("jump")`. Use `input.keyStatus(action)` when you
want the raw held/not-held state regardless of locking.

### A poll can miss a press entirely

`isKeyPressed` is sampled once per frame, and `keyup` decrements the key's
counter the moment it arrives — locked or not. A press that goes down and up
between two frames therefore leaves the counter back at zero and is never
seen. At 60fps that is anything under ~16ms: rare from a human finger, routine
from a synthetic event, and more likely the slower the frame rate.

For a screen where a missed press is a dead end — a splash, a "press any key",
a notice to acknowledge — listen for the event instead, which cannot be missed:

```js
import { event } from "melonjs";

// action is the bound action name, or undefined for an unbound key
const onKey = (action) => { if (action === "menuSelect") continue(); };
event.on(event.KEYDOWN, onKey);      // in onResetEvent
event.off(event.KEYDOWN, onKey);     // in onDestroyEvent — it does not self-remove
```

`KEYDOWN` fires for *every* key, bound or not, so matching on `action` is what
narrows it; it also repeats while the key is held, so guard anything that must
happen once. Keep polling for movement and for a menu cursor, where one step
per press and a key held across a state change are the things that matter.

When the window loses the focus or the page is hidden, every key and
`bindPointer` button still held is released, since its real release goes to
another window: polling sees it up when the player comes back, and a key still
held then is pressed again by its next `keydown`. No `KEYUP` is sent for it,
so code moved by `KEYDOWN` / `KEYUP` rather than by polling should also listen
to `event.BLUR`. A gamepad's presses are left to the gamepad, which is read
every frame.

The full signature is `bindKey(keyCode, action, lock?, preventDefault?)`;
`preventDefault` defaults to `input.preventDefault` (itself `true`). Pass the
fourth argument per binding, or change the global default, for the keys bound
after it, with `input.setPreventDefault(false)` — **assigning
`input.preventDefault = false` does not work**, it is a read-only module
binding. The same flag covers the keys the UI focus takes while a widget has
it, and a button's own `bindKey` key (20.15.1, read on each press): with it
off, the browser keeps its action for them too, such as scrolling the page
around the game.

### A mouse button as a key

`bindPointer` makes a mouse button press a bound key, so a click fires the same
action and `isKeyPressed` sees it:

```js
input.bindKey(input.KEY.X, "fire");
input.bindPointer(input.KEY.X);                       // the left button
input.bindPointer(input.pointer.RIGHT, input.KEY.X);  // or another button
input.unbindPointer(input.pointer.RIGHT);             // LEFT when omitted
```

As with `bindGamepad`, the key needs its `bindKey` first, or `bindPointer`
throws `no action defined for keycode N`. Turning the wheel neither presses
nor releases a bound button's key (before 20.14 it released the left
button's).

**This is the trap.** `Renderable.isKinematic` defaults to `true`, and both the
broadphase and the pointer dispatcher skip any candidate whose `isKinematic` is
still `true`. The handler registers successfully and simply never fires.

```js
class Button extends Renderable {
    constructor(x, y, w, h) {
        super(x, y, w, h);
        this.isKinematic = false;               // ← required
    }
    onActivateEvent() {
        input.registerPointerEvent("pointerdown", this, this.onDown.bind(this));
    }
    onDeactivateEvent() {
        input.releasePointerEvent("pointerdown", this);
    }

```

It gates pointer **events**, not `camera.pick()`: under a `Camera3d`, `pick()`
finds the nearest mesh under a pixel whatever its `isKinematic`, and a mesh is
left out of it with **`pickable = false`** instead (an opt-out, default
`true`), which touches neither its events nor its collisions — `melonjs-3d`
compares the two side by side. Do not clear `isKinematic` just to make a mesh
pickable: that also files it in the collision broadphase.

```js

input.registerPointerEvent("pointerdown", crate, onCrate);

const hit = camera.pick(pointer.gameScreenX, pointer.gameScreenY, app.world);
```

to `false` for you, and so does giving it a physics body (a `bodyDef` on any
adapter, or a `Body`) — so plain `Renderable` and `Sprite` subclasses with no
body are the ones that catch people. Before melonJS 20.14, matter-adapter
1.6.0 and planck-adapter 1.7.0, a `bodyDef` under matter or planck left
`isKinematic` at `true`, so set it yourself there.

constructor — pooled objects are reused and would otherwise accumulate handlers.

`app.viewport` works as a whole-screen region when you want global clicks. Note
it is asked **before** everything else, not as a fallback after nothing matched:
the dispatcher appends it to the candidate list and walks that list from the
end. So a viewport handler must not return `false` unless it really means to
swallow every pointer event in the game.

A state has its own viewport: the loading screen's is not the one the game's
state brings. Register on `app.viewport` once the state is in place (in the
stage's `onResetEvent`, or after `state.change(state.PLAY, true)`), not in the
`loader.preload` callback before it: that handler stays on the loading
screen's viewport and never fires.

The accepted event names are exactly `"pointerdown"`, `"pointerup"`,
`"pointermove"`, `"pointercancel"`, `"pointerenter"`, `"pointerover"`,
`"pointerleave"` and `"wheel"`. Anything else — `"click"`, `"mousedown"`,
`"touchstart"` — makes both `registerPointerEvent` and `releasePointerEvent`
throw `invalid event type`. melonJS maps the canonical name onto whichever
mouse/touch events the device actually supports, so you always register the
pointer name.

A region can listen to `"pointerup"` alone, to act on release: it gets the
release of a press made on it. With several fingers on one region, each finger
that pressed it gets its own `pointerup` / `pointercancel`; `pointerenter` and
`pointerleave` still follow one pointer per region.

The dispatcher collects the regions near the pointer from the broadphase,

topmost first, walking down until something consumes.

A handler consumes by returning `false`. This is the DOM sense and it reads
backwards: `false` means handled, and anything else, `undefined` included, lets
the walk carry on to whatever is underneath.

```js

    this.fire();
    return false;        // nothing under this gets the click
});
```

  under a `Camera3d`, where the world sorts on `"depth"` and the regions follow
  that sort: a `floating` region is ordered by `|z|` alone, the **smaller** on
  top, so a dialog at depth 1 is asked before a full-screen region at depth 4.

  container-local, since `autoDepth` numbers each container's children from 1,
  so a button at `z = 8` inside one panel does not outrank a second panel at

  comparing the two siblings there, which is exactly how drawing resolves it.
  Raise a whole panel with `ancestor.moveToTop(panel)`, not by inflating a
  child's `z`.
- **A child is asked before the container holding it**, since it draws over it.

act on it (no shot, no throw). Each finger has its own `pointerId`.

Do not use a raw `globalThis.addEventListener("pointerup", …)` for this any
more: it hands over the browser's coordinates, not the game's, and is easy to
forget to remove.

For plain drag-and-drop, `Draggable` / `DropTarget` already wire all of this up
(`pointerdown` / `pointerup` / `pointercancel` regions plus a global
`POINTERMOVE` listener) and emit `event.DRAGSTART` / `event.DRAGEND`, and
follow the pointer under any camera, scrolled or zoomed. `DRAGEND` still
originates from a region handler, so it only fires when the release lands on
the draggable itself.

## Gamepad

Gamepad input maps onto the same action strings, so game code does not branch:

```js
input.bindGamepad(0,
    { type: "buttons", code: input.GAMEPAD.BUTTONS.FACE_1 },
    input.KEY.X);        // → the "jump" action bound above
```

**Order matters:** `bindGamepad` throws `no action defined for keycode N` if the
keycode has not already been passed to `bindKey`.

Axes use the same call with a threshold, and bind **one half of the axis each**
— the sign selects which half:

```js
input.bindGamepad(0, { type: "axes", code: input.GAMEPAD.AXES.LX, threshold: -0.15 }, input.KEY.LEFT);
input.bindGamepad(0, { type: "axes", code: input.GAMEPAD.AXES.LX, threshold:  0.15 }, input.KEY.RIGHT);
```

**`threshold` is added to the deadzone, it does not replace it.** The test is
`abs(value) >= deadzone + abs(threshold)`, so with the default deadzone of 0.1
a threshold of `0.5` does not fire until 0.6 of full travel, and `0.15` fires at
0.25. Pick the number you want the stick to break at and subtract the deadzone.
Raising `setGamepadDeadzone` moves every axis binding with it.

`unbindGamepad(index, button, type?)`, `setGamepadDeadzone(value)` and
`setGamepadMapping(id, mapping)` complete the surface.

### Which index to bind

Bindings are per pad **index**, and the index is plug order, not identity —
nothing reports which pad is "the" controller. Slot 0 is a guess: a wheel, a
spare pad or a keyboard-shaped device left plugged in can hold it for a whole
session while the player presses buttons on slot 1.

So a one-player game binds **every slot it will accept** to the same actions,
and lets `activeGamepad()` say which one is in use when something has to go
back the other way:

```js
for (let pad = 0; pad < 4; pad++) {
    input.bindGamepad(pad, { type: "buttons", code: input.GAMEPAD.BUTTONS.FACE_1 }, input.KEY.X);
}
input.activeGamepad();   // the last pad to produce a bound input, else the
                         // first connected one, else -1
```

Binding spare slots costs nothing: the poll skips a bound index with no pad in
it. `activeGamepad()` follows **bound inputs only**, which is what makes it an
answer about the player rather than about electrical noise — a worn stick at
rest reports movement for ever and would otherwise claim to be the active pad.

### Rumble

```js
input.vibrateGamepad(input.activeGamepad(), {
    duration: 120, strongMagnitude: 0.6, weakMagnitude: 0.9,
});
input.stopGamepadVibration(index);   // cut a long effect short
input.hasGamepadVibration(index);    // for an options-screen toggle
```

Safe to call blind: no pad, no motors, or no Gamepad API at all resolves
`false` and does nothing, so game code never branches on support. Magnitudes
default to **full** and `duration` to 200 ms — the underlying web API defaults
every parameter to zero, which makes a bare `playEffect` a silent no-op. A
second call preempts the first on the same pad, so a rapid series of hits
reads as a rapid series of hits rather than as a queue. For a SUSTAINED rumble issue one effect with a
long `duration` instead of calling every frame.

Hot-plugging needs no polling of your own — the engine listens for the browser's
own events and republishes them:

```js
import { event } from "melonjs";

event.on(event.GAMEPAD_CONNECTED,    (gamepad) => { /* gamepad.id, .index */ });
event.on(event.GAMEPAD_DISCONNECTED, (gamepad) => { /* pause, show a prompt */ });
```

Bindings survive a disconnect: they are attached to the index, not to the
device, so a pad unplugged and plugged back into the same slot keeps working.
A pad unplugged with a button or the stick held lets go of the keys bound to
them, as releasing them would.

## Virtual controls

For on-screen touch controls, use `@melonjs/gamepad-plugin` (it needs melonJS
20.12 or later) rather than writing them: sticks and buttons drawn over the
game and reported as a pad in a gamepad slot, so the `bindGamepad` bindings
above answer to them unchanged.

```js
import { GamepadPlugin } from "@melonjs/gamepad-plugin";

// once the application is created: a stick and two buttons, on touch screens
plugin.register(GamepadPlugin, "gamepad", {
    buttons: [{ label: "A" }, { label: "B" }],
});
```

The left stick presses the D-pad buttons (`GAMEPAD.BUTTONS.UP` ...) in 8
directions and reports `AXES.LX`/`LY`; the buttons press `FACE_1`, `FACE_2`...
in turn, or a key with `{ key: input.KEY.SPACE }`. Each finger is followed on
its own, a touch starting on the controls does not reach the game, and they
hide while a real pad is in use. `plugin.cache.gamepad.visible` says whether
they show, to word a prompt ("tap" or a key name).

Sticks and buttons are fixed in a corner by default. **`floating: true`**
puts one under the finger wherever it lands inside its `area` (`"half"`, its
own half of the screen, by default; `"screen"`; or `{ x, y, width, height }`),
and **`hideAtRest: true`** draws it only while held. The usual mobile
two-thumb layout, nothing on screen until touched (1.1):

```js
plugin.register(GamepadPlugin, "gamepad", {
    sticks: [{ floating: true, hideAtRest: true }],                 // left half
    buttons: [{ floating: true, hideAtRest: true, label: "A" }],    // right half
});
```

Or one thumb for both: a stick over the whole screen whose quick tap (lifted
within `tap.time`, 250 ms, without leaning to `dpadThreshold`) presses a key
or button for one frame, and no button at all:

```js
plugin.register(GamepadPlugin, "gamepad", {
    sticks: [{ floating: true, area: "screen", hideAtRest: true,
               tap: { key: input.KEY.SPACE } }],
    buttons: 0,
});
```

Where areas overlap, a finger takes the first free control there: fixed
buttons, fixed sticks, floating buttons, floating sticks. So a floating button
on its `"half"` carves the right half out of a `"screen"` stick, and several
floating buttons sharing an area split it by distance to where each rests.
Every press lasts at least one frame, so a 15 ms thumb tap still reaches
`isKeyPressed`, and Safari's pinch gesture is cancelled while the controls
show, so a second thumb works on iOS.

To match the game's artwork (1.2), pass an already-loaded `TextureAtlas` as
`skin` to `GamepadPlugin`, with `base` / `thumb` region names on sticks
and `region` / optional `pressed` names on buttons. Omitted parts keep
their shapes. Regions scale to the controls' sizes without changing hit areas;
labels, floating controls, opacity, hiding and dimming keep working.

A single key can also be pressed directly, reaching the same actions:

```js
input.triggerKeyEvent(input.KEY.LEFT, true);    // press
input.triggerKeyEvent(input.KEY.LEFT, false);   // release
```

## Symptom → cause

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| a drag stays stuck when released off its region or off the canvas | it ends on the region's own `"pointerup"`, which only fires over it: end it on `event.POINTERUP`, heard anywhere |
| a drag stays stuck after a touch turned into a scroll or a pinch | it ends on `POINTERUP` alone: the browser sent a cancel, `event.POINTERCANCEL` |
| clicks on a 3D mesh land in the wrong place or not at all (before 20.16) | meshes were hit-tested by their 2D bounds, which a perspective camera makes meaningless: update — they are hit-tested by the pointer's ray now |
| a click on a mesh also reaches the floor or mesh behind it | the handler did not `return false` |
| moving the mouse got slow under a `Camera3d` | a big mesh or `InstancedMesh` listens for `pointermove` / `pointerenter` / `pointerleave`: each move ray-tests all its triangles. Listen for presses only, or hover with `camera.pick` on a smaller set |
| `pointer.hit3d` is `null` | not a mesh's event, a `pointerleave`, or read after the callback returned (the record is reused) |
| pointer handler never fires | `isKinematic` left at its `true` default |
| under a `Camera3d`, a full-screen `floating` region takes the presses meant for a button drawn over it (before 20.16) | regions were asked by raw z, highest first, though a `Camera3d` draws the smaller depth on top: update |
| touches never arrive where there is no DOM (nx.js, a Web Worker) | melonJS older than 20.14 listened for mouse events there; update. Touch is then read from `TouchEvent`s dispatched on the canvas given as `settings.canvas` |
| handlers fire twice, or on dead objects | registered in the constructor instead of `onActivateEvent` |
| camera drag jumps around | using world coordinates instead of `gameScreenX`/`gameScreenY` |
| `gameX` holds screen coords where world coords were expected | read on `event.POINTERMOVE`, or on a floating region — use `gameWorldX`/`gameWorldY` |
| drag stops when leaving the object | region events end at the region — use `event.POINTERMOVE` |
| jump fires every frame while held | `bindKey` without its third `lock` argument |
| the arrow keys or Space scroll the page around the game, in a portal's frame | the key is read from `event.KEYDOWN` without a binding, bound with `preventDefault` `false`, or bound after `input.setPreventDefault(false)`; before 20.15.1, also the keys the UI focus takes: bind the key, leaving its `preventDefault` and `input.setPreventDefault` on |
| the hero keeps walking after an Alt-Tab, until the key is pressed again (before 20.14) | the key's release went to another window: update, held keys are now released on blur |
| a region with only a `"pointerup"` callback never gets it, or the first fing

# 2D dynamic lighting

> `Light2d` is a world renderable that cuts through a stage's ambient darkness.
> The glow and the cutout work on every backend; only per-pixel normal-map
> shading needs a GPU one. It is 2D-only.

## The model: ambient darkness plus cutouts

The `Stage` holds an ambient colour — a dark sheet painted over the scene after
the world is drawn — and each active `Light2d` punches a hole in it at its
visible area. The lights themselves are drawn additively on top.

```js
class PlayScreen extends Stage {
    onResetEvent(app) {
        this.ambientLight.parseCSS("#1a1a2e");     // the darkness

        app.world.addChild(new Light2d(x, y, radiusX, radiusY, "#ffddaa", 0.9));
    }
}
```

The constructor is `Light2d(x, y, radiusX, radiusY = radiusX, color = "#FFF",
intensity = 0.7)`, and `pos` is the light's **centre** — its `anchorPoint` is
`(0.5, 0.5)`, and `centerX` / `centerY` are overridden to return `pos` directly.
Give `radiusY` a different value for a stretched, elliptical light.

Resize a light with `light.setRadii(radiusX, radiusY)`, which resizes its
bounds too. Writing `radiusX` alone changes nothing you can see: the glow, the
hole in the darkness and the normal-map shading are all sized from the bounds,
on every backend.

A `Light2d` added to the world **registers itself with the stage's ambient
overlay on activate**, so you add it like any other renderable and it takes part
in the lighting pass. It draws additively (`blendMode = "lighter"`); set
`light.illuminationOnly = true` to suppress the visible glow while still lighting
normal-mapped sprites.

`Stage.ambientLight` defaults to fully transparent black, and `drawLighting()`
returns immediately while its alpha is 0 — so with no ambient colour set there
is nothing to cut through and the lights just look like soft additive blobs.

## Soft edges: `softness`

A light's hole in the darkness is hard-edged by default: full light inside its
radius, full darkness outside. `light.softness` (0 to 1) fades it instead:

```js
const torch = new Light2d(x, y, 220, 220, "#ffb46a", 0.4);
torch.softness = 0.8;      // lit core of 20% of the radius, then fading out
```

- `1` thins the darkness straight from the centre to the edge, the same falloff
  as the glow; in between, a fully lit core of `1 - softness` of the radius.
- Hard and soft lights mix in one scene. Where lights overlap, what is left of the
  darkness is what each leaves, multiplied, so two half-lights make three
  quarters light.
- The hole is the light's size. For an opening wider than the glow (a torch whose
  light reaches further than its flame's halo), add a second, bigger light with
  `illuminationOnly = true`: it cuts the darkness and draws nothing.
- Up to 32 lights in view are cut by one soft pass; lights outside the view do not
  count. A scene with no soft light draws exactly as before.
- To keep a camera out of the darkness (a minimap showing the level lit),
  override `drawLighting` on the stage and skip that camera.
- To keep one light out of a camera, put it, or a container it is in, on a
  `visibilityLayer` the camera's `cullMask` leaves out: there it neither glows,
  nor cuts the darkness, nor lights normal-mapped sprites (see
  `melonjs-camera-and-drawing`). This is for a `Light2d`: a `Light3d` lights
  the meshes of every camera.

## Multiple lights

Add as many as you need — the glow quads and the ambient cutouts accumulate with
no fixed cap.

The **normal-map** pipeline is capped: lights are packed into a std140 uniform
block sized for `MAX_LIGHTS = 32`, and anything past the 32nd is silently dropped
from the per-pixel shading (it still draws its glow and punches its cutout). The
cap is an allocation, not a budget — the fragment loop still runs once per pixel
per live light.

Lights are positioned like any renderable, so they can follow an entity by
updating `pos`, or be added as children of one.

## Per-pixel lighting with normal maps

For sprites that respond to light direction rather than just brightness, supply a
normal map alongside the diffuse texture:

```js
await loader.preload([
    { name: "hero",     type: "image", src: "data/img/hero.png" },
    { name: "hero_n",   type: "image", src: "data/img/hero_n.png" },
]);

const hero = new Sprite(x, y, {
    image: "hero",
    normalMap: "hero_n",       // ← enables per-pixel lighting on this sprite
    framewidth: 32, frameheight: 32,
});
```

`normalMap` takes a loader key, or any image-like source (`HTMLImageElement`,
canvas, `ImageBitmap`, a `Texture2d`). Assigning anything else — including an
`HTMLVideoElement`, which would freeze on frame 0 — throws a `TypeError`.

It is lit on the GPU renderers, **WebGL and WebGPU**. On Canvas the sprite is
drawn unlit and a warning says so once (see "What needs a GPU backend" below).

A normal map is a still image, uploaded once. A sprite that **animates** takes
its normals from one static sheet laid out exactly like its colour sheet: the
animation picks the frame, and the same region of both is sampled. There is no
video or per-frame normal source to set up.

How grazing the light is comes from `light.lightHeight`, its height above the
sprite plane in the same units as its radius (default `max(radiusX, radiusY) *
0.075`). Lower it for light raking across the surface, which shows the relief
off; raise it for flatter, more even shading.

Normal maps are typically authored in **SpriteIlluminator**. The sidecar pattern
above — one `_n` image beside each diffuse image — is the simplest setup, but an
atlas can carry one too: `new TextureAtlas(json, image, { normalMap })` pairs a
normal texture sharing the colour texture's UVs, and a `Sprite` built from that
atlas picks it up in preference to its own `settings.normalMap`.

## Specular highlights

A normal map gives a sprite **shape**: the light knows which way each texel
faces, so a torch reveals bumps and crevices. `shininess` decides whether it
also **shines**:

```js
const sword = new Sprite(x, y, {
    image: "sword",
    normalMap: "sword_n",
    shininess: 64,        // 0 (the default) is matte
});
```

The difference is what the highlight *does*. Diffuse brightness depends only on
the angle between the surface and the light, so a torch moving past just makes
the sprite brighter. A specular highlight only appears where a texel reflects
the light **toward the screen**, so it slides across the surface as the light
moves: armour that glints as you walk by, rather than armour that is merely lit.

Low values give a broad sheen (worn metal, wet stone); high values a tight glint
(polished steel, glass). It is gated on the exponent exactly as MTL `Ns` is on
the 3D path, so `0` means matte however bright the scene, and a sprite that
never sets it renders exactly as it always did.

Three things worth knowing:

- **It needs a `normalMap`.** With no surface directions there is nothing to
  reflect, and the sprite stays matte whatever `shininess` says.
- **The normal map's alpha channel masks it per texel.** 255 is fully
  reflective, 0 is dead matte, so one sprite can be a shiny blade with a matte
  leather grip. A normal map with no alpha detail (the usual case) shines
  uniformly. Note the corollary: if your normal map already uses alpha for
  something, that channel now also decides gloss. The mask is in the **normal
  map's** alpha, never the colour image's: making the grip transparent there
  would hide it, not dull it.
- **It accumulates per light.** Each light contributes its own highlight in its
  own colour, so a sprite between a warm lamp and a cool one carries two
  distinct glints that move independently.

The highlight takes the light's own colour and is *added* on top of the lit
result rather than multiplied into it, which is why a glint blows out toward
white on a dark sprite instead of tinting with it.

### A matte texel still needs its direction

In a normal map the alpha is a material, not a hole. A texel with an alpha of 0
is matte, and is still shaded by the direction in its RGB. That direction has to
survive all the way to the GPU, and image tools are built to assume the opposite
(that nothing matters under a transparent pixel):

| the normal map comes from | directions under a low alpha |
|---|---|
| an image file through the loader (a PNG) | **kept**: the engine uploads normal maps with premultiplied alpha off |
| `createImageBitmap(source, { premultiplyAlpha: "none" })` | **kept**: the way to build a masked normal map in code |
| `createImageBitmap(source)`, default options | **wrong** as soon as the alpha is below 255: WebGL uploads a bitmap as it was made, so the directions arrive multiplied by the mask |
| a canvas you drew or `putImageData` into | **lost** at an alpha of 0, and rounded at a low one: a canvas stores its pixels multiplied by their alpha |

```js
// a masked normal map made in code: from pixels, never through a canvas
const pixels = new ImageData(width, height);
// ... rgb = the direction, a = how much it shines ...
sprite.normalMap = await createImageBitmap(pixels, { premultiplyAlpha: "none" });
```

Before the file reaches the game, the same goes for the pipeline: an optimiser
or a packer that "cleans" or "bleeds" the colour of fully transparent pixels, or
that premultiplies, erases the directions of every matte texel. Export the
normal sheet with those options off, and with the same layout as the colour one.

See it running: [Normal Map example](https://melonjs.github.io/melonJS/examples/#/normal-map).

Unlit areas of a normal-mapped sprite render pure black unless you raise
`Stage.ambientLightingColor` (default black) — that is the base level added to
every lit pixel, and it is a different knob from `Stage.ambientLight`.

Without a normal map a sprite is not shaded at all: it takes the unlit path on
every backend, and a light changes how it looks only through its additive glow
and its cutout in the ambient darkness.

## What needs a GPU backend, and what does not

Less than you would expect. `Light2d` is renderer-agnostic: it just calls
`renderer.drawLight(this)`, and every backend implements it — the GPU backends
through a shared procedural radial-falloff shader, the Canvas renderer by
rasterising a cached `Gradient` into one shared render target and compositing it
with `drawImage`. The hard ambient cutout pass is plain `setMask` + `fillRect`;
the soft one is one shader pass on the GPU backends and an offscreen canvas on
Canvas. So the lit-spot look, soft or hard, works everywhere, Canvas included.

What Canvas cannot do is **per-pixel normal-map lighting**:
`renderer.setLightUniforms()` is a no-op there, and the first normal-mapped
sprite drawn while lights are on logs a one-shot warning (a scene with lights
and no normal maps stays quiet). Normal-mapped sprites simply render unlit — no
error.

```js
if (app.renderer.shaderLanguage === null) {
    // Canvas fallback: lights and ambient still work, but `normalMap` is ignored
}
```

## Do not combine with `Camera3d`

`Camera3d` extends `Camera2d` and therefore still runs the 2D lighting pass, but
nothing in that pass is projection-aware: the ambient fill is a screen-space
`fillRect`, the cutout is a 2D `Ellipse` mask, and light positions are packed as
2D world coordinates minus the camera translate. Under a perspective projection
none of that lines up with what the camera actually draws.

For 3D scenes use `Light3d` instead — it is the counterpart for the mesh
lighting path, with `"directional"`, `"ambient"`, `"point"` and `"spot"` types.
See the `melonjs-3d` skill.

## Symptom → cause

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| lights added but the scene never darkens | no ambient colour set — `ambientLight` alpha is 0, so the pass returns early |
| the lit area has a hard rim | `softness` is 0 (the default): set it on the light |
| the darkness opens no wider than the glow | the hole is the light's size: add a bigger `illuminationOnly` light for the opening |
| a minimap or second camera is dark too | every camera draws the stage's darkness: override `drawLighting` and skip that camera |
| a light should show in one camera only | put it on a `visibilityLayer` the other camera's `cullMask` leaves out |
| sprite not shaded by a light, only glowed over | no `normalMap` on the sprite, or the Canvas backend is active |
| normal-mapped sprite is pure black where unlit | `Stage.ambientLightingColor` left at black |
| the 33rd light shades nothing | `MAX_LIGHTS = 32` for the normal-map pipeline |
| changing `radiusX` / `radiusY` does nothing | everything is sized from the bounds, which `setRadii()` updates and a bare field write does not |
| normal-mapped relief looks flat under a light | `lightHeight` is high relative to the radius; lower it for a grazing light |
| `TypeError` assigning `normalMap` | not an image-like value (a video element is rejected outright) |
| the whole sprite glints, not just the metal | the normal map is opaque, which is a full mask: paint the matte parts with a lower alpha in the **normal map** |
| `shininess` is set and nothing glints | no `normalMap`, an alpha of 0 over the whole normal map, the light behind the surface, or the Canvas backend |
| the matte part of a sprite (normal alpha 0) is black, or lit from the wrong side | its directions were erased: an optimiser cleared the colour of transparent pixels, or the map came from a canvas or from `createImageBitmap` with its default options. Load the file as it was exported, or build it with `premultiplyAlpha: "none"` |
| an animated sprite's shading does not follow its pose | the normal sheet is not laid out like the colour sheet: same size, same frames in the same places |
| lighting misaligned under a 3D camera | the 2D light pass is not projection-aware — use `Light3d` |

## Related skills

- `melonjs-3d` — `Light3d` for perspective scenes
- `melonjs-sprites-and-animation` — sprite settings and atlases
