// the adapter is chosen at construction …
const app = new Application(800, 600, {
    parent: "screen",
    physic: await PlanckAdapter.create({ gravity, pixelsPerMeter }),
});

// … the plugin is registered once the renderer exists
await app.init();
plugin.register(DebugPanelPlugin, "debugPanel");
```

## `register` in detail

```js
plugin.register(PluginClass, "name", ...constructorArgs);
plugin.cache.name;              // the instance
plugin.get(PluginClass);        // by class — or by registered name string
```

- **The name is optional** — it falls back to the class name.
- **The registry is global, not per-application.** It is a module-level object,
  so registering the same name twice throws `plugin <name> already registered`.
  A plugin *instance* does hold an `app` reference, but it defaults to `game` —
  **whichever Application most recently finished `init()`**, since that is where
  `game` is assigned. On a multi-application page, pass the app explicitly
  through the constructor args:
  `plugin.register(DebugPanelPlugin, "debugPanel", input.KEY.S, myApp)`.
- **`BasePlugin.version` is a floor, not an identity.** It declares the
  *minimum melonJS version the plugin needs*, and `register` throws
  `Plugin version mismatch, expected: <floor>, got: <engine>` when the running
  engine is older. That gate is the real enforcement — a peer-dependency range
  only warns at install time, and not at all for CDN or pre-bundled use. If you
  see that error, upgrade the engine or pin an older plugin. The check runs
  *after* the instance is constructed, so a plugin whose constructor has side
  effects will already have run them when it throws.

Register after `await app.init()`: a plugin binds to an Application and reads
renderer and frame state that does not exist before init.

## The official plugins

### `@melonjs/debug-plugin`

An in-game panel — frame time, draw and object counts — plus toggles for
hitbox/bounding-box overlays, velocity vectors and quadtree visualisation. The
first thing to reach for when something is slow or a collision is not landing
where you expect.

```js
import { DebugPanelPlugin } from "@melonjs/debug-plugin";
plugin.register(DebugPanelPlugin, "debugPanel");   // default toggle key: S
```

### `@melonjs/tiled-inflate-plugin`

**Required**, not optional, for Tiled maps using gzip, zlib or zstd layer
compression. It installs the inflate hook `TMXUtils` calls; without it a
compressed `.tmx` fails to parse — a map that opens fine in Tiled and refuses to
load in melonJS is nearly always this.

```js
import { TiledInflatePlugin } from "@melonjs/tiled-inflate-plugin";
plugin.register(TiledInflatePlugin);
```

### `@melonjs/spine-plugin`

Spine 4.x skeletal animation as a melonJS renderable, on all three backends.
This is the answer for deforming animated characters — glTF import does not read
vertex skinning. It also registers a Tiled object class, so Spine skeletons can
be placed from a map.

```js
import Spine, { SpinePlugin } from "@melonjs/spine-plugin";

await app.init();
plugin.register(SpinePlugin);   // after init: it reads app.renderer
// preloaded as { name: "hero.atlas", type: "spine", src: … }, and the same for
// "hero.json" (a binary "hero.skel" also goes in jsonFile)
const hero = new Spine(100, 100, { atlasFile: "hero.atlas", jsonFile: "hero.json" });
```

Register it after `await app.init()` like any plugin: its constructor builds
an asset manager on the application's renderer, which does not exist before.

### `@melonjs/gamepad-plugin`

On-screen touch controls, reported as a gamepad: one or two sticks and any
number of buttons, drawn over the game and read by the engine as a pad in a
gamepad slot. The game's `bindGamepad` bindings drive it unchanged, so one set
of bindings covers a real pad and a touch screen.

```js
import { GamepadPlugin } from "@melonjs/gamepad-plugin";
plugin.register(GamepadPlugin, "gamepad", {
    buttons: [{ label: "A" }, { label: "B" }],
});
// plugin.cache.gamepad.visible — showing, to word prompts ("tap" or a key)
```

Shown on touch screens by default (`enabled`), hidden while a real pad is in
use. The left stick also presses the D-pad; a button can press a key instead
of a pad button. Since 1.1 a stick or button can be `floating` (shows up
under the finger anywhere in its `area`), `hideAtRest` (drawn only while
held), and a stick can take a `tap` (a quick touch that does not steer presses
a key or button) — so the mobile layouts, two thumbs or one thumb with
tap-to-act, need no code of their own. Since 1.2 a `skin` texture atlas draws
them from the game's own art (`base` / `thumb` regions on a stick, `region` /
`pressed` on a button). It needs melonJS 20.12 or later. See `melonjs-input`
for the bindings, the layouts and the overlap rules.

### `@melonjs/pathfinding-plugin`

A* on a grid of open and solid cells, each with a weight to cross. The grid
is the part to get right; the search is one call:

```js
import { Grid } from "@melonjs/pathfinding-plugin";

// a layer of walls: a tile makes its cell solid (a tile's `weight` property, or attribute, sets its weight)
const grid = Grid.fromTileLayer(app.world.getChildByName("walls")[0]);
// a floor layer: decide from the tile instead
Grid.fromTileLayer(floor, { solid: (tile) => tile === null || isWall(tile) });
// or the level's collision shapes (WORLD_SHAPE bodies, a Tiled collision layer)
Grid.fromBodies(app.world, { cols, rows, tileWidth, tileHeight });

grid.diagonalMode = "onlyIfNoObstacles";    // never cut a corner past a wall
grid.getIdPath(fromCell, toCell);           // cells (Vector2d, x the column)
grid.getPointPath(fromCell, toCell);        // world points (cell centre + grid.offset)
const { path, found } = grid.findPath(enemy.pos, player.pos, {
    smooth: true,                // straight lines across open ground
    maxNodes: 300,               // a cap, so an unreachable goal cannot stall a frame
    allowPartialPath: true,      // unreachable: the way to the nearest cell (found false)
    avoid: others.map((o) => o.pos), avoidWeight: 6,   // spread out, this search only
});
// path[0] is the start: head for path[1]
```

The plugin keeps a grid for each level loaded, so a game that gets its grid
from the level never builds one by hand:

```js
import { PathfindingPlugin } from "@melonjs/pathfinding-plugin";

// from the "walls" tile layer, or (no `layer`) from the collision shapes;
// `subdivide` cuts each tile into 4 x 4 cells (1.1+), for doorways narrower
// than a tile
plugin.register(PathfindingPlugin, "pathfinding", { subdivide: 4 });

// once a level is loaded (null for a level it could not build a grid for)
const grid = plugin.cache.pathfinding.grid;

// a door opens: a body that collides with nothing is no wall (1.1+)
door.body.setCollisionMask(collision.types.NO_OBJECT);
grid.refresh();
```

Following a path is the game's part. Walk to each point in turn, and when the
agent stops getting closer (its body caught on a corner the point-sized path
runs past), find a new path from where it stands:

```js
update(dt) {
    const next = this.route[0];
    if (next) {
        const d = next.distance(this.pos);
        if (d < SPEED * 1.5) {
            this.route.shift();                          // reached: on to the next
            this.closest = Infinity;
        } else if (d < this.closest - 0.5) {
            this.closest = d; this.stuck = 0;            // getting there
        } else if (++this.stuck > 12) {
            this.route = grid.findPath(this.pos, this.destination,
                { smooth: true, diagonalMode: "onlyIfNoObstacles" }).path.slice(1);
            this.closest = Infinity; this.stuck = 0;     // a new way from here
        }
        // ... set the velocity toward route[0]
    }
    return super.update(dt);
}
```

- **The grid is a snapshot.** A tile changed with `setTile` / `clearTile`, or
  a wall body added, is not seen until `grid.refreshCell(col, row)` or
  `grid.refresh()`; `setSolid` / `setWeight` (and `fillSolidRegion` /
  `fillWeightRegion`) change cells directly.
- **`fromTileLayer` makes every non-empty cell solid by default** (a walls
  layer). On a floor layer, where every cell has a tile, pass `solid`, or
  everything is solid.
- **Paths include the start**, and are empty when the goal cannot be reached
  unless `allowPartialPath` is set.
- **Build `fromBodies` after the level loads.** It scans the shapes, not a
  physics query, so it works before the world first steps; it reads `bodyDef`
  shapes too, so it is the same on every adapter.
- **The walls are `WORLD_SHAPE` bodies that collide with something.** The
  type and the mask are read from the live body before its `bodyDef` (which
  keeps what it was written with), so a door opened with
  `body.setCollisionMask(collision.types.NO_OBJECT)` is open after
  `grid.refresh()`, with no `solid` callback. Before 1.1 it stayed a wall.
  Pass `solid: (renderable) => ...` for any other rule.
- **Walls off the tile grid need smaller cells.** A doorway narrower than a
  tile, between walls part of a tile deep, is closed on a grid of whole
  tiles: `{ subdivide: 4 }` on the plugin, or smaller `tileWidth` /
  `tileHeight` for `fromBodies`. A search crosses `n` times more cells along
  a path, `n²` more in all, so subdivide no further than the walls need.
- **The grid sees an agent as a point**, and a smoothed path runs right along
  the walls: a body with width catches on corners. Find a new path from where
  it stands when it stops getting closer (above), rather than giving up.
- A weight is 1 or more and finite: block with `setSolid`, not `Infinity`.
- `PathfindingPlugin` builds the grid from `layer` (a tile layer's name),
  from the collision shapes without it (with `subdivide`), or with
  `build: (container) => grid`. It only rebuilds when a level loads (and at
  once if one is loaded): call `grid.refresh()` after the level changes, or
  `rebuild()` for a new grid. A `Grid` works on its own. On a level it cannot
  build for (staggered, hexagonal, or a bad `subdivide`) it warns and keeps
  `grid` null.
- `PathfindingDebug` draws solid and heavy cells, the cells a search looked
  at (`trace: true`) and the paths.
- **Isometric maps work**: `fromTileLayer` and the plugin (from a layer or
  the shapes) see an isometric map and lay the cells out as diamonds; for
  `new Grid` or `fromBodies`, pass `cellShape: "isometric"`. Staggered and hexagonal maps are not
  supported (`fromTileLayer` throws).

### `@melonjs/capacitor-plugin`

Bridges Capacitor's native lifecycle and hardware-back events into the engine:

```js
import { CapacitorPlugin } from "@melonjs/capacitor-plugin";
plugin.register(CapacitorPlugin, "capacitor", options);
// plugin.cache.capacitor.teardown()  — detach every listener
```

It also exports helpers usable on their own: `onBackButton`, `bindStageBack`,
`lockOrientation` / `unlockOrientation`, `hideSplash`. See `melonjs-platforms`
for native apps and the other platforms.

With `pauseOnBackground` (the default), going to the background pauses the
game and coming back resumes it, but only if this pause was the plugin's: a
game the player had paused stays paused.

## Physics adapters

`@melonjs/planck-adapter`, `@melonjs/matter-adapter` and
`@melonjs/rapier2d-adapter` swap the physics world wholesale, and
`@melonjs/rapier3d-adapter` does it for a `Camera3d` game whose bodies turn in
3D (3D shapes only). Pick **one** per game (`app.world.setAdapter()` can switch it later). The portable surface — the
declarative `renderable.bodyDef`, `world.adapter.queryAABB(rect)` and
`world.adapter.raycast(from, to)` — works unchanged across the built-in world and
every adapter, so entity code does not have to branch. The exceptions are in
`melonjs-physics`: `Box3d`, `Sphere` and `Point` shapes are built-in only,
`type: "kinematic"` is planck and Rapier only, and the adapters' `queryAABB`
returns only renderables with a body. The Rapier adapter's WebAssembly loads
asynchronously, so it must be made with `await RapierAdapter.create()`.
`create()` is on every adapter from planck-adapter 1.7, matter-adapter 1.6 and
rapier2d-adapter 1.0 (an older planck or matter adapter is made with
`new X(options)`), and `world.setAdapter()` from melonJS 20.14.

Two queries are **not** portable: `querySphere` and `raycast3d` exist only on the
built-in and Rapier 3D adapters (planck, matter and Rapier 2D are 2D-only and
deliberately omit them).
`queryAABB` is the one region query every adapter must implement, so call the
others optionally — `app.world.adapter.querySphere?.(center, radius)`. For rays
there is a real flag: `app.world.adapter.capabilities.raycasts3d`.

Behaviour genuinely differs: velocity units, force magnitudes and where a body's
position is measured from all change. See `melonjs-physics`.

## Writing your own

There is **no `init()` lifecycle hook** — the constructor is where setup goes,
and `register` instantiates it for you.

```js
import { plugin, event } from "melonjs";

class MyPlugin extends plugin.BasePlugin {
    constructor(app = undefined) {
        super(app);              // stores it as this.app
        this.version = "20.0.0"; // MINIMUM engine version this needs
        event.on(event.GAME_UPDATE, () => { /* … */ });
    }
}

plugin.register(MyPlugin, "myPlugin");
```

`this.version` defaults to the running engine version, which means it always
passes — set it deliberately to the oldest version you actually support.

To wrap an existing engine method, `plugin.patch` keeps the original reachable
as `this._patched()`:

```js
plugin.patch(app, "update", function (time) {
    const result = this._patched(time);
    return result;
});
```

`patch` takes a class *or* an instance: given a constructor it patches the
prototype (that is how the debug plugin decorates `Renderable.postDraw`), given a
plain object it patches that object. `this._patched` is only bound for the
synchronous duration of your replacement — it is set before the call and nulled
straight after — so call it inline, never after an `await`.

```js
plugin.patch(Renderable, "postDraw", function (renderer) {
    this._patched(renderer);
    // draw an overlay on top of every renderable
});
```

A plugin is the right shape when you need to augment engine classes or hook the
engine lifecycle globally. For anything that is just game code, a `Renderable`
or a `Stage` is simpler and easier to test.

## Symptom → cause

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| `plugin <name> already registered` | the registry is global; registered twice, often across hot reloads |
| `Plugin version mismatch` | the plugin's `version` floor is above the running engine |
| `Plugin should extend the BasePlugin Class !` | the class does not extend `plugin.BasePlugin` |
| the panel reports another app's numbers | `app` defaulted to `game`, the last Application to finish `init()` |
| `world.adapter.querySphere is not a function` | built-in and Rapier 3D adapters only; planck, matter and Rapier 2D are 2D-only |
| a Tiled map opens in Tiled but not melonJS | compressed layers, tiled-inflate plugin missing |
| a path goes through walls | the grid does not know them: a floor layer needs `solid`, a changed tile needs `refreshCell`, `fromBodies` walls must be `WORLD_SHAPE` bodies (or pass `solid`) |
| a path cuts across a wall corner | `diagonalMode` is `"always"` or `"atLeastOneWalkable"`: use `"onlyIfNoObstacles"` |
| no path found (empty path, `found` false) | the goal is walled off, solid, or past `maxNodes`; `allowPartialPath: true` returns the way to the nearest point |
| everything is solid on a `fromTileLayer` grid | a floor layer, where every cell has a tile: pass `solid` |
| an agent turns back at the start | `path[0]` is where it stands: head for `path[1]` |
| an opened door still blocks the path | pathfinding-plugin < 1.1 counted it a wall (it read the `bodyDef`, and ignored the mask): upgrade, and `grid.refresh()` once it opens |
| every doorway is closed on the grid | doorways narrower than a cell: `subdivide` on the plugin |
| searches got slow after `subdivide` | `n` times finer is `n²` times the cells: subdivide no further than the walls need, or cap with `maxNodes` |
| an agent stops at a wall corner | it is not a point: on getting no closer, find a new path from where it stands |
| a path is offset from an isometric map | the grid is square: `new Grid` / `fromBodies` without `cellShape: "isometric"` |
| `plugin.cache.pathfinding.grid` is null, with a warning | a staggered or hexagonal level, `layer` names no layer of it, or `subdivide` is not a whole number of 1 or more |
| a path is offset from the map | the grid's `x` / `y` are not the layer's: built before the layer was in its container, or the container moved since |
| plugin setup never runs | setup written in an `init()` method — there is no such hook |
| `Plugin should extend the BasePlugin Class !` when registering an adapter | adapters are a construction setting (or `world.setAdapter()`), not a plugin |
| `PlanckAdapter.create is not a function` (or `MatterAdapter`) | planck-adapter < 1.7 or matter-adapter < 1.6; upgrade, or `new PlanckAdapter(options)` |
| `TypeError` reading `renderer` from `plugin.register(SpinePlugin)` | registered before `await app.init()`; the plugin's `app` is still unset |
| physics behaves differently after adding an adapter | expected — units and force scales differ; re-tune |
| a Spine object slides off screen when the camera moves, or ignores its container (WebGL / WebGPU) | spine-plugin < 4.0.1 drew without the camera's and the parents' transform; upgrade |
| a Spine object ignores `setOpacity()` / `alpha` | spine-plugin < 4.0.1; upgrade |
| a game paused from its menu is running again after the app comes back from the background | capacitor-plugin < 1.0.1 resumed on every return; upgrade |
| touch controls miss the finger after browser zoom or a move to another screen | gamepad-plugin < 1.2.1; upgrade |

# Renderables, input and effects

> Subclassing `Renderable`, custom drawing, receiving pointer events, and
> applying post effects — with the traps that produce silently wrong output
> rather than an error.

Everything here is a **silent failure**: the code runs, nothing throws, and the
result is wrong. Those are the cases worth memorising, because nothing in the
type signatures warns you.

## 1. A custom `draw()` must position itself from `this.pos`

The renderer is **not** pre-translated to the renderable's position when `draw()`
is called. `Container.draw` translates by the *container's* own `pos` and then
calls `child.preDraw` / `draw` / `postDraw`; `preDraw` never translates by the
child's `pos`. Read `this.pos` and draw relative to it.

```js
class Marker extends Renderable {
    draw(renderer) {
        // ✗ draws at the parent container's origin, not at the marker
        renderer.fillRect(0, 0, this.width, this.height);

        // ✓
        renderer.fillRect(this.pos.x, this.pos.y, this.width, this.height);
    }
}
```

The symptom is an object that renders correctly at position (0, 0) and appears
stuck at the top-left as soon as you move it.

**Zero the anchor in custom-draw renderables.** `preDraw` does not translate to
`pos`, but it *does* apply the anchor offset `(-width * anchorPoint.x,
-height * anchorPoint.y)`. With the default centred anchor, drawing at
`this.pos` therefore lands half a size off:

```js
constructor(x, y, w, h) {
    super(x, y, w, h);
    this.anchorPoint.set(0, 0);   // ← or every custom draw is offset by -w/2, -h/2
}
```

## 2. `isKinematic` must be `false` to receive input or collisions

`Renderable.isKinematic` **defaults to `true`**, which means *"physics collision
and input events will not impact this renderable"*. A kinematic renderable is
skipped by the pointer-event dispatcher entirely.

```js
class Button extends Renderable {
    constructor(x, y) {
        super(x, y, 100, 40);
        this.isKinematic = false;          // ← required, or clicks never arrive
        input.registerPointerEvent("pointerdown", this, () => { /* … */ });
    }
}
```

The symptom is a handler that is registered, looks correct, and never fires.

Note that `Container`, `Camera2d`, `Draggable`, `DropTarget` and the `UI*`
elements set it to `false` for you, and so does giving a renderable a body (a
`bodyDef`, on every physics adapter, or a `Body`, which covers `Entity`) — so a
plain `Renderable` or `Sprite` subclass with no body is the case that catches
people. Before melonJS 20.14, matter-adapter 1.6.0 and planck-adapter 1.7.0,
only the built-in adapter cleared it: under matter or planck a renderable with
a `bodyDef` stayed kinematic and missed pointer events.

The same flag has a second, less obvious effect: it is also the opt-in to the
world **broadphase**. The quadtree/octree insert skips any child with
`isKinematic === true`, so body-less objects you want `adapter.queryAABB` /
`querySphere` to find need `isKinematic = false` as well. That is the built-in
adapter; the `queryAABB` of matter, planck and Rapier only ever returns
renderables with a body. The builtin
narrowphase likewise requires *both* partners to be non-kinematic.

## 3. Draw order: only `addChild(child, z)` works

There are three separate traps here and they compound.

```js
world.addChild(sprite, 10);   // ✓ the only reliable form
```

1. **`renderable.z` does not exist.** There is no `z` accessor anywhere on
   `Renderable` (nor on `Rect`/`Polygon` above it) — only `depth`, which proxies
   `pos.z`, and the container's default `sortOn: "z"` comparator reads `pos.z`.
   Writing `sprite.z = 100` creates an inert property that nothing reads: a
   HUD that sets `this.z = Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` draws on top only if it
   happens to be added last. (A `z` key in a `Sprite`/`ImageLayer` *settings*
   object is a different thing and is real — it assigns `pos.z` in the
   constructor — but trap 2 then overwrites it.)
2. **Setting `depth` *before* `addChild` is overwritten.** With `autoDepth` on
   (the default), `addChild` without an explicit `z` assigns
   `child.pos.z = children.length` after the push, discarding whatever you set.
3. **Setting `depth` *after* `addChild` does not reorder.** A `"z"` sort runs
   when a child is added (`autoSort`, deferred to the next tick), not when
   `pos.z` changes. If you must change it later, call `container.sort()`
   yourself, or use `moveToTop` / `moveUp` / `moveDown` / `moveToBottom`, which
   reorder the children themselves. (An `"x"` / `"y"` sort is different: see
   below.)

### Sorting on `"y"` (or `"x"`), and `sortOffset`

A container with `sortOn = "y"` draws its children from the smallest `pos.y` to
the largest, so whatever is lower on screen covers what is above it (top-down and
isometric games). `"x"` does the same along x. A different `pos.z` still decides
first, so keep the children that should interleave at one z.

- **Moving a child re-sorts by itself.** With `autoSort` on (the default), the
  container checks its order at the end of every update, after physics and the
  children's own updates, and re-sorts when anything is out of place: a walking
  character needs no `sort()` call. A frame where nothing moved costs one pass
  over the children and does not cause a redraw. Turn `autoSort` off to keep
  the children in the order you put them.
- **Ties keep insertion order, and the child added LAST is drawn BEHIND.** A
  torch placed at its wall's exact position disappears behind the wall.

`sortOffset` changes the ORDER only, never where anything is: the child is lined
up as if it stood that many pixels lower (positive) or higher (negative), and is
drawn exactly where it was. Use it when `pos` is not the point to sort by:

```js
torch.sortOffset = 1;                        // win the tie with the wall it hangs on
dust.sortOffset = door.pos.y - dust.pos.y;   // an emitter's pos is the top of its
                                             // spawn area: line it up with the door
prop.sortOffset = prop.height;               // sort by the bottom of the image
```

A container that keeps itself sorted picks a change up at its next update (with
`autoSort` off, call its `sort()`). `"z"` and `"depth"` sorting ignore it. It must be a finite number (a string
or `NaN` throws, rather than scrambling every sibling), and a pooled renderable
starts again at `0`.

The exception: under `Camera3d` the world's `sortOn` is `"depth"`, and the
camera calls `container.sortNow(true)` every frame. Note that mode does **not**
sort by `pos.z` as a layer index — it sorts by squared distance from the camera
in world space (nearest first in the array, painted far→near). So changing
`depth` does reorder there, but as a position change, not as a layer number.

```js
// ✗ overwritten by autoDepth
sprite.depth = 10;
world.addChild(sprite);

// ✗ no resort happens (except under Camera3d)
world.addChild(sprite);
sprite.depth = 10;

// ✓
world.addChild(sprite, 10);
```

## 4. `removePostEffect()` destroys the effect

To disable an effect temporarily, toggle it. Removing it frees its GPU
resources and leaves you holding a dead object.

```js
// ✗ effect is destroyed; re-adding it will not work
sprite.removePostEffect(effect);

// ✓
effect.enabled = false;
```

Exception worth knowing: an effect with `effect.shared === true` opts out of
auto-destroy, because it is reused across renderables.

Use `addPostEffect()` / `getPostEffect()` / `removePostEffect()`. Assigning
`renderable.shader = …` is deprecated since 19.2.0.

Post effects need a programmable pipeline. A `ShaderEffect` constructed against
the Canvas renderer (`renderer.shaderLanguage === null`) stays at
`enabled === false` and no-ops every method rather than throwing — and
`beginPostEffect` filters disabled effects out. The first one logs a warning,
the rest stay quiet, so a decorative effect needs no renderer check. Since `video.AUTO` picks the
backend at runtime, an effect that works on your machine may do nothing on
another.

## 5. Opacity cascades; `setChildsProperty` assigns

`alpha` composes down the tree. Fading a container fades everything inside
it, and the values multiply — a child at `0.5` inside a parent at `0.5` draws
at `0.25`. Each renderable keeps its own value; the composition happens at
draw time and is undone when the renderable is finished.

```js
model.alpha = 0.3;                             // fades the whole rig
container.setChildsProperty("alpha", 0.3, true); // REWRITES each child's alpha
```

The two are not interchangeable. `setChildsProperty` is a bulk assignment: it
changes what the children *are*, so their own `alpha` now reads `0.3` and
stays that way after the container goes back to full. Reach for it when you
mean to change the children, and for `alpha` when you mean to fade a subtree.

Do not assign alpha down a hierarchy by hand. The renderer composes it as it
walks the tree, so setting it at more than one level multiplies: in a rig
nested three deep, `0.3` applied at every level lands parts on `0.3`, `0.09`
and `0.027` depending where they sit. The symptom does not look like an
opacity problem — a model whose parts hold *different* opacities, and which
appears to change opacity as it turns, because turning changes which parts
face the camera.

A useful consequence: a `GLTFModel` is a `Container`, so `model.alpha` fades
every part of a loaded rig — which is what you want for a ghost, a fade-in,
or a reflection.

## 6. `Vector3d.set(x, y)` silently zeroes `z`

```js

v.set(10, 20, v.z);   // keep it
```

`pos` is an `ObservableVector3d`, whose `set(x = 0, y = 0, z = 0)` does the same
— so `this.pos.set(x, y)` wipes the object's depth.

`Renderable#setPosition(x, y, z?)` is the renderable-level form and does not:

reference without recycling it: the same instance may still be masking
something else, so the engine has no claim on it. If you pool masks, release

could not be destroyed or removed without keepalive at all.

## Update and draw

```js

```

`obj.alwaysUpdate === true`. An off-screen object with the default
`alwaysUpdate = false` does not tick at all.

unless it has a size of its own (`resize`) or `enableChildBoundsUpdate` is on.

and, while the group is off screen, before each culling check — so a squad that

at a point (screen pixels for a floating one). A clip inside a clip shows
their overlap, on WebGL and WebGPU as on Canvas.

  forces `(0, 0)`. Mixing them up shifts children by half their size.

# Renderables, input and effects

> Subclassing `Renderable`, custom drawing, receiving pointer events, and
> applying post effects — with the traps that produce silently wrong output
> rather than an error.

Everything here is a **silent failure**: the code runs, nothing throws, and the
result is wrong. Those are the cases worth memorising, because nothing in the
type signatures warns you.

## 1. A custom `draw()` must position itself from `this.pos`

The renderer is **not** pre-translated to the renderable's position when `draw()`
is called. `Container.draw` translates by the *container's* own `pos` and then
calls `child.preDraw` / `draw` / `postDraw`; `preDraw` never translates by the
child's `pos`. Read `this.pos` and draw relative to it.

```js
class Marker extends Renderable {
    draw(renderer) {
        // ✗ draws at the parent container's origin, not at the marker
        renderer.fillRect(0, 0, this.width, this.height);

        // ✓
        renderer.fillRect(this.pos.x, this.pos.y, this.width, this.height);
    }
}
```

The symptom is an object that renders correctly at position (0, 0) and appears
stuck at the top-left as soon as you move it.

**Zero the anchor in custom-draw renderables.** `preDraw` does not translate to
`pos`, but it *does* apply the anchor offset `(-width * anchorPoint.x,
-height * anchorPoint.y)`. With the default centred anchor, drawing at
`this.pos` therefore lands half a size off:

```js
constructor(x, y, w, h) {
    super(x, y, w, h);
    this.anchorPoint.set(0, 0);   // ← or every custom draw is offset by -w/2, -h/2
}
```

`Renderable.isKinematic` **defaults to `true`**, which means *"physics collision
and input events will not impact this renderable"*. A kinematic renderable is
skipped by the pointer-event dispatcher entirely.

```js

    constructor(x, y) {
        super(x, y, 100, 40);
        this.isKinematic = false;          // ← required, or clicks never arrive
        input.registerPointerEvent("pointerdown", this, () => { /* … */ });
    }

```

The symptom is a handler that is registered, looks correct, and never fires.

Note that `Container`, `Camera2d`, `Draggable`, `DropTarget` and the `UI*`
elements set it to `false` for you, and so does giving a renderable a body (a
`bodyDef`, on every physics adapter, or a `Body`, which covers `Entity`) — so a
plain `Renderable` or `Sprite` subclass with no body is the case that catches
people. Before melonJS 20.14, matter-adapter 1.6.0 and planck-adapter 1.7.0,
only the built-in adapter cleared it: under matter or planck a renderable with
a `bodyDef` stayed kinematic and missed pointer events.

The same flag has a second, less obvious effect: it is also the opt-in to the
world **broadphase**. The quadtree/octree insert skips any child with
`isKinematic === true`, so body-less objects you want `adapter.queryAABB` /
`querySphere` to find need `isKinematic = false` as well. That is the built-in
adapter; the `queryAABB` of matter, planck and Rapier only ever returns
renderables with a body. The builtin
narrowphase likewise requires *both* partners to be non-kinematic.

## 3. Draw order: only `addChild(child, z)` works

There are three separate traps here and they compound.

```js
world.addChild(sprite, 10);   // ✓ the only reliable form
```

1. **`renderable.z` does not exist.** There is no `z` accessor anywhere on
   `Renderable` (nor on `Rect`/`Polygon` above it) — only `depth`, which proxies
   `pos.z`, and the container's default `sortOn: "z"` comparator reads `pos.z`.

   happens to be added last. (A `z` key in a `Sprite`/`ImageLayer` *settings*

   constructor — but trap 2 then overwrites it.)
2. **Setting `depth` *before* `addChild` is overwritten.** With `autoDepth` on

   `child.pos.z = children.length` after the push, discarding whatever you set.
3. **Setting `depth` *after* `addChild` does not reorder.** A `"z"` sort runs

   `pos.z` changes. If you must change it later, call `container.sort()`
   yourself, or use `moveToTop` / `moveUp` / `moveDown` / `moveToBottom`, which
   reorder the children themselves. (An `"x"` / `"y"` sort is different: see
   below.)

### Sorting on `"y"` (or `"x"`), and `sortOffset`

A container with `sortOn = "y"` draws its children from the smallest `pos.y` to
the largest, so whatever is lower on screen covers what is above it (top-down and
isometric games). `"x"` does the same along x. A different `pos.z` still decides
first, so keep the children that should interleave at one z.

- **Moving a child re-sorts by itself.** With `autoSort` on (the default), the
  container checks its order at the end of every update, after physics and the
  children's own updates, and re-sorts when anything is out of place: a walking
  character needs no `sort()` call. A frame where nothing moved costs one pass
  over the children and does not cause a redraw. Turn `autoSort` off to keep
  the children in the order you put them.
- **Ties keep insertion order, and the child added LAST is drawn BEHIND.** A

up as if it stood that many pixels lower (positive) or higher (negative), and is
drawn exactly where it was. Use it when `pos` is not the point to sort by:

```js
torch.sortOffset = 1;                        // win the tie with the wall it hangs on

A container that keeps itself sorted picks a change up at its next update (with

sprite.depth = 10;

// ✗ no resort happens (except under Camera3d)
world.addChild(sprite);

```

# Renderer backends and graceful degradation

> `video.AUTO` picks a backend at **runtime**. The same code runs on a different
> renderer depending on the machine, and several subsystems degrade to nothing
> rather than erroring. This is the root cause of most "works on my machine"
> reports.

## The ladder

`video.AUTO` (the default) tries **WebGPU → WebGL 2 → Canvas** and uses the first
that initialises.

```js
const app = new Application(800, 600, {
    parent: "screen",
    renderer: video.AUTO,     // or video.WEBGPU / video.WEBGL / video.CANVAS
});
await app.init();
```

WebGL 1 is not in the ladder — 20.x made WebGL 2 the baseline, and pinning
`video.WEBGL` **rejects** on a WebGL-1-only device rather than degrading.

A GPU backend also counts as unavailable when the browser says it would run
far slower than native — a software rasterizer, a blocklisted driver. The
`failIfMajorPerformanceCaveat` setting (`true` by default, stricter than
WebGL's own default) refuses such a context, and the WebGPU backend refuses a
software adapter the same way: under `AUTO` that machine gets Canvas, and
under `video.WEBGL` or `video.WEBGPU` `init()` rejects. Set it `false` to accept
the slow context instead.

## What each backend can do

| | WebGPU | WebGL 2 | Canvas |
|---|---|---|---|
| sprites, tilemaps, text | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| blend modes | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ except `"none"` |
| shaders and post effects | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ inert |
| `Light2d` glow (`drawLight`) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ cached radial gradient |
| normal-map lighting, `Light3d` | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ inert |
| `Mesh` | ✅ | ✅ | ⚠️ last resort: 2D camera only, CPU-projected, no depth, unlit |
| `Camera3d` / depth sorting | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ warns, renders wrong |
| `InstancedMesh` | ✅ | ✅ | ⚠️ one draw per instance |
| GPU tilemap rendering | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ per-tile CPU path |
| `textureFilter: "linear-mipmap"` | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ no mipmaps |
| `hdr` (headroom through the effects) | ✅ | ✅ where the driver can render and filter half-float | ❌ |
| `hdrOutput` (HDR presentation) | ✅ with `hdr` on too | ❌ | ❌ |
| `state.transition("pixelate", …)` | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ the state changes with no transition |

The Canvas column is the problem: none of it throws. Most of those paths warn
once and then degrade or no-op, and some (the pixelate transition, `hdr`) do
so without a word, so the game runs and looks wrong.

Two Canvas rows are worth spelling out because they are easy to misread as total
failures. A `Light2d` still *draws* — the Canvas renderer bakes a radial gradient
per light and blits it — what disappears is per-pixel normal-map shading, which
warns once (`Light2d normal-map lighting requires a GPU backend`), the first time
a normal-mapped sprite is drawn under a light, and then renders sprites unlit. A `Mesh` under a 2D camera still draws too, textured,
sorted with the painter's algorithm and no depth buffer, so convex models look
right and a self-overlapping one can draw a few triangles over the wrong ones.
That is a last resort so a game does not go blank, not a target: anything
built on meshes should run on WebGPU or WebGL 2. `"none"` (replace, alpha included) is the one blend
mode Canvas cannot express — there is no `globalCompositeOperation` that
disables blending for the drawn area alone — so it resolves to `"normal"`, and
`setBlendMode` reports that back.

```js
app.renderer.type;                    // "WebGPU" | "WebGL2" | "CANVAS"
app.renderer.supportsDepthBuffer;     // the practical "is this a GPU backend" test
app.renderer.shaderLanguage;          // "wgsl" | "glsl" | null (null on Canvas)
```

There are narrower flags for the features that do not travel together:
`supportsShaderTileLayers`, `supportsRetainedMesh` and `supportsInstancing` —
all three `false` on Canvas, `true` on both GPU backends. `supportsHDR` and
`supportsHDROutput` say what the `hdr` and `hdrOutput` settings were actually
granted, which can be less than was asked. Prefer a capability
flag over comparing `type` against a string; `type` is an identity check for
code coupled to one backend's machinery.

For a scene that genuinely requires a GPU backend, fail loudly rather than
rendering something broken:

```js
await app.init();

    throw new Error("this game needs WebGL 2 or WebGPU");
}
```

## Writing code that degrades well

**Decorative effects** — let them no-op. A missing vignette is fine.

**Load-bearing effects** — guard the carrier. If a shader draws your content
rather than decorating it, the carrier renderable shows through raw when the
effect is disabled: a 1×1 white texture stretched to fill a quad renders as a
white box exactly where the effect should have been.

```js

    // draw the carrier the shader consumes
}
```

**Dual-language shaders** — a `ShaderEffect` compiles the body matching
`renderer.shaderLanguage`. With no matching body — a GLSL-only effect on WebGPU,
any effect on Canvas — the constructor warns once, leaves `enabled === false`,
and every method becomes a no-op. Pass `{ glsl, wgsl }` rather than a bare
string, or gate on `renderer.shaderLanguage`.

## Pinning a backend

Pin only with a reason. `video.WEBGL` costs you the WebGPU path *and* the Canvas
fallback, so a WebGL-1-only device gets nothing at all.

Legitimate reasons: reproducing a backend-specific bug, a benchmark, or a known
driver issue in the field.

For one-off testing you do not need to touch the settings at all: the URI
fragments `#webgpu`, `#webgl` (or `#webgl2`) and `#canvas` override the
`renderer` setting for that run, and behave exactly like passing the matching
constant — `#webgl` on a WebGL-1-only device rejects rather than falling back.

## Context loss

A GPU context can be lost at any time — tab backgrounding, driver reset, memory
pressure. melonJS handles restoration on both GPU backends: WebGL recompiles
every live `GLShader` and replays its uniform snapshot, WebGPU renegotiates a
device and rebuilds its batchers, and both then emit
`event.ONCONTEXT_RESTORED` (the paired loss event is `event.ONCONTEXT_LOST`).

What you must handle is your own GPU-side state. If you cached a raw texture or
program handle, re-acquire it on restore rather than holding the stale one:

```js
import { event } from "melonjs";

event.on(event.ONCONTEXT_RESTORED, (renderer) => {
    // re-acquire anything you were holding by raw handle
});
```

## Test on the backend your users get, not the one your harness picks

`video.AUTO` prefers WebGPU where it exists. Headless Chromium usually has no
GPU adapter and falls back to WebGL, so an automated suite can pass every run
while the WebGPU path is broken — the two differ in real, throwing ways (see
below). Pin the backend explicitly when it matters: `renderer: video.WEBGPU`,
or the `#webgpu` / `#webgl` URI fragment on a page you can open by hand.

## Practical differences

- **Frame capture orientation differs**: row 0 of a `toFrameTexture()` capture is
  the bottom of the frame under WebGL and the *top* under WebGPU, so a GLSL body
  that flips with `1.0 - uv.y` must not do so in its WGSL twin. The WebGPU
  capture also preserves alpha, where the WebGL one captures into an opaque RGB
  texture.
- **The advanced blend modes cost far more than they look.** `overlay`,
  `difference`, `hard-light`, `soft-light`, `color-dodge`, `color-burn`,
  `darken` and `lighten` cannot be expressed as fixed-function blending, so on
  both GPU backends each such draw is bracketed individually: capture the
  destination, redraw offscreen, composite through `BlendEffect`. Fine for
  accents, ruinous for hundreds of objects. `normal`, `additive`, `multiply`,
  `screen` and `exclusion` are ordinary fixed-function state and cost nothing
  extra.
- **WebGPU rejects a zero-sized image source; WebGL shrugs at it.** Uploading a
  0-width or 0-height canvas throws
  `OperationError: GPUQueue.copyExternalImageToTexture: External image state is
  not valid`, from a stack that reads `drawImage → addQuad → getBinding`. WebGL
  uploads the same source without complaint, so this is a class of bug that
  cannot appear on one backend and stops the game dead on the other. Check
  any canvas the game sizes from content that can be empty before it is drawn.
  An empty or whitespace-only `Text` did this before 20.11; its glyph canvas
  is now at least 32 pixels on each side.
- **3D meshes do not honour the advanced blend modes.** The mesh pass draws
  with its own depth/blend state; asking for one of them logs a one-time
  `blend mode "…" is not supported for 3D meshes` warning and falls back to
  `"normal"`. Gradient fills warn the same way.

## Symptom → cause

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| effect works locally, not for a user | they got the Canvas fallback, or a different GPU backend |
| sprites render unlit though lights are in the scene | Canvas fallback — normal-map shading is inert (check the console) |
| a few triangles of a mesh drawn over the wrong ones where it overlaps itself | Canvas fallback — painter's algorithm sorts whole triangles, no depth buffer |
| a mesh shows its far side through its near one (looks inside-out) on Canvas | melonJS older than 20.14 sorted the triangles the wrong way round; update |
| a textured OBJ + MTL mesh is a white silhouette on Canvas | melonJS older than 20.14 filled it with its material color and skipped the texture; update |
| a low-poly (palette) model looks faceted on Canvas, with faint lines between its triangles | melonJS older than 20.14 filled each of its triangles with one texel; update |
| shader works on one machine only | GLSL-only effect, AUTO chose WebGPU elsewhere — the console carries the warning |
| a solid box where an effect should be | carrier drawn while the effect is disabled |
| nothing renders at all on an old device | `video.WEBGL` pinned; WebGL 1 is rejected, not downgraded |
| ported shader is vertically flipped | the WebGL capture is bottom-up, the WebGPU one top-down |
| `copyExternalImageToTexture: External image state is not valid` | a zero-sized upload source: a canvas sized from empty content (an empty `Text` before 20.11) |
| Canvas renderer on a machine that has a GPU, or `init()` rejects with a pinned backend | software rendering or a blocklisted driver, refused by `failIfMajorPerformanceCaveat` (default `true`) |
| runs on the test machine, dies on the dev's | the harness fell back to WebGL and never exercised WebGPU |
| an advanced blend mode is ignored on a mesh | meshes fall back to `"normal"` for those; look for the one-time warning |
| textures vanish after the tab is restored | cached raw GPU handles not re-acquired on context restore |

- `melonjs-getting-started` — renderer selection in the Application settings
- `melonjs-effects-and-shaders` — dual-language shaders and the Canvas no-op
- `melonjs-3d` — the tier that requires a GPU backend outright

# Scenes, game state and timing

## Stages and the state manager

A `Stage` is a screen. Register it against a state id, then change to it:

```js
import { Stage, state } from "melonjs";

class PlayScreen extends Stage {
    onResetEvent(app) { /* build the scene */ }
    onDestroyEvent(app) { /* tear it down */ }
}

state.set(state.PLAY, new PlayScreen());   // register first
state.change(state.PLAY);                   // then switch
```

Built-in ids: `state.LOADING`, `state.MENU`, `state.READY`, `state.PLAY`,
`state.GAMEOVER` (no underscore), `state.GAME_END`, `state.SCORE`,
`state.CREDITS`, `state.SETTINGS`, `state.DEFAULT`. `state.USER` (100) is the
base for your own ids — `const CUTSCENE = state.USER + 1`.

**Build scene content in `onResetEvent`, not the constructor.** `onResetEvent`
runs on *every* entry to the state; the constructor runs once. Scene content
created in the constructor exists once and is not rebuilt when you return.

`onResetEvent(app)` receives the `Application` — use that rather than importing
the global `game`.

Extra arguments to `state.change` are forwarded:

```js
state.change(state.PLAY, false, { level: 2 });   // → onResetEvent(app, { level: 2 })
```

The second argument is `forceChange`: pass `true` to switch immediately instead
of on a deferred tick, which is what you want when changing state right after a
preload completes. It is ignored when a transition is configured — a transition
always drives the switch from its own completion callback.

`onResetEvent` runs when the switch is made. The first frame, `STATE_CHANGE` and
a transition's reveal follow once the shaders the stage queued are ready, which
is a few milliseconds once the browser has compiled them before, and at most
1.5s on a first visit. So build the stage in `onResetEvent`: an object a
`STATE_CHANGE` listener adds is not waited for, and its first draw may still
compile what it needs. That first frame steps the world once before drawing it,
however short it is, so everything `onResetEvent` added is in it (the same goes
for the frame after a `level.load` made while the game runs). Before 20.12 it
was drawn unstepped, and showed the stage's background alone for one frame.

`state.change` **throws** `Undefined Stage for state '<id>'` if nothing was
registered for that id, and `state.set` throws if the second argument is not a
`Stage` instance. Neither fails quietly.

A change to the state that is **already current does nothing**: no
`onDestroyEvent`, no `onResetEvent`, no transition. So a "Retry" that calls
`state.change(state.PLAY)` from `PLAY` is ignored. Build the current stage
again with `state.reload()` (since 20.16): `onDestroyEvent`, the world reset and
`onResetEvent`, with the arguments the state was entered with, or new ones.
`level.reload()` reloads just the Tiled map, keeping the stage.

```js
// "Play again" on the game-over card, from inside PLAY
new UITextButton(x, y, { text: "AGAIN", onClick: () => state.reload() });
// restart on another level: replaces the arguments for later reloads too
state.reload(false, { level: 2 });
```

Like `state.change`, it waits for the next frame unless `forceChange` is
`true`, and it throws when no state has been entered yet. It plays no
transition.

### Always leave `state.LOADING` — it is transitional

`loader.preload()` switches to `state.LOADING` for you. Building your scene in
the preload callback and then *staying there* looks like it works, and is one
of the easiest mistakes to make:

```js
// WRONG — the game now runs inside the loading stage, forever
loader.preload(assets, () => {
    app.world.addChild(new Player(...));
});
```

Nothing ever destroys that stage, so the built-in loading screen's logo and
progress bar are never removed and sit on top of your game. (Eight of this
repository's own examples did this before it was noticed, so it is not an
obscure trap.)

Give the scene a stage of its own and switch to it:

```js
class PlayScreen extends Stage {
    onResetEvent(app) {
        app.world.addChild(new Player(...));
    }
}

await loader.preload(assets);
state.set(state.PLAY, new PlayScreen());
state.change(state.PLAY);
```

The awaited form reads better here than the callback, because "load, then
switch" is exactly what the code then says. If you genuinely want to keep using
the loading stage as your scene, `state.change(state.DEFAULT)` at least gets
you out of it — but a stage of your own is what you want.

## Persistent objects across levels

```js
if (typeof this.HUD === "undefined") {
    this.HUD = new Container();         // construct once (or UIBaseElement)
}
this.HUD.isPersistent = true;           // survives level changes
this.HUD.floating = true;               // screen coordinates, not world
app.world.addChild(this.HUD, 100);      // explicit z — see melonjs-renderables
```

Everything inside a persistent container is kept with it, physics bodies
included (before 20.13 the children's bodies were dropped by the reset).

## Transitions and pausing

```js
state.transition("fade", "#FFFFFF", 250);
state.transition("mask", "#000", 500, new Ellipse(0, 0, 1, 1));  // shape required
state.transition("mask", "#000", 500, "star_mask");          // a preloaded image's silhouette
state.transition("mask", "#000", 500, player, { center: player }); // the player's shape, closing on it
state.transition("mask", "#000", 400, new Ellipse(0, 0, 1, 1), { center: player, invert: true });
state.transition("pixelate", "#000", 300);  // blocks up to 32px; a 4th argument sets the size
state.pause();                               // freeze update, keep drawing
state.resume();
app.freeze(150);                             // brief hit-stop (proxies state.freeze)
```

`state.transition` is global and sticky — once set it applies to every later
`state.change`; `state.setTransition(id, false)` turns it off for changes
into one state.
The duration (1000 ms when omitted) is for each half: the cover, then the
reveal. The `"mask"` form needs its fourth argument, the shape: an `Ellipse`
or `Polygon` (unit-sized, centred on the origin), an image or the name of a
preloaded one (its silhouette: transparent pixels are covered, the rest shows
the scene; colours do not matter and gaps inside the outline are filled), or a
`Sprite` (the silhouette of the frame it shows, facing its way). Without a
shape it warns and falls back to a direct switch. Its fifth argument is
`{ center, invert }`: `center` is where the shape closes and the reveal opens,
a renderable (where it is drawn on screen as the transition starts) or a
screen point, the centre of the screen by default; `invert: true` makes the
shape the cover, filled with the colour and growing out of `center`. The
shape grows about its thickest part (a U or a sprite drawn off-centre in its
frame too), until the screen is wholly inside it, so the reveal ends with the
scene uncovered.

A sprite or renderable given here is read when the transition starts, and
the reveal reuses what the hide read, so the old stage destroying the player
in between is fine. Whether it is kept depends on whose it is:

- **a sprite the game keeps for itself** (never added to a level, such as
  `atlas.createSpriteFromName("logo")`, or a persistent one in the world): set
  it once, it shapes every change, with the frame it shows by then.
- **a sprite that is part of the level** (the player): the change destroys it,
  so it is let go after that one transition, and later changes are an iris on
  the centre of the screen until you set it again. Give it this level's
  player right before each `state.change`.

```js
// once, at startup: every change wears the logo
state.transition("mask", "#000", 500, atlas.createSpriteFromName("logo"));

// before each change: this level's player
state.transition("mask", "#000", 500, player, { center: player });
state.change(state.GAME_END);
```

The `"pixelate"` form breaks the screen up into blocks (its fourth argument is the
largest block size in pixels; the color is not used). It is a shader effect,
so on Canvas it does nothing and the state changes directly.

A level change is not a state change, so `state.transition` does not apply to
it. A Tiled `Trigger` that loads a level has a transition of its own, set on
the trigger: `color` and `duration` (both needed, or the level loads with
none), and `transition: "fade"` (the default) or `"mask"` with a `shape`,
plus `center` and `invert` as above. On a trigger, `shape: "touching"` and
`center: "touching"` mean whoever walked in: the player's own silhouette
closing on the player, with no code to find it. A `"mask"` without a `shape`
fades instead, without a warning, and there is no pixelate form for a
trigger. See `melonjs-tilemaps`.

A `state.change` asked for while a transition covers the screen (Enter pressed
twice on a menu, a timer firing as the player skips a screen) needs no guard:
the transition already under way makes it, switching to the last state asked
for with the last arguments, and a second cover never goes up. A change to a
state with no transition of its own (`state.setTransition(id, false)`) is made
at once, and the cover comes down with it. Before 20.12 the second change left
the first cover on the camera for good, the screen black over a running game.

### A Stage's own `update()` is NOT paused

This one is easy to get wrong and hard to see. `Application.update` calls both
of these **unconditionally**:

```js
this.isDirty = this.world.update(this.updateDelta);
this.isDirty = state.current().update(this.updateDelta) || this.isDirty;
```

Only `Container.update` consults the pause — it reads `state.isPaused()` and
skips every child that is not `updateWhenPaused`. So world children (entities,
sprites, meshes, a `GLTFModel`) freeze correctly, while **the Stage subclass's
own `update()` keeps running**. (`event.GAME_UPDATE` is not emitted while
paused, so logic hung off it stops with the world.)

A game that keeps its logic in entities pauses for free and never notices. A
game that drives the simulation from `Stage.update` — common for an endless
runner, where one object moves and the world scrolls past it — keeps simulating
through `pauseOnBlur` with its world frozen. The signature is bizarre and very
misleading: the scenery scrolls on, the player character stands still in world
space and slides off the screen, and it all snaps back on focus. It reads as a
culling or animation bug, not a pause bug.

Guard it explicitly:

```js
update(dt) {
    super.update(dt);
    if (state.isPaused()) {
        return true;        // world children are already frozen for you
    }
    // …simulation…
}
```

Worth knowing that `pauseOnBlur` (default `true`) fires on a window `blur`, not
only on tab `visibilitychange` — so clicking another window on the same screen
triggers it while the canvas is still fully visible.

On focus, `resumeOnFocus` (default `true`) undoes only the pause the
application applied on blur. A game the player paused from its own menu stays
paused when the window comes back; before 20.9 it resumed underneath the menu.

**Who reports the focus, and what the game does.** Two separate settings:

| setting | decides | default |
|---|---|---|
| `device.setFocusEvents()` | **who** reports that the player switched away: the browser window (`blur`, `focus`, `visibilitychange` become `event.BLUR` / `event.FOCUS`), or nobody, leaving it to the game's host | the window |
| `app.pauseOnBlur`, `stopOnBlur`, `resumeOnFocus` | **what** the game does on every `event.BLUR` / `event.FOCUS`, wherever it comes from | pause on blur, resume on focus |

- **To keep the game running while the player is away**, turn the flags off
  (`app.pauseOnBlur = false`). The window still reports; nothing pauses.
- **To let a host decide when the game runs**, turn the window off and keep the
  flags. Turning the flags off would not do it: they cannot tell the window's
  `event.BLUR` from the host's, so the host's pause would do nothing either.

**When a host decides, not the window.** A game embedded by a host that says
when it runs, such as a web game portal's SDK (YouTube Playables forbids
pausing on the page's visibility) or a native wrapper, stops the window
reporting with `device.setFocusEvents(false)` and emits the engine's own
events from the host's callbacks:

```js
device.setFocusEvents(false);   // the window's blur, focus and visibilitychange no longer count
app.stopOnBlur = true;          // a pause stops drawing too; pauseOnBlur keeps drawing
app.pauseOnBlur = false;
ytgame.system.onPause(() => event.emit(event.BLUR));
ytgame.system.onResume(() => event.emit(event.FOCUS));
```

Everything else is as with the window: `pauseOnBlur`, `stopOnBlur` and
`resumeOnFocus` decide what happens, the sound effects are silenced and held
keys released, and only a pause the engine applied is undone. It can be called
before or after creating the application.

## The update loop

There is no loop you own. Logic goes in `update(dt)` overrides, or a
`GAME_UPDATE` subscription for scene-level animation:

```js
event.on(event.GAME_UPDATE, () => { /* per frame */ });
```

`update(dt)` must **return `true`** when the object changed and needs redrawing.
Returning nothing is falsy and the object can appear frozen while its state moves.

`dt` is milliseconds since the last frame and is the right basis for motion —
the engine already paces it. Do not reach for `performance.now()`.

**Smooth a value toward a target with `math.damp`, not with `lerp` per
frame.** `lerp(current, target, 0.1)` once per frame moves further on a slow
frame than on a fast one, so the feel drifts with the frame rate:

```js
this.speed = math.damp(this.speed, targetSpeed, 5, dt / 1000);
```

`damp(current, target, lambda, dt)` takes SECONDS, so divide `dt`. Higher
`lambda` converges faster. See `melonjs-camera-and-drawing` for the camera's
own `follow()` damping, which is already frame-rate independent for you.

A common idiom for a per-frame game controller with nothing to draw is a
`Renderable(0, 0, 1, 1)` with `alwaysUpdate = true` and an empty `draw()`.

## Timers: use the engine's, not the window's

```js
import { timer } from "melonjs";

timer.setTimeout(fn, 1000);
const id = timer.setInterval(fn, 500);
timer.clearInterval(id);        // in the Stage's onDestroyEvent
```

`Stage` has only `onResetEvent` and `onDestroyEvent` — there is no
`onActivateEvent` / `onDeactivateEvent` on a stage. Those two are `Renderable`
hooks; put per-renderable teardown there instead.

**The outgoing stage is destroyed before the incoming one is reset.** That
ordering is what makes "each stage owns what it started" work: a scene can
release a resource in `onDestroyEvent` and the next scene can claim the same
one in `onResetEvent` without the teardown arriving late and undoing it.

What a stage starts, it must end: `input.registerPointerEvent` regions,
`event.on` subscriptions and running `Tween`s all outlive the stage that made
them. Music is the exception rather than the rule, since `audio.playTrack()`
stops the track it replaces, so `stopTrack()` in `onDestroyEvent` is only
needed where the next screen has no music of its own.

Engine timers are **pause-aware**. `window.setTimeout` keeps firing while the
game is paused, which produces enemies spawning behind a pause menu. Pass
`false` as the third argument — `timer.setInterval(fn, 500, false)` — for one
that keeps running through a pause, which is what a pause-menu animation or a
countdown that should not freeze needs. (That argument was ignored by
`setInterval` before 20.3.)

## Tweens

### You are hand-rolling a tween if you write this

The shape, in any of its spellings. If you are adding a field that counts
milliseconds and dividing it by a constant to get a `0..1`, stop:

```js
// ✗ a tween, written out longhand
private flashMs = 0;
// ... in update(dt)
if (this.flashMs > 0) {
    this.flashMs -= dt;
    const k = this.flashMs / FLASH_MS;      // ← the 0..1
    effect.setUniform("uIntensity", k * k); // ← and a curve, by hand
}
```

```js
// ✓ the same thing
const driver = { k: 1 };
new Tween(driver)
    .to({ k: 0 }, { duration: FLASH_MS })
    .easing(Tween.Easing.Quadratic.In)      // the curve, named
    .onUpdate(() => effect.setUniform("uIntensity", driver.k))
    .start();
```

The tells, any one of which is enough: a `*Ms` or `*Age` field that only
`update()` touches; a division by a `*_MS` constant; `k * k`, `(1 - k) ** 2` or
`** 1.4` written inline, which is an easing curve spelled by hand; an
`if (x <= 0)` arm that exists only to clean up at the end, which is
`onComplete`; a second timer counting the same duration to chain what happens
next, which is `delay`.

It matters beyond tidiness: a hand-rolled fade needs something to tick it, and
an effect that is NOT a renderable (one living on the camera, say) has nothing
that will. That forces an `update(dt)` method and a call site in the game loop
whose only job is to drive the fade. A tween updates itself, so both disappear.

### When NOT to reach for one

Four shapes that look similar and are not tweens:

| shape | what it is | use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| approaching a value that keeps MOVING | a follow, not an animation | `math.damp` |
| a loop that never ends | oscillation | a sine of your own clock |
| a gate: cooldown, spawn interval, invulnerability window | a timer, nothing is interpolated | a plain countdown |
| the same effect on dozens of live objects | per-instance churn | a hand-rolled countdown really is cheaper |

The rule in one line: **fixed duration, known endpoint, one-shot, few
instances.** All four, or it is not a tween.


```js
import { getPool, Tween } from "melonjs";

const t = getPool("tween").get(sprite.pos) // typed pool, release when done
    .to({ x: 300 }, { duration: 500 })     // options object, not a number
    .easing(Tween.Easing.Quadratic.Out)
    .onComplete(() => { /* … */ })
    .start();                    // ← without this, nothing happens
```

Four traps:

- **A tween without `.start()`** (or `autoStart: true` in the `to()` options)
  silently does nothing.
- **`to()`'s second argument is an options object**
  (`{ duration, easing, yoyo, repeat, delay, repeatDelay, interpolation,
  autoStart }`). Passing a bare number is not a duration — it is read for a
  `.duration` property, finds none, and the tween silently runs the default
  1000 ms.
- **Tweens freeze during `state.pause()` / `freeze()`** unless
  `tween.updateWhenPaused = true` — which is how you get an effect that decays
  *through* a hit-stop.
- **Stop a tween before destroying its target**, or `onUpdate` fires against a
  dead renderable.

**A target can be an array: a path.** `to({ x: [200, 120, 300] })` runs from
the current value through each entry in turn, and
`interpolation: Tween.Interpolation.CatmullRom` smooths the corners. Each
`start()` builds the path afresh from the current value, so a replay or a chain
that comes back round runs the same path, and with `yoyo` the return leg plays
it back the way it came. Before 20.13 a restart ran a longer path each time and
a `yoyo` path turned the property into `NaN`.

**To animate something that is not a property, tween a holder and push the
value in `onUpdate`.** A shader uniform and a light's intensity are both set
through a method, so there is nothing for `to()` to interpolate directly. The
callback is invoked with the tweened object as `this` and the eased progress
`0..1` as its argument:

```js
const fade = { level: 1 };
getPool("tween").get(fade)
    .to({ level: 0 }, { duration: 400 })
    .easing(Tween.Easing.Quadratic.Out)
    .onUpdate(function () {
        effect.setUniform("uIntensity", this.level);
        muzzleLight.intensity = this.level * 3;
    })
    .start();
```

Use a `function`, not an arrow, if you want `this` to be the tweened object;
an arrow keeps the enclosing `this` and you read the holder by name instead.
For a handful of pooled objects a hand-rolled countdown in `update()` is
cheaper than a `Tween` each — this is the right tool for one-off effects, not
for every particle.

### Pick the easing, not just the duration

Eleven families, each with `In`, `Out` and `InOut`. `Out` is what most UI
wants: the value arrives decisively instead of creeping in. The two worth
knowing by name beyond the power curves:

| family | what it does |
| --- | --- |
| `Back` | **overshoots past the target and settles back**, which is impact: a stamp, a button press, anything that should LAND rather than arrive |
| `Bounce` | lands and bounces, for something dropping onto a surface |

```js
// a stamp: scale falls to 1 and springs through it
const driver = { scale: 5 };
new Tween(driver)
    .to({ scale: 1 }, { duration: 420 })
    .easing(Tween.Easing.Back.Out)
    .onUpdate(() => { label.currentTransform.identity(); label.scale(driver.scale); })
    .onComplete(() => camera.shake(12, 400))     // the thump, when it truly lands
    .start();
```

`Back` and `Elastic` **leave the range** between your start and end, so clamp
anything that cannot take it, an opacity or a colour channel above all. The
overshoot follows the direction of travel: a value tweened DOWN overshoots
below its target.

Reach for `onComplete` for anything that must happen on arrival, rather than a
second timer counting the same duration. `delay` in the `to()` options chains
the next one without a timer either.

## Guard teardown-adjacent callbacks

Callbacks can fire while a stage is being torn down, when the current state is
already something else:

```js
if (!state.isCurrent(state.PLAY)) return;
```

Without the guard, a "children emptied" handler can reset the wrong stage.

## Persistence

```js
import { save } from "melonjs";

save.add({ hiscore: 0 });      // once; idempotent, loads any stored value
save.hiscore = 1200;           // plain assignment writes to localStorage
save.remove("hiscore");        // gone from localStorage; set it again to save it again
```

**In TypeScript, keep what `add()` returns.** The namespace carries a
`[key: string]: unknown` index for keys registered anywhere, so reading
`save.hiscore` off it gives you `unknown`. `add()` hands back the same
namespace typed with the keys you just registered, which is the handle to
keep:

```ts
const store = save.add({ hiscore: 0, lives: 3 });
store.hiscore = 1200;          // number, no cast
if (score > store.hiscore) { /* ... */ }
```

Chained calls accumulate, so `save.add({ a: 0 }).add({ b: "" })` is typed with
both.

**No `localStorage`, no error.** Where there is none, or reading it throws (a
sandboxed iframe such as an embedded playable page, cookies blocked), `save`
keeps the keys in memory for the session: `add`, reads and writes all work,
and nothing outlives the page. No `try` / `catch` is needed around it;
`device.localStorage` is `false` when the keys will not be kept.

# Scenes, game state and timing

## Stages and the state manager

A `Stage` is a screen. Register it against a state id, then change to it:

```js
import { Stage, state } from "melonjs";

class PlayScreen extends Stage {
    onResetEvent(app) { /* build the scene */ }
    onDestroyEvent(app) { /* tear it down */ }
}

state.set(state.PLAY, new PlayScreen());   // register first
state.change(state.PLAY);                   // then switch
```

Built-in ids: `state.LOADING`, `state.MENU`, `state.READY`, `state.PLAY`,
`state.GAMEOVER` (no underscore), `state.GAME_END`, `state.SCORE`,
`state.CREDITS`, `state.SETTINGS`, `state.DEFAULT`. `state.USER` (100) is the
base for your own ids — `const CUTSCENE = state.USER + 1`.

**Build scene content in `onResetEvent`, not the constructor.** `onResetEvent`
runs on *every* entry to the state; the constructor runs once. Scene content
created in the constructor exists once and is not rebuilt when you return.

`onResetEvent(app)` receives the `Application` — use that rather than importing
the global `game`.

Extra arguments to `state.change` are forwarded:

```js
state.change(state.PLAY, false, { level: 2 });   // → onResetEvent(app, { level: 2 })
```

The second argument is `forceChange`: pass `true` to switch immediately instead
of on a deferred tick, which is what you want when changing state right after a
preload completes. It is ignored when a transition is configured — a transition
always drives the switch from its own completion callback.

`onResetEvent` runs when the switch is made. The first frame, `STATE_CHANGE` and
a transition's reveal follow once the shaders the stage queued are ready, which
is a few milliseconds once the browser has compiled them before, and at most
1.5s on a first visit. So build the stage in `onResetEvent`: an object a
`STATE_CHANGE` listener adds is not waited for, and its first draw may still
compile what it needs. That first frame steps the world once before drawing it,
however short it is, so everything `onResetEvent` added is in it (the same goes
for the frame after a `level.load` made while the game runs). Before 20.12 it
was drawn unstepped, and showed the stage's background alone for one frame.

`state.change` **throws** `Undefined Stage for state '<id>'` if nothing was
registered for that id, and `state.set` throws if the second argument is not a
`Stage` instance. Neither fails quietly.

A change to the state that is **already current does nothing**: no
`onDestroyEvent`, no `onResetEvent`, no transition. So a "Retry" that calls
`state.change(state.PLAY)` from `PLAY` is ignored. Build the current stage
again with `state.reload()` (since 20.16): `onDestroyEvent`, the world reset and
`onResetEvent`, with the arguments the state was entered with, or new ones.
`level.reload()` reloads just the Tiled map, keeping the stage.

```js
// "Play again" on the game-over card, from inside PLAY
new UITextButton(x, y, { text: "AGAIN", onClick: () => state.reload() });
// restart on another level: replaces the arguments for later reloads too
state.reload(false, { level: 2 });
```

Like `state.change`, it waits for the next frame unless `forceChange` is
`true`, and it throws when no state has been entered yet. It plays no
transition.

### Always leave `state.LOADING` — it is transitional

`loader.preload()` switches to `state.LOADING` for you. Building your scene in
the preload callback and then *staying there* looks like it works, and is one
of the easiest mistakes to make:

```js
// WRONG — the game now runs inside the loading stage, forever
loader.preload(assets, () => {
    app.world.addChild(new Player(...));
});
```

Nothing ever destroys that stage, so the built-in loading screen's logo and
progress bar are never removed and sit on top of your game. (Eight of this
repository's own examples did this before it was noticed, so it is not an
obscure trap.)

Give the scene a stage of its own and switch to it:

```js
class PlayScreen extends Stage {
    onResetEvent(app) {
        app.world.addChild(new Player(...));
    }
}

await loader.preload(assets);
state.set(state.PLAY, new PlayScreen());
state.change(state.PLAY);
```

The awaited form reads better here than the callback, because "load, then
switch" is exactly what the code then says. If you genuinely want to keep using
the loading stage as your scene, `state.change(state.DEFAULT)` at least gets
you out of it — but a stage of your own is what you want.
