at once, and the cover comes down with it. Before 20.12 the second change left
the first cover on the camera for good, the screen black over a running game.

### A Stage's own `update()` is NOT paused

This one is easy to get wrong and hard to see. `Application.update` calls both
of these **unconditionally**:

```js
this.isDirty = this.world.update(this.updateDelta);
this.isDirty = state.current().update(this.updateDelta) || this.isDirty;
```

Only `Container.update` consults the pause — it reads `state.isPaused()` and
skips every child that is not `updateWhenPaused`. So world children (entities,
sprites, meshes, a `GLTFModel`) freeze correctly, while **the Stage subclass's
own `update()` keeps running**. (`event.GAME_UPDATE` is not emitted while
paused, so logic hung off it stops with the world.)

A game that keeps its logic in entities pauses for free and never notices. A
game that drives the simulation from `Stage.update` — common for an endless
runner, where one object moves and the world scrolls past it — keeps simulating
through `pauseOnBlur` with its world frozen. The signature is bizarre and very
misleading: the scenery scrolls on, the player character stands still in world
space and slides off the screen, and it all snaps back on focus. It reads as a
culling or animation bug, not a pause bug.

Guard it explicitly:

```js
update(dt) {
    super.update(dt);
    if (state.isPaused()) {
        return true;        // world children are already frozen for you
    }
    // …simulation…
}
```

Worth knowing that `pauseOnBlur` (default `true`) fires on a window `blur`, not
only on tab `visibilitychange` — so clicking another window on the same screen
triggers it while the canvas is still fully visible.

On focus, `resumeOnFocus` (default `true`) undoes only the pause the
application applied on blur. A game the player paused from its own menu stays
paused when the window comes back; before 20.9 it resumed underneath the menu.

**Who reports the focus, and what the game does.** Two separate settings:

| setting | decides | default |
|---|---|---|
| `device.setFocusEvents()` | **who** reports that the player switched away: the browser window (`blur`, `focus`, `visibilitychange` become `event.BLUR` / `event.FOCUS`), or nobody, leaving it to the game's host | the window |
| `app.pauseOnBlur`, `stopOnBlur`, `resumeOnFocus` | **what** the game does on every `event.BLUR` / `event.FOCUS`, wherever it comes from | pause on blur, resume on focus |

- **To keep the game running while the player is away**, turn the flags off
  (`app.pauseOnBlur = false`). The window still reports; nothing pauses.
- **To let a host decide when the game runs**, turn the window off and keep the
  flags. Turning the flags off would not do it: they cannot tell the window's
  `event.BLUR` from the host's, so the host's pause would do nothing either.

**When a host decides, not the window.** A game embedded by a host that says
when it runs, such as a web game portal's SDK (YouTube Playables forbids
pausing on the page's visibility) or a native wrapper, stops the window
reporting with `device.setFocusEvents(false)` and emits the engine's own
events from the host's callbacks:

```js
device.setFocusEvents(false);   // the window's blur, focus and visibilitychange no longer count
app.stopOnBlur = true;          // a pause stops drawing too; pauseOnBlur keeps drawing
app.pauseOnBlur = false;
ytgame.system.onPause(() => event.emit(event.BLUR));
ytgame.system.onResume(() => event.emit(event.FOCUS));
```

Everything else is as with the window: `pauseOnBlur`, `stopOnBlur` and
`resumeOnFocus` decide what happens, the sound effects are silenced and held
keys released, and only a pause the engine applied is undone. It can be called
before or after creating the application.

## The update loop

There is no loop you own. Logic goes in `update(dt)` overrides, or a
`GAME_UPDATE` subscription for scene-level animation:

```js
event.on(event.GAME_UPDATE, () => { /* per frame */ });
```

`update(dt)` must **return `true`** when the object changed and needs redrawing.
Returning nothing is falsy and the object can appear frozen while its state moves.

`dt` is milliseconds since the last frame and is the right basis for motion —
the engine already paces it. Do not reach for `performance.now()`.

**Smooth a value toward a target with `math.damp`, not with `lerp` per
frame.** `lerp(current, target, 0.1)` once per frame moves further on a slow
frame than on a fast one, so the feel drifts with the frame rate:

```js
this.speed = math.damp(this.speed, targetSpeed, 5, dt / 1000);
```

`damp(current, target, lambda, dt)` takes SECONDS, so divide `dt`. Higher
`lambda` converges faster. See `melonjs-camera-and-drawing` for the camera's
own `follow()` damping, which is already frame-rate independent for you.

A common idiom for a per-frame game controller with nothing to draw is a
`Renderable(0, 0, 1, 1)` with `alwaysUpdate = true` and an empty `draw()`.

## Timers: use the engine's, not the window's

```js
import { timer } from "melonjs";

timer.setTimeout(fn, 1000);
const id = timer.setInterval(fn, 500);
timer.clearInterval(id);        // in the Stage's onDestroyEvent
```

`Stage` has only `onResetEvent` and `onDestroyEvent` — there is no
`onActivateEvent` / `onDeactivateEvent` on a stage. Those two are `Renderable`
hooks; put per-renderable teardown there instead.

**The outgoing stage is destroyed before the incoming one is reset.** That
ordering is what makes "each stage owns what it started" work: a scene can
release a resource in `onDestroyEvent` and the next scene can claim the same
one in `onResetEvent` without the teardown arriving late and undoing it.

What a stage starts, it must end: `input.registerPointerEvent` regions,
`event.on` subscriptions and running `Tween`s all outlive the stage that made
them. Music is the exception rather than the rule, since `audio.playTrack()`
stops the track it replaces, so `stopTrack()` in `onDestroyEvent` is only
needed where the next screen has no music of its own.

Engine timers are **pause-aware**. `window.setTimeout` keeps firing while the
game is paused, which produces enemies spawning behind a pause menu. Pass
`false` as the third argument — `timer.setInterval(fn, 500, false)` — for one
that keeps running through a pause, which is what a pause-menu animation or a
countdown that should not freeze needs. (That argument was ignored by
`setInterval` before 20.3.)

## Tweens

### You are hand-rolling a tween if you write this

The shape, in any of its spellings. If you are adding a field that counts
milliseconds and dividing it by a constant to get a `0..1`, stop:

```js
// ✗ a tween, written out longhand
private flashMs = 0;
// ... in update(dt)
if (this.flashMs > 0) {
    this.flashMs -= dt;
    const k = this.flashMs / FLASH_MS;      // ← the 0..1
    effect.setUniform("uIntensity", k * k); // ← and a curve, by hand
}
```

```js
// ✓ the same thing
const driver = { k: 1 };
new Tween(driver)
    .to({ k: 0 }, { duration: FLASH_MS })
    .easing(Tween.Easing.Quadratic.In)      // the curve, named
    .onUpdate(() => effect.setUniform("uIntensity", driver.k))
    .start();
```

The tells, any one of which is enough: a `*Ms` or `*Age` field that only
`update()` touches; a division by a `*_MS` constant; `k * k`, `(1 - k) ** 2` or
`** 1.4` written inline, which is an easing curve spelled by hand; an
`if (x <= 0)` arm that exists only to clean up at the end, which is
`onComplete`; a second timer counting the same duration to chain what happens
next, which is `delay`.

It matters beyond tidiness: a hand-rolled fade needs something to tick it, and
an effect that is NOT a renderable (one living on the camera, say) has nothing
that will. That forces an `update(dt)` method and a call site in the game loop
whose only job is to drive the fade. A tween updates itself, so both disappear.

### When NOT to reach for one

Four shapes that look similar and are not tweens:

| shape | what it is | use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| approaching a value that keeps MOVING | a follow, not an animation | `math.damp` |
| a loop that never ends | oscillation | a sine of your own clock |
| a gate: cooldown, spawn interval, invulnerability window | a timer, nothing is interpolated | a plain countdown |
| the same effect on dozens of live objects | per-instance churn | a hand-rolled countdown really is cheaper |

The rule in one line: **fixed duration, known endpoint, one-shot, few
instances.** All four, or it is not a tween.


```js
import { getPool, Tween } from "melonjs";

const t = getPool("tween").get(sprite.pos) // typed pool, release when done
    .to({ x: 300 }, { duration: 500 })     // options object, not a number
    .easing(Tween.Easing.Quadratic.Out)
    .onComplete(() => { /* … */ })
    .start();                    // ← without this, nothing happens
```

Four traps:

- **A tween without `.start()`** (or `autoStart: true` in the `to()` options)
  silently does nothing.
- **`to()`'s second argument is an options object**
  (`{ duration, easing, yoyo, repeat, delay, repeatDelay, interpolation,
  autoStart }`). Passing a bare number is not a duration — it is read for a
  `.duration` property, finds none, and the tween silently runs the default
  1000 ms.
- **Tweens freeze during `state.pause()` / `freeze()`** unless
  `tween.updateWhenPaused = true` — which is how you get an effect that decays
  *through* a hit-stop.
- **Stop a tween before destroying its target**, or `onUpdate` fires against a
  dead renderable.

**A target can be an array: a path.** `to({ x: [200, 120, 300] })` runs from
the current value through each entry in turn, and
`interpolation: Tween.Interpolation.CatmullRom` smooths the corners. Each
`start()` builds the path afresh from the current value, so a replay or a chain
that comes back round runs the same path, and with `yoyo` the return leg plays
it back the way it came. Before 20.13 a restart ran a longer path each time and
a `yoyo` path turned the property into `NaN`.

**To animate something that is not a property, tween a holder and push the
value in `onUpdate`.** A shader uniform and a light's intensity are both set
through a method, so there is nothing for `to()` to interpolate directly. The
callback is invoked with the tweened object as `this` and the eased progress
`0..1` as its argument:

```js
const fade = { level: 1 };
getPool("tween").get(fade)
    .to({ level: 0 }, { duration: 400 })
    .easing(Tween.Easing.Quadratic.Out)
    .onUpdate(function () {
        effect.setUniform("uIntensity", this.level);
        muzzleLight.intensity = this.level * 3;
    })
    .start();
```

Use a `function`, not an arrow, if you want `this` to be the tweened object;
an arrow keeps the enclosing `this` and you read the holder by name instead.
For a handful of pooled objects a hand-rolled countdown in `update()` is
cheaper than a `Tween` each — this is the right tool for one-off effects, not
for every particle.

### Pick the easing, not just the duration

Eleven families, each with `In`, `Out` and `InOut`. `Out` is what most UI
wants: the value arrives decisively instead of creeping in. The two worth
knowing by name beyond the power curves:

| family | what it does |
| --- | --- |
| `Back` | **overshoots past the target and settles back**, which is impact: a stamp, a button press, anything that should LAND rather than arrive |
| `Bounce` | lands and bounces, for something dropping onto a surface |

```js
// a stamp: scale falls to 1 and springs through it
const driver = { scale: 5 };
new Tween(driver)
    .to({ scale: 1 }, { duration: 420 })
    .easing(Tween.Easing.Back.Out)
    .onUpdate(() => { label.currentTransform.identity(); label.scale(driver.scale); })
    .onComplete(() => camera.shake(12, 400))     // the thump, when it truly lands
    .start();
```

`Back` and `Elastic` **leave the range** between your start and end, so clamp
anything that cannot take it, an opacity or a colour channel above all. The
overshoot follows the direction of travel: a value tweened DOWN overshoots
below its target.

Reach for `onComplete` for anything that must happen on arrival, rather than a
second timer counting the same duration. `delay` in the `to()` options chains
the next one without a timer either.

## Guard teardown-adjacent callbacks

Callbacks can fire while a stage is being torn down, when the current state is
already something else:

```js
if (!state.isCurrent(state.PLAY)) return;
```

Without the guard, a "children emptied" handler can reset the wrong stage.

## Persistence

```js
import { save } from "melonjs";

save.add({ hiscore: 0 });      // once; idempotent, loads any stored value
save.hiscore = 1200;           // plain assignment writes to localStorage
save.remove("hiscore");        // gone from localStorage; set it again to save it again
```

**In TypeScript, keep what `add()` returns.** The namespace carries a
`[key: string]: unknown` index for keys registered anywhere, so reading
`save.hiscore` off it gives you `unknown`. `add()` hands back the same
namespace typed with the keys you just registered, which is the handle to
keep:

```ts
const store = save.add({ hiscore: 0, lives: 3 });
store.hiscore = 1200;          // number, no cast
if (score > store.hiscore) { /* ... */ }
```

Chained calls accumulate, so `save.add({ a: 0 }).add({ b: "" })` is typed with
both.

**No `localStorage`, no error.** Where there is none, or reading it throws (a
sandboxed iframe such as an embedded playable page, cookies blocked), `save`
keeps the keys in memory for the session: `add`, reads and writes all work,
and nothing outlives the page. No `try` / `catch` is needed around it;
`device.localStorage` is `false` when the keys will not be kept.

**Somewhere other than `localStorage`.** Two calls, one for each kind of
storage:

| call | for |
|---|---|
| `save.setStorage(storage)` | keeping the keys in anything with `getItem`, `setItem` and `removeItem` (the `SaveStorage` type), called synchronously, as `localStorage` is |
| `save.createCloudStorage({ data, write })` | making such a storage out of a platform's cloud save (YouTube Playables, Facebook Instant Games), which loads and saves asynchronously |

`localStorage` stays the default, and `save.setStorage(localStorage)` goes back
to it. A storage is handed the same items `localStorage` would hold:
`me.save.<key>` with the key's value as JSON, and `me.save`, the list of keys.

A platform's cloud save: load it before the game reads `save`, then hand it
over. `data` is what the platform loaded (an object, its JSON, or nothing the
first time); `write(items)` saves every item back:

```js
// YouTube Playables: the save is one string
const cloud = save.createCloudStorage({
    data: await ytgame.game.loadData(),
    write: (items) => ytgame.game.saveData(JSON.stringify(items)),
});
save.setStor

# Sprites, animation and atlases

> Creating sprites from images or atlases, driving frame animation, and the
> positioning trap that catches almost everyone.

## `pos` is the centre, not the top-left

`Renderable.anchorPoint` defaults to **`(0.5, 0.5)`**, so a sprite's `pos` is its
**centre**. `Container` forces `(0, 0)` instead, which is why containers and
sprites appear to disagree.

```js
// a 64×64 sprite at (100, 100) covers 68..132, not 100..164
const s = new Sprite(100, 100, { image: "hero", framewidth: 64, frameheight: 64 });

s.anchorPoint.set(0, 0);   // switch to top-left positioning if you prefer

// or in the settings, by name: "top-left", "bottom" (the feet), "center",
// "top", "left", "right", "top-right", "bottom-left", "bottom-right"
const hero = new Sprite(x, y, { image: "hero", anchorPoint: "bottom" });
```

Writing top-left maths against the centred default puts everything half a sprite
off, with no error. It is the most common source of "close but subtly wrong"
placement.

## Constructing a sprite

From a plain image:

```js
const hero = new Sprite(x, y, {
    image: "hero",          // preloaded asset name
    framewidth: 32,
    frameheight: 32,
});
```

From a texture atlas region:

```js
const atlas = new TextureAtlas(loader.getJSON("sprites"), loader.getImage("sprites"));
const coin = new Sprite(x, y, { image: atlas, region: "coin_01.png" });
```

`framewidth` / `frameheight` define the animation grid on a sheet. Omit them and
the whole image is one frame.

## Animation

```js
hero.addAnimation("idle", [0, 1, 2, 3], 100);   // frames, ms per frame
hero.addAnimation("walk", [4, 5, 6, 7]);
hero.addAnimation("die",  [8, 9], 150);

hero.setCurrentAnimation("walk");
hero.setCurrentAnimation("die", "idle");                          // chain to idle when it ends
hero.setCurrentAnimation("die", { loop: false });                 // play once, hold the last frame
hero.setCurrentAnimation("die", { loop: false, onComplete: fn }); // …and call fn when it does
hero.setCurrentAnimation("use", { next: "idle", onComplete: fn }); // call fn, then chain to idle
hero.setCurrentAnimation("run", { onFrame: (frame) => {            // each frame playback reaches
    if (frame === 3 || frame === 8) footstep();
} });

if (hero.isCurrentAnimation("walk")) { /* … */ }
```

Frame indices are into the `framewidth`/`frameheight` grid. With an atlas, use
`atlas.getAnimationSettings([regionNames])` and spread it into the Sprite
settings, or `atlas.createAnimationFromName([regionNames])`, which returns a
ready-made Sprite. On a fixed-cell spritesheet only numeric indices are
accepted — passing region names throws.

The second argument to `setCurrentAnimation` is polymorphic. A **string** chains
to that animation when this one ends. An **options object** takes
`{ loop, next, speed, onComplete, onFrame }`, and only an explicit `loop: false`
stops the looping. A **bare function** is the legacy form: it fires at *every* cycle end,
and only holds the last frame if it returns `false`. Omit the argument entirely
and the animation loops forever. The options type also has a `crossfade`, which
only a 3D `GLTFModel` reads (see `melonjs-3d-assets`); a sprite ignores it.

`onFrame(frame)` is called with frame 0 when the animation starts, then with each
frame playback reaches, so a footstep or a hit lands on its frame without polling
`getCurrentAnimationFrame()`. A long tick reports every frame it goes past. It is
not called for a frame set with `setAnimationFrame`, nor for the frame 0 a
play-once animation would wrap to. Keep the callback in a field when you call
`setCurrentAnimation` every frame: re-selecting keeps the first one anyway.

With both `next` and `onComplete`, the callback runs first and the chained
animation starts with none of its own, so a one-off action (a pickup, an
attack) needs no manual switch back to idle.

Re-selecting the animation that is already current is a no-op, so calling
`setCurrentAnimation` every frame is safe, and an `isCurrentAnimation` check
around it adds nothing. **The exception is a `loop: false` run that has
finished**: selecting it again plays it again, so a death animation selected
every frame replays forever. Select a play-once animation once, on the event
that starts it. An unknown id throws.

A frame can carry its own delay, as `{ name, delay }` in place of the index or
region name: `[{ name: 3, delay: 200 }, { name: 4, delay: 100 }]`.
`play(name?, options?)` switches and plays (or, with no name, resumes),
`pause()` freezes the current frame and `stop()` rewinds to the first one and
pauses there; the options are `setCurrentAnimation`'s.

`addAnimation` with an id that exists replaces it, which is how you change an
animation's frames or speed (`hero.addAnimation("walk", [4, 5, 6, 7], 200)`).
Redefining the one that is playing takes effect at once: the playing frame is
kept if the new strip still has it, playback restarts on frame 0 if not, a
finished `loop: false` run holds the new last frame, and the
`setCurrentAnimation` options stay. Before 20.13 it kept the old frame count, so
a shorter strip threw on the next `update()` and a longer one never reached its
new frames.

Since 20.14, a frame the texture does not have (a number past the end of the
sheet, a name the atlas does not hold) is left out with a console warning
naming it, and the frames that exist play in order; `addAnimation` returns how
many it kept.

## Texture atlases

`TextureAtlas` reads several formats:

| source | how |
|---|---|
| TexturePacker / Free Texture Packer JSON, "JSON (Array)" or "JSON (Hash)" | `new TextureAtlas(loader.getJSON(name), loader.getImage(name))` |
| Aseprite **JSON export** | same as TexturePacker — the format is detected from `meta.app` |
| another tool writing either layout (spritesheet.dev, your own exporter) | same call. Since 20.18 an unknown `meta.app` is recognised from the file's structure: `meta.frameTags` reads as Aseprite, frames with a `frame` rectangle as TexturePacker. Before, it threw `Unknown texture atlas format` |
| Aseprite **`.aseprite` / `.ase` binary** | loader type `"aseprite"`, which stores the composited image *and* a JSON sidecar under the one asset name |
| ShoeBox | JSON export using the melonJS exporter settings file; same call as TexturePacker |
| fixed-cell spritesheet | `new TextureAtlas({ framewidth, frameheight, anchorPoint }, loader.getImage(name))` |
| multi-page | pass an array of atlas JSON objects as the first argument |

Helpers: `createSpriteFromName(name)`, `createAnimationFromName([names])`,
`getAnimationSettings([names])`.

Atlases matter for performance: the GPU batchers bind several textures at once
(up to `renderer.maxTextures`), so a handful of separate images still batch —
but once a frame crosses that many distinct textures the batch has to flush.
Packing into one atlas keeps everything on a single binding.

## Visual properties

```js
sprite.setTint("#ff8000");   // multiply tint
sprite.alpha = 0.5;
sprite.flipX(true);                   // mirror horizontally
sprite.flipY(true);
sprite.blendMode = "additive";        // see the effects skill for the full list
sprite.scale(2, 2);                   // ← multiplicative, see below
sprite.flicker(1000, function () {    // blink for a second, then…
    this.ancestor.removeChild(this);  // …`this` is the sprite; the flicker has ended
});
```

**A tint multiplies, so it can only darken.** It cannot turn a red sprite blue,
or flash it white. For one sprite drawn in several palettes (a team colour, an
elite enemy, a frozen one) use a `GradientMapEffect`, which redraws it from its
brightness in the colours you list; for a white hit flash, a `FlashEffect`. Both
are in `melonjs-effects-and-shaders`.

```js
// the same art as a second team
enemy.addPostEffect(new GradientMapEffect(app.renderer, {
    colors: [[0.1, 0.05, 0.3], [0.3, 0.4, 0.9], [0.8, 0.9, 1]],
}));
```

**`scale()` is multiplicative, not absolute.** Calling it every frame compounds.
For absolute scaling reset first:

```js
sprite.currentTransform.identity();
sprite.currentTransform.scale(s, s, 1);
```

This bites hardest with pooled sprites, which arrive carrying their previous
life's transform.

## `NineSliceSprite`

For panels and dialogue boxes that stretch without distorting their corners:

```js
new NineSliceSprite(x, y, {
    image: "panel", width: 300, height: 120,
    insetx: 12, insety: 12,     // lowercase x/y — `insetX` is silently ignored
});
```

`width` and `height` are mandatory and the constructor throws without them.
The insets default to a quarter of the frame.

## Pooling

Frequently spawned sprites should be pooled:

```js
import { createPool } from "melonjs";

const bulletPool = createPool((x, y) => {    // me.pool is deprecated
    const instance = new Bullet(x, y);
    return { instance, reset: (x, y) => instance.onResetEvent(x, y) };
});
const b = bulletPool.get(x, y);             // new Bullet(x, y), or reset(x, y) on a reused one
world.removeChild(b);                       // returns it to bulletPool automatically
```

Two consequences:

- A recyclable class's `onResetEvent` must reset **everything** its lifetime
  mutates — alpha, tint, scale, animation state. Anything you forget carries
  over to the next use.
- Pool-recycled objects do **not** fire `onDestroyEvent` on removal. Pair event
  subscriptions with `onActivateEvent` / `onDeactivateEvent` instead.

## Symptom → cause

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| everything offset by half a sprite | top-left maths against the centred `anchorPoint` |
| sprite grows every frame | `scale()` is multiplicative — reset the transform |
| a recycled sprite keeps its old look | `onResetEvent` does not restore every mutated property |
| event handlers leak on pooled objects | bound in the constructor rather than `onActivateEvent` |
| animation never advances | no `framewidth`/`frameheight`, so the sheet is one frame |
| animation plays once and stops | `{ loop: false }`, or a callback that returned `false` |
| a `loop: false` animation keeps replaying | `setCurrentAnimation` called every frame: a finished play-once run is restarted by selecting it again |
| a one-frame animation never calls its `onComplete` | a looping one-frame animation does not step; play it with `loop: false` or `next` (before 20.12 even those never completed) |
| `TypeError` reading `offset` or `delay` in `update()` after re-adding the playing animation with fewer frames, or a longer one never shows its new frames | before 20.13 redefining the current animation kept its old frame count; upgrade |
| a console warning `addAnimation("walk"): no frame … in the texture`, or a `TypeError` reading `delay` / `offset` on an older melonJS | a frame number or name the sheet or atlas does not have (often an atlas re-exported without one of its images): fix the frame list or re-export the atlas |
| `this` is wrong in a `flicker(ms, callback)` callback, or a flicker started from it stops at once | before 20.13.0 the callback ran on an internal object and the flicker was stopped after it; now `this` is the sprite and the flicker has already ended |
| sprites do not batch | more distinct textures in one frame than `renderer.maxTextures` |
| nine-slice corners stretch anyway | `insetX`/`insetY` instead of `insetx`/`insety` |
| an atlas animation blinks: the sprite vanishes on some of its frames (before 20.17) | the frames the packer stored rotated were drawn off the screen unless the sprite was at (0, 0); a nine-slice sprite from a rotated frame was stretched along the wrong axis. Update; on an older version, turn rotation off in the packer |
| `Unknown texture atlas format: <name or URL>` from `new TextureAtlas` | before 20.18, an atlas whose `meta.app` named a tool the engine did not know, even in the TexturePacker or Aseprite layout (and `ShoeBox`, matched in lowercase only); since 20.18, a file that is in neither layout: no `meta.size`, a frame with no `frame` rectangle, or a list of frames with no `filename` |
| `frames.forEach is not a function` from `new TextureAtlas` | before 20.18, a TexturePacker "JSON (Hash)" export; re-export as "JSON (Array)" or update |
| a frame of an Aseprite JSON export is not found by its name | exported as "Array": the frames are then named by their position (`"0"`, `"1"`…); export as "Hash" to keep the names |
| a tint will not turn the sprite the colour asked for, only a darker one | a tint multiplies the art's own colours: recolour with a `GradientMapEffect`, flash with a `FlashEffect` |

# Sprites, animation and atlases

> Creating sprites from images or atlases, driving frame animation, and the
> positioning trap that catches almost everyone.

## `pos` is the centre, not the top-left

`Renderable.anchorPoint` defaults to **`(0.5, 0.5)`**, so a sprite's `pos` is its
**centre**. `Container` forces `(0, 0)` instead, which is why containers and
sprites appear to disagree.

```js
// a 64×64 sprite at (100, 100) covers 68..132, not 100..164
const s = new Sprite(100, 100, { image: "hero", framewidth: 64, frameheight: 64 });

s.anchorPoint.set(0, 0);   // switch to top-left positioning if you prefer

// or in the settings, by name: "top-left", "bottom" (the feet), "center",
// "top", "left", "right", "top-right", "bottom-left", "bottom-right"
const hero = new Sprite(x, y, { image: "hero", anchorPoint: "bottom" });
```

Writing top-left maths against the centred default puts everything half a sprite
off, with no error. It is the most common source of "close but subtly wrong"
placement.

## Constructing a sprite

From a plain image:

```js
const hero = new Sprite(x, y, {
    image: "hero",          // preloaded asset name
    framewidth: 32,
    frameheight: 32,
});
```

From a texture atlas region:

```js
const atlas = new TextureAtlas(loader.getJSON("sprites"), loader.getImage("sprites"));
const coin = new Sprite(x, y, { image: atlas, region: "coin_01.png" });
```

`framewidth` / `frameheight` define the animation grid on a sheet. Omit them and
the whole image is one frame.

## Animation

```js
hero.addAnimation("idle", [0, 1, 2, 3], 100);   // frames, ms per frame
hero.addAnimation("walk", [4, 5, 6, 7]);
hero.addAnimation("die",  [8, 9], 150);

hero.setCurrentAnimation("walk");
hero.setCurrentAnimation("die", "idle");                          // chain to idle when it ends
hero.setCurrentAnimation("die", { loop: false });                 // play once, hold the last frame
hero.setCurrentAnimation("die", { loop: false, onComplete: fn }); // …and call fn when it does
hero.setCurrentAnimation("use", { next: "idle", onComplete: fn }); // call fn, then chain to idle
hero.setCurrentAnimation("run", { onFrame: (frame) => {            // each frame playback reaches
    if (frame === 3 || frame === 8) footstep();
} });

if (hero.isCurrentAnimation("walk")) { /* … */ }
```

Frame indices are into the `framewidth`/`frameheight` grid. With an atlas, use
`atlas.getAnimationSettings([regionNames])` and spread it into the Sprite
settings, or `atlas.createAnimationFromName([regionNames])`, which returns a
ready-made Sprite. On a fixed-cell spritesheet only numeric indices are
accepted — passing region names throws.

The second argument to `setCurrentAnimation` is polymorphic. A **string** chains
to that animation when this one ends. An **options object** takes
`{ loop, next, speed, onComplete, onFrame }`, and only an explicit `loop: false`
stops the looping. A **bare function** is the legacy form: it fires at *every* cycle end,
and only holds the last frame if it returns `false`. Omit the argument entirely
and the animation loops forever. The options type also has a `crossfade`, which
only a 3D `GLTFModel` reads (see `melonjs-3d-assets`); a sprite ignores it.

`onFrame(frame)` is called with frame 0 when the animation starts, then with each
frame playback reaches, so a footstep or a hit lands on its frame without polling
`getCurrentAnimationFrame()`. A long tick reports every frame it goes past. It is
not called for a frame set with `setAnimationFrame`, nor for the frame 0 a
play-once animation would wrap to. Keep the callback in a field when you call
`setCurrentAnimation` every frame: re-selecting keeps the first one anyway.

With both `next` and `onComplete`, the callback runs first and the chained
animation starts with none of its own, so a one-off action (a pickup, an
attack) needs no manual switch back to idle.

Re-selecting the animation that is already current is a no-op, so calling
`setCurrentAnimation` every frame is safe, and an `isCurrentAnimation` check
around it adds nothing. **The exception is a `loop: false` run that has
finished**: selecting it again plays it again, so a death animation selected
every frame replays forever. Select a play-once animation once, on the event
that starts it. An unknown id throws.

A frame can carry its own delay, as `{ name, delay }` in place of the index or
region name: `[{ name: 3, delay: 200 }, { name: 4, delay: 100 }]`.
`play(name?, options?)` switches and plays (or, with no name, resumes),
`pause()` freezes the current frame and `stop()` rewinds to the first one and
pauses there; the options are `setCurrentAnimation`'s.

`addAnimation` with an id that exists replaces it, which is how you change an
animation's frames or speed (`hero.addAnimation("walk", [4, 5, 6, 7], 200)`).
Redefining the one that is playing takes effect at once: the playing frame is
kept if the new strip still has it, playback restarts on frame 0 if not, a
finished `loop: false` run holds the new last frame, and the
`setCurrentAnimation` options stay. Before 20.13 it kept the old frame count, so
a shorter strip threw on the next `update()` and a longer one never reached its
new frames.

Since 20.14, a frame the texture does not have (a number past the end of the
sheet, a name the atlas does not hold) is left out with a console warning
naming it, and the frames that exist play in order; `addAnimation` returns how
many it kept.

## Texture atlases

`TextureAtlas` reads several formats:

| source | how |
|---|---|
| TexturePacker / Free Texture Packer JSON, "JSON (Array)" or "JSON (Hash)" | `new TextureAtlas(loader.getJSON(name), loader.getImage(name))` |
| Aseprite **JSON export** | same as TexturePacker — the format is detected from `meta.app` |
| another tool writing either layout (spritesheet.dev, your own exporter) | same call. Since 20.18 an unknown `meta.app` is recognised from the file's structure: `meta.frameTags` reads as Aseprite, frames with a `frame` rectangle as TexturePacker. Before, it threw `Unknown texture atlas format` |
| Aseprite **`.aseprite` / `.ase` binary** | loader type `"aseprite"`, which stores the composited image *and* a JSON sidecar under the one asset name |
| ShoeBox | JSON export using the melonJS exporter settings file; same call as TexturePacker |
| fixed-cell spritesheet | `new TextureAtlas({ framewidth, frameheight, anchorPoint }, loader.getImage(name))` |
| multi-page | pass an array of atlas JSON objects as the first argument |

Helpers: `createSpriteFromName(name)`, `createAnimationFromName([names])`,
`getAnimationSettings([names])`.

Atlases matter for performance: the GPU batchers bind several textures at once
(up to `renderer.maxTextures`), so a handful of separate images still batch —
but once a frame crosses that many distinct textures the batch has to flush.
Packing into one atlas keeps everything on a single binding.

## Visual properties

```js
sprite.setTint("#ff8000");   // multiply tint
sprite.alpha = 0.5;
sprite.flipX(true);                   // mirror horizontally
sprite.flipY(true);
sprite.blendMode = "additive";        // see the effects skill for the full list
sprite.scale(2, 2);                   // ← multiplicative, see below
sprite.flicker(1000, function () {    // blink for a second, then…
    this.ancestor.removeChild(this);  // …`this` is the sprite; the flicker has ended
});
```

**A tint multiplies, so it can only darken.** It cannot turn a red sprite blue,
or flash it white. For one sprite drawn in several palettes (a team colour, an
elite enemy, a frozen one) use a `GradientMapEffect`, which redraws it from its
brightness in the colours you list; for a white hit flash, a `FlashEffect`. Both
are in `melonjs-effects-and-shaders`.

```js
// the same art as a second team
enemy.addPostEffect(new GradientMapEffect(app.renderer, {
    colors: [[0.1, 0.05, 0.3], [0.3, 0.4, 0.9], [0.8, 0.9, 1]],
}));
```

**`scale()` is multiplicative, not absolute.** Calling it every frame compounds.
For absolute scaling reset first:

```js
sprite.currentTransform.identity();
sprite.currentTransform.scale(s, s, 1);
```

This bites hardest with pooled sprites, which arrive carrying their previous
life's transform.

## `NineSliceSprite`

For panels and dialogue boxes that stretch without distorting their corners:

```js
new NineSliceSprite(x, y, {
    image: "panel", width: 300, height: 120,
    insetx: 12, insety: 12,     // lowercase x/y — `insetX` is silently ignored
});
```

`width` and `height` are mandatory and the constructor throws without them.
The insets default to a quarter of the frame.

## Pooling

Frequently spawned sprites should be pooled:

```js
import { createPool } from "melonjs";

const bulletPool = createPool((x, y) => {    // me.pool is deprecated
    const instance = new Bullet(x, y);
    return { instance, reset: (x, y) => instance.onResetEvent(x, y) };
});
const b = bulletPool.get(x, y);             // new Bullet(x, y), or reset(x, y) on a reused one
world.removeChild(b);                       // returns it to bulletPool automatically
```

Two consequences:

- A recyclable class's `onResetEvent` must reset **everything** its lifetime
  mutates — alpha, tint, scale, animation state. Anything you forget carries
  over to the next use.
- Pool-recycled objects do **not** fire `onDestroyEvent` on removal. Pair event
  subscriptions with `onActivateEvent` / `onDeactivateEvent` instead.

## Symptom → cause

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| everything offset by half a sprite | top-left maths against the centred `anchorPoint` |
| sprite grows every frame | `scale()` is multiplicative — reset the transform |
| a recycled sprite keeps its old look | `onResetEvent` does not restore every mutated property |
| event handlers leak on pooled objects | bound in the constructor rather than `onActivateEvent` |
| animation never advances | no `framewidth`/`frameheight`, so the sheet is one frame |
| animation plays once and stops | `{ loop: false }`, or a callback that returned `false` |
| a `loop: false` animation keeps replaying | `setCurrentAnimation` called every frame: a finished play-once run is restarted by selecting it again |
| a one-frame animation never calls its `onComplete` | a looping one-frame animation does not step; play it with `loop: false` or `next` (before 20.12 even those never completed) |
| `TypeError` reading `offset` or `delay` in `update()` after re-adding the playing animation with fewer frames, or a longer one never shows its new frames | before 20.13 redefining the current animation kept its old frame count; upgrade |
| a console warning `addAnimation("walk"): no frame … in the texture`, or a `TypeError` reading `delay` / `offset` on an older melonJS | a frame number or name the sheet or atlas does not have (often an atlas re-exported without one of its images): fix the frame list or re-export the atlas |
| `this` is wrong in a `flicker(ms, callback)` callback, or a flicker started from it stops at once | before 20.13.0 the callback ran on an internal object and the flicker was stopped after it; now `this` is the sprite and the flicker has already ended |
| sprites do not batch | more distinct textures in one frame than `renderer.maxTextures` |
| nine-slice corners stretch anyway | `insetX`/`insetY` instead of `insetx`/`insety` |
| an atlas animation blinks: the sprite vanishes on some of its frames (before 20.17) | the frames the packer stored rotated were drawn off the screen unless the sprite was at (0, 0); a nine-slice sprite from a rotated frame was stretched along the wrong axis. Update; on an older version, turn rotation off in the packer |
| `Unknown texture atlas format: <name or URL>` from `new TextureAtlas` | before 20.18, an atlas whose `meta.app` named a tool the engine did not know, even in the TexturePacker or Aseprite layout (and `ShoeBox`, matched in lowercase only); since 20.18, a file that is in neither layout: no `meta.size`, a frame with no `frame` rectangle, or a list of frames with no `filename` |
| `frames.forEach is not a function` from `new TextureAtlas` | before 20.18, a TexturePacker "JSON (Hash)" export; re-export as "JSON (Array)" or update |
| a frame of an Aseprite JSON export is not found by its name | exported as "Array": the frames are then named by their position (`"0"`, `"1"`…); export as "Hash" to keep the names |
| a tint will not turn the sprite the colour asked for, only a darker one | a tint multiplies the art's own colours: recolour with a `GradientMapEffect`, flash with a `FlashEffect` |

# Checking that a game works

> Most melonJS mistakes are silent: the game starts, logs nothing in red, and
> draws the wrong thing or nothing. Code that compiles has therefore told you
> very little. Run the game, read what the engine printed, and look at a
> frame, before reporting that it works.

## Run it in a headless browser

A scaffolded project is a Vite project: `npm run dev` serves it and prints the
address. Open that address with a browser automation library and collect what
the page says. With Playwright:

```js
import { chromium } from "playwright";

const browser = await chromium.launch();
const page = await browser.newPage();

const lines = [];
page.on("console", (m) => lines.push(`[${m.type()}] ${m.text()}`));
page.on("pageerror", (e) => lines.push(`[pageerror] ${e}`));

await page.goto("http://localhost:5173/");
// the game is ready once init() has resolved (see below for `app`)
await page.waitForFunction(() => globalThis.app?.isInitialized === true);

await page.locator("canvas").screenshot({ path: "frame.png" });
console.log(lines.join("\n"));
await browser.close();
```

Collect **every** console message, whatever its type, and uncaught errors
through `pageerror`. Filtering on `error` alone misses the engine's own
complaints, most of which are warnings.

A headless page has the focus and runs its frames, so the game is not paused:
`requestAnimationFrame` fires, tweens and physics advance, and two screenshots
a second apart differ if anything moves.

## Let the harness reach the game

Module code is not reachable from outside the page. Put the application on
`globalThis`, in development only, and the harness can ask the game what it
thinks is going on rather than guess from pixels:

```js
const app = new Application(800, 600, { parent: "screen" });
await app.init();
if (import.meta.env.DEV) {
    globalThis.app = app;
}
```

```js
await page.evaluate(() => app.renderer.type);                // "WebGL2", "WebGPU" or "CANVAS"
await page.evaluate(() => app.world.getChildren().length);   // what is in the world
```

Expose a particular object the same way (`globalThis.player = player`) to read
its position or its state after driving it.

## Read the console the engine writes

A clean start prints, as plain `log` lines:

```
melonJS 2 (v20.17.0) | http://melonjs.org
WebGL2 renderer (ANGLE (…)) | Web Audio | pixel ratio 1 | desktop | landscape
resolution: requested 800x600 (SDR), got 800x600 (SDR)
physics: builtin
```

The second line names the renderer the run got: `WebGPU`, `WebGL2` or
`CANVAS`. Read it every time: the same code draws differently on each (see
below).

What to act on:

- **An uncaught error** (`pageerror`): the game stopped, or a callback did.
- **Text containing `is deprecated`.** A deprecation arrives as a collapsed
  group, of type `startGroupCollapsed`, whose text is the engine's message
  with its arguments after it (`melonJS: %s is deprecated since version %s,
  please use %s` then the names), followed by a `warning` that is only a
  stack trace. Filter on `warning` and you get an anonymous `Error at
  warning (…)`: match on the text of every message instead. The message
  names the replacement.
- **A `melonJS:` warning**, printed once however often it happens: a feature
  that is doing nothing on this renderer, an asset that failed to load, a
  setting that was ignored. Each skill's symptom table starts from these.

What is noise, in a headless browser:

- `No available adapters.` and `AUTO: WebGPU unavailable (…) — falling back`:
  the machine has no GPU the browser will use, so the engine took the next
  renderer. Expected; it tells you which one below.
- `GL Driver Message (…): GPU stall due to ReadPixels`: caused by the
  screenshot itself.
- `The AudioContext was not allowed to start`: no one has clicked yet. Sound
  starts after the first input, in a real browser too.

## Know which renderer you checked

A headless browser has no graphics card. What it falls back to depends on the
browser and how it was launched, and changes what the run proves:

| the console says | what was checked |
|---|---|
| `WebGL2 renderer (… SwiftShader …)` | the WebGL path, on a software rasterizer: shaders and post effects ran. Timings mean nothing. |
| `CANVAS renderer` | the fallback only. Shader effects, lit sprites, meshes and everything else that needs a GPU did **nothing**, silently. A screenshot without the effect you added is this, not a bug in your code. |
| `WebGPU renderer` | the WebGPU path. |

The engine refuses a software GPU by default (`failIfMajorPerformanceCaveat`),
which is how a run lands on Canvas. To check GPU features in a harness, accept
the slow context there and only there:

```js
const app = new Application(800, 600, {
    parent: "screen",
    // a test harness has no graphics card: take the software one
    failIfMajorPerformanceCaveat: import.meta.env.DEV ? false : true,
});
```

A run on WebGL says nothing about WebGPU, which the engine prefers on a real
machine. `melonjs-renderer-backends` covers pinning a backend (the `#webgl`,
`#webgpu` and `#canvas` fragments of the page's address do it without a code
change) and what each can and cannot do.

## Drive the keyboard and the pointer

Real input events reach the game, so drive it as a player would:

```js
// hold a key for half a second
await page.keyboard.down("ArrowRight");
await page.waitForTimeout(500);
await page.keyboard.up("ArrowRight");

// click a point given in game coordinates: the canvas may be scaled
const box = await page.locator("canvas").boundingBox();
const toPage = (x, y, width, height) => [
    box.x + (x / width) * box.width,
    box.y + (y / height) * box.height,
];
await page.mouse.click(...toPage(160, 120, 320, 240));
```

Then check the effect on the game's own state, not only on the picture:

```js
const before = await page.evaluate(() => player.pos.x);
// … hold ArrowRight …
const after = await page.evaluate(() => player.pos.x);   // greater, or the binding is wrong
```

A key held for too short a time can fall between two frames: hold it across
several. To press one from inside the page instead, expose `input` as `app`
is and call `input.triggerKeyEvent(input.KEY.LEFT, true)`, then `false`. A renderable that never gets its pointer events has `isKinematic` left
at `true`, the third rule of `melonjs`.

## Look at a frame

`page.locator("canvas").screenshot()` captures what was drawn, on every
renderer. Take it after the scene has had time to start (assets load behind a
loading screen), and read it: an image is the only check for draw order,
scaling, an effect, a camera that looks at the wrong place.

To see the collision shapes and the bounds, register the debug panel in
development and toggle it before the screenshot (`melonjs-plugins`):

```js
import { DebugPanelPlugin } from "@melonjs/debug-plugin";
plugin.register(DebugPanelPlugin, "debugPanel");   // toggled with S
```

## What a check has to cover

Before saying a game works, in this order:

1. The page loads with no `pageerror` and no text containing `is deprecated`.
2. The console header is there, and names the renderer you meant to check.
3. A screenshot after the loading screen shows the scene, not a blank canvas.
4. Each control does what it should, read from the game's state.
5. The path through the game you changed: a level change, a game over and a
   restart, whatever the task was about.

Say which of these you ran, and on which renderer. "It builds" is not one of
them.

## Symptom → cause

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| the harness waits for ever on `app.isInitialized` | `app` was never put on `globalThis`, or `init()` rejected: read the console |
| a blank canvas and a clean console | `await app.init()` is missing, or nothing was added to `app.world`: the first rule of `melonjs` |
| the effect just added is not in the screenshot | the run is on `CANVAS renderer`, where shader effects are inert: accept the software GPU in the harness |
| the only complaint is an anonymous `Error at warning (…)` | a deprecation, whose message is in the collapsed group before it: match console text on `is deprecated` |
| a key press does nothing in the harness, and works by hand | pressed and released inside one frame: hold it across several |
| a click lands beside its target | page coordinates were used as game coordinates: scale by the canvas's bounding box |
| the game runs in the harness and stalls for a user | timings on a software rasterizer mean nothing: measure on a real GPU (`melonjs-performance`) |
| it passes here and fails on a user's machine | the harness got WebGL and the user WebGPU, or the reverse: pin each with the address fragment and check both |

## Related skills

- `melonjs-renderer-backends` — which renderer a machine gets, and what each can do
- `melonjs-plugins` — the debug panel
- `melonjs-performance` — measuring, and why not on a software rasterizer
- `melonjs-input` — bindings, pointer events, `triggerKeyEvent`

physics: builtin
```

The second line names the renderer the run got: `WebGPU`, `WebGL2` or
`CANVAS`. Read it every time: the same code draws differently on each (see
below).

What to act on:

- **An uncaught error** (`pageerror`): the game stopped, or a callback did.
- **Text containing `is deprecated`.** A deprecation arrives as a collapsed
  group, of type `startGroupCollapsed`, whose text is the engine's message
  with its arguments after it (`melonJS: %s is deprecated since version %s,
  please use %s` then the names), followed by a `warning` that is only a
  stack trace. Filter on `warning` and you get an anonymous `Error at
  warning (…)`: match on the text of every message instead. The message
  names the replacement.
- **A `melonJS:` warning**, printed once however often it happens: a feature
  that is doing nothing on this renderer, an asset that failed to load, a
  setting that was ignored. Each skill's symptom table starts from these.

What is noise, in a headless browser:

- `No available adapters.` and `AUTO: WebGPU unavailable (…) — falling back`:
  the machine has no GPU the browser will use, so the engine took the next
  renderer. Expected; it tells you which one below.
- `GL Driver Message (…): GPU stall due to ReadPixels`: caused by the
  screenshot itself.
- `The AudioContext was not allowed to start`: no one has clicked yet. Sound
  starts after the first input, in a real browser too.

## Know which renderer you checked

A headless browser has no graphics card. What it falls back to depends on the
browser and how it was launched, and changes what the run proves:

| the console says | what was checked |
|---|---|
| `WebGL2 renderer (… SwiftShader …)` | the WebGL path, on a software rasterizer: shaders and post effects ran. Timings mean nothing. |
| `CANVAS renderer` | the fallback only. Shader effects, lit sprites, meshes and everything else that needs a GPU did **nothing**, silently. A screenshot without the effect you added is this, not a bug in your code. |
| `WebGPU renderer` | the WebGPU path. |

The engine refuses a software GPU by default (`failIfMajorPerformanceCaveat`),
which is how a run lands on Canvas. To check GPU features in a harness, accept
the slow context there and only there:

```js
const app = new Application(800, 600, {
    parent: "screen",
    // a test harness has no graphics card: take the software one
    failIfMajorPerformanceCaveat: import.meta.env.DEV ? false : true,
});
```

A run on WebGL says nothing about WebGPU, which the engine prefers on a real
machine. `melonjs-renderer-backends` covers pinning a backend (the `#webgl`,
`#webgpu` and `#canvas` fragments of the page's address do it without a code
change) and what each can and cannot do.

## Drive the keyboard and the pointer

Real input events reach the game, so drive it as a player would:

```js
// hold a key for half a second
await page.keyboard.down("ArrowRight");
await page.waitForTimeout(500);
await page.keyboard.up("ArrowRight");

// click a point given in game coordinates: the canvas may be scaled
const box = await page.locator("canvas").boundingBox();
const toPage = (x, y, width, height) => [
    box.x + (x / width) * box.width,
    box.y + (y / height) * box.height,
];
await page.mouse.click(...toPage(160, 120, 320, 240));
```

Then check the effect on the game's own state, not only on the picture:

```js
const before = await page.evaluate(() => player.pos.x);
// … hold ArrowRight …
const after = await page.evaluate(() => player.pos.x);   // greater, or the binding is wrong
```

A key held for too short a time can fall between two frames: hold it across
several. To press one from inside the page instead, expose `input` as `app`
is and call `input.triggerKeyEvent(input.KEY.LEFT, true)`, then `false`. A renderable that never gets its pointer events has `isKinematic` left
at `true`, the third rule of `melonjs`.

## Look at a frame

`page.locator("canvas").screenshot()` captures what was drawn, on every
renderer. Take it after the scene has had time to start (assets load behind a
loading screen), and read it: an image is the only check for draw order,
scaling, an effect, a camera that looks at the wrong place.

To see the collision shapes and the bounds, register the debug panel in
development and toggle it before the screenshot (`melonjs-plugins`):

```js
import { DebugPanelPlugin } from "@melonjs/debug-plugin";
plugin.register(DebugPanelPlugin, "debugPanel");   // toggled with S
```

## What a check has to cover

Before saying a game works, in this order:

1. The page loads with no `pageerror` and no text containing `is deprecated`.
2. The console header is there, and names the renderer you meant to check.
3. A screenshot after the loading screen shows the scene, not a blank canvas.
4. Each control does what it should, read from the game's state.
5. The path through the game you changed: a level change, a game over and a
   restart, whatever the task was about.

Say which of these you ran, and on which renderer. "It builds" is not one of
them.

## Symptom → cause

| symptom | cause |
|---|---|
| the harness waits for ever on `app.isInitialized` | `app` was never put on `globalThis`, or `init()` rejected: read the console |
| a blank canvas and a clean console | `await app.init()` is missing, or nothing was added to `app.world`: the first rule of `melonjs` |
| the effect just added is not in the screenshot | the run is on `CANVAS renderer`, where shader effects are inert: accept the software GPU in the harness |
| the only complaint is an anonymous `Error at warning (…)` | a deprecation, whose message is in the collapsed group before it: match console text on `is deprecated` |
| a key press does nothing in the harness, and works by hand | pressed and released inside one frame: hold it across several |
| a click lands beside its target | page coordinates were used as game coordinates: scale by the canvas's bounding box |
| the game runs in the harness and stalls for a user | timings on a software rasterizer mean nothing: measure on a real GPU (`melonjs-performance`) |
| it passes here and fails on a user's machine | the harness got WebGL and the user WebGPU, or the reverse: pin each with the address fragment and check both |

## Related skills

- `melonjs-renderer-backends` — which renderer a machine gets, and what each can do
- `melonjs-plugins` — the debug panel
- `melonjs-performance` — measuring, and why not on a software rasterizer
- `melonjs-input` — bindings, pointer events, `triggerKeyEvent`

# Tiled maps

> melonJS's flagship content pipeline. Maps are authored in
> [Tiled](https://www.mapeditor.org/) and loaded through the `level` director —
> you rarely touch the `TMX*` classes directly.
>
> Levels made with [LDtk](https://ldtk.io) load the same way, from the
> `.ldtk` project file as the editor saves it: see "LDtk levels" below. What
> this skill says of tile layers, the level director and the object registry
> holds for them too.
>
> A map made with [Sprite Fusion](https://www.spritefusion.com) loads as it is
> exported, `map.json` or `map.tmx`, under the asset type `"spritefusion"`:
> see "Sprite Fusion maps" below.

## Loading a level

Preload the map **and** everything it references — the `.tmx`, any external
`.tsx` tilesets, and the tileset images:

```js
await loader.preload([
    { name: "map1",    type: "tmx", src: "data/map/map1.tmx" },
    { name: "tileset", type: "tsx", src: "data/map/tileset.tsx" },
    { name: "tiles",   type: "image", src: "data/img/tiles.png" },
]);

level.load("map1");           // inside Stage.onResetEvent
```

**A game with several maps** keeps each map and the images only it uses in a
bundle of its own, beside a `common` bundle for the shared tileset, the player
and the sounds: an assets file exporting `{ common: [...], map1: [...],
map2: [...] }`, passed as it is to `loader.preload()`. A map's level can then be
freed with `loader.unload("map1")` and brought back with
`await loader.load("map1")` before `level.load("map1")`; a game whose maps
loop back simply keeps them all loaded. `melonjs-loading-assets` covers the
pattern.

Asset `type` is `"tmx"` for maps and `"tsx"` for external tilesets (`"tilemap"`
is another name for `"tmx"`, see "A map written by another tool" below). The
*file* can be `.tmx` / `.tsx`
(XML), or `.json` / `.tmj` / `.tsj`; the parser branches on the extension, not
on the type. `type: "tmj"` throws `unknown or invalid resource type`. You can
also skip `src` and pass the map inline via `data`, as the parsed JSON object
of a Tiled JSON export (not an XML string).

**Prefer JSON where there is no DOM.** XML maps and tilesets are parsed with
`DOMParser`, which only a page has: in a Web Worker, or on nx.js (the Nintendo
Switch, see `melonjs-platforms`), loading one fails, and `preload()` rejects
with "Failed loading resource …" whose `cause` (also logged to the console)
says to export it as JSON. Export the map *and* its external tilesets as
`.tmj` / `.tsj` (Tiled: File → Export As, or set JSON as the format in the
project).

`level.load(levelId, options)` accepts `container` (default `game.world`),
`onLoaded` (default `game.onLevelLoaded`), `flatten` (default `game.mergeGroup`),
`setViewportBounds` (default **`true`**), `objects` (default `true`, see
below) and `async` (default `false`). It throws
`level <id> not found` for an unknown id — synchronously, in both forms, because
that is a typo rather than a load failure.

Those `game.` defaults are the engine's own, and `game` is whichever
`Application` finished `init()` last. **Pass `container` explicitly** from a
`Stage`, which has the right one: `level.load("map", { container: this.app.world })`.

**`level.load` is deferred while the game loop is running.** It calls
`state.stop()` and finishes the load on a timer, after the current frame, so by
default it returns `true` before anything is in the world. Two ways to sequence
work after it:

```js
// await it
await level.load("map1", { async: true });
// the world is populated here

// ...or use the callback / event, which fire in both forms
level.load("map1", { onLoaded: () => this.spawnPlayer() });
```

`async: true` is the only thing that changes the return value — everything else
behaves identically, `onLoaded` included. Without it the call returns a boolean,
so `await level.load("map1")` is not an error and does not await the load:
`await true` resolves immediately, while the load is still sitting on a timer.
Pass the flag when you mean to await.

`level.reload()`, `level.next()` and `level.previous()` take the same `async`
option and resolve the same value they return — so `if (level.next())` becomes
`if (await level.next({ async: true }))`. Running out of levels reports `false`
either way rather than throwing. `level.getCurrentLevelId()` and
`level.levelCount()` round out the namespace. `flatten: false` wraps each Tiled
object layer and group layer in its own `Container` named after it.

## Spawning entities from Tiled objects

Objects are matched against a factory registry, in this order: the object's
Tiled **class**, then its **name**, then, for a tile object with no class of
its own, its **tile's class**, then the structural fallbacks `"text"`,
`"tile"` and `"shape"`.

```js
import { registerObjectClass, registerObjectFactory } from "melonjs";

registerObjectClass("Enemy", Enemy);   // ← matches Tiled class OR name
registerObjectFactory("Spine", (settings, map) => { /* → Renderable */ });
level.load("map1");
```

The registry is the same for every kind of level: a class registered here is
also built for an LDtk entity of that name. (`registerTiledObjectClass` and
`registerTiledObjectFactory` are the older names of these two functions,
deprecated since 20.18 and still working.)

These are the entry points to use. The registry is the level loader's, held by
the object factory, and has nothing to do with object pooling.

`pool.register(className, classObj)` **also** works and registers a Tiled
factory as a side effect, under the name and again under an `me.`-prefixed
alias, unless you set `pool.autoRegisterTiled = false`. That is the older
spelling, kept working for maps and games written against it, and it now
prints a one-off deprecation notice: `me.pool` is deprecated since 18.0.0.

Its third argument no longer buys anything here. It used to make Tiled
objects recyclable; they are constructed directly now, and the container
returns children to typed pools rather than to the name-keyed one. To pool a
class you spawn constantly, give it a `createPool` and register it for Tiled
separately:

```js
registerObjectClass("mainPlayer", PlayerEntity);
```

Register **before** loading. With no match the object falls through to the
structural factory and becomes a plain `Renderable` with a static body — it does
not error, it just has none of your behaviour.

`registerObjectClass` **throws** if you register a *different* constructor
under a name already taken (re-registering the same one is a no-op).
`registerObjectFactory` overwrites and only `console.warn`s, so it is the
one to use for replacing something already registered.

**Overriding a built-in name always works.** The engine's own classes are
DEFAULTS: they fill a name nothing else has claimed, and yours takes it over
whenever you register, before or after a map has loaded.

```js
registerObjectClass("Trigger", MyTrigger);   // whenever you like
```

The throw is for a clash between two of *your* classes under one name. For
that case `registerObjectFactory` overwrites and only warns.

### Finding an object, and choosing which are built

An object in the world is found as any child is, by the name or the id its
level gives it, whatever class built it and whatever the editor:

```js
const [player] = app.world.getChildByName("Player");
const [door] = app.world.getChildByProp("id", 12);   // Tiled's object id; LDtk's iid, a string
```

The id is put on the object for you when its class does not take it (a class
that sets its own `id` keeps it). The name is the class's business: a `Sprite`
or an `Entity` takes the level's, a `Trigger` is always named "Trigger" (find
one by its id, or with `getChildByType(Trigger)`).

`objects` chooses which objects a load builds: `false` for none, or a function
given each object's settings, the same its class would be given, before
anything is built:

```js
// a level that comes back without what the player took
level.load("map1", { objects: (settings) => !taken.has(settings.id) });
```

### Classes and properties set on tiles

In Tiled, a tile can carry a class and custom properties (tileset editor), and
every object placed from that tile shows them as its own. melonJS follows:

- **The tile's class.** A tile object with no class is built by the class
  registered under its tile's class, so a designer sets "Chest" once on the
  chest tile and every chest dropped in the map is a `Chest`. The object's
  own class or registered name still comes first, and a tile classed like a
  built-in (`Sprite`, `Trigger`, `shape`...) stays a plain tile.
- **The tile's properties.** Read them with `settings.resolvedProperty(name)`
  or `settings.resolvedProperties()`, which merge the tile's properties under
  the object's own, as Tiled's scripting API of the same names does. They are
  **not** set on `settings` by name: only the object's own properties are,
  as before, so a tile property named like a sprite setting never reaches a
  plain tile sprite.

```ts
import { registerObjectClass, Sprite, type TMXObject } from "melonjs";

// the custom properties set on the object itself, by name
interface DoorSettings extends TMXObject {
    locked?: boolean;
}

class Door extends Sprite {
    locked: boolean;
    facing: string;
    constructor(x: number, y: number, settings: DoorSettings) {
        super(x, y, { image: "door" });
        this.locked = settings.locked ?? false;
        // on the object, or else on the door tile in the tileset
        this.facing = settings.resolvedProperty("facing") ?? "N";
    }
}
registerObjectClass("Door", Door);   // and give the door tile the class "Door"
```

`TMXObject` is the type of the `settings` a registered class (or factory)
receives: the object as read from the map, with `tile` (a `Tile`) on a tile
object. Extend it with the properties your class reads.

For a class that is not a `Sprite` itself (a `Container` holding the tile and
something else, say), `settings.tile.getRenderable()` returns the tile's sprite
as a plain tile object would get it: from a tileset image, an image collection
or an animated tile alike, with no region names to build by hand.

melonJS pre-registers `Renderable`, `Sprite`, `NineSliceSprite`, `Text`,
`BitmapText`, `ImageLayer`, `ColorLayer`, `Light2d`, `Collectable`, `Trigger`
and `Entity` as Tiled classes, so `Collectable` and `Trigger` work out of the
box. A rectangle object of class `ColorLayer` with a `color` property is
filled with that color (20.18). Each is registered under its `me.`-prefixed alias as well, so a map
authored against melonJS 1.x finds them where it looks.

A `Trigger` forwards a **fixed list** of settings to `level.load()` — not
whatever you pass it. Today that list is `container`, `onLoaded`, `flatten`,
`setViewportBounds`, `objects` and the glTF scene options: `scale`, `rightHanded`,
`lights`, `lightIntensityScale` and the ground-shadow settings
(`castGroundShadow`, `shadowGroundY`, `shadowOpacity`, `shadowScale`,
`shadowOffset`, `shadowStretch`, `shadowDirectionX`, `shadowDirectionZ`,
`shadowGroundNormal`, `shadowLight`, but not `shadowGroundPoint`); see the 3D
assets skill. Anything outside it is **dropped silently**, which is worth
knowing before you spend an afternoon on a map that loads at the wrong scale.
`async` is excluded deliberately — the trigger needs to sequence its own
transition.

That transition is the trigger's own, and every part of it can be a property
of the trigger object in Tiled, with no code: `color` and `duration` (both, or
there is none), `transition` (`"fade"` or `"mask"`), and for a mask `shape`,
`center` and `invert`. A `shape` property is text, so it names a preloaded
image (its silhouette) or is `"touching"`; `center: "touching"` closes the
mask on whoever walked in. So a door that closes the player's own silhouette
onto the player is the properties `transition = mask`, `shape = touching`,
`center = touching`, `color = #000`, `duration = 400`. See
`melonjs-scenes-and-state` for the shapes and what `invert` does.

## Reading and changing tiles at run time

A tile layer is a live grid, not just a picture: read it as the game board,
and change cells while the game runs — a door opening, a floor panel lighting
up, a wall blown away. A loaded tile layer is a `TMXLayer` in the world, under
the name it has in Tiled:

```js
await level.load("map1", { container: this.app.world, async: true });
const board = this.app.world.getChildByName("ground")[0];   // a TMXLayer
board.cols; board.rows;              // the grid, in cells
board.tilewidth; board.tileheight;   // a cell, in pixels
```

Two coordinate systems, and the methods do not share one:

| method | takes | returns |
|---|---|---|
| `cellAt(col, row)` | column and row | the `Tile` there, or `null` for an empty cell or outside the grid |
| `getTile(x, y)` | **world pixels** | the same `Tile` object `cellAt` gives, or `null` |
| `setTile(tile, col, row)` | column and row | puts `tile` there, and returns it |
| `clearTile(col, row)` | column and row | empties the cell: `cellAt` then returns `null` |
| `getTileById(gid, col, row)` | a global tile id, column and row | a new `Tile`, to pass to `setTile` |

Columns and rows are the map's tile coordinates, the ones Tiled shows. On an
**infinite** map a layer can hold tiles left of or above the map's origin:
there `board.startx` / `board.starty` are negative, its cells run from
`startx` to `startx + cols - 1` (and `starty` to `starty + rows - 1`), and
`cellAt(-3, -2)` is the tile Tiled shows at (-3, -2), drawn where Tiled draws
it. On a finite map both are 0:

```js
for (let row = board.starty; row < board.starty + board.rows; row++) {
    for (let col = board.startx; col < board.startx + board.cols; col++) {
        const tile = board.cellAt(col, row);   // every cell, infinite maps included
    }
}
```

An infinite map's `getBounds()` (and its `width` / `height`) covers the map's
own area and every painted tile, so a level loaded with `setViewportBounds`
lets the camera reach tiles painted past the map's size, or left of or above
its origin. Empty chunk cells past the last painted tile are not part of it.
Size a camera you set up yourself from `map.getBounds()`, not from
`cols * tilewidth`, which is only right for an orthogonal map:

```js
const b = level.getCurrentLevel().getBounds();
app.viewport.setBounds(b.left, b.top, b.width, b.height);
```

A `Tile` carries `tileId` (its **global** id), `col`, `row` and `tileset`.
Tiled shows a tile's *local* id in the tileset editor; the global id is
`tileset.firstgid + localId`, and only the global one works with `setTile`.
The properties of the tile in a cell come from the layer (20.18), whatever
the map was made with: a Tiled tile's custom properties, an LDtk tile's custom
data and tags, a Sprite Fusion tile's attributes.

```js
const props = board.getTileProperties(col, row);   // { kind: "floor" }, or undefined
```

It is a method of a `TileLayer`. An LDtk layer that stacks tiles or places
them off its grid is a `PlacedTileLayer`, which has no cells to ask: test
`layer instanceof TileLayer` on an LDtk level before calling it.

They are those of the tile in its tileset, with those the one cell has of its
own over them: `board.setTileProperties(col, row, { locked: true })` gives a
cell some, which last until the cell is written (`setTile`, `setCell`,
`clearTile`). Read the object, do not write to it: it may be the tileset's.

The tileset's alone, and the tile's class, come from the tileset by global id:

```js
const tile = board.cellAt(col, row);
const props = tile && tile.tileset.getTileProperties(tile.tileId);  // { kind: "floor" } or undefined
const cls = tile && tile.tileset.getTileClass(tile.tileId);
```

To swap a cell for another tile of the tileset, build the tile and set it. Look
global ids up by property once, rather than hard-coding them, so a designer
can rearrange the tileset:

```js
const tileset = board.tilesets.getTilesetByIndex(0);   // the layer's first tileset
const gidByKind = new Map();
for (let gid = tileset.firstgid; gid <= tileset.lastgid; gid++) {
    const kind = tileset.getTileProperties(gid)?.kind;
    if (kind !== undefined) gidByKind.set(kind, gid);
}

// light a floor panel up
board.setTile(board.getTileById(gidByKind.get("floor-lit"), col, row), col, row);
// knock a wall down
board.clearTile(col, row);
```

The layer redraws the changed cell by itself. What it does **not** change is
collision: solid ground comes from collision object layers (below), so a tile
set or cleared changes what is drawn and what `cellAt` returns, not what a body
runs into. Keep a layer you edit often off `preRender` (see the symptom table).

A tile layer moves with its `pos`. It starts where its offset in Tiled puts
it (Layer → Offset), and the game moves it from there; its tiles are drawn
where it is, and `getTile(x, y)` answers for where they are drawn. Move it
by a difference, not to a point: `pos` is not (0, 0) to begin with on every
map (an infinite one, an oblique one).

```js
board.pos.y -= 8;                    // the whole layer, 8 pixels up
board.getTile(pointer.x, pointer.y); // still the tile under the pointer
```

The other layers follow their offset in Tiled too: an image layer is placed by
it, an object layer's objects are created that far from where they were drawn
(collision shapes with them), and a group layer's offset moves the layers
inside it, on top of their own.

A group layer holds layers of any kind: tile layers, object layers, image
layers and other groups (object layers, image layers and nested groups since
20.18). As in Tiled, the group gives the layers inside it its offset, its
opacity, its parallax factor, its blend mode, and its tint where a layer has
none of its own. Every layer takes a depth (`pos.z`) of its own in Tiled's
order, the ones inside a group included, so the layer that follows a group
draws over everything in the group. With `flatten: false`, a group is a
`Container` named after it, holding its tile and image layers, and a
container for each object layer or group inside it.

The map's own custom properties (Map → Map Properties in Tiled) are set on the
map object, which `level.getCurrentLevel()` returns once it is loaded: a
`theme` string property is `level.getCurrentLevel().theme`. They are set
**over** the map's own fields, so a property named like one replaces it: a
custom `name` property becomes the level's `name`. Give level settings names of
their own (`title`, not `name`).

## Camera bounds

`level.load` sets the viewport bounds to the map's bounds for you (on an
infinite map, every painted tile, see above) —
`setViewportBounds` defaults to `true`, and the handler is re-run on every
viewport resize, centring the map when it is smaller than the screen. You only
need to do it by hand when you opted out:

```js
level.load("map1", { setViewportBounds: false });
app.viewport.setBounds(0, 0, mapWidth, mapHeight);   // now it's on you
```

The same is true if you drive `TileMap.addTo(container, flatten, setViewportBounds)`
directly — note that method's `setViewportBounds` defaults to **`false`**, the
opposite of `level.load`'s.

## Collision shapes

Draw collision geometry in Tiled on an object layer and melonJS turns it into
world shapes automatically — rectangles, polygons, polylines, ellipses and
points all work. On an isometric map they are projected with the map's tile
ratio; a circle stays an `Ellipse`, but any other ellipse comes out tilted and
becomes a `Polygon`, so code that checks a shape's type should expect either.

The contract is the **layer name**: melonJS lowercases it and checks whether it
*contains* `"collision"` (so `collision`, `Collision`, `world collision` all
match). Inside such a layer, objects **with no name** get
`collisionType = collision.types.WORLD_SHAPE` and `type = "static"`. A *named*
object in a collision layer keeps whatever its factory gave it — that is how you
mix triggers into the collision layer.

An object that matches no factory and carries no text or tile data falls to the
`"shape"` factory: a plain `Renderable` with a static `bodyDef` built from its
geometry, which the world auto-registers with the active adapter on `addChild`.

For per-object physics, set the object's custom properties in Tiled; they arrive
on the settings object passed to your entity's constructor. Properties set on
the object's tile are read with `settings.resolvedProperty(name)`. One is also
applied to the object the map creates: an `int` property named
`visibilityLayer` sets which cameras draw it (see `melonjs-camera-and-drawing`).

### Solid tile layers: the `collider` property

A tile layer is solid when it has a boolean custom property named `collider`
set to true (20.18): each run of its tiles becomes one static `WORLD_SHAPE`
body, as an unnamed shape of a collision layer does. No object layer to draw.

```js
// in Tiled: select the tile layer, add a custom property `collider` (bool), check it
level.load("map1");   // the layer's tiles hold the player up
```

- The walls are built when the level is loaded, from the tiles the layer has
  then: `setTile` / `clearTile` afterwards does not change them.
- Each wall carries the layer's name as `wall.layer`, to tell them apart in a
  collision handler. The layer itself is still the only thing found by
  `getChildByName`.
- They are part of the layer, not objects: `objects: false` leaves them in.
- Orthogonal maps only; on another orientation the property is ignored, with
  a warning.

### Sprite Fusion maps

A map made with [Sprite Fusion](https://www.spritefusion.com) loads as the
editor exports it, under the asset type `"spritefusion"` (20.18). Either
export does: `map.json` ("JSON") or `map.tmx` ("TMX"). Unzip the export, keep
`spritesheet.png` next to the map, and give the loader the map alone:

```js
await loader.preload([
    { name: "level1", type: "spritefusion", src: "maps/level1/map.json" },
    { name: "level2", type: "spritefusion", src: "maps/level2/map.json" },
]);
level.load("level1");
```

- **The spritesheet comes with the map**: it is loaded from the map's folder,
  kept for that map (two maps each have their own `spritesheet.png`), and
  freed with it. Nothing to preload.
- **Collider layers are solid**: a layer with the editor's "collider" box
  checked gets walls, as above.
- **Tile attributes** are read by the cell, each value of its type:
  `layer.getTileProperties(col, row)` gives
  `{ type: "lava", damage: 25, isSolid: false }`. That one call reads both
  exports. (The TMX export puts them on the tile in the tileset, the JSON on
  each placed tile: `tileset.getTileProperties` only finds the first.)
- **Per-tile instance attributes** (the project setting that gives one placed
  tile its own) are in the JSON export only: the editor refuses a TMX export
  while it is on. Use `map.json` for those.
- The layers are in the editor's order, the bottom one first,
