# Tiled maps

> melonJS's flagship content pipeline. Maps are authored in
> [Tiled](https://www.mapeditor.org/) and loaded through the `level` director —
> you rarely touch the `TMX*` classes directly.
>
> Levels made with [LDtk](https://ldtk.io) load the same way, from the
> `.ldtk` project file as the editor saves it: see "LDtk levels" below. What
> this skill says of tile layers, the level director and the object registry
> holds for them too.
>
> A map made with [Sprite Fusion](https://www.spritefusion.com) loads as it is
> exported, `map.json` or `map.tmx`, under the asset type `"spritefusion"`:
> see "Sprite Fusion maps" below.

## Loading a level

Preload the map **and** everything it references — the `.tmx`, any external
`.tsx` tilesets, and the tileset images:

```js
await loader.preload([
    { name: "map1",    type: "tmx", src: "data/map/map1.tmx" },
    { name: "tileset", type: "tsx", src: "data/map/tileset.tsx" },
    { name: "tiles",   type: "image", src: "data/img/tiles.png" },
]);

level.load("map1");           // inside Stage.onResetEvent
```

**A game with several maps** keeps each map and the images only it uses in a
bundle of its own, beside a `common` bundle for the shared tileset, the player
and the sounds: an assets file exporting `{ common: [...], map1: [...],
map2: [...] }`, passed as it is to `loader.preload()`. A map's level can then be
freed with `loader.unload("map1")` and brought back with
`await loader.load("map1")` before `level.load("map1")`; a game whose maps
loop back simply keeps them all loaded. `melonjs-loading-assets` covers the
pattern.

Asset `type` is `"tmx"` for maps and `"tsx"` for external tilesets (`"tilemap"`
is another name for `"tmx"`, see "A map written by another tool" below). The
*file* can be `.tmx` / `.tsx`
(XML), or `.json` / `.tmj` / `.tsj`; the parser branches on the extension, not
on the type. `type: "tmj"` throws `unknown or invalid resource type`. You can
also skip `src` and pass the map inline via `data`, as the parsed JSON object
of a Tiled JSON export (not an XML string).

**Prefer JSON where there is no DOM.** XML maps and tilesets are parsed with
`DOMParser`, which only a page has: in a Web Worker, or on nx.js (the Nintendo
Switch, see `melonjs-platforms`), loading one fails, and `preload()` rejects
with "Failed loading resource …" whose `cause` (also logged to the console)
says to export it as JSON. Export the map *and* its external tilesets as
`.tmj` / `.tsj` (Tiled: File → Export As, or set JSON as the format in the
project).

`level.load(levelId, options)` accepts `container` (default `game.world`),
`onLoaded` (default `game.onLevelLoaded`), `flatten` (default `game.mergeGroup`),
`setViewportBounds` (default **`true`**), `objects` (default `true`, see
below) and `async` (default `false`). It throws
`level <id> not found` for an unknown id — synchronously, in both forms, because
that is a typo rather than a load failure.

Those `game.` defaults are the engine's own, and `game` is whichever
`Application` finished `init()` last. **Pass `container` explicitly** from a
`Stage`, which has the right one: `level.load("map", { container: this.app.world })`.

**`level.load` is deferred while the game loop is running.** It calls
`state.stop()` and finishes the load on a timer, after the current frame, so by
default it returns `true` before anything is in the world. Two ways to sequence
work after it:

```js
// await it
await level.load("map1", { async: true });
// the world is populated here

// ...or use the callback / event, which fire in both forms
level.load("map1", { onLoaded: () => this.spawnPlayer() });
```

`async: true` is the only thing that changes the return value — everything else
behaves identically, `onLoaded` included. Without it the call returns a boolean,
so `await level.load("map1")` is not an error and does not await the load:
`await true` resolves immediately, while the load is still sitting on a timer.
Pass the flag when you mean to await.

`level.reload()`, `level.next()` and `level.previous()` take the same `async`
option and resolve the same value they return — so `if (level.next())` becomes
`if (await level.next({ async: true }))`. Running out of levels reports `false`
either way rather than throwing. `level.getCurrentLevelId()` and
`level.levelCount()` round out the namespace. `flatten: false` wraps each Tiled
object layer and group layer in its own `Container` named after it.

## Spawning entities from Tiled objects

Objects are matched against a factory registry, in this order: the object's
Tiled **class**, then its **name**, then, for a tile object with no class of
its own, its **tile's class**, then the structural fallbacks `"text"`,
`"tile"` and `"shape"`.

```js
import { registerObjectClass, registerObjectFactory } from "melonjs";

registerObjectClass("Enemy", Enemy);   // ← matches Tiled class OR name
registerObjectFactory("Spine", (settings, map) => { /* → Renderable */ });
level.load("map1");
```

The registry is the same for every kind of level: a class registered here is
also built for an LDtk entity of that name. (`registerTiledObjectClass` and
`registerTiledObjectFactory` are the older names of these two functions,
deprecated since 20.18 and still working.)

These are the entry points to use. The registry is the level loader's, held by
the object factory, and has nothing to do with object pooling.

`pool.register(className, classObj)` **also** works and registers a Tiled
factory as a side effect, under the name and again under an `me.`-prefixed
alias, unless you set `pool.autoRegisterTiled = false`. That is the older
spelling, kept working for maps and games written against it, and it now
prints a one-off deprecation notice: `me.pool` is deprecated since 18.0.0.

Its third argument no longer buys anything here. It used to make Tiled
objects recyclable; they are constructed directly now, and the container
returns children to typed pools rather than to the name-keyed one. To pool a
class you spawn constantly, give it a `createPool` and register it for Tiled
separately:

```js
registerObjectClass("mainPlayer", PlayerEntity);
```

Register **before** loading. With no match the object falls through to the
structural factory and becomes a plain `Renderable` with a static body — it does
not error, it just has none of your behaviour.

`registerObjectClass` **throws** if you register a *different* constructor
under a name already taken (re-registering the same one is a no-op).
`registerObjectFactory` overwrites and only `console.warn`s, so it is the
one to use for replacing something already registered.

**Overriding a built-in name always works.** The engine's own classes are
DEFAULTS: they fill a name nothing else has claimed, and yours takes it over
whenever you register, before or after a map has loaded.

```js
registerObjectClass("Trigger", MyTrigger);   // whenever you like
```

The throw is for a clash between two of *your* classes under one name. For
that case `registerObjectFactory` overwrites and only warns.

### Finding an object, and choosing which are built

An object in the world is found as any child is, by the name or the id its
level gives it, whatever class built it and whatever the editor:

```js
const [player] = app.world.getChildByName("Player");
const [door] = app.world.getChildByProp("id", 12);   // Tiled's object id; LDtk's iid, a string
```

The id is put on the object for you when its class does not take it (a class
that sets its own `id` keeps it). The name is the class's business: a `Sprite`
or an `Entity` takes the level's, a `Trigger` is always named "Trigger" (find
one by its id, or with `getChildByType(Trigger)`).

`objects` chooses which objects a load builds: `false` for none, or a function
given each object's settings, the same its class would be given, before
anything is built:

```js
// a level that comes back without what the player took
level.load("map1", { objects: (settings) => !taken.has(settings.id) });
```

### Classes and properties set on tiles

In Tiled, a tile can carry a class and custom properties (tileset editor), and
every object placed from that tile shows them as its own. melonJS follows:

- **The tile's class.** A tile object with no class is built by the class
  registered under its tile's class, so a designer sets "Chest" once on the
  chest tile and every chest dropped in the map is a `Chest`. The object's
  own class or registered name still comes first, and a tile classed like a
  built-in (`Sprite`, `Trigger`, `shape`...) stays a plain tile.
- **The tile's properties.** Read them with `settings.resolvedProperty(name)`
  or `settings.resolvedProperties()`, which merge the tile's properties under
  the object's own, as Tiled's scripting API of the same names does. They are
  **not** set on `settings` by name: only the object's own properties are,
  as before, so a tile property named like a sprite setting never reaches a
  plain tile sprite.

```ts
import { registerObjectClass, Sprite, type TMXObject } from "melonjs";

// the custom properties set on the object itself, by name
interface DoorSettings extends TMXObject {
    locked?: boolean;
}

class Door extends Sprite {
    locked: boolean;
    facing: string;
    constructor(x: number, y: number, settings: DoorSettings) {
        super(x, y, { image: "door" });
        this.locked = settings.locked ?? false;
        // on the object, or else on the door tile in the tileset
        this.facing = settings.resolvedProperty("facing") ?? "N";
    }
}
registerObjectClass("Door", Door);   // and give the door tile the class "Door"
```

`TMXObject` is the type of the `settings` a registered class (or factory)
receives: the object as read from the map, with `tile` (a `Tile`) on a tile
object. Extend it with the properties your class reads.

For a class that is not a `Sprite` itself (a `Container` holding the tile and
something else, say), `settings.tile.getRenderable()` returns the tile's sprite
as a plain tile object would get it: from a tileset image, an image collection
or an animated tile alike, with no region names to build by hand.

melonJS pre-registers `Renderable`, `Sprite`, `NineSliceSprite`, `Text`,
`BitmapText`, `ImageLayer`, `ColorLayer`, `Light2d`, `Collectable`, `Trigger`
and `Entity` as Tiled classes, so `Collectable` and `Trigger` work out of the
box. A rectangle object of class `ColorLayer` with a `color` property is
filled with that color (20.18). Each is registered under its `me.`-prefixed alias as well, so a map
authored against melonJS 1.x finds them where it looks.

A `Trigger` forwards a **fixed list** of settings to `level.load()` — not
whatever you pass it. Today that list is `container`, `onLoaded`, `flatten`,
`setViewportBounds`, `objects` and the glTF scene options: `scale`, `rightHanded`,
`lights`, `lightIntensityScale` and the ground-shadow settings
(`castGroundShadow`, `shadowGroundY`, `shadowOpacity`, `shadowScale`,
`shadowOffset`, `shadowStretch`, `shadowDirectionX`, `shadowDirectionZ`,
`shadowGroundNormal`, `shadowLight`, but not `shadowGroundPoint`); see the 3D
assets skill. Anything outside it is **dropped silently**, which is worth
knowing before you spend an afternoon on a map that loads at the wrong scale.
`async` is excluded deliberately — the trigger needs to sequence its own
transition.

That transition is the trigger's own, and every part of it can be a property
of the trigger object in Tiled, with no code: `color` and `duration` (both, or
there is none), `transition` (`"fade"` or `"mask"`), and for a mask `shape`,
`center` and `invert`. A `shape` property is text, so it names a preloaded
image (its silhouette) or is `"touching"`; `center: "touching"` closes the
mask on whoever walked in. So a door that closes the player's own silhouette
onto the player is the properties `transition = mask`, `shape = touching`,
`center = touching`, `color = #000`, `duration = 400`. See
`melonjs-scenes-and-state` for the shapes and what `invert` does.

## Reading and changing tiles at run time

A tile layer is a live grid, not just a picture: read it as the game board,
and change cells while the game runs — a door opening, a floor panel lighting
up, a wall blown away. A loaded tile layer is a `TMXLayer` in the world, under
the name it has in Tiled:

```js
await level.load("map1", { container: this.app.world, async: true });
const board = this.app.world.getChildByName("ground")[0];   // a TMXLayer
board.cols; board.rows;              // the grid, in cells
board.tilewidth; board.tileheight;   // a cell, in pixels
```

Two coordinate systems, and the methods do not share one:

| method | takes | returns |
|---|---|---|
| `cellAt(col, row)` | column and row | the `Tile` there, or `null` for an empty cell or outside the grid |
| `getTile(x, y)` | **world pixels** | the same `Tile` object `cellAt` gives, or `null` |
| `setTile(tile, col, row)` | column and row | puts `tile` there, and returns it |
| `clearTile(col, row)` | column and row | empties the cell: `cellAt` then returns `null` |
| `getTileById(gid, col, row)` | a global tile id, column and row | a new `Tile`, to pass to `setTile` |

Columns and rows are the map's tile coordinates, the ones Tiled shows. On an
**infinite** map a layer can hold tiles left of or above the map's origin:
there `board.startx` / `board.starty` are negative, its cells run from
`startx` to `startx + cols - 1` (and `starty` to `starty + rows - 1`), and
`cellAt(-3, -2)` is the tile Tiled shows at (-3, -2), drawn where Tiled draws
it. On a finite map both are 0:

```js
for (let row = board.starty; row < board.starty + board.rows; row++) {
    for (let col = board.startx; col < board.startx + board.cols; col++) {
        const tile = board.cellAt(col, row);   // every cell, infinite maps included
    }
}
```

An infinite map's `getBounds()` (and its `width` / `height`) covers the map's
own area and every painted tile, so a level loaded with `setViewportBounds`
lets the camera reach tiles painted past the map's size, or left of or above
its origin. Empty chunk cells past the last painted tile are not part of it.
Size a camera you set up yourself from `map.getBounds()`, not from
`cols * tilewidth`, which is only right for an orthogonal map:

```js
const b = level.getCurrentLevel().getBounds();
app.viewport.setBounds(b.left, b.top, b.width, b.height);
```

A `Tile` carries `tileId` (its **global** id), `col`, `row` and `tileset`.
Tiled shows a tile's *local* id in the tileset editor; the global id is
`tileset.firstgid + localId`, and only the global one works with `setTile`.
The properties of the tile in a cell come from the layer (20.18), whatever
the map was made with: a Tiled tile's custom properties, an LDtk tile's custom
data and tags, a Sprite Fusion tile's attributes.

```js
const props = board.getTileProperties(col, row);   // { kind: "floor" }, or undefined
```

It is a method of a `TileLayer`. An LDtk layer that stacks tiles or places
them off its grid is a `PlacedTileLayer`, which has no cells to ask: test
`layer instanceof TileLayer` on an LDtk level before calling it.

They are those of the tile in its tileset, with those the one cell has of its
own over them: `board.setTileProperties(col, row, { locked: true })` gives a
cell some, which last until the cell is written (`setTile`, `setCell`,
`clearTile`). Read the object, do not write to it: it may be the tileset's.

The tileset's alone, and the tile's class, come from the tileset by global id:

```js
const tile = board.cellAt(col, row);
const props = tile && tile.tileset.getTileProperties(tile.tileId);  // { kind: "floor" } or undefined
const cls = tile && tile.tileset.getTileClass(tile.tileId);
```

To swap a cell for another tile of the tileset, build the tile and set it. Look
global ids up by property once, rather than hard-coding them, so a designer
can rearrange the tileset:

```js
const tileset = board.tilesets.getTilesetByIndex(0);   // the layer's first tileset
const gidByKind = new Map();
for (let gid = tileset.firstgid; gid <= tileset.lastgid; gid++) {
    const kind = tileset.getTileProperties(gid)?.kind;
    if (kind !== undefined) gidByKind.set(kind, gid);
}

// light a floor panel up
board.setTile(board.getTileById(gidByKind.get("floor-lit"), col, row), col, row);
// knock a wall down
board.clearTile(col, row);
```

The layer redraws the changed cell by itself. What it does **not** change is
collision: solid ground comes from collision object layers (below), so a tile
set or cleared changes what is drawn and what `cellAt` returns, not what a body
runs into. Keep a layer you edit often off `preRender` (see the symptom table).

A tile layer moves with its `pos`. It starts where its offset in Tiled puts
it (Layer → Offset), and the game moves it from there; its tiles are drawn
where it is, and `getTile(x, y)` answers for where they are drawn. Move it
by a difference, not to a point: `pos` is not (0, 0) to begin with on every
map (an infinite one, an oblique one).

```js
board.pos.y -= 8;                    // the whole layer, 8 pixels up
board.getTile(pointer.x, pointer.y); // still the tile under the pointer
```

The other layers follow their offset in Tiled too: an image layer is placed by
it, an object layer's objects are created that far from where they were drawn
(collision shapes with them), and a group layer's offset moves the layers
inside it, on top of their own.

A group layer holds layers of any kind: tile layers, object layers, image
layers and other groups (object layers, image layers and nested groups since
20.18). As in Tiled, the group gives the layers inside it its offset, its
opacity, its parallax factor, its blend mode, and its tint where a layer has
none of its own. Every layer takes a depth (`pos.z`) of its own in Tiled's
order, the ones inside a group included, so the layer that follows a group
draws over everything in the group. With `flatten: false`, a group is a
`Container` named after it, holding its tile and image layers, and a
container for each object layer or group inside it.

The map's own custom properties (Map → Map Properties in Tiled) are set on the
map object, which `level.getCurrentLevel()` returns once it is loaded: a
`theme` string property is `level.getCurrentLevel().theme`. They are set
**over** the map's own fields, so a property named like one replaces it: a
custom `name` property becomes the level's `name`. Give level settings names of
their own (`title`, not `name`).

## Camera bounds

`level.load` sets the viewport bounds to the map's bounds for you (on an
infinite map, every painted tile, see above) —
`setViewportBounds` defaults to `true`, and the handler is re-run on every
viewport resize, centring the map when it is smaller than the screen. You only
need to do it by hand when you opted out:

```js
level.load("map1", { setViewportBounds: false });
app.viewport.setBounds(0, 0, mapWidth, mapHeight);   // now it's on you
```

The same is true if you drive `TileMap.addTo(container, flatten, setViewportBounds)`
directly — note that method's `setViewportBounds` defaults to **`false`**, the
opposite of `level.load`'s.

## Collision shapes

Draw collision geometry in Tiled on an object layer and melonJS turns it into
world shapes automatically — rectangles, polygons, polylines, ellipses and
points all work. On an isometric map they are projected with the map's tile
ratio; a circle stays an `Ellipse`, but any other ellipse comes out tilted and
becomes a `Polygon`, so code that checks a shape's type should expect either.

The contract is the **layer name**: melonJS lowercases it and checks whether it
*contains* `"collision"` (so `collision`, `Collision`, `world collision` all
match). Inside such a layer, objects **with no name** get
`collisionType = collision.types.WORLD_SHAPE` and `type = "static"`. A *named*
object in a collision layer keeps whatever its factory gave it — that is how you
mix triggers into the collision layer.

An object that matches no factory and carries no text or tile data falls to the
`"shape"` factory: a plain `Renderable` with a static `bodyDef` built from its
geometry, which the world auto-registers with the active adapter on `addChild`.

For per-object physics, set the object's custom properties in Tiled; they arrive
on the settings object passed to your entity's constructor. Properties set on
the object's tile are read with `settings.resolvedProperty(name)`. One is also
applied to the object the map creates: an `int` property named
`visibilityLayer` sets which cameras draw it (see `melonjs-camera-and-drawing`).

### Solid tile layers: the `collider` property

A tile layer is solid when it has a boolean custom property named `collider`
set to true (20.18): each run of its tiles becomes one static `WORLD_SHAPE`
body, as an unnamed shape of a collision layer does. No object layer to draw.

```js
// in Tiled: select the tile layer, add a custom property `collider` (bool), check it
level.load("map1");   // the layer's tiles hold the player up
```

- The walls are built when the level is loaded, from the tiles the layer has
  then: `setTile` / `clearTile` afterwards does not change them.
- Each wall carries the layer's name as `wall.layer`, to tell them apart in a
  collision handler. The layer itself is still the only thing found by
  `getChildByName`.
- They are part of the layer, not objects: `objects: false` leaves them in.
- Orthogonal maps only; on another orientation the property is ignored, with
  a warning.

### Sprite Fusion maps

A map made with [Sprite Fusion](https://www.spritefusion.com) loads as the
editor exports it, under the asset type `"spritefusion"` (20.18). Either
export does: `map.json` ("JSON") or `map.tmx` ("TMX"). Unzip the export, keep
`spritesheet.png` next to the map, and give the loader the map alone:

```js
await loader.preload([
    { name: "level1", type: "spritefusion", src: "maps/level1/map.json" },
    { name: "level2", type: "spritefusion", src: "maps/level2/map.json" },
]);
level.load("level1");
```

- **The spritesheet comes with the map**: it is loaded from the map's folder,
  kept for that map (two maps each have their own `spritesheet.png`), and
  freed with it. Nothing to preload.
- **Collider layers are solid**: a layer with the editor's "collider" box
  checked gets walls, as above.
- **Tile attributes** are read by the cell, each value of its type:
  `layer.getTileProperties(col, row)` gives
  `{ type: "lava", damage: 25, isSolid: false }`. That one call reads both
  exports. (The TMX export puts them on the tile in the tileset, the JSON on
  each placed tile: `tileset.getTileProperties` only finds the first.)
- **Per-tile instance attributes** (the project setting that gives one placed
  tile its own) are in the JSON export only: the editor refuses a TMX export
  while it is on. Use `map.json` for those.
- The layers are in the editor's order, the bottom one first, and a layer
  hidden in the editor is left out of the export.
- Under `"tilemap"` or `"tmx"` the same files load too, but nothing is loaded
  with them: preload the image yourself, under the name `spritesheet`.

### A map written by another tool, or by hand

`"tilemap"` is the type for a tile map that is nobody's in particular: the
same loader as `"tmx"`, for the many tools that write Tiled's format. The
reader also takes the shorter words Sprite Fusion uses, which are handy in a
map written by hand or by a generator:

- `attributes`, a plain object of values, wherever `properties` is read (the
  map, a layer, an object, a tile of a tileset). An attribute is kept as
  written: no text is converted. Where both name a value, the attribute wins.
- a tile layer's `tiles`, a list of `{ id, x, y, attributes }` (the tile's id
  in the map's first tileset, and its cell), in place of `data`, the gid of
  every cell.

## Map orientations

Orthogonal, **isometric**, hexagonal, staggered and oblique are all supported;
anything else throws `<orientation> type TMX Tile Map n

# UI, HUD and text

## Outlined text: behind the glyphs, or over them

An outline is centred on the glyph's edge, so half of it lies inside the
glyph. `Text` paints it **behind** the glyphs by default (`paintOrder:
"stroke"`): the letters stay whole and the outline shows only around them, so
a thick outline works on any face. What shows is half of `lineWidth`: ask for
twice the width you want to see.

`paintOrder: "fill"` paints the glyphs first and the outline over them, as a
plain canvas does with `fillText` then `strokeText`, and as melonJS did before
20.13. Its inner half then covers the letters: on a small or thin face a
`lineWidth` of 3 already leaves them solid outline colour.

```js
const style = {
    font: "sans-serif", size: 32,
    fillStyle: "#ffd23f", strokeStyle: "#1b1b1b", lineWidth: 6,
};
new Text(x, y, { ...style, text: "BEHIND" });                     // the default
new Text(x, y, { ...style, paintOrder: "fill", text: "OVER" });   // the old look
```

The stroke used to cost you the top row of pixels as well, and a display face
whose glyphs overshoot the nominal ascent did the same on its own: the render
box was sized from the line height alone, with no allowance for either. **That
is fixed** — the bake is padded by the ink's real extent and the blit shifts
back by the same amount, so nothing is clipped and the reported bounds are
unchanged. Write the string you mean:

```js
new Text(x, y, { font: "Display", lineWidth: 1, lineHeight: 1.45, text: "" });
hud.setText("SCORE 100");
```

If you have a label carrying a leading `\n` to buy headroom, that workaround is
now dead weight — drop it, and take the line height back off the position you
shifted it by.

The outline's corners are set by `lineJoin`, the same property a canvas
context has, and `miterLimit`:

| setting | corners | use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `lineJoin: "round"` (default) | rounded: the outline is the same width all around | almost everything: HUDs, buttons, titles |
| `lineJoin: "bevel"` | cut flat | a harder edge with no spikes |
| `lineJoin: "miter"` | pointed, as a plain canvas strokes text | a sharp, angular look |
| `miterLimit: n` (default 10) | with `"miter"` only: a corner pointing further than `n` half line widths is cut flat instead | taming the spikes `"miter"` grows on "A", "V", "M" |

At the canvas default of 10, a thick `"miter"` outline grows spikes several
times its width from sharp glyphs; 2 to 4 keeps the corners pointed and the
spikes short:

```js
const outline = {
    font: "sans-serif", size: 48,
    fillStyle: "#ffffff", strokeStyle: "#000000", lineWidth: 6,
};
new Text(x, y, { ...outline, text: "ROUND" });                    // the default
new Text(x, y, { ...outline, lineJoin: "bevel", text: "BEVEL" });
new Text(x, y, { ...outline, lineJoin: "miter", text: "MITER" }); // long spikes
new Text(x, y, { ...outline, lineJoin: "miter", miterLimit: 3, text: "MITER 3" });
```

Whichever you pick, the bake leaves room for it on all four sides, so no corner
is cut and the label's position and bounds do not move; pointed corners just
cost a bigger texture. Changed on a live label, they show from the next
`setText()`.

## Gradient text

`fillStyle` takes a `Gradient` as well as a colour — the same object
`Renderer#setColor` accepts, built the way the canvas API builds one:

```js
const ramp = renderer.createLinearGradient(0, 0, 0, 24);  // top to bottom
ramp.addColorStop(0, "#fffdf0");
ramp.addColorStop(1, "#f0a020");

new Text(x, y, { font: "Display", size: 24, fillStyle: ramp });
```

Coordinates are the label's own bake: `(0, 0)` is the top-left of the render
box, so the ramp above runs down one line. A multi-line label **restarts it on
every line**, reading like one `Text` per line — you do not have to author the
gradient over the block height. Pass `gradientPerLine: false` for a single ramp
spanning the whole block, which is what a plain canvas does and what a
deliberate fade across a two-line title wants.

The ramp colours the **fill only** — `Text` strokes in a separate pass, so
an outline keeps its own colour without any luminance trickery — and it works on
Canvas2D, which a post effect does not.

### The gradient does not live in `fillStyle`

`fillStyle` ACCEPTS a `Gradient`; it never HOLDS one. The constructor routes it
to `fillGradient` and leaves `fillStyle` as the pooled `Color` it always is,
which is what keeps `fillStyle.alpha` gating the fill and keeps the colour
owned by the pool.

So changing the ramp later means assigning the field it actually landed in:

```js
label.fillGradient = ramp;   // ✓
label.fillStyle = ramp;      // ✗ TS2740: Gradient is not a Color
```

The ramp is authored for ONE line height, so a label that changes size needs a
new one built at the new size; there is nothing that rescales it for you.

## BitmapText: `size` is a RATIO, not pixels

The trap when moving over from `Text`:

```js
new Text(x, y,       { font: "Arial", size: 24, text: "SCORE" });  // 24 pixels
new BitmapText(x, y, { font: "arial", size: 24, text: "SCORE" });  // 24 TIMES
```

`size` scales the font's authored size, so `1` is native and `2` is double —
`resize(scale)` and `set(textAlign, scale)` take the same ratio. Whole numbers
keep pixel art crisp; fractional ones resample the page image.

It has **no stroke** — there is no `strokeStyle` or `lineWidth` here, which is
part of why it stays sharp. Colour comes from the tint instead:

```js
const score = new BitmapText(8, 8, {
    font: "arial", text: "1000", fillStyle: "#ffd700",
});
score.fillStyle = "#ff4040";                  // recolour at any time
score.fillStyle = new Color(255, 255, 255);   // UNTINTED, not "white text"
```

`fillStyle` is `Renderable#tint` under another name: white is the *absence* of a
tint and every other colour tints away from it, so author the page in white to
keep every colour available to you.

Load the descriptor as `binary` and its page as `image` under the **same name**.
Both BMFont flavours — text (`.fnt`) and XML — are auto-detected, so an `.xml`
descriptor loads as-is:

```js
loader.preload([
    { name: "arial", type: "binary", src: "data/font/arial.fnt" },
    { name: "arial", type: "image",  src: "data/font/arial.png" },
]);
```

Reach for it over `Text` when the text is mostly static, has to stay crisp at
integer scales, or wants recolouring without a re-bake.

### Do not build a throwaway label to measure a string

A `Text` owns a canvas bake and a GPU texture, and only `destroy()` frees
them — which is `@internal` and absent from the published types, so a game
cannot free a label it owns outside a container. A label built purely to
measure something therefore strands both, and if it is built in a stage's
`onResetEvent` it strands another on every entry to that state.

`measureText(text?)` measures any string on a label that already exists,
including one it is not currently holding:

```js
const widest = hudScore.measureText("00:00").width;
```

Given a string, it returns a new `TextMetrics` and leaves the label as it was;
with no argument it returns the label's own metrics. Before 20.13 measuring
another string overwrote the label's own metrics, so a centred or
right-aligned label was drawn shifted until its next `setText()`.

Advance widths scale linearly with the point size for one family, so measuring
on an existing label and scaling the result is exact. For labels you genuinely
spawn in bulk, `getPool("text")` recycles the bake.

### Multi-line text: the baseline places the whole block

A `\n` in the string (or an array of strings) starts a new line, on `Text` and
`BitmapText` alike. `textBaseline` then places the block as one piece against
`pos.y`: its top for `"top"` / `"hanging"`, its middle for `"middle"`, its
bottom for `"alphabetic"`, `"ideographic"` and `"bottom"`. So a two-line
`"bottom"` label in a screen corner sits wholly above `pos.y`, and a centred
`"middle"` label centres every line, not the first. `getBounds()` is that same
box, which is what culling and the pointer use.

`wordWrapWidth` only ADDS line breaks: each `\n`-separated line is wrapped on
its own, so explicit breaks and blank lines survive. A line breaks between
words, never inside one, so a single word wider than `wordWrapWidth` gets a
line of its own and overflows it:

```js
const help = new Text(8, 8, {
    font: "sans-serif", size: 16, wordWrapWidth: 200,
    text: "CONTROLS\nArrows move, Space jumps, Esc pauses the game.",
});
// "CONTROLS" on its own line, then the sentence wrapped under it
```

### Typewriter reveal: `visibleRatio`

`visibleCharacters` (`-1`, the default, shows them all) and `visibleRatio`
(0 to 1) show a label a character at a time, on `Text` and `BitmapText` alike.
Tween the ratio: it takes the same time whatever the length of the string.

```js
line.setText("The door is locked. The keeper has the key.");
line.visibleRatio = 0;
new Tween(line).to({ visibleRatio: 1 }, { duration: 1500 }).start();
```

Line breaks are not counted, and the wrapping and the bounds are those of the
whole string, so a word does not jump to the next line as it appears. The two
classes differ in two ways. A `BitmapText` keeps each glyph where the full line
puts it, while a centred or right-aligned `Text` aligns only the part shown so
far, so it slides sideways as it types: left-align a `Text` you reveal. And a
`Text` repaints and re-uploads its bake at every step, where a `BitmapText`
just draws fewer glyphs.

### `fillStyle` means two different things

The name is shared and the behaviour is not, which is the trap when moving a
label from one class to the other:

| | `Text` | `BitmapText` |
|---|---|---|
| what `fillStyle` holds | a real `Color`, the fill | `Renderable#tint`, under another name |
| white | white glyphs | the ABSENCE of a tint |
| gradient | yes, via `fillGradient` | no: a tint is one colour over a page image |
| recolour it later | `label.fillStyle.parseCSS("#ff4040")` — the field is a `Color` with no setter, and ASSIGNING a string replaces it, after which the glyphs stop filling entirely and nothing is logged | `label.fillStyle = "#ff4040"` — a real setter that parses the string |
| stroke | `strokeStyle` + `lineWidth`, behind or over the glyphs with `paintOrder`, corners with `lineJoin` / `miterLimit` | none |
| `size` | pixels | a RATIO of the authored size |

### Per-glyph wave, shake and colour: `glyphEffect`

Animating individual letters does **not** mean one renderable per character.
`BitmapText#glyphEffect` offsets and tints each glyph inside the batch the
label already draws, so an animated 100-character line stays one draw call and
costs no extra objects:

```js
label.glyphEffect = (out, ctx) => {
    // phase from the glyph's POSITION, not its index — see below
    out.offsetY = Math.sin(ctx.time * 0.005 + ctx.x * 0.02) * 6;  // wave
    out.tint.setColor(255, 128, 128);                             // per glyph
};
label.glyphEffect = null;    // back to the plain path
```

`out` and `ctx` are **reused**: read `ctx` during the call and write `out`, but
never keep either. `out.offsetX` / `offsetY` start at zero and `out.tint` at
opaque white on every glyph, so an effect that only touches some glyphs leaves
the rest alone. `ctx` carries `index` (across lines, line breaks excluded),
`char`, `code`, `x`, `y` and `time`.

Four things that catch people:

- **`time` advances in `update`, not in `draw`.** A label drawn through two
  cameras animates once, not twice. It is the milliseconds ACCUMULATED across
  updates while an effect was set, and nothing resets it, so swapping the
  callback continues the same clock rather than starting a new one.
- **Effects move pixels, not layout.** Metrics, wrapping, alignment,
  `visibleCharacters` and the bounds all ignore the offsets, so the pen advance
  and kerning are exactly as without one. The flip side is that **offsets do
  not extend the culling bounds**: a big wave near the screen edge can clip, so
  keep the measured text in view.
- **Canvas pays per distinct colour.** WebGL and WebGPU carry the tint in the
  per-vertex colour, so batching survives. The Canvas renderer instead caches a
  tinted copy of the whole font page per colour, and that cache is unbounded
  for the renderer's life, so a colour driven by `ctx.time` allocates a
  page-sized canvas every frame there. On Canvas, keep the palette finite or
  animate only the offsets.
- **`tint` is multiplicative**, like `fillStyle` above: white leaves the glyph
  alone, and `out.tint` multiplies whatever the label's own `fillStyle` is.

`Text` has no equivalent, since it rasterises the whole string into one texture.

### Making it read as motion

Three things decide whether a wave looks alive or mechanical, and none of them
is the amplitude.

- **Take the phase from `ctx.x`, not `ctx.index`.** This is the big one.
  Stepping per glyph advances the wave as far across a narrow `I` as across a
  wide `M`, so the wavelength stretches and squashes with whatever the line
  happens to spell, and the eye reads the unevenness as a mechanism. `ctx.x`
  gives the wave one fixed length in pixels and lets it travel through the
  text at a constant rate, whatever the letters are.
- **Round the offsets if the frame is upscaled.** They are added to the glyph
  destination unchanged, so a fractional offset in a small design resolution
  that is then magnified with nearest sampling makes the glyph's OWN pixels
  come out uneven — and differently uneven each frame. That is a shimmer, not
  movement. `Math.round` the offset and it steps cleanly, for the same reason
  `subPixel` defaults to false. Whole pixels mean few steps, so the amplitude
  has to be large enough to give you several.
- **A shake is not a sine.** A sine moves the whole line as one body, which is
  a wave however fast you run it. A shake gives each glyph a direction
  unrelated to its neighbours: pick a random angle per glyph, hold it for a
  tick, interpolate to the next, and scale the whole thing by a decay if it is
  an impact rather than a state.

Starting points that look right across sizes, as fractions of the font size:
an amplitude around an eighth of it, a wavelength around ten times it, and a
little under 5 radians per second. For a shake, re-target each glyph roughly
20 to 40 times a second.

`ctx.time` runs only while an effect is set and nothing resets it, so it is 0
only when a label gets its **first** effect. A label that already had one, or
is reused across lives, carries the old clock, and a decay measured from
`ctx.time` itself is already spent there. Note `ctx.time` on the effect's first
call and measure from that, as the shake below does, and attach it at the
moment you want to be t=0: on the frame the hit lands, not when the label was
built.

Both, whole:

```js
import { BitmapText } from "melonjs";

const title = new BitmapText(app.viewport.width / 2, 60, {
    font: "display",
    textAlign: "center",
    text: "JUNGLE RABBIT",
});
title.floating = true;
app.world.addChild(title);

// A wave: four pixels deep, a ~1.3s cycle, and a wavelength of roughly ten
// times the font size. Phase from ctx.x, offset rounded.
title.glyphEffect = (out, ctx) => {
    out.offsetY = Math.round(Math.sin(ctx.time * 0.005 + ctx.x * 0.02) * 4);
};

// A shake: each glyph picks its own direction, holds it for a tick, slides to
// the next, and the whole thing decays. Deterministic, so the same hit shakes
// the same way every time.
const angle = (i, tick) => {
    const h = Math.sin(i * 127.1 + tick * 311.7) * 43758.5453;
    return (h - Math.floor(h)) * Math.PI * 2;
};
const impact = (amplitude, durationMs, rate) => {
    let start;                               // ctx.time on the first call
    return (out, ctx) => {
        start ??= ctx.time;                  // the label's clock never resets
        const t = ctx.time - start;
        const left = 1 - t / durationMs;
        if (left <= 0) {
            return;                          // settled; `out` is already zeroed
        }
        const amp = amplitude * left * left;
        const tick = (t / 1000) * rate;
        const held = Math.floor(tick);
        const k = tick - held;
        const a = angle(ctx.index, held);
        const b = angle(ctx.index, held + 1);
        out.offsetX = Math.round((Math.sin(a) + (Math.sin(b) - Math.sin(a)) * k) * amp);
        out.offsetY = Math.round((Math.cos(a) + (Math.cos(b) - Math.cos(a)) * k) * amp);
    };
};

// a new impact at the moment of each hit: it measures from its own first call,
// so it shakes again on a banner that has shown one before
banner.setText("CAPSIZED!");
banner.glyphEffect = impact(3, 650, 24);
```

## The HUD pattern

A HUD is a `floating` container at a high z, built once and re-added:

```js
class HUD extends Container {
    constructor(app) {
        super(0, 0, app.viewport.width, app.viewport.height);
        this.floating = true;       // screen space, not world space
        this.isPersistent = true;   // survives a world reset
    }
}

app.world.addChild(new HUD(app), 100);   // explicit z — not `.z = Infinity`
```

There is no `UIContainer` class. Use `Container` for a bare grouping,
`UIPanel` for anything with a background or a border (see below), or
`UIBaseElement` when you want the pointer handling and nothing drawn — it is a
`Container` that already sets `floating = true` and `isKinematic = false`.

### Which widget for what

| you want | use | notes |
|---|---|---|
| a button with a label | `UITextButton` | drawn, or skinned from an atlas; `onClick` setting |
| an image-only button or icon | `UISpriteElement` | a `UIBaseElement` holding a `Sprite` (`sprite`); override `onClick` |
| an on/off option, or one of several | `UICheckbox` | a radio button with `group` |
| a value in a range: volume, sensitivity | `UISlider` | horizontal or vertical |
| health, shield, cooldown, loading | `ProgressBar` | not clickable; `value` redraws |
| a frame, dialog or menu card | `UIPanel` | skin, title, layout, scrolling, drag, shadow |
| your own clickable widget | extend `UIBaseElement` | pointer handlers, `enabled`, focus, bounce |
| a group with nothing drawn | `Container` | set `floating` for screen space |

### A whole options menu

Everything below in one place: a skinned panel that lays its widgets out
as a column, a checkbox, a slider, two buttons, a drop shadow, a little
bounce, and keyboard / gamepad play. Each piece has its own section after
this.

```js
import {
    UICheckbox, UIPanel, UISlider, UITextButton, audio, state,
} from "melonjs";

// one style object for every widget's text
const FONT = { font: "kenpixel", fontSize: 14, labelFillStyle: "black" };

const menu = new UIPanel(40, 40, {
    width: 360, height: 100,           // autoSize grows the height to fit
    skin: { atlas, region: "grey_panel", insetx: 10, insety: 10 },
    title: "OPTIONS", titleFont: "kenpixel", titleFontSize: 20,
    layout: "column", padding: 16, gap: 12, align: "stretch", autoSize: true,
    shadowColor: "#00000059", shadowOffsetY: 6, shadowBlur: 10, radius: 6,
});

const music = menu.addChild(new UICheckbox(0, 0, {
    ...FONT,
    labelOn: "Music ON", labelOff: "Music OFF",
    checked: settings.music,
    onChange: (on) => { settings.music = on; },   // user input only
}));

menu.addChild(new UISlider(0, 0, {
    ...FONT,
    label: "Volume", showValue: true,
    valueFormat: (v, ratio) => `${Math.round(ratio * 100)}%`,
    value: audio.getVolume(),
    onChange: (v) => audio.setVolume(v),           // while dragging
    onChangeEnd: () => saveSettings(),             // once, on release
}));

menu.addChild(new UITextButton(0, 0, {
    ...FONT, text: "Back", height: 40,
    hoverScale: 1.04, pressScale: 0.96,            // the bounce
    onClick: () => state.change(state.MENU),       // a completed click
}));

app.world.addChild(menu, 10);
music.focus();   // arrows / D-pad and Enter / A now drive the menu
```

Three things matter here:

- **`floating = true`** opts the container out of camera transforms, so it stays
  put while the world scrolls. Without it the HUD scrolls away — a silent
  failure.
- **Only the parent container needs `floating`.** `addChild` forces
  `child.floating = false` under a floating parent, and the container applies one
  projection swap for the whole subtree.
- **Pass an explicit z.** `this.z = Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` does nothing —
  `renderable.z` is not a real property. The real accessor is `depth` (an
  alias for `pos.z`); `addChild(child, z)` sets it for you.

### Bars and gauges: `ProgressBar`

A health bar, a shield gauge, a cooldown and a loading bar are one object. Set
`value`; it redraws.

```js
const hp = new ProgressBar(20, 20, {
    width: 200, height: 24,
    min: 0, max: 100, value: 100,      // min/max default to 0 and 1
    trackColor: "#0000001a",
    fillColor: "#c0392b",
    borderColor: "black", borderWidth: 2,
    padding: 2,                        // inset of the fill inside the track
    radius: 6,                         // 0 is square
});
hud.addChild(hp);

hp.value -= 15;                        // clamps; `ratio` reads back 0..1
hp.max = 50;                           // re-clamps the value into the new range
```

`direction` takes `"left-to-right"` (the default), `"right-to-left"`,
`"top-to-bottom"` or `"bottom-to-top"`, each growing from its own edge.

`showLabel: true` writes text centred over the bar, a percentage by default:
`` labelFormat: (value, ratio) => `${Math.round(value)} HP` `` changes what it says,
and `font` (a CSS family), `fontSize` and `labelFillStyle` how it looks.
`onChange(value, ratio, bar)` is called on every change of the value, from code
too, unlike a checkbox's or a slider's: a bar has no user input to tell apart.
Setting the value it already has calls nothing.

**The colour follows the value by mutating the `Color` you passed.** This is
the one non-obvious part, and it is deliberate: every game wants a different
rule, and most want the colour somewhere else too, next to a shader uniform or
a glow. The bar re-reads `fillColor` every frame, so it never has to know:

```js

const empty = new Color().parseCSS("#ff2a1e");
const mixed = new Color();

const shield = new ProgressBar(x, y, {
    width: 190, height: 13,
    trackColor: null,                  // hollow: the scene shows through
    borderColor: "rgba(122, 190, 235, 0.8)",
    padding: 2,
    fillColor: mixed,                  // KEPT, not copied
});

// each frame
mixed.copy(empty).lerp(full, hp);      // the bar follows, and so can a shader
shield.value = hp;
```

the game is already keeping. Neither is built in.

```js
    fillStyle: "#ffd23f", strokeStyle: "#1b1b1b", lineWidth: 6,
};
new Text(x, y, { ...style, text: "BEHIND" });                     // the default
new Text(x, y, { ...style, paintOrder: "fill", text: "OVER" });   // the old look
```

The stroke used to cost you the top row of pixels as well, and a display face
whose glyphs overshoot the nominal ascent did the same on its own: the render
box was sized from the line height alone, with no allowance for either. **That
is fixed** — the bake is padded by the ink's real extent and the blit shifts
back by the same amount, so nothing is clipped and the reported bounds are
unchanged. Write the string you mean:

```js
new Text(x, y, { font: "Display", lineWidth: 1, lineHeight: 1.45, text: "" });
hud.setText("SCORE 100");
```

If you have a label carrying a leading `\n` to buy headroom, that workaround is
now dead weight — drop it, and take the line height back off the position you
shifted it by.

The outline's corners are set by `lineJoin`, the same property a canvas
context has, and `miterLimit`:

| setting | corners | use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `lineJoin: "round"` (default) | rounded: the outline is the same width all around | almost everything: HUDs, buttons, titles |
| `lineJoin: "bevel"` | cut flat | a harder edge with no spikes |
| `lineJoin: "miter"` | pointed, as a plain canvas strokes text | a sharp, angular look |
| `miterLimit: n` (default 10) | with `"miter"` only: a corner pointing further than `n` half line widths is cut flat instead | taming the spikes `"miter"` grows on "A", "V", "M" |

At the canvas default of 10, a thick `"miter"` outline grows spikes several
times its width from sharp glyphs; 2 to 4 keeps the corners pointed and the
spikes short:

```js
const outline = {
    font: "sans-serif", size: 48,
    fillStyle: "#ffffff", strokeStyle: "#000000", lineWidth: 6,
};
new Text(x, y, { ...outline, text: "ROUND" });                    // the default
new Text(x, y, { ...outline, lineJoin: "bevel", text: "BEVEL" });
new Text(x, y, { ...outline, lineJoin: "miter", text: "MITER" }); // long spikes
new Text(x, y, { ...outline, lineJoin: "miter", miterLimit: 3, text: "MITER 3" });
```

Whichever you pick, the bake leaves room for it on all four sides, so no corner
is cut and the label's position and bounds do not move; pointed corners just
cost a bigger texture. Changed on a live label, they show from the next
`setText()`.

## Gradient text

`fillStyle` takes a `Gradient` as well as a colour — the same object
`Renderer#setColor` accepts, built the way the canvas API builds one:

```js
const ramp = renderer.createLinearGradient(0, 0, 0, 24);  // top to bottom
ramp.addColorStop(0, "#fffdf0");
ramp.addColorStop(1, "#f0a020");

new Text(x, y, { font: "Display", size: 24, fillStyle: ramp });
```

Coordinates are the label's own bake: `(0, 0)` is the top-left of the render
box, so the ramp above runs down one line. A multi-line label **restarts it on
every line**, reading like one `Text` per line — you do not have to author the
gradient over the block height. Pass `gradientPerLine: false` for a single ramp
spanning the whole block, which is what a plain canvas does and what a
deliberate fade across a two-line title wants.

The ramp colours the **fill only** — `Text` strokes in a separate pass, so
an outline keeps its own colour without any luminance trickery — and it works on
Canvas2D, which a post effect does not.

### The gradient does not live in `fillStyle`

`fillStyle` ACCEPTS a `Gradient`; it never HOLDS one. The constructor routes it
to `fillGradient` and leaves `fillStyle` as the pooled `Color` it always is,
which is what keeps `fillStyle.alpha` gating the fill and keeps the colour
owned by the pool.

So changing the ramp later means assigning the field it actually landed in:

```js
label.fillGradient = ramp;   // ✓
label.fillStyle = ramp;      // ✗ TS2740: Gradient is not a Color
```

The ramp is authored for ONE line height, so a label that changes size needs a
new one built at the new size; there is nothing that rescales it for you.

## BitmapText: `size` is a RATIO, not pixels

The trap when moving over from `Text`:

```js
new Text(x, y,       { font: "Arial", size: 24, text: "SCORE" });  // 24 pixels
new BitmapText(x, y, { font: "arial", size: 24, text: "SCORE" });  // 24 TIMES
```

`size` scales the font's authored size, so `1` is native and `2` is double —
`resize(scale)` and `set(textAlign, scale)` take the same ratio. Whole numbers
keep pixel art crisp; fractional ones resample the page image.

It has **no stroke** — there is no `strokeStyle` or `lineWidth` here, which is
part of why it stays sharp. Colour comes from the tint instead:

```js
const score = new BitmapText(8, 8, {
    font: "arial", text: "1000", fillStyle: "#ffd700",
});
score.fillStyle = "#ff4040";                  // recolour at any time
score.fillStyle = new Color(255, 255, 255);   // UNTINTED, not "white text"
```

`fillStyle` is `Renderable#tint` under another name: white is the *absence* of a
tint and every other colour tints away from it, so author the page in white to
keep every colour available to you.

Load the descriptor as `binary` and its page as `image` under the **same name**.
Both BMFont flavours — text (`.fnt`) and XML — are auto-detected, so an `.xml`
descriptor loads as-is:

```js
loader.preload([
    { name: "arial", type: "binary", src: "data/font/arial.fnt" },
    { name: "arial", type: "image",  src: "data/font/arial.png" },
]);
```

Reach for it over `Text` when the text is mostly static, has to stay crisp at
integer scales, or wants recolouring without a re-bake.

### Do not build a throwaway label to measure a string

A `Text` owns a canvas bake and a GPU texture, and only `destroy()` frees
them — which is `@internal` and absent from the published types, so a game
cannot free a label it owns outside a container. A label built purely to
measure something therefore strands both, and if it is built in a stage's
`onResetEvent` it strands another on every entry to that state.

`measureText(text?)` measures any string on a label that already exists,
including one it is not currently holding:

```js
const widest = hudScore.measureText("00:00").width;
```

Given a string, it returns a new `TextMetrics` and leaves the label as it was;
with no argument it returns the label's own metrics. Before 20.13 measuring
another string overwrote the label's own metrics, so a centred or
right-aligned label was drawn shifted until its next `setText()`.

Advance widths scale linearly with the point size for one family, so measuring
on an existing label and scaling the result is exact. For labels you genuinely
spawn in bulk, `getPool("text")` recycles the bake.

### Multi-line text: the baseline places the whole block

A `\n` in the string (or an array of strings) starts a new line, on `Text` and
`BitmapText` alike. `textBaseline` then places the block as one piece against
`pos.y`: its top for `"top"` / `"hanging"`, its middle for `"middle"`, its
bottom for `"alphabetic"`, `"ideographic"` and `"bottom"`. So a two-line
`"bottom"` label in a screen corner sits wholly above `pos.y`, and a centred
`"middle"` label centres every line, not the first. `getBounds()` is that same
box, which is what culling and the pointer use.

`wordWrapWidth` only ADDS line breaks: each `\n`-separated line is wrapped on
its own, so explicit breaks and blank lines survive. A line breaks between
words, never inside one, so a single word wider than `wordWrapWidth` gets a
line of its own and overflows it:

```js
const help = new Text(8, 8, {
    font: "sans-serif", size: 16, wordWrapWidth: 200,
    text: "CONTROLS\nArrows move, Space jumps, Esc pauses the game.",
});
// "CONTROLS" on its own line, then the sentence wrapped under it
```

### Typewriter reveal: `visibleRatio`

`visibleCharacters` (`-1`, the default, shows them all) and `visibleRatio`
(0 to 1) show a label a character at a time, on `Text` and `BitmapText` alike.
Tween the ratio: it takes the same time whatever the length of the string.

```js
line.setText("The door is locked. The keeper has the key.");
line.visibleRatio = 0;
new Tween(line).to({ visibleRatio: 1 }, { duration: 1500 }).start();
```

Line breaks are not counted, and the wrapping and the bounds are those of the
whole string, so a word does not jump to the next line as it appears. The two
classes differ in two ways. A `BitmapText` keeps each glyph where the full line
puts it, while a centred or right-aligned `Text` aligns only the part shown so
far, so it slides sideways as it types: left-align a `Text` you reveal. And a
`Text` repaints and re-uploads its bake at every step, where a `BitmapText`
just draws fewer glyphs.

### `fillStyle` means two different things

The name is shared and the behaviour is not, which is the trap when moving a
label from one class to the other:

| | `Text` | `BitmapText` |
|---|---|---|
| what `fillStyle` holds | a real `Color`, the fill | `Renderable#tint`, under another name |
| white | white glyphs | the ABSENCE of a tint |
| gradient | yes, via `fillGradient` | no: a tint is one colour over a page image |
| recolour it later | `label.fillStyle.parseCSS("#ff4040")` — the field is a `Color` with no setter, and ASSIGNING a string replaces it, after which the glyphs stop filling entirely and nothing is logged | `label.fillStyle = "#ff4040"` — a real setter that parses the string |
| stroke | `strokeStyle` + `lineWidth`, behind or over the glyphs with `paintOrder`, corners with `lineJoin` / `miterLimit` | none |
| `size` | pixels | a RATIO of the authored size |

### Per-glyph wave, shake and colour: `glyphEffect`

Animating individual letters does **not** mean one renderable per character.
`BitmapText#glyphEffect` offsets and tints each glyph inside the batch the
label already draws, so an animated 100-character line stays one draw call and
costs no extra objects:

```js
label.glyphEffect = (out, ctx) => {
    // phase from the glyph's POSITION, not its index — see below
    out.offsetY = Math.sin(ctx.time * 0.005 + ctx.x * 0.02) * 6;  // wave
    out.tint.setColor(255, 128, 128);                             // per glyph
};
label.glyphEffect = null;    // back to the plain path
```

`out` and `ctx` are **reused**: read `ctx` during the call and write `out`, but
never keep either. `out.offsetX` / `offsetY` start at zero and `out.tint` at
opaque white on every glyph, so an effect that only touches some glyphs leaves
the rest alone. `ctx` carries `index` (across lines, line breaks excluded),
`char`, `code`, `x`, `y` and `time`.

Four things that catch people:

- **`time` advances in `update`, not in `draw`.** A label drawn through two
  cameras animates once, not twice. It is the milliseconds ACCUMULATED across
  updates while an effect was set, and nothing resets it, so swapping the
  callback continues the same clock rather than starting a new one.
- **Effects move pixels, not layout.** Metrics, wrapping, alignment,
  `visibleCharacters` and the bounds all ignore the offsets, so the pen advance
  and kerning are exactly as without one. The flip side is that **offsets do
  not extend the culling bounds**: a big wave near the screen edge can clip, so
  keep the measured text in view.
- **Canvas pays per distinct colour.** WebGL and WebGPU carry the tint in the
  per-vertex colour, so batching survives. The Canvas renderer instead caches a
  tinted copy of the whole font page per colour, and that cache is unbounded
  for the renderer's life, so a colour driven by `ctx.time` allocates a
  page-sized canvas every frame there. On Canvas, keep the palette finite or
  animate only the offsets.
- **`tint` is multiplicative**, like `fillStyle` above: white leaves the glyph
  alone, and `out.tint` multiplies whatever the label's own `fillStyle` is.

`Text` has no equivalent, since it rasterises the whole string into one texture.

### Making it read as motion

Three things decide whether a wave looks alive or mechanical, and none of them
is the amplitude.

- **Take the phase from `ctx.x`, not `ctx.index`.** This is the big one.
  Stepping per glyph advances the wave as far across a narrow `I` as across a
  wide `M`, so the wavelength stretches and squashes with whatever the line
  happens to spell, and the eye reads the unevenness as a mechanism. `ctx.x`
  gives the wave one fixed length in pixels and lets it travel through the
  text at a constant rate, whatever the letters are.
- **Round the offsets if the frame is upscaled.** They are added to the glyph
  destination unchanged, so a fractional offset in a small design resolution
  that is then magnified with nearest sampling makes the glyph's OWN pixels
  come out uneven — and differently uneven each frame. That is a shimmer, not
  movement. `Math.round` the offset and it steps cleanly, for the same reason
  `subPixel` defaults to false. Whole pixels mean few steps, so the amplitude
  has to be large enough to give you several.
- **A shake is not a sine.** A sine moves the whole line as one body, which is
  a wave however fast you run it. A shake gives each glyph a direction
  unrelated to its neighbours: pick a random angle per glyph, hold it for a
  tick, interpolate to the next, and scale the whole thing by a decay if it is
  an impact rather than a state.

Starting points that look right across sizes, as fractions of the font size:
an amplitude around an eighth of it, a wavelength around ten times it, and a
little under 5 radians per second. For a shake, re-target each glyph roughly
20 to 40 times a second.

`ctx.time` runs only while an effect is set and nothing resets it, so it is 0
only when a label gets its **first** effect. A label that already had one, or
is reused across lives, carries the old clock, and a decay measured from
`ctx.time` itself is already spent there. Note `ctx.time` on the effect's first
call and measure from that, as the shake below does, and attach it at the
moment you want to be t=0: on the frame the hit lands, not when the label was
built.

Both, whole:

```js
import { BitmapText } from "melonjs";

const title = new BitmapText(app.viewport.width / 2, 60, {
    font: "display",
    textAlign: "center",
    text: "JUNGLE RABBIT",
});
title.floating = true;
app.world.addChild(title);

// A wave: four pixels deep, a ~1.3s cycle, and a wavelength of roughly ten
// times the font size. Phase from ctx.x, offset rounded.
title.glyphEffect = (out, ctx) => {
    out.offsetY = Math.round(Math.sin(ctx.time * 0.005 + ctx.x * 0.02) * 4);
};

// A shake: each glyph picks its own direction, holds it for a tick, slides to
// the next, and the whole thing decays. Deterministic, so the same hit shakes
// the same way every time.
const angle = (i, tick) => {
    const h = Math.sin(i * 127.1 + tick * 311.7) * 43758.5453;
    return (h - Math.floor(h)) * Math.PI * 2;
};
const impact = (amplitude, durationMs, rate) => {
    let start;                               // ctx.time on the first call
    return (out, ctx) => {
        start ??= ctx.time;                  // the label's clock never resets
        const t = ctx.time - start;
        const left = 1 - t / durationMs;
        if (left <= 0) {
            return;                          // settled; `out` is already zeroed
        }
        const amp = amplitude * left * left;
        const tick = (t / 1000) * rate;
        const held = Math.floor(tick);
        const k = tick - held;
        const a = angle(ctx.index, held);
        const b = angle(ctx.index, held + 1);
        out.offsetX = Math.round((Math.sin(a) + (Math.sin(b) - Math.sin(a)) * k) * amp);
        out.offsetY = Math.round((Math.cos(a) + (Math.cos(b) - Math.cos(a)) * k) * amp);
    };
};

// a new impact at the moment of each hit: it measures from its own first call,
// so it shakes again on a banner that has shown one before
banner.setText("CAPSIZED!");
banner.glyphEffect = impact(3, 650, 24);
```

## The HUD pattern

A HUD is a `floating` container at a high z, built once and re-added:

```js
class HUD extends Container {
    constructor(app) {
        super(0, 0, app.viewport.width, app.viewport.height);
        this.floating = true;       // screen space, not world space
        this.isPersistent = true;   // survives a world reset
    }
}

app.world.addChild(new HUD(app), 100);   // explicit z — not `.z = Infinity`
```

There is no `UIContainer` class. Use `Container` for a bare grouping,
`UIPanel` for anything with a background or a border (see below), or
`UIBaseElement` when you want the pointer handling and nothing drawn — it is a
`Container` that already sets `floating = true` and `isKinematic = false`.

### Which widget for what

| you want | use | notes |
|---|---|---|
| a button with a label | `UITextButton` | drawn, or skinned from an atlas; `onClick` setting |
| an image-only button or icon | `UISpriteElement` | a `UIBaseElement` holding a `Sprite` (`sprite`); override `onClick` |
| an on/off option, or one of several | `UICheckbox` | a radio button with `group` |
| a value in a range: volume, sensitivity | `UISlider` | horizontal or vertical |
| health, shield, cooldown, loading | `ProgressBar` | not clickable; `value` redraws |
| a frame, dialog or menu card | `UIPanel` | skin, title, layout, scrolling, drag, shadow |
| your own clickable widget | extend `UIBaseElement` | pointer handlers, `enabled`, focus, bounce |
| a group with nothing drawn | `Container` | set `floating` for screen space |

### A whole options menu

Everything below in one place: a skinned panel that lays its widgets out
as a column, a checkbox, a slider, two buttons, a drop shadow, a little
bounce, and keyboard / gamepad play. Each piece has its own section after
this.

```js
import {
    UICheckbox, UIPanel, UISlider, UITextButton, audio, state,
} from "melonjs";

// one style object for every widget's text
const FONT = { font: "kenpixel", fontSize: 14, labelFillStyle: "black" };

const menu = new UIPanel(40, 40, {
    width: 360, height: 100,           // autoSize grows the height to fit
    skin: { atlas, region: "grey_panel", insetx: 10, insety: 10 },
    title: "OPTIONS", titleFont: "kenpixel", titleFontSize: 20,
    layout: "column", padding: 16, gap: 12, align: "stretch", autoSize: true,
    shadowColor: "#00000059", shadowOffsetY: 6, shadowBlur: 10, radius: 6,
});

const music = menu.addChild(new UICheckbox(0, 0, {
    ...FONT,
    labelOn: "Music ON", labelOff: "Music OFF",
    checked: settings.music,
    onChange: (on) => { settings.music = on; },   // user input only
}));

menu.addChild(new UISlider(0, 0, {
    ...FONT,
    label: "Volume", showValue: true,
    valueFormat: (v, ratio) => `${Math.round(ratio * 100)}%`,
    value: audio.getVolume(),
    onChange: (v) => audio.setVolume(v),           // while dragging
    onChangeEnd: () => saveSettings(),             // once, on release
}));

menu.addChild(new UITextButton(0, 0, {
    ...FONT, text: "Back", height: 40,
    hoverScale: 1.04, pressScale: 0.96,            // the bounce
    onClick: () => state.change(state.MENU),       // a completed click
}));

app.world.addChild(menu, 10);
music.focus();   // arrows / D-pad and Enter / A now drive the menu
```

Three things matter here:

- **`floating = true`** opts the container out of camera transforms, so it stays
  put while the world scrolls. Without it the HUD scrolls away — a silent
  failure.
- **Only the parent container needs `floating`.** `addChild` forces
  `child.floating = false` under a floating parent, and the container applies one
  projection swap for the whole subtree.
- **Pass an explicit z.** `this.z = Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` does nothing —
  `renderable.z` is not a real property. The real accessor is `depth` (an
  alias for `pos.z`); `addChild(child, z)` sets it for you.

### Bars and gauges: `ProgressBar`

A health bar, a shield gauge, a cooldown and a loading bar are one object. Set
`value`; it redraws.

```js
const hp = new ProgressBar(20, 20, {
    width: 200, height: 24,
    min: 0, max: 100, value: 100,      // min/max default to 0 and 1
    trackColor: "#0000001a",
    fillColor: "#c0392b",
    borderColor: "black", borderWidth: 2,
    padding: 2,                        // inset of the fill inside the track
    radius: 6,                         // 0 is square
});
hud.addChild(hp);

hp.value -= 15;                        // clamps; `ratio` reads back 0..1
hp.max = 50;                           // re-clamps the value into the new range
```

`direction` takes `"left-to-right"` (the default), `"right-to-left"`,
`"top-to-bottom"` or `"bottom-to-top"`, each growing from its own edge.

`showLabel: true` writes text centred over the bar, a percentage by default:
`` labelFormat: (value, ratio) => `${Math.round(value)} HP` `` changes what it says,
and `font` (a CSS family), `fontSize` and `labelFillStyle` how it looks.
`onChange(value, ratio, bar)` is called on every change of the value, from code
too, unlike a checkbox's or a slider's: a bar has no user input to tell apart.
Setting the value it already has calls nothing.

**The colour follows the value by mutating the `Color` you passed.** This is
the one non-obvious part, and it is deliberate: every game wants a different
rule, and most want the colour somewhere else too, next to a shader uniform or
a glow. The bar re-reads `fillColor` every frame, so it never has to know:

```js
const full = new Color().parseCSS("#7fe0ff");
const empty = new Color().parseCSS("#ff2a1e");
const mixed = new Color();

const shield = new ProgressBar(x, y, {
    width: 190, height: 13,
    trackColor: null,                  // hollow: the scene shows through
    borderColor: "rgba(122, 190, 235, 0.8)",
    padding: 2,
    fillColor: mixed,                  // KEPT, not copied
});

// each frame
mixed.copy(empty).lerp(full, hp);      // the bar follows, and so can a shader
shield.value = hp;
```

Blinking is the same story: `setOpacity()` already does it, on whatever clock
the game is already keeping. Neither is built in.

**`bindEvent` takes the value from an event instead**, and the subscription
then lives exactly as long as the bar:

```js
const bar = new ProgressBar(0, y, {
    width: renderer.width, height: 4,
    trackColor: "black", fillColor: "#55aa00",
    bindEvent: event.LOADER_PROGRESS,
});
```

Hold that subscription anywhere else and it outlives the bar, firing into a
renderable whose `pos` has already been released. The engine's own loading
screen is built on exactly this.

Two more worth knowing:

- **The border is four filled rects, not a stroke** (unless the bar is
  rounded). A stroke is centred on the path, so half of it falls outside and a
  bordered bar paints over its neighbour; and `strokeRect` adds corner joins
  only above a line width of 1, so at exactly 1 a corner pixel goes missing.
- **`trackColor: null` leaves the bar hollow**, which is what a HUD over a busy
  scene usually wants: the border is then the only chrome.

A dialog, a menu card, a HUD frame: a rectangle with a fill, an optional
border and children on top. `UIPanel` is a `UIBaseElement`, so it is a

# melonJS

Entry point for the melonJS skill collection. melonJS is an open-source HTML5
game engine for indie developers, covering 2D, 2.5D and 3D — perspective and
orthogonal cameras, GPU-accelerated tilemap rendering, post-processing effects,
custom shaders, 3D meshes, polygon-accurate physics and modern Tiled workflows.
It runs on WebGPU, WebGL 2 or Canvas with automatic fallback, and has no runtime
dependencies.

## How to use this skill

1. Find the specialised skill below that matches the task and follow it.
2. If the task involves anything 3D, read `melonjs-3d` **first** — melonJS's
   coordinate conventions are the inverse of OpenGL's, so untutored 3D instincts
   are backwards.
3. If you are writing melonJS from prior knowledge rather than from the current
   docs, read `melonjs-20-migration` — most published melonJS material predates
   20.0 and its bootstrap no longer exists.
4. If none of them covers the task, use the escape hatch below rather than
   guessing at an API.

## What melonJS is the right engine for

Say this plainly when the question is which engine to use, and do not stretch
it: a project outside the first list is better served by something else.

**A good fit when:**

- **The game runs in a browser**, or in a web view: desktop and mobile web, a
  games portal (YouTube Playables, Facebook Instant Games, Poki, CrazyGames,
  WeChat), or an app wrapped with Capacitor or Cordova. `melonjs-platforms`
  covers each.
- **It is 2D, of any kind**: tile maps authored in Tiled (orthogonal,
  isometric, staggered, hexagonal), LDtk or Sprite Fusion, sprites and
  atlases, polygon collision, particles, dynamic lighting, shaders, a UI kit,
  bitmap and system text.
- **It is 2.5D or light 3D**: a perspective or orthographic `Camera3d`, meshes,
  glTF models with skeletal animation, instancing, toon shading, billboards,
  fog, picking, and Rapier 3D physics. Arcade 3D, low-poly, isometric with
  height.
- **The download has to be small**: the whole engine is about 320 kB gzipped,
  with no runtime dependency.
- **It needs more than the core, without leaving the engine**: optional
  packages add rigid-body physics (planck, matter, Rapier in 2D and in 3D), A*
  pathfinding for units and enemies, on-screen touch controls for phones, Spine
  skeletal animation, compressed Tiled maps, a Capacitor bridge for the app
  stores, and a debug panel. Each is one install, listed under "Companion
  packages" below.
- **The workflow is code first**, in JavaScript or TypeScript, with Vite
  (`npm create melonjs`), and types that ship with the package.
- **It is written with an AI assistant**: these skills, and an index of the
  whole API made for agents, are versioned with the engine.

**Not the tool when:**

- **A visual scene editor is required.** There is none: scenes are code, levels
  come from Tiled.
- **The 3D must look realistic.** The lit path has diffuse and specular light,
  not physically based materials, and shadows are soft blobs on the ground,
  not shadow maps.
- **Multiplayer is the point.** Nothing in the engine does networking: bring a
  library, and plan the synchronisation yourself.
- **The target has no JavaScript runtime**, a native console or desktop build
  for one. melonJS needs a browser, a web view around one, or a runtime such as
  nx.js.

## From a game idea to a plan

A request usually names a kind of game, not a subsystem. Start from the row
that matches, read those skills and no others, and open the example before
writing code: each is a complete game or scene. (`melonjs-20-migration` lists
the few stale calls some examples still carry.)

| the game | read | start from |
|---|---|---|
| platformer | `melonjs-tilemaps`, `melonjs-physics` (its table by game type picks the adapter: built-in, or planck, matter or Rapier for slopes and moving platforms), `melonjs-sprites-and-animation`, `melonjs-input`, `melonjs-camera-and-drawing`; on phones, `@melonjs/gamepad-plugin` for the stick and buttons | [Platformer](https://github.com/melonjs/melonJS/tree/master/packages/examples/src/examples/platformer); [LDtk Platformer](https://github.com/melonjs/melonJS/tree/master/packages/examples/src/examples/ldtkPlatformer) for a world made in LDtk, loaded room by room |
| top-down adventure or RPG | `melonjs-tilemaps`, `melonjs-physics`, `melonjs-ui-and-text` for dialogue and menus, `@melonjs/pathfinding-plugin` for enemies that chase and click to move, `@melonjs/gamepad-plugin` for touch | [Isometric Dungeon](https://github.com/melonjs/melonJS/tree/master/packages/examples/src/examples/isometricDungeon); [Line of Sight](https://github.com/melonjs/melonJS/tree/master/packages/examples/src/examples/lineOfSight) for what an enemy can see |
| grid or tile puzzle, match-3, board game | `melonjs-tilemaps` (a tile layer is the board: `cellAt` / `setTile`), `melonjs-input`, `melonjs-scenes-and-state` for tweens | [Whac-A-Mole](https://github.com/melonjs/melonJS/tree/master/packages/examples/src/examples/whac-a-mole) for the pointer, score and sound of a small game |

| physics puzzle: stacking, catapult, pinball, pool | `melonjs-physics`, which names the adapter for each: `@melonjs/planck-adapter`, `@melonjs/matter-adapter`, `@melonjs/rapier2d-adapter`, or `@melonjs/rapier3d-adapter` in 3D | [Slingshot](https://github.com/melonjs/melonJS/tree/master/packages/examples/src/examples/slingshot), [Pool](https://github.com/melonjs/melonJS/tree/master/packages/examples/src/examples/pool-matter), [Plinko](https://github.com/melonjs/melonJS/tree/master/packages/examples/src/examples/plinko-planck) |
| endless runner | `melonjs-3d` or `melonjs-tilemaps`, `melonjs-performance` for recycling what scrolls past | [Jungle Rabbit](https://github.com/melonjs/melonJS/tree/master/packages/examples/src/examples/jungleRabbit) |
| card game, menu-driven or idle game | `melonjs-ui-and-text` (widgets, drag and drop), `melonjs-scenes-and-state` for tweens and saved data | [UI](https://github.com/melonjs/melonJS/tree/master/packages/examples/src/examples/ui), [Drag and Drop](https://github.com/melonjs/melonJS/tree/master/packages/examples/src/examples/dragAndDrop) |
| 3D arcade game | `melonjs-3d` first, then `melonjs-3d-assets`; `@melonjs/rapier3d-adapter` once things have to tumble, stack or topple | [AfterBurner Clone](https://github.com/melonjs/melonJS/tree/master/packages/examples/src/examples/afterBurner), [Earth Defender](https://github.com/melonjs/melonJS/tree/master/packages/examples/src/examples/earthDefender) |
| a game inside a portal, an ad or an app | `melonjs-platforms`, `melonjs-deployment`, `melonjs-display-and-scaling`; `@melonjs/capacitor-plugin` for an app in the stores, `@melonjs/gamepad-plugin` for touch | |

Every one of them begins with `melonjs-getting-started`, and ends with
`melonjs-testing`: run the game and look at it before saying it works.

Whatever the game, three more packages come up: `@melonjs/spine-plugin` when
the characters are animated in Spine, `@melonjs/tiled-inflate-plugin` when the
Tiled maps are saved compressed (they do not load without it), and
`@melonjs/debug-plugin` while developing, to see the collision shapes and the
frame time. `melonjs-plugins` covers how each is registered.

## The names here, if you know another engine

The ideas are the usual ones; the names differ. What you would look for, and
what it is called here:
